The patterns behind the mistakes

Ten cross-domain lessons

These are not facts about Claude. They are patterns your own exam log identified in how you answer — the reasoning habits that produced wrong picks across several domains at once. They are the highest-leverage thing on this page.

"Sounds like the fix, isn't" — a probabilistic prompt- or parameter-level fix chosen over the structural guarantee

You keep choosing the better-worded instruction, the extra worked example, or the boolean the agent is supposed to set, over the mechanism that makes the wrong behaviour impossible. Ask one question of every option: after this change, can the model still do the wrong thing? If yes, you bought guidance, not enforcement. Read the stem for a compliance percentage — '9% of calls', '~90% of the time', '11% of blocking statuses' — because a number like that is the exam telling you the probabilistic layer has already been tried and failed. The corollary that has cost marks twice: a prompt can never grant a capability the configuration withholds.

Evidence Named explicitly in EXAM-LOG.md's Exam 4 Professor's Note: 'Q34 (prompt instruction chosen over `allowed_tools` whitelist), Q19 (prompt instruction chosen over `tool_choice:any`), Q52 (uniform backoff chosen over categorized retryable/non-retryable) all share the same shape: a probabilistic prompt-level fix chosen over the structural/configuration-level guarantee the corpus favors.' Exam 5's Professor's Note records it 'recurring across two consecutive scored exams' (Q54, KD #12), and Exam 6's note calls the identical shape in Q12 'the single most persistent trap in this learner's history'. Also Exam 4 Q2 and Exam 7 Q3 (Task-tool grant read as a prompt-wording problem).

Over-engineering / symptom-patching chosen over the proportionate direct move

When something misbehaves you reach for the heavier mechanism — a hook, a mode, a composite tool, a louder reminder — instead of the smallest move that addresses the actual cause. Name the cause in one clause before you read the options: 'we do not know what is actually loaded' means diagnose, never re-instruct; 'it is doing the right thing across two turns instead of one' means prompt-level bundling, not new machinery; 'single file, fully specified, already decided' means execute directly. Hold this against the structural-guarantee lesson, because the two point in opposite directions and the exam tests both — heavy wins when the requirement is a guarantee (irreversibility, mandatory ordering, capability grant), light wins when the requirement is diagnosis, efficiency, or organisation.

Evidence Named verbatim in EXAM-LOG.md's Exam 8 Observations: 'A discernible meta-pattern in roughly half the misses: over-engineering / symptom-patching over the proportionate root-cause move' — Q11 (§2.8) chose a `PreToolUse` hook over prompt-bundling, Q12 (§3.1) chose re-typing the instruction over running `/memory`, Q13 (§3.6) chose plan mode over direct execution on a fully-scoped one-liner, Q51 (§3.11) chose a half-measure partial split over the clean full split. The Exam 8 Professor's Note calls for 'a deliberate cluster of "proportionate first response" items across D3'. The pattern recurred at Exam 10 Q6 (§2.8 again — recommending the simpler bundling fix over building a composite tool), which Insights Round 2 logs as a repeat.

Trusting the more dramatic-sounding wrong explanation

Given two candidate diagnoses, you lean toward the one that sounds more consequential rather than the one the evidence supports. In practice this shows up as blaming a tool description when every subagent succeeded and the coordinator's own decomposition was at fault, and as believing a real, still-supported mechanism had been made obsolete. Prefer the boring diagnosis that fits the stated facts, and be especially sceptical of any option asserting that something you know exists has stopped working.

Evidence Named in EXAM-LOG.md's Exam 5 Professor's Note, item 3: 'A "trust the more dramatic-sounding wrong explanation" pattern in D1/D3, not a domain-level weakness (D1 is 93.8%, D3 is 91.7%) — Q21 blamed a tool description instead of the coordinator's own decomposition, and Q36 believed a real, still-supported mechanism was fabricated-obsolete. Worth a light touch next paper, not a section reweight.'

A weak domain is usually a breadth gap, not one narrow trap

When a domain scores badly, check whether the misses cluster on one concept or scatter across many sections — the answer changes the remedy entirely. Misses spread across six different facts are a coverage gap that needs broad re-reading; misses landing repeatedly on one concept are a single misconception to re-teach. This project has now made the same diagnosis twice, first about D2 and later about D3 and D4, and both times narrowing study to the known-missed sections would have under-served the actual gap.

Evidence First named in EXAM-LOG.md's Exam 4 Professor's Note: '6 misses across 6 distinct facts... Not one repeated trap — a genuine coverage gap across the domain's tool-design mechanics.' Restated in Exam 8's Observations: 'The weakness is domain-wide breadth, not four narrow traps... D3's three misses span §3.1/§3.6/§3.11; D4's span §4.2/§4.6/§4.9. This is the same "genuine breadth gap, not one misconception" diagnosis Exam 4 first made about D2 — now recurring in D3 and D4', with the Exam 8 note adding 'Do NOT re-narrow to only the four originally-flagged sections.' Insights Round 2 applies it prospectively to D2's 3-exam decline.

The targeted re-test is the diagnostic that separates a real gap from attempt-specific noise

One miss tells you almost nothing; the same concept missed again on a fresh re-test in a different scenario tells you a great deal. Treat a single bad result as a hypothesis and let a deliberately re-tested question decide it. That mechanism has now resolved several cases in both directions in this project — some dips proved to be noise and recovered on their own, while others survived a fresh re-test and turned out to be real misconceptions worth direct study.

Evidence EXAM-LOG.md Exam 8 Observations: 'The targeted re-test worked as a diagnostic — and the verdict is decisive... D3 §3.1 (Q12) missed again, D3 §3.6 (Q13) missed again, D4 §4.6 (Q17) missed again — and only D4 §4.4 (Q16, prefilling) recovered to correct... three of these four are real, persistent gaps, not attempt-specific noise — they survived a fresh re-test in a different scenario.' Both directions are documented: D5's Exam 6 dip to 71.4% fully recovered to 9/9 in Exam 7 ('confirming Exam 6's dip was attempt-specific'), and D3 §3.1/§3.6 both recovered on their third re-test in Exam 10.

Three consecutive misses is the escalation threshold — stop relying on exam exposure and read the section

A concept you have now missed three times across three genuinely different concrete situations is no longer being tested wrong, it is being understood wrong. At that point another practice question is unlikely to move it, because you have already had three independent chances to reason your way there. The prescribed response is to go read the corpus section directly before the next attempt, and only then re-test it.

Evidence EXAM-LOG.md Insights Round 2 Focus Recommendation: 'Primary: D4 §4.6. Three consecutive misses across three different concrete situations (a Claude Code CI structured-output-guarantee framing, a review-bot precondition-gating framing, and a retry-with-stale-tool-list framing) is this project's first genuinely stubborn single-section trap. Recommend Ram directly re-read `Domain-4_v2.md` §4.6 (`tool_choice` forcing a specific tool vs. `"any"`) before Exam 11, rather than relying on a fourth exam attempt alone to close it.' The criterion itself was pre-stated in Exam 8's Professor's Note and Exam 10's Observations apply it ('per the Exam 8 note's own stated criterion, three straight misses across three different concrete situations is no longer "attempt-specific noise"'). Misses: Exam 7 Q51, Exam 8 Q17, Exam 10 Q48.

Adjacent misses in one mechanism family are one gap, not two coincidences

When two wrong answers land back to back and both sit in the same family of mechanisms, read them as a single clustered gap rather than as unrelated slips. The tell is that the two options you confused are near-identical on the page and only the stem decides between them — conflating a system-prompt instruction with prefilling, or a specifically forced tool with the configuration that only guarantees some tool. Study the family as a set of promises with exact scopes rather than revisiting each question in isolation.

Evidence EXAM-LOG.md Exam 7 Observations: 'Q50 and Q51 are adjacent, back-to-back misses in the Claude Code CI block, both in the D4 structured-output-guarantee mechanism family (prefilling vs. system-prompt instructions; `tool_choice: "any"` vs. a specific forced tool) — worth watching as a possible clustered gap rather than two unrelated misses.' The Exam 7 Professor's Note repeats the framing, and the subsequent Exam 8 result partly confirmed it — §4.4 prefilling recovered while §4.6 missed again, and §4.6 went on to become the project's first three-exam stubborn trap.

Pace is not the constraint — the wrong answers are considered, not rushed

Your clean attempts run at roughly a third of the available per-question budget, and the log has repeatedly checked whether misses correlate with speed. They do not: several of the most persistent misses were among the slowest questions on their papers. That rules out a pacing or fatigue explanation and confirms these are knowledge gaps. Spend the surplus time running an explicit decision rule on each option rather than answering on first impression.

Evidence EXAM-LOG.md Exam 8 Observations: 'the three re-missed sections were not rushed (Q12 took 77s, the second-slowest question on the paper; Q13 37s; Q17 37s) — these are considered wrong answers, not careless ones, which strengthens the "real gap" reading.' Exam 10 Observations make the same check ('slowest: Q27 at 114s — notably one of the two D3 misses, considered rather than rushed'). Insights Round 2 Pace Trend: Exams 8 and 10 are clean at 35.4s and 39.3s per question, 'suggesting this is now the learner's genuine steady-state pace' against a ~120s/question budget. Insights Round 1 had reached only an inconclusive verdict because two of its three exams were break-confounded.

A three-exam window catches trends a single-exam review cannot see

Some patterns only exist across papers, so reviewing each result in isolation will miss them by construction. A section missed once in each of two different exams looks like two unrelated slips inside either exam's own review, and a domain sliding steadily downward can stay above every alarm threshold at each individual sitting. Zoom out periodically and trend the same concept and the same domain across several attempts before concluding anything is fine.

Evidence EXAM-LOG.md Insights Round 2 Repeated Missed Traps: 'D2 §2.8 (composite tool vs. prompt-bundling) — missed in Exam 8 (Q11) and Exam 10 (Q6), not tested in Exam 7. A new repeat this round surfaced that neither exam's own Professor's Note flagged in isolation — exactly the kind of cross-exam pattern a 3-exam window is meant to catch and a single-exam note can miss.' The same round surfaced D2's smooth 100% → 90.9% → 81.8% decline, which GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md Session 13 records as 'a real 3-exam declining trend that a single-exam Professor's Note would not have caught in isolation.'

The gaps have migrated off the Key Distinctions and onto whole corpus sections

Use this Key Distinctions inventory as maintenance, not as your main repair work. Every tracked distinction is currently clean, and the concepts that still cost marks live in whole corpus sections rather than in any named trap. That changes what to do with a list like this one: skim it to hold the ground you have already won, and spend your best study hours on the sections the exam log names as still open.

Domain 1 · 27% of the exam · 16 of 60 questions

Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

This is the biggest domain on the exam and it is about one question asked many different ways: when an agent system misbehaves, which architectural layer is actually at fault, and what is the smallest structural change that fixes it? You will be shown a coordinator delegating to subagents, or a single agentic loop calling tools, and something will be wrong — wasted round-trips, missing citations, a coverage gap, a duplicated refund, a human re-asking questions the bot already answered. Almost every correct answer moves the fix down a level: from prompt wording to configuration, from configuration to code-level enforcement, from cleanup-after to partition-before. The reliably wrong answers are the ones that sound responsible — a stronger instruction, more examples, more subagents, a bigger context window, an after-the-fact audit — because they leave the structure that caused the failure completely intact.

32 concepts85/94 lifetime (90%)

Recall check — D1

Answer out loud before you open each one. Retrieval is what moves a concept from recognised to owned.

  1. A tempting answer says Rewrite the system prompt with stronger, more explicit wording, or add a few-shot example of correct behavior.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: A system prompt cannot grant a capability the configuration withholds, and cannot withhold one the configuration grants.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Prompt wording is behavioral guidance, not a capability restriction. If two prompt revisions already failed, a third is the same fix repeated.

  2. A tempting answer says Rewrite the coordinator's system prompt with more explicit delegation instructions.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Without the Task tool granted, a coordinator cannot spawn a single subagent — no matter how well its prompt describes them.

    Why the tempting answer fails: The prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds. Delegation stays impossible regardless of wording.

  3. A tempting answer says Instruct the subagent to ask the coordinator for the findings whenever it needs them mid-task.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Telling a subagent to 'use the findings from the earlier step' gives it nothing — the findings must be inside its prompt.

    Why the tempting answer fails: The findings-on-request pattern starts from the same gap, adds an avoidable round-trip, and nothing guarantees the coordinator supplies real data rather than another pointer.

D1 §1.3

A coordinator needs "Task" in allowed_tools to delegate at all

Still open

Without the Task tool granted, a coordinator cannot spawn a single subagent — no matter how well its prompt describes them.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Subagents are spawned by the `Task` tool. If `"Task"` is absent from the coordinator's `allowed_tools`, delegation is structurally impossible, and the observable symptom is a coordinator that reasons about handing off and then does everything itself in one long response. The exam presents this with a deliberate decoy: the subagent descriptions in the coordinator's system prompt are detailed and well-written, tempting you to conclude the prompt needs to be more persuasive. It does not. Descriptions help the coordinator choose among subagents once delegation is possible; the `Task` grant is what makes delegation possible at all.

Why it works that way

This is the cleanest instance of the domain's governing principle — a structural gap misread as a wording problem. Recognizing it saves you from the most attractive distractor on the page.

Decision rule

"Coordinator never delegates" → check for `"Task"` in allowed_tools before touching the prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rewrite the coordinator's system prompt with more explicit delegation instructions.The prompt cannot grant a tool the configuration withholds. Delegation stays impossible regardless of wording.Exam 4, Exam 7 (missed)
  • Add more detailed subagent descriptions to the coordinator's prompt so it recognizes when delegation is worthwhile.Descriptions inform selection among available subagents; they do not enable spawning. In these scenarios the prompt already describes them in detail.Exam 4, Exam 7
  • The coordinator needs a larger context window to reason through when delegation is warranted.Context window size has no bearing on whether a tool appears in a whitelist — this misdiagnoses a configuration gap as a capacity problem.Exam 4 (§1.3)
  • Give subagents the `Task` tool so they can hand cases to each other directly.`Task` is the coordinator's spawning tool, not a peer-to-peer channel — and direct subagent handoff breaks hub-and-spoke anyway.Exam 8 (§1.3)

Your record on it

Missed on Exam 7 — that exam's Professor's Note names it directly: 'D1 §1.3 (Task tool grant) — mistook a coordinator's missing Task tool grant (a structural, allowed_tools-level gap) for a prompt-wording problem.' Exam 4 carried two Task-grant items and answered both correctly (Exam 4's single §1.3 miss, Q34, was the least-privilege-guarantee framing — see D1-05), so this is a regression, not a first exposure. The Task-grant facet has not been re-tested on a scored exam since (Exam 8's §1.3 item was the description-routing facet, Exam 10's was the config-over-prompt facet), so no recovery is on record.

D1 §1.5

Pass complete findings, not references to findings

Still open

Telling a subagent to 'use the findings from the earlier step' gives it nothing — the findings must be inside its prompt.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Because subagent context is isolated (§1.2), a coordinator that delegates by reference — 'use the compliance-cost findings from the filing-review step' — hands the subagent an instruction with no data attached. What it produces next is worse than an error: plausible-sounding figures that trace to no actual source. The rule is to include the complete findings of prior agents directly in the subagent's prompt, in structured form with the metadata attached, and to require subagents to carry that metadata through in their own structured outputs.

Why it works that way

Fabrication here is silent and confident. Unlike a missing tool or a failed call, nothing in the pipeline signals that the synthesis agent was working from nothing.

Decision rule

If a subagent's prompt refers to findings rather than containing them, that is the bug.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Instruct the subagent to ask the coordinator for the findings whenever it needs them mid-task.The findings-on-request pattern starts from the same gap, adds an avoidable round-trip, and nothing guarantees the coordinator supplies real data rather than another pointer.Exam 10 (§1.5)
  • Have the subagent re-run its own search to independently verify the figures before writing.Duplicates work the upstream subagent already did and risks producing a different, conflicting set of figures.Exam 10 (§1.5)

Your record on it

MISSED on scored Exam 10 (Q35) — EXAM-LOG names it as that exam's sole D1 miss: 'told a synthesis subagent to "use the findings from the filing-review step" without including those findings in the prompt; subagents have isolated context and cannot see prior findings by reference alone. A fresh, first-time miss for this specific facet of §1.5.' Exam 10 is the most recent scored paper and this delegate-by-reference facet has appeared on no other scored exam, so there is no recovery data. The sibling §1.5 facets (content/metadata separation, conflict preservation) were answered correctly.

D1 §1.8

The coordinator's iterative refinement loop

Still open

A gap in a synthesis draft belongs to the coordinator: it evaluates the draft, re-delegates a targeted query to the subagent that can actually gather the evidence, then re-invokes synthesis.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a synthesis draft comes back with a coverage gap, the coordinator owns the response. It evaluates the output, sends a targeted query aimed specifically at what is missing back to the research or analysis subagents best suited to it, then re-invokes synthesis with the enriched findings. Two details carry most of the marks. First, re-invoking synthesis alone cannot help: it produces hedged filler because the evidence was never gathered — the re-delegation has to go to the agents that can actually fetch it, and only for the missing piece, not the whole investigation. Second, know the §1.8/§1.10 boundary. Shipping the report with 'further research needed' is a coverage annotation, and coverage annotation is reserved for gaps that cannot be recovered. When re-delegation is available and has not even been tried, a caveat skips the loop prematurely — that exact substitution is the one D1 item missed on Exam 8. Gap evaluation and loop control stay with the coordinator; when to stop is its own question (see D1-18).

Why it works that way

Gap evaluation and loop termination are part of the coordinator's aggregation-and-validation responsibility. Pushing either onto the synthesis agent breaks separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling in one move.

Decision rule

Recoverable gap → targeted re-delegation by the coordinator. Unrecoverable gap → coverage annotation.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Give the synthesis agent its own search or retrieval tool so it can fill the gaps it notices while drafting.It turns the synthesizer into a second researcher, breaking separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling. Gap-filling research belongs to the research subagents.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Ship the report with a note that further research is needed.Coverage annotation (§1.10) is for gaps that are genuinely unrecoverable. When re-delegation is available and has not even been tried, a caveat skips the loop prematurely.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Keep re-invoking synthesis with a stronger instruction, or loop again automatically whenever any gap remains, with no upper bound.Looping the wrong stage produces hedged text with no new evidence, and an unbounded loop has no sufficiency criterion — the coordinator needs defined quality criteria to know when to stop.Exam 6, Exam 9 (§1.8)
  • Re-delegate the entire investigation from scratch, or have the coordinator run the lookup itself.Re-running everything wastes still-valid findings; the coordinator investigating directly blurs its delegating role and duplicates what the owning subagent is positioned to do.Exam 7, Exam 8 (§1.8)

Your record on it

MISSED on scored Exam 8 — EXAM-LOG names that exam's sole D1 miss as '§1.8 re-delegate-vs-ship-with-caveat', i.e. a recoverable gap treated as a §1.10 coverage annotation. Answered correctly on Exam 7 (sole D1 miss §1.3) and again on Exam 10 (sole D1 miss §1.5), so the most recent data point is correct. It is not marked recovered because §1.8 is the only D1 section missed on two different scored papers (Exam 6 on the termination facet — see D1-18 — and Exam 8 on this one), a relapse pattern rather than a clean close.

D1 §1.8

Knowing when to stop the refinement loop

Still open

The loop terminates when the coordinator's own quality criteria are met — not after a fixed number of passes, and not never.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The refinement loop needs a defined sufficiency condition, and the coordinator owns it. That condition is the coordinator's own quality criteria — the same goal-plus-criteria formulation §1.4 requires of its prompt — so 'should the coordinator re-delegate a fourth time?' has exactly one correct answer: only if the quality criteria still are not met. Both failure modes are offered as options and both sound reasonable. Looping automatically whenever any gap remains, with no upper bound, is a loop with no stopping condition at all. Stopping at an arbitrary pass count — 'after two re-delegations, ship it with a note' — substitutes a number for a criterion and reaches for §1.10 coverage annotation while the gap is still recoverable. Note the asymmetry that makes this tricky: the pass count is never the reason to stop, but repeated failure of the same targeted re-delegation is real information, and if the criteria remain unmet with no new evidence arriving, that is an escalation trigger (§1.12), not a reason to loop again.

Why it works that way

This is where the loop stops being a diagram and becomes a control system. Without a sufficiency criterion the same architecture either runs forever or stops arbitrarily, and both look identical in a design review — which is why the exam asks about the fourth pass rather than the first.

Decision rule

Stop when the coordinator's quality criteria are met — never on a pass count, in either direction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Yes — always re-delegate again automatically whenever any gap remains, with no upper bound.A loop with no stopping condition is the named failure mode. The coordinator needs defined quality criteria to know when coverage is sufficient.Exam 6 Q25 (missed), Exam 9 (§1.8)
  • No — after two re-delegations, ship the report with a note that further research is needed.An arbitrary pass cap is not a sufficiency criterion, and coverage annotation (§1.10) is for unrecoverable gaps — not a way out of a loop that is still making progress.Exam 6 Q25 (missed), Exam 8, Exam 9 (§1.8)
  • Have the synthesis subagent search for the missing material itself instead of looping back through the coordinator.Moves termination and gap-filling onto the synthesizer, breaking separation of responsibilities and least-privilege tooling in one move.Exam 6 Q25, Exam 9, Exam 10 (§1.8)
  • Remove the refinement loop entirely once the synthesis agent can self-correct.Deletes the coordinator's only defined mechanism for evaluating coverage and deciding a report is sufficient — the sufficiency criterion disappears with it.Exam 10 (§1.8)

Your record on it

MISSED on scored Exam 6 (Q25) — EXAM-LOG names it as that exam's sole D1 miss: 'the coordinator's refinement loop needs a defined sufficiency criterion, not an open-ended "keep re-delegating" or an arbitrary re-delegation cap. Domain-1_v2 §1.8.' The termination facet has not been re-tested on a scored paper since — the §1.8 items on Exams 7, 8 and 10 all test the re-delegation mechanic (D1-17), and the only later appearance of the sufficiency idea is a distractor in unscored Exam 9. No recovery on record.

D1 §1.10

Coverage annotation — graceful degradation

Recovered

When some inputs are missing, complete the work with what you have, mark exactly where the gaps are, and propagate the uncertainty upward.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Upstream inputs arrive incomplete all the time: three of five source categories return, eight of eleven files are readable, two of three verification checks come back. The correct behavior has three parts and you need all three. Complete the synthesis using the available data. Annotate coverage — mark which conclusions are well-supported and where data is missing. Propagate that uncertainty upward so whoever reads it can tell an eighteen-file review from a twenty-two-file one. There are exactly two failure modes, and the exam offers both: returning an error because the input is incomplete, and proceeding as though nothing is missing. A subtler third form also appears — silently dropping every conclusion that would have drawn on the missing sources, which is the 'proceed without noting the gaps' failure in subtractive disguise.

Why it works that way

Honesty about coverage is what keeps a partial result usable. An unannotated partial report is indistinguishable from a complete one, which quietly converts a known gap into a false confidence.

Decision rule

Incomplete input → complete + annotate + propagate. Never error out, never hide it, never block on it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Return an error or failure status because the input set is incomplete.Named as the wrong response. It discards genuinely complete, usable data for no benefit.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Proceed and produce the report with no mention of what was missing.The other named wrong response — it hides a real limitation from every reader of the output.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 10
  • Wait, or retry the missing sources repeatedly, until everything eventually returns.Blocks the pipeline on sources that already timed out or are offline for the whole window, with no guarantee they return. Graceful degradation exists to proceed now.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Drop the conclusions that depended on the missing sources so the draft contains only fully supported claims.The subtractive form of proceeding-without-noting. The reader cannot tell the report's scope was reduced, or where.Exam 9 (§1.10)
  • Substitute cached results from a prior run, or bypass the access control that blocked the read.Fabricates coverage instead of annotating the real gap, and turns a permissions boundary into a security workaround.Exam 4, Exam 10 (§1.10)

Your record on it

MISSED on Exam 4 (Q17) — EXAM-LOG: 'partial subagent failure should produce coverage-annotated synthesis, not an error-out or a silent omission. Domain-1_v2 §1.10.' Re-tested and correct on every scored paper since: Exam 6 (sole D1 miss §1.8), Exam 7 (§1.3), Exam 8 (§1.8) and Exam 10 (§1.5). Four clean re-tests — recovered.

D1 §1.12

The four escalation triggers — and never inventing policy

Recovered

Escalate on a policy gap, an explicit human request, repeated inability to progress, or high-stakes ambiguity — and treat policy silence as undefined, not as permission or denial.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Four conditions warrant handing a case to a human: the agent cannot determine the correct action within defined policy; the user explicitly asks for a human; multiple attempts have failed and it cannot make progress; or the decision is high-stakes enough that getting it wrong causes significant harm. The classic stem is a policy gap — policy covers own-site price drops but says nothing about competitor matching; it authorizes domestic damage waivers but is silent on international shipping. The trap comes in a matched pair: applying the nearest existing rule, and treating silence as a denial. Both invent policy. So does inventing a middle-ground remedy such as store credit, or a plausible-sounding default. And 'not explicitly forbidden' is not the same as 'safe to do autonomously' — a 42-order bulk refund is the high-stakes-ambiguity trigger, not a green light.

Why it works that way

Escalation is a defined architectural behavior, not a failure. An agent that guesses at an undefined rule to protect a first-contact-resolution metric is making an unauthorized policy decision on the organization's behalf.

Decision rule

Policy silent, or repeated failure, or high stakes → escalate. Never fill a policy gap yourself, in either direction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Apply the closest matching existing rule, since the underlying situation is the same.Stretching a rule onto a case it was never written to cover is exactly the invented interpretation the agent is not authorized to make.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Refuse or deny, since policy makes no explicit provision for it.The mirror-image invented interpretation — silence means undefined, not 'no'.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7
  • Offer a reasonable middle-ground default — store credit, the higher of two tiers, include-by-default — until policy is updated.Invents a remedy policy never authorized. A plausible-sounding default is still an unauthorized decision.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7
  • Keep retrying on a longer backoff, or on later scheduled runs, until the blocking system recovers.Repeated failure is an escalation signal, not a retry signal. Continuing with no new information neither resolves the case nor surfaces it to anyone who can.Exam 9, Exam 10 (§1.12)
  • Mark the item permanently out of scope, close the case, or silently skip and report completion.Suppresses an unresolved problem so no human ever learns of it — dodging the escalation trigger and hiding the gap at once.Exam 5, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Escalate immediately because the customer sounds frustrated.A first expression of dissatisfaction is not a request for a human. Acknowledge the emotion, offer the concrete resolution you are authorized to give, and escalate only if they reiterate wanting a person.Exam 2 (D1-tagged, cites Domain-5_v2 §5.8)

Your record on it

The most heavily tested D1 section (10 rationale records) — and MISSED on Exam 4 (Q14), where EXAM-LOG records 'high-stakes ambiguity is an escalation trigger even absent an explicit policy prohibition' (the 42-order bulk-refund stem). That is the high-stakes-ambiguity trigger specifically, not the policy-gap trigger. Correct on every scored paper since — Exams 5 (sole D1 miss §1.6), 6 (§1.8), 7 (§1.3), 8 (§1.8) and 10 (§1.5) — so five clean re-tests: recovered.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.12 · Domain-5_v2 §5.8 · Exam 2 · Exam 4 Q14 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10 · EXAM-LOG Exam 4 scored observations

D1 §1.3

allowed_tools is the enforcement lever, not the prompt

Recovered

A system prompt cannot grant a capability the configuration withholds, and cannot withhold one the configuration grants.

The full lesson

What is actually true

An `AgentDefinition` has three levers: `description` (what the orchestration layer routes on), `system_prompt` (how the agent behaves once selected), and `allowed_tools` (what it can actually touch). Only the third is enforcement. If a subagent keeps calling a tool outside its role, the tool is still in its whitelist — rewriting the prompt a second and third time will not change that, and neither will a few-shot example of it declining. Conversely, if an agent never performs a step its prompt demands, check whether the tool that step requires is even in its `allowed_tools`; an instruction to run a test suite is unexecutable when `Bash` was never granted. Read the configuration before you read the prompt.

Why it works that way

Prompt compliance is probabilistic; a whitelist is deterministic. When the exam wants a guarantee — 'can never modify a file even if a prompt asks it to' — only the configuration can provide one.

Decision rule

Configuration beats prompt for anything that must be guaranteed — check `allowed_tools` first.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rewrite the system prompt with stronger, more explicit wording, or add a few-shot example of correct behavior.Prompt wording is behavioral guidance, not a capability restriction. If two prompt revisions already failed, a third is the same fix repeated.Exam 4 Q34 (missed), Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Give every subagent the full tool catalog so any can substitute for another during a bottleneck.Backwards reasoning — per-subagent tool restriction IS the mechanism for separation of responsibilities and least privilege, not a limitation to work around.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 9 (§1.3)
  • Wrap the risky calls in a PreToolUse hook requiring manual approval, or add a coordinator review step that flags bad output.A gate still permits the action when approved, and after-the-fact detection does not stop recurrence. Scoping `allowed_tools` makes the call structurally impossible.Exam 4 (§1.3), Exam 10
  • Add a description of the needed tool to the prompt so the step is known.Descriptions tell the orchestration layer what an agent type is for; they do not add a tool to any whitelist.Exam 9 (§1.3)

Your record on it

Missed on Exam 4 Q34, named in that exam's Professor's Note as 'prompt instruction chosen over allowed_tools whitelist'. Retested on Exam 5 (reject-the-full-catalog framing) where the sole D1 miss was §1.6 — so it was correct — and again on Exams 6 and 10 with no miss named.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.3 · Exam 4 Q34 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 9 · Exam 10 · EXAM-LOG Professor's Note — Intent for Exam 5

D1 §1.6

All subagents succeeded, output is wrong → blame the decomposition

Recovered

When every subagent executes correctly but the result covers the wrong ground, the root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the single most recognizable stem shape in D1. You are told explicitly that each subagent completed successfully, and then shown output that misses whole categories: a creative-industries report covering only visual art, a checkout map covering only SQL and not caching or billing, an extraction pipeline handling invoices and receipts while purchase orders fall through. The coordinator's logs will show the decomposition, and it will be narrower than the question asked. Task decomposition is the coordinator's most critical responsibility, and when it is too narrow the subagents cannot compensate — they were never assigned the missing ground. The fix is the coordinator's prompt, not the subagents.

Why it works that way

The distractors all name plausible subagent-level defects — query wording, document filters, tool descriptions, context window size, reasoning capability. Every one of them describes a failure inside an assigned scope, which cannot explain the absence of a scope that was never assigned.

Decision rule

Every subagent succeeded + coverage is wrong → the coordinator's decomposition, every time.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The search subagent's queries were worded too narrowly, or the document filters excluded the missing topics.Query wording and filters are subagent-execution concerns. The corpus explicitly rules them out for this failure shape — the subagents performed correctly on the narrow scope they were given.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 7, Exam 8
  • The synthesis agent failed to flag that its input covered only one dimension.Synthesis cannot flag gaps for subtopics it was never given findings about — there was no signal to surface.Exam 3, Exam 7, Exam 8; KD #7
  • A tool description doesn't clearly define the thing that was missed.A description problem causes misrouting between existing categories, not the wholesale absence of a category from the decomposition.Exam 5 Q21 (missed), Exam 6
  • The subagents lacked tool access, needed a bigger context window, or lacked the reasoning capability.All three misattribute the gap to capacity. The subagents were simply never told to look.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 8

Your record on it

Missed TWICE, on consecutive scored papers. Exam 4 Q39 — EXAM-LOG: 'when subagents all succeed but coverage is wrong, the root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition, not subagent execution.' Then Exam 5 Q21 — that exam's Professor's Note records it as 'blamed a tool description instead of the coordinator's own decomposition'. Recovered from there and held: correct on Exam 6 (whose sole D1 miss is §1.8), Exam 7 (sole D1 miss §1.3) and Exam 8 (sole D1 miss §1.8). Three clean re-tests after two misses — recovered, but it was this learner's most-missed D1 concept before it closed.

Where this was taught
