Key Distinction #7

D1 §1.16

fork_session for comparing approaches

Not yet tested

Fork to evaluate two approaches from one expensive shared baseline — both branches inherit context up to the fork point, then diverge with no live link.

The full lesson

What is actually true

After a costly analysis, `fork_session` creates two independent branches that both start from that completed work and then evolve separately. It is the right tool when you want to compare two designs — Redux versus Context API, an idempotency key versus a server-side dedup window, two testing strategies — without re-running the analysis twice and without the two explorations contaminating each other. The property the exam probes hardest is what happens after the branch point: the branches share nothing afterward. A dependency discovered in branch A does not appear in branch B and must be passed in explicitly. Believing forks share a live context is the specific misconception this section corrects.

Why it works that way

Independence after the fork is the whole value — it is what keeps the second evaluation from being biased by the first's conclusions. That same independence is why post-fork discoveries do not propagate.

Decision rule

One expensive baseline + two approaches to compare independently → fork_session.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Both branches share one live context, so a post-fork discovery is already visible in the other.Forks do not share a live context past the branch point. The second evaluation would silently proceed without a constraint that could change its verdict.Exam 9 (§1.16)
  • Evaluate both approaches sequentially in the same session, since the analysis is already in context.The second evaluation happens with the first's reasoning and conclusions already present — it is biased by them, the opposite of an independent comparison.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 9
  • Open two brand-new sessions and re-run the analysis in each.Each must redo the expensive shared baseline that forking exists to reuse.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 9
  • Use `--resume` twice on the same named session, treating each resume as a fresh perspective.Resuming continues one accumulating linear history — the second evaluation still sees everything reasoned about the first. Resume does not branch.Exam 3 (§1.16)
  • Run one approach, `/compact`, then run the second over the compacted context.Still one lineage, so the second is contaminated, and compaction risks losing analysis precision. Solves neither independence nor reuse.Exam 2 (§1.16)

Your record on it

The fork_session facet appears only in Exams 2, 3 and 9 — all three generated but never attempted, so no scored data exists. Adjacent §1.16 facets (resume-with-delta, fresh-plus-summary) were tested on Exams 7 and 10 and answered correctly, but fork_session itself has never appeared on a scored paper.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.16 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 9 · DASHBOARD-DATA.jsonl (Exams 2, 3, 9 unattempted)

D1 §1.1

stop_reason drives the agentic loop

Solid

The loop continues or stops based on the structured stop_reason field — never on the text Claude wrote, a call count, or a timer.

The full lesson

What is actually true

An agentic loop is a sequence of API calls where Claude's own response decides the next action. After every call your orchestrator inspects `stop_reason`: if it is `tool_use`, extract the tool_use blocks, execute the tools, append `tool_result` blocks to the message list, and call Claude again; if it is `end_turn`, Claude has finished — stop and return the answer. That is the entire control mechanism. Every alternative you will be offered is a heuristic standing in for a signal the API already gives you explicitly, and each one fails in both directions: it keeps looping after Claude has finished, and it cuts off a case that legitimately needed one more tool call.

Why it works that way

The API hands you a deterministic completion signal, so any inference you build on top of the response text or on timing is strictly less reliable than the thing it replaces. Loop control is the one place in an agent where you get a guarantee — spending it on string matching is how sessions hang in staging.

Decision rule

If an answer option infers completion from anything other than `stop_reason`, it is wrong.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Scan Claude's reply for a closing phrase — 'done', 'complete', 'issue resolved', 'Is there anything else?' — and stop when it appears.Phrasing varies run to run, so the check fires late, early, or never. This is the single most repeated D1 trap in the corpus: control flow keys off structured stop_reason, not natural-language parsing.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8; KD #5
  • Cap the loop at a fixed number of iterations or tool calls to guarantee termination.An iteration cap is a safety backstop, not a completion signal. A hard limit truncates legitimate multi-tool resolutions and still wastes a call on cases that already finished.Exam 2 Q, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 8
  • Stop once a particular tool has been called — e.g. treat any `process_refund` or `escalate_to_human` block as final.Tying termination to a tool name invents a rule the API does not use. Many valid resolutions never call that tool, and Claude may have intended a follow-up call after it.Exam 2, Exam 6
  • Use a wall-clock timeout, or wait a fixed number of seconds after the last tool result and assume completion.Timing is unrelated to whether Claude intends another tool call. A finished case lingers to the timeout while an in-progress case is cut off.Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 8

Your record on it

§1.1 was tested on every scored exam (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10) and is never named as a miss in any EXAM-LOG Professor's Note. On Exam 5 and Exam 7 the single D1 miss is separately identified (§1.6 and §1.3 respectively), so this section was answered correctly on both.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.1 · KD #5 · Exam 2 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 10

Key Distinction #5

D1 §1.1

Every stop_reason value needs its own handling

Solid

One iteration handles every tool_use block in a response, and max_tokens means truncated — not finished.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Two mechanics of the loop get tested separately from the basic continue/stop decision. First, a single response can carry several `tool_use` blocks: you extract them all, execute each tool, and append a `tool_result` for each one before calling Claude again. Executing only the first block and letting Claude re-request the rest costs a full extra round-trip on most multi-tool turns. Second, `stop_reason` has four values and only `end_turn` means Claude finished. `max_tokens` means the response was cut off mid-output — it needs an explicit continuation or retry, and treating it like `end_turn` ships a half-written payload downstream. `stop_sequence` is application-defined behavior.

Why it works that way

These are the two ways a technically-correct stop_reason check still produces a broken agent: right signal, wrong granularity. Truncated JSON forwarded to a human queue and an extra API call on every multi-tool turn are both silent, expensive, and entirely avoidable in the loop structure.

Decision rule

Handle the whole response in one iteration, and give each stop_reason value its own branch.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Execute only the first tool_use block — Claude will re-request anything else it still needs, so the loop converges anyway.It converges, but each ignored block costs a full extra API round-trip. Rationalizing the defect is not the same as handling the response.Exam 10 (§1.1)
  • Force `tool_choice` to a single named tool so each response can only contain one tool call for the harness to run.This misuses a routing control as a loop fix — it locks every turn to one tool and cannot express a request that legitimately needs two lookups.Exam 10 (cites D2 §2.1)
  • Treat `max_tokens` the same as `end_turn` since the response is complete enough to forward.A truncated response is not a finished one. Each stop_reason value demands its own handling; forwarding half a structured payload is exactly the bug.Exam 7 (§1.1)
  • Parse the partial JSON for a closing brace to decide whether the response actually finished.Inspecting output content to infer completeness is the same anti-pattern as text-matching for 'done' — decide from stop_reason.Exam 7 (§1.1)
  • When an agent splits two obviously-needed lookups across two turns, raise the per-session loop limit or build a composite tool.The lighter documented fix is to prompt the agent to bundle related tool requests into a single turn — Claude can emit multiple tool calls simultaneously. Raising the limit accommodates the wasted loop instead of removing it; a composite tool works but hides the composition.Exam 2 (D1-tagged, cites Domain-2_v2 §2.8)

Your record on it

The multi-tool-block facet was tested on Exam 10 and the max_tokens facet on Exam 7; neither appears as a named miss. Every scored D1 miss in EXAM-LOG is named to a section (Exam 4: §1.3, §1.6, §1.10, §1.12; Exam 5: §1.6; Exam 6: §1.8; Exam 7: §1.3; Exam 8: §1.8; Exam 10: §1.5), so Exam 7's and Exam 10's §1.1 items are both confirmed correct, not merely inferred.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.1 · Domain-2_v2 §2.8 · Exam 2 · Exam 7 · Exam 10

D1 §1.11

Least privilege — fix over-broad tools at the interface

Solid

Each subagent gets only the tools its scope needs, and an over-broad tool is replaced with a constrained one — not wrapped in an instruction.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tool restriction per subagent is the mechanism for separation of responsibilities, so when a subagent starts doing work outside its role, look at what its tools let it do. Two shapes recur. Either a tool it should never have had was granted 'for convenience' — remove it. Or the tool it legitimately needs is defined too broadly — a free-form `run_report_query`, a general `fetch_url`, an `update_shipping_address` that also accepts `refund_amount` — in which case replace it with a narrowly scoped, validating alternative: `get_return_eligibility`, `load_document` that checks the URL points at a document, `load_approved_excerpt` that only accepts registered IDs. Both fixes work at the interface level, which makes the out-of-scope behavior impossible rather than merely discouraged.

Why it works that way

A prompt telling an agent not to misuse a tool it still holds is probabilistic — the corpus's own `fetch_url` case rejects exactly this. Halving misuse is not eliminating it, and the capability survives every future prompt change.

Decision rule

Tool misuse → change what the tool accepts or remove it. Never instruct around a capability you can revoke.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a prompt instruction telling the subagent not to use the tool that way — the first instruction already cut misuse in half.Prompt instructions against tool misuse are probabilistic, not deterministic. The documented rejected fix.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Keep the broad tool but add a denylist, reject the one bad parameter value, or log every invocation for audit.Pattern-based patches catch only the misuse already observed, leave the permissive interface intact, and detect rather than prevent.Exam 4, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Give every subagent the full tool catalog so any can substitute for another.The inverse of least privilege — it produces exactly the scope creep described. Agents outside their specialization misuse tools they were not scoped for.Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Route every call through the coordinator for approval, or require human approval before any tool call.Disproportionate infrastructure that slows routine calls and still leaves the over-broad capability in place.Exam 4, Exam 10 (§1.11)
  • Split the subagent into two, or use a larger model less likely to misuse a broad toolset.Separation theater — the broad interface survives the split, and a bigger model does not fix a tool-scoping problem.Exam 4, Exam 10 (§1.11)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 7's sole D1 miss is §1.3, so the §1.11 item there was correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.11 · Exam 3 · Exam 4 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.11

The sanctioned exception: a scoped cross-role tool for high-frequency simple needs

Solid

When ~80-90% of a need is trivial and routing it through the coordinator costs a round-trip every time, give a narrow tool for the simple case and keep routing the complex remainder.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Strict role scoping has one documented exception, and the exam signals it with a split statistic: 85% simple single-fact lookups, 15% complex cross-referencing; or 78% one-off confirmations, 22% multi-filing traces. The correct configuration is a narrowly scoped tool — `verify_fact` — for the high-frequency simple case, with the rare complex case still routed through the coordinator to the research subagents. That applies least privilege without paying a full extra loop on the overwhelming majority of the need. Note both extremes are wrong: full search access is cross-specialization misuse, and routing everything through the coordinator preserves scoping in principle while ignoring the round-trip cost this exception exists to avoid.

Why it works that way

Least privilege is a design principle, not a purity test. Recognizing where a narrow, validating tool serves the principle better than a strict routing rule is the difference between an architecture that works and one that just looks correct.

Decision rule

A large simple majority plus a small complex remainder → narrow tool for the majority, coordinator routing for the remainder.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Give the synthesis agent full web-search access so it can resolve any verification itself.Cross-specialization misuse — the synthesizer starts doing open-ended research instead of synthesizing, which is exactly the scope creep least privilege prevents.Exam 3, Exam 7 (§1.11)
  • Batch all verification to the end of drafting and resolve it in one pass.Blocking — later drafting steps may depend on facts verified earlier, so deferring everything stalls the synthesis itself.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7 (§1.11)
  • Route every verification, simple or complex, through the coordinator to preserve strict role separation.Correct scoping in principle, but ignores the round-trip overhead on a high-frequency need — the precise situation the exception addresses.Exam 3 (§1.11)
  • Move verification to a different agent entirely, e.g. have report-generation verify every claim.Shifts responsibility to an agent with less context on the draft's specific claims rather than fixing the scoping problem.Exam 7 (§1.11)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 7, whose sole D1 miss is separately identified as §1.3 — so this was answered correctly. Also taught in unscored Exam 3.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.11 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D1 §1.13

Structured handoff protocol for escalations

Solid

The human receiving an escalation has no transcript access — the structured summary is everything they see, so it must be complete and self-contained.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Escalating is not just calling `escalate_to_human`. The agent must compile a structured handoff summary, because the human on the other end cannot see the conversation. The exam names the core fields: an identifier (customer ID, claim ID, module), a root-cause analysis, the relevant amount or scope, and a recommended action — plus the actions already taken and the escalation reason. A partial payload produces a specific, testable symptom: once IDs are present the human stops re-asking for basics, but still spends minutes reconstructing what the bot tried and what it concluded, which tells you `actions_taken` and `recommended_action` are the missing fields.

Why it works that way

Information the agent already gathered is expensive to gather twice. A handoff that omits it converts every escalation into a fresh investigation, which is the difference between an assist and a restart.

Decision rule

Handoff payload = identifier + root cause + amount/scope + actions taken + recommended action + escalation reason.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Give the human access to the raw conversation transcript, session, or reasoning trace.Rejected on two counts: humans lack transcript access by design, and a raw transcript forces re-reading the whole conversation to find what a summary would state directly.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Have the human re-run the agent's tools to rebuild the context.Duplicates work already done and slows resolution — and it describes the current failing behavior rather than changing it.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Escalate earlier, before much context accumulates, so there is less for the human to catch up on.The named wrong answer for this symptom. It does not fix the information loss — the same generic note arrives, just sooner — and it degrades the autonomous resolution rate.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Send only a flag or one-line note, since the human can ask follow-up questions.A bare flag forces the receiver to re-derive everything through follow-ups, defeating the purpose of a self-contained handoff.Exam 3, Exam 6 (§1.13)
  • Add a case-priority field so agents can triage which escalations to open first.Priority helps decide which case to open; it does nothing about the time cost once the agent is already inside a case, which is the actual complaint.Exam 8 (§1.13)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 6, 8 and 10, and taught in unscored Exams 2 and 3. Never named as a miss in any Professor's Note — and every scored D1 miss on those three papers is separately named (§1.8, §1.8, §1.5), so these are confirmed correct rather than inferred.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.13 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.14

Programmatic preconditions for mandatory sequencing

Solid

When an order must hold every time, enforce it in code — a prompt instruction is probabilistic and plateaus above zero.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The stem is always the same shape: a rule that lives only in the system prompt, an audit showing it is violated some single-digit percentage of the time, and real consequences — the wrong account refunded, an unverified caller told order details, a release corrupted, a refund issued while a human was reviewing it for denial. The fix is a programmatic precondition that blocks the downstream call until the required step has returned success: block `lookup_order` until `get_customer` verifies identity, block `commit_changes` until `format_code` succeeds on the same changeset, block any further tool call once `escalate_to_human` returns. For security-, safety-, or correctness-critical sequencing, enforce at the code level, not the prompt level. Watch for the version of this stem where prompt strengthening already ran twice and violations fell from 12% to 3% and stopped — that plateau is what a probabilistic control looks like, not evidence one more revision will finish the job.

Why it works that way

Prompt compliance is a distribution; a precondition is a guarantee. When the requirement is 'this must never happen', only the code-level version can deliver it.

Decision rule

'Must always happen before' + a nonzero violation rate → programmatic precondition, never a better prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Reword the instruction more emphatically — stronger MUST language, all caps, moved to the top of the prompt.Still prompt-level enforcement. Compliance stays probabilistic regardless of phrasing intensity, which is why the current rule already fails.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10; KD #11
  • Add few-shot examples showing the correct call order.Examples influence behavior rather than constraining it. They make the correct order likelier, not guaranteed — a residual violation rate survives.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Have the agent self-report that it performed the step, and proceed only when it says yes.A self-report is a claim, not an enforced precondition — it is the same probabilistic instance making the same judgment it already skips.Exam 2, Exam 9 (§1.14)
  • Log or alert on every violation for same-day correction, or add a nightly job that reverses bad outcomes.After-the-fact detection does not prevent the disclosure, the corrupted release, or the refund a human was still reviewing. The requirement is to make the call impossible.Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 10 (§1.14)
  • Move the rule from the system prompt into the first user message, or repeat the reminder more often during long cases.Changes where the instruction sits, not the enforcement mechanism — the failure mode persists.Exam 4, Exam 7 (§1.14)

Your record on it

One of the two most-tested D1 sections (10 rationale records), on scored Exams 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so both were correct. Never named as a miss — notable because the related 'prompt-level fix over structural guarantee' reflex was flagged as a cross-domain pattern in Exam 4's and Exam 5's Professor's Notes.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.14 · KD #11 · Exam 2 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

Key Distinction #11

D1 §1.15

Parallel execution requires one coordinator response

Solid

Multiple Task calls run in parallel only when emitted together in a single coordinator response — issued across turns, they run sequentially no matter how independent the work is.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Independent subtasks — three unrelated documents to extract, three analyses of one PR, three separate issues in one customer message, three legacy modules to investigate — should be decomposed and run concurrently, with the coordinator aggregating once all return. The mechanism is specific and it is the point of the question: the `Task` calls must appear in the same coordinator response. A coordinator that emits one Task call, waits for the result, then emits the next in a following turn has serialized the work regardless of how independent it is. The stems make the symptom obvious — latency roughly triples versus a single-item case — and every distractor treats a symptom of the serial structure rather than the structure itself.

Why it works that way

This is a free latency win that costs nothing architecturally, and the exam wants you to know it is about turn structure, not agent count, model speed, or token budget.

Decision rule

Independent work running slowly → emit all the Task calls in one response.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Merge the independent items into one prompt or one subagent call.Cuts round-trips but keeps the work sequential inside that call, reintroduces cross-item attention dilution, and mixes scopes a specialized subagent should not hold at once.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 8, Exam 10
  • Keep the calls sequential but make each one faster — a faster model, a smaller diff, fewer fields, pre-fetched content, shorter prompts.All shorten each step while preserving the serial structure. The bottleneck is that independent calls are forced to run one after another.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 10
  • Add more subagents, or give the coordinator a larger token budget.Parallelism is determined by whether the calls appear together in one response — not by agent count or available tokens.Exam 5, Exam 8 (§1.15)
  • Move the work to the Message Batches API for the cost discount.Batch has no latency SLA (up to 24 hours) — the opposite of what a latency complaint or a blocking pre-merge check needs.Exam 3 (cites Domain-4_v2 §4.11)
  • Have each subagent hand its result directly to the next to skip coordinator round-trips.Breaks hub-and-spoke — subagents never communicate directly; all results flow through the coordinator, which owns the synthesis.Exam 2 (cites §1.2)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 5, 8 and 10. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6, so the §1.15 item there was correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.15 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 5 · Exam 8 · Exam 10

D1 §1.16

Resume a named session — and say exactly what changed

Solid

When most prior context is still valid, resume with --resume and tell the agent precisely which files changed so it re-analyzes only those.

The full lesson

What is actually true

`claude --resume <session-name>` continues a specific prior conversation with its saved context, which is what makes multi-day investigations practical. The risk is that its tool results are snapshots: if files changed since, the session reasons over stale evidence as though it were current. So when you resume after code modifications, name the changed files explicitly. The agent then performs a targeted re-analysis of just those, instead of either trusting stale results or re-exploring everything. Both wrong answers are recognizable: resuming as-is because 'it's only a day old', and discarding the session to re-analyze the whole codebase 'to be safe'.

Why it works that way

Resumption is a tradeoff between reusing expensive analysis and trusting old evidence. Naming the delta is what lets you keep the first without paying for the second.

Decision rule

Mostly-valid context + a known delta → resume and name the changed files.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Resume and continue as-is — the mapping is recent and the session's saved context is why it was named.The agent reasons over stale tool results for the changed files. The exam's explicit wrong choice once files have changed.Exam 2, Exam 10 (§1.16)
  • Discard the session and re-analyze everything from scratch.Wasteful when most of the analysis is still valid — a full re-run discards days of good context because one module changed.Exam 2, Exam 10 (§1.16)
  • Resume and run `/compact` first to shrink the old context.Compaction compresses context and risks losing precision; it does nothing to refresh the stale analysis of the changed files. Wrong problem.Exam 2 (§1.16)
  • Use `fork_session` to branch, keeping one branch on the old code and one on the new.Forking compares divergent approaches from a shared baseline; it does not refresh stale results — neither branch would reflect the rewritten module.Exam 10 (§1.16)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 10 (D1 15/16) and taught in unscored Exam 2. Exam 10's sole D1 miss is named in EXAM-LOG as §1.5, so this item is confirmed correct rather than inferred. Never named as a miss.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.16 · Exam 2 · Exam 10

D1 §1.16

Fresh session plus injected summary when results are stale

Solid

When the prior session's tool results no longer reflect reality, start fresh and inject a structured summary — carry the conclusions forward, leave the evidence behind.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Resumption stops being the right answer once the underlying evidence has decayed badly enough: a module substantially rewritten across dozens of files, weeks elapsed, policy and data both changed, or context degraded. In that case start a new session and inject a short structured summary of what the prior investigation concluded. The reason is precise — a resumed session reasons over old tool results as if they were current, whereas a structured summary carries the conclusions forward without the stale evidence attached to them. Note the contrast with the resume case: the choice turns on whether the prior tool results are mostly still valid, not on how long ago the session ran.

Why it works that way

Conclusions and evidence age at different rates. Separating them is what lets you keep the thinking from an expensive investigation while discarding observations that are now simply wrong.

Decision rule

Prior tool results invalid → fresh session + structured summary of conclusions.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Resume the named session as-is and let it reconcile differences as it notices them.A resumed session treats its old tool results as valid unless told otherwise — exactly the failure mode that produces wrong conclusions from a rewritten module.Exam 7 (§1.16)
  • Resume, but instruct it to re-read every file in the module first.Still carries the old session's stale reasoning, and re-reading everything is wasteful next to a clean summary-based restart.Exam 7 (§1.16)
  • Fork the stale session so two branches can each attempt the reconciliation.Forking branches two approaches off a still-valid shared baseline. It does not help when the baseline itself is known to be stale.Exam 7 (§1.16)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 7 in two forms — the §1.16 mechanics question and the §1.18 named-pattern question ('Fresh-plus-summary'). Exam 7's sole D1 miss is separately identified as §1.3, so both were answered correctly.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.16 · Domain-1_v2 §1.18 · Exam 7

D1 §1.17

Independent review instances beat self-review

Solid

A second instance that never sees the generator's reasoning is the only fix for self-check confirmation bias — and giving it the transcript destroys the independence.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A model that generates code retains the reasoning that convinced it the code was correct, so asking that same session to review its own work reliably reaffirms the original decision. The scenario is always the same: Claude Code considers an edge case in its reasoning, talks itself out of it, self-reviews clean, and the bug surfaces in production weeks later while a human reviewing the diff cold spots it immediately. The fix mirrors human peer review — route the artifact to a second, independent instance that receives only the diff and the review criteria, with no access to the first instance's reasoning. The exam also tests the inverse: a reviewing instance that IS fed the generator's transcript concurs every time, and the fix is to withhold that transcript, not to instruct the reviewer to challenge it.

Why it works that way

This is a structural limitation, not an effort problem. No amount of extra reasoning by an anchored instance produces independent scrutiny, because the anchoring is what needs removing.

Decision rule

Self-review missed it → second independent instance, artifact and criteria only, no generator reasoning.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Enable extended thinking on the generation stage so it reasons harder about edge cases.More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny — it still starts from the conclusion it already reached.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Add a self-review instruction to the generation prompt, or a stronger 'look for race conditions' directive.Same instance, same confirmation bias. It already 'considered' the case and dismissed it, so asking it to re-check repeats the failure.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Ask for a second review pass in the same conversation, framed as an independent look.The second pass still carries the full generation reasoning in context — the model re-reads and reaffirms its own justification. Relabeling is not independence.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 7
  • Keep passing the generator's reasoning transcript to the reviewer, but instruct it to challenge every assumption.An instruction cannot undo the contamination — the reviewer is still reasoning from the generator's own justification. The fix is withholding that context, not prompting against it.Exam 9 (§1.17)
  • Have the same session write extra unit tests, or raise max_tokens so it can write more defensive code.Tests for cases it already considered will not surface an interaction it never reasoned about, and output length has nothing to do with a biased self-assessment.Exam 2, Exam 10 (§1.17)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 7 and 10. Exam 7's sole D1 miss is separately identified as §1.3, so the §1.17 item there was correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.17 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 7 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.18

Naming the architecture patterns on sight

Solid

A recurring question type gives you a described system and asks which named pattern it is — you need the vocabulary, not just the behavior.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The corpus maintains a named-pattern table and the exam tests recognition directly: 'which named architecture pattern does this reflect?' Learn each name against its one distinguishing feature. Hub-and-spoke: central coordinator, no direct inter-agent comms. Agentic loop: stop_reason-driven. Parallel execution: multiple Task calls in one response. Context isolation: subagents receive only what the coordinator passes. Evaluator-optimizer: generator followed by an independent critic. Structured error propagation: type + params + partial results + alternatives. Coverage annotation: synthesis marks supported vs data-gap conclusions. Least-privilege tooling: minimum tools per scope. Goal-oriented delegation: goals and quality criteria instead of steps. Content/metadata separation: sources carried alongside content. Prompt chaining: fixed sequential pipeline for predictable work. Dynamic adaptive decomposition: subtasks generated from intermediate findings. Iterative refinement loop: coordinator evaluates, re-delegates, re-invokes. Structured handoff: self-contained escalation summary. Session forking: independent branches from a shared baseline. Fresh-plus-summary: new session with an injected summary when prior results are stale.

Why it works that way

In these questions all four options name real patterns from the table, so you cannot eliminate on plausibility — only on which distinguishing feature the stem actually describes. The stem always states it: 'nothing depends on what any step discovers' is prompt chaining; 'never learns what the other found unless the coordinator copies it' is context isolation.

Decision rule

Match the stem's one distinguishing clause to the pattern's defining feature — all four options will be real patterns.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Calling a fixed four-step chore 'dynamic adaptive decomposition' because an agent runs it.Dynamic adaptive decomposition generates subtasks from intermediate findings. The stem states the sequence depends on nothing any step discovers — that is prompt chaining.Exam 9 (§1.18)
  • Calling a fixed linter step in a pipeline 'evaluator-optimizer'.Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with an *independent* critic stage. A fixed step in the chain is not an independent review instance.Exam 9 (§1.18)
  • Answering 'least-privilege tooling' or 'structured handoff' for a scenario about information flow between subagents.Least privilege scopes tool access, not information; structured handoff is the summary built for a human reviewer during escalation. Neither describes a subagent-to-subagent information gap — that is context isolation.Exam 5, Exam 8 (§1.18)
  • Answering 'session forking' or 'coverage annotation' for a stalled session restarted with a pasted summary.Forking branches two approaches off a still-valid baseline; coverage annotation marks gaps within one synthesis pass. Neither resolves stale evidence — that is fresh-plus-summary.Exam 7 (§1.18)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 5, 7 and 8. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so the pattern-naming items on both were correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.18 · Exam 5 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9

D1 §1.2

Hub-and-spoke: no direct subagent-to-subagent channels

Solid

All inter-agent communication flows through the coordinator — any side channel, however convenient, breaks visibility, uniform error handling, and information control at once.

The full lesson

What is actually true

In hub-and-spoke, one coordinator orchestrates specialized subagents and subagents never communicate with each other directly. The coordinator exists to buy four things: visibility (it observes every interaction), uniform error handling (it decides retry vs skip vs escalate consistently), information control (it decides what each subagent receives), and separation of responsibilities (each subagent keeps a narrow scope). A side channel removes all four simultaneously — and it does not matter what shape the channel takes. A direct message, a shared queue, a shared file, a database one agent writes and another polls, or read access to another agent's transcript are all the same violation wearing different clothes. The correct fix is always the same: route the output back through the coordinator and let it forward.

Why it works that way

Every failure you will be shown — a double refund, a lost finding, a run summary that no longer reflects reality, an escalation missing the reasoning that produced it — is a downstream symptom of the coordinator not having seen something. Restore the hub and the symptom cannot recur; patch the symptom and it recurs in a new shape.

Decision rule

If the fix leaves any agent-to-agent path open — message, file, queue, database, transcript — it is not the fix.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Let the two subagents message each other first to confirm neither has already acted, or have one write to a shared DB the other polls.Still a direct inter-agent channel, just routed differently. The coordinator remains blind to the exchange, which is the actual defect.Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Add a shared lock file, a schema validation at the consumer, a retry policy on the queue, or a daily reconciliation job.These are infrastructure patched around the missing coordinator visibility. They catch the problem after the fact (or treat an architecture problem as a data-quality problem) instead of restoring the architecture that would have prevented it.Exam 6, Exam 9
  • Give each subagent its own error-handling logic so it can detect a stalled sibling independently.That is exactly the fragmented per-agent error handling the coordinator hub exists to replace with a uniform decision.Exam 5; KD #6
  • Merge the two subagents into one so no handoff is needed.Removes the handoff by removing the specialization. It sacrifices separation of responsibilities and leaves the coordinator no better able to observe the work.Exam 5, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Forward the first subagent's early findings onward without waiting for the other Task calls in the round.The coordinator aggregates only once every Task call in a delegation round completes. Splitting a downstream agent's input across two deliveries defeats coordinated aggregation.Exam 10 (§1.2)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so the hub-topology items on both were correct. Never named as a miss anywhere in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.2 · KD #6 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

Key Distinction #6

D1 §1.2

Context isolation between subagents

Solid

A subagent sees only what the coordinator explicitly puts in its prompt — nothing else, ever.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Subagents spawned via `Task` run with isolated context. They do not see the coordinator's conversation history, and they do not see another subagent's output, unless the coordinator copies it into their prompt. This is the defining information-flow property of hub-and-spoke, and it produces a very recognizable exam symptom: a downstream agent that reports 'no data to validate', or generated tests that never mock a dependency an upstream agent already discovered, or a synthesis step writing about something it was never given. The root cause is never the downstream agent's capability or tooling — it is a context-passing gap in the coordinator's prompt.

Why it works that way

Isolation is a feature, not a bug: it is what keeps each subagent's context small and its scope narrow. But it makes the coordinator solely responsible for propagation, so any finding it forgets to forward simply does not exist downstream.

Decision rule

If a subagent lacks information another subagent already found, the coordinator's prompt is the defect.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The downstream subagent needs a `session_id` to retrieve the prior agent's turn.No such parameter exists — the API is stateless and there is no server-side retrieval of another agent's turn. Context is shared only by the coordinator putting it in the prompt.Exam 2 (§1.2); KD #25
  • Give the downstream subagent its own tool so it can re-derive the information itself.A validator that re-extracts is no longer validating, and a test-writer that re-maps duplicates work. It breaks separation of responsibilities instead of closing the context gap.Exam 2 (cites §1.11), Exam 8
  • Give every worker read access to the coordinator's full conversation history so each can reconstruct what the others did.This inverts the context-passing principle — it destroys information control and floods each worker with context irrelevant to its narrow scope.Exam 9 (§1.2)
  • Subagent runs are just non-deterministic, so some coverage will always be missed at random.This is not random variation. It is a specific, traceable context-passing gap between two turns with a clear architectural fix.Exam 8 (§1.2)

Your record on it

The context-isolation facet was tested on scored Exam 8 (D1 15/16) and in unscored Exams 2 and 9. Exam 8's sole D1 miss is named in EXAM-LOG as §1.8, so this item is confirmed correct rather than inferred. Never named as a miss anywhere.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.2 · Exam 2 · Exam 8 · Exam 9

D1 §1.3

The description field is what routing runs on

Solid

The orchestration layer picks which subagent type to invoke from its description — so two subagents sharing a generic description will be routed to interchangeably.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Each of the three AgentDefinition levers answers a different question, and the exam tests whether you can tell them apart. `description` decides which subagent type gets invoked. `system_prompt` governs behavior after selection. `allowed_tools` bounds capability. So when a coordinator routes billing cases to the returns agent a third of the time — while both agents have correctly scoped tools and accurate system prompts — the defect is that both descriptions read 'Handles customer requests.' Give each a distinct, specific description and the routing signal exists.

Why it works that way

Selection and behavior are separate stages. Fixing the wrong stage is the classic near-miss here: a better system prompt makes a subagent behave well once chosen, which does nothing about how often it gets chosen wrongly.

Decision rule

Misrouting between subagent types → fix the descriptions; misbehavior within a type → fix the prompt; capability leaks → fix allowed_tools.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rewrite each subagent's system prompt to state its specialty more explicitly.The system prompt governs behavior after a subagent type is already selected — it has no influence on the coordinator's initial choice.Exam 8 (§1.3)
  • Give both subagent types the full tool set so either can complete any case.Broadening access does not change which one gets picked, and it abandons least privilege without touching the root cause.Exam 8 (§1.3)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 8 (D1 15/16), never named as a miss in any Professor's Note. Exam 8's sole D1 miss is named in EXAM-LOG as §1.8, so this item is confirmed correct rather than inferred.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.3 · Exam 8

D1 §1.4

Goal-oriented coordinator prompts, not procedural scripts

Solid

State the goal and the quality criteria; a numbered script breaks the moment reality deviates from it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A coordinator prompt should say what to achieve and how good the result must be — 'a comprehensive, cited overview, with at least three independent sources per claim, covering production, distribution and composition' — not 'Step 1: search X. Step 2: open the first five results. Step 3: summarize each in 100 words.' The procedural version locks the system into a decision tree written before anything was known, so it produces checklist-shaped output and silently drops findings its own subagents surfaced but no step asked for. The goal-oriented version is model-driven decision-making applied at the orchestration level: the same principle as the agentic loop, one layer up. The tell in a stem is shallow, thin, or template-shaped results from subagents that each executed correctly.

Why it works that way

Adaptability is the whole reason to use an agent instead of a script. A procedural coordinator prompt spends the model's judgment and keeps the brittleness — the worst of both.

Decision rule

Shallow, checklist-like output from correctly-executing subagents → rewrite the coordinator prompt as goals + quality criteria.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add more granular steps, or one more checklist item covering the case that was just missed.The corpus is explicit: more detailed step-by-step instructions deepen the rigidity that caused the problem. The next unanticipated discovery hits the same wall.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Increase the number of subagents so more of the script runs in parallel.More agents executing a bad script does not fix the script — it runs the flawed procedure in more places at once.Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Keep the script but wrap the fragile step in try/except, or add a final step saying 'use good judgment'.Still a rigid procedural script underneath. Swallowing the error avoids the crash without letting the subagent reason about what the situation actually needs; a vague escape hatch states no goal and no quality criteria.Exam 4, Exam 5 (§1.4)
  • Add a review pass afterward, or a dedicated subagent that watches for the specific thing that was missed.Adds infrastructure to patch a symptom instead of fixing the coordinator prompt that produced the shallow plan.Exam 6, Exam 7 (§1.4)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so the §1.4 items on both were correct. Never named as a miss.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.4 · Exam 3 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9

D1 §1.5

Separate content from source metadata

Solid

Attribution survives aggregation only when the claim and its source live in separate fields — never inside the same sentence.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When agents hand findings to each other, use a structured format that keeps the content in one field and the metadata — source URL, document name, page number, file path, line number, retrieval date — in another. The moment findings are concatenated into free-text paragraphs, or the source is folded into the prose ('resistance rose 18% (hospital bulletin)'), the claim-to-source mapping is destroyed by the next rewrite or merge. That is the actual root cause behind every missing-or-wrong-citation stem: attribution was lost during aggregation because it was never captured in a form that survives it. Notice this generalizes past research — a file path and line number are source metadata for a code finding exactly as a URL is for a web finding.

Why it works that way

A downstream agent cannot cite metadata it never received in structured form. No amount of instruction downstream can recover information that was destroyed upstream — which is why the fix always belongs at the producing end of the pipeline.

Decision rule

Citations wrong or missing → fix the inter-agent data format upstream, never the downstream instruction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Instruct the synthesis agent to 'remember to cite the source for every claim'.It cannot cite metadata it never received in structured form. This is the corpus's named wrong answer for this exact symptom.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 7, Exam 9 (§1.5)
  • Have the report-generation agent re-search afterward to find a plausible source for each uncited claim.Duplicated, expensive work that can attach a claim to the wrong source entirely — the very failure being reported.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Add a disclaimer that some figures may be unsourced, or a post-generation check flagging uncited numbers.A blanket disclaimer does not restore claim-level attribution and undermines the properly-sourced claims too; a post-hoc check catches the symptom after fabricated figures are already written.Exam 3, Exam 10 (§1.5)
  • Have the coordinator merge overlapping findings into one deduplicated narrative before synthesis.Merging into narrative is precisely where attribution is lost — this compounds the loss rather than reducing it.Exam 9 (§1.5)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 7's sole D1 miss is §1.3, so the §1.5 item there was correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.5 · Exam 3 · Exam 4 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.5

Conflicting sources: preserve both, annotate the conflict

Solid

When two sources disagree, keep both values with their attribution and flag the conflict — never pick, average, or re-run.

The full lesson

What is actually true

If two subagents return contradictory figures or dates, each accurately reporting what its own source says, the merge step must not resolve the conflict on its own. Preserve both values with their source attribution in the structured output, annotate that they disagree, and let the coordinator — which has visibility across both subagents — decide or escalate. Silently choosing the one that 'looks more authoritative' discards a legitimate, differently-sourced data point; averaging manufactures a third value that neither source reported and hides the discrepancy entirely.

Why it works that way

A genuine conflict between two real source systems is information. Collapsing it during aggregation destroys the one signal that tells a human something needs looking at.

Decision rule

Conflicting statistics → preserve both with attribution and annotate; the coordinator decides.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Report whichever value the synthesis step trusts more, without surfacing the other.This is the arbitrary-pick failure the rule exists to prevent — it drops a legitimate data point instead of preserving it.Exam 8 (§1.5)
  • Average the two conflicting values to give one consistent answer.Fabricates a third value neither source reported — worse than either original, and it conceals the discrepancy.Exam 8 (§1.5)
  • Re-run both subagents and expect the values to converge.Each subagent is accurately reporting its own source, so a retry reproduces the same two values.Exam 8 (§1.5)
  • Treat whichever subagent reported first as authoritative going forward.Report order has no bearing on which figure is correct — an arbitrary tiebreak dressed as a rule.Exam 6, Exam 7 (§1.5)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 8 (D1 15/16); never named as a miss. Exam 8's sole D1 miss is named in EXAM-LOG as §1.8, so this item is confirmed correct rather than inferred.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.5 · Exam 8

D1 §1.6

Partition the work space before delegating

Solid

Assign distinct, non-overlapping scopes up front — deduplicating afterward has already paid the cost.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The other half of decomposition is partitioning. Before delegating, the coordinator must explicitly divide the research space or work list, assigning each agent distinct subtopics or source types. Skip this and two agents investigate the same ground: token usage doubles, run time doubles, edits collide, and coverage does not improve at all. The exam is precise about the fix's timing — partition before delegation, not deduplication after — because by the time a merge or dedup step runs, the duplicated work is already spent.

Why it works that way

Partitioning is what prevents duplication and missed coverage with one action. It is also the only mechanism available: a subagent cannot avoid its sibling's territory, because context isolation means it has no idea what its sibling was assigned.

Decision rule

Two agents covering the same ground → partition before delegating, never deduplicate after.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a dedup or merge step that reconciles the overlapping outputs after both agents finish.The documented wrong answer for this exact symptom — the doubled effort and run time were already spent, and reconciliation widens no coverage.Exam 9, Exam 10 (§1.6)
  • Instruct each worker to skip anything another worker might already be handling.Pushes a coordinator responsibility onto workers as a probabilistic instruction. A subagent has no visibility into its sibling's assignment, so it cannot reliably decide what to skip.Exam 9 (§1.6)
  • Run the agents sequentially so the second can see what the first changed, or merge them into one agent.Serializing removes the parallelism without addressing the unpartitioned delegation; merging collapses the specialization hub-and-spoke depends on.Exam 9, Exam 10 (§1.6, §1.2)
  • Restrict one agent's tools so it can no longer touch the overlapping topic.Removes its ability to contribute at all, rather than simply assigning it a distinct scope.Exam 10 (§1.6)

Your record on it

The partitioning facet was tested on scored Exam 10 (D1 15/16) and unscored Exam 9. Exam 10's sole D1 miss is named in EXAM-LOG as §1.5, so this item is confirmed correct rather than inferred. Never named as a miss.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.6 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.7

Fixed pipeline vs dynamic adaptive decomposition

Solid

Predictable structure known up front → fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining); scope discovered as you go → dynamic adaptive decomposition.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Two named decomposition patterns, and picking between them is a repeated exam skill. Use a fixed sequential pipeline — prompt chaining — when every instance follows the same known steps in the same order: classify, extract, validate, enrich, format. You get stability and reproducibility, which is exactly what a 40,000-case-a-quarter refund flow or a template-driven claims intake needs. Use dynamic adaptive decomposition when the full scope is unknown at the outset and each step depends on what the previous one found: an open-ended investigation, a dead-code sweep, adding tests to an undocumented legacy module. The deciding factor is always whether the steps are knowable in advance — not how important, high-stakes, or auditable the task is. Some questions give you both workloads at once and ask you to assign each correctly.

Why it works that way

Each pattern fails in the other's territory in a specific way: a fixed script cannot react to a dependency nobody knew existed, and dynamic re-planning on a fully predictable flow is pure overhead that costs you the reproducibility you chose the pipeline for.

Decision rule

Ask only one thing: are all the steps knowable before starting? Yes → fixed pipeline. No → dynamic adaptive.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use dynamic adaptive decomposition everywhere — it can always fall back to a fixed order once discoveries stop.It adds planning overhead a predictable flow does not need, and sacrifices the reproducibility that is the whole point of the pipeline. Unnecessary complexity, not a safety net.Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 8, Exam 9
  • Use a fixed pipeline for the open-ended task because predefined steps guarantee coverage and keep it on budget.A predetermined script cannot react to what the work discovers; enumeration order guarantees nothing when an unanticipated dependency blocks whole paths.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • This flow is high-stakes, so it needs the reproducibility of a fixed pipeline.Stakes do not determine the pattern. The deciding factor is whether the steps are predictable up front.Exam 6 (§1.7)
  • Add the newly-discovered dependency as a required first step of the fixed pipeline.You could not have known that dependency existed before the work started — it was found partway through. This still forces an unknown-scope task into a predetermined sequence.Exam 3 (§1.7)
  • Run the fixed pipeline twice and merge the outputs so the second pass catches what the first missed.Both passes inherit the same rigidity; adaptivity, not repetition, is the fix.Exam 2 (§1.7)

Your record on it

§1.7 is the most heavily taught D1 section (15 rationale records) and was tested on scored Exams 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so the §1.7 items on both were correct. Never named as a miss.

Domain-1_v2 §1.7 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 5 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D1 §1.7

The shape of an adaptive investigation plan

Solid

Map the structure first, prioritize the high-risk areas, then adapt the plan as dependencies surface.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When dynamic adaptive decomposition is the right answer, the exam usually wants you to recognize its concrete shape too. Given 'add tests to a legacy codebase', the pattern runs: map the structure with Glob and Grep; discover which modules have no coverage and which have partial; prioritize by risk (start with payments); then, when the work reveals an undocumented dependency on an external API, adapt — add a mock before continuing. Subtasks are generated from intermediate findings rather than declared up front, and the plan is revised mid-flight when a discovery invalidates part of it.

Why it works that way

This is what makes the pattern more than 'be flexible'. The map-first, prioritize, adapt sequence is what lets an agent handle scope it could not have estimated, without either freezing on a script or wandering.

Decision rule

Unknown scope → map first, prioritize by risk, replan as discoveries land.

Traps that have caught you here

  • One giant single-pass prompt that attempts the whole task at once.Attention dilutes across the work — deep on some parts, shallow on others. It is the documented anti-pattern for large multi-part work and finds the hidden dependency no faster.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 9
  • Assign one subagent to investigate everything in a single unscoped pass so nothing is prematurely excluded.An unscoped pass risks attention dilution and lacks the explicit partitioning that prevents missed coverage.Exam 7 (cites §1.6)
  • Use adaptive decomposition, but first double the number of subagents on the investigation.More subagents running the same fixed sequence adds no adaptability — the fix is the decomposition strategy, not the agent count.Exam 6 (§1.7)

Your record on it

Taught in unscored Exams 2 and 3 and tested within the §1.7 items on scored Exams 5, 6, 7 and 9's sibling framings. Exam 5 and Exam 7's D1 misses are separately identified (§1.6, §1.3), so these were correct. Never named as a miss.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.7 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D1 §1.7

Multi-pass code review beats one big pass

Solid

Split a large PR into per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass — a bigger context window does not fix attention.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Prompt chaining applied to review: for a PR touching 10+ files, run one pass per file for local issues, then a distinct integration pass that examines relationships between them (inconsistent types, circular dependencies). The failure mode of a single pass over everything is diagnostic — deep feedback on the first few files and shallow feedback on the rest, an obvious bug missed, and the same pattern flagged in one file while approved in another. That inconsistency is attention dilution, and the trap answer is to reach for a larger model with a bigger context window. More tokens available is not the same as consistent attention per token; the fix is structural, not capacity.

Why it works that way

This is the clearest case in the domain where 'give the model more room' is explicitly debunked. Recognizing inconsistent-depth symptoms as an architecture problem rather than a capacity problem generalizes to any large multi-item analysis.

Decision rule

Inconsistent depth across many items → split into per-item passes plus one integration pass.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Switch to a larger model with a bigger context window so all the files fit comfortably in one pass.A bigger context window does not fix attention quality. This is the explicitly debunked 'bigger context' trap.Exam 2, Exam 5; KD #17
  • Require developers to split the PR into several smaller PRs.Shifts the burden onto humans instead of fixing the review architecture, and still does not address cross-file issues inside a legitimately large change.Exam 2 (§1.7)
  • Run the same full-PR pass twice and keep only findings that appear in both runs.Consensus filtering across two diluted passes suppresses real single-run findings and leaves the underlying attention problem untouched.Exam 2, Exam 5
  • Review a random sample of the files to keep attention concentrated.Trades thoroughness for focus and guarantees some files are never reviewed — it shrinks the problem instead of restructuring it.Exam 5 (§1.7)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 5 (block 3, 12-file scaffold review). Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6, so this was answered correctly. Also taught twice in unscored Exam 2.

Where this was taught

Domain-1_v2 §1.7 · KD #17 · Exam 2 · Exam 5

Key Distinction #17

D1 §1.9

Structured error context, never a generic failure status

Solid

A failing subagent returns failure type, what it attempted, partial results, and possible alternatives — four fields, not one flag.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a subagent fails, the coordinator has to choose between retry, reroute, continue with partial results, and escalate. It can only do that if the error payload carries four things: the failure type (timeout vs syntax error vs access denied vs rate limit), exactly what was attempted (the query string, the parameters, the malformed code), whatever partial results were completed before the failure, and the viable alternatives (retry later? different source? narrow the trace?). A bare `{"status":"failed"}` forces the coordinator to guess, which in practice means it retries everything identically — burning cycles on failures that can never succeed — or aborts work that was nearly done.

Why it works that way

The coordinator's uniform error handling (§1.2) is only as good as the information it receives. Structured error context is what converts an agent failure from a dead end into a decision.

Decision rule

Failure payload must answer: what kind, what was tried, what came back, what else could work.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Return a generic 'unavailable' or `{"status":"error"}` so the coordinator can apply one uniform recovery policy.A single undifferentiated code collapses failure types that need opposite responses, allowing only a crude retry-or-abort instead of an informed decision.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 6; KD #8
  • Add a single `retryable: true` boolean and let the coordinator infer the rest.A blanket retryable flag wastes retries on permanent failures and still hides what was attempted and what partial work exists.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7; KD #9
  • Return only the failing file path or item and let the coordinator diagnose the cause itself.Pushes cause-diagnosis back onto the coordinator for every failure, adding work the subagent is far better positioned to do automatically.Exam 5 (§1.9)
  • Present a timed-out, unfinished branch exactly like a branch that legitimately had nothing left to check.Erases the distinction between a valid result and an unresolved failure — the coordinator would believe the trace finished.Exam 8 (§1.9)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 5's sole D1 miss is §1.6 and Exam 7's is §1.3, so these items were correct on both. Never named as a miss.

Where this was taught

Key Distinction #8

D1 §1.9

Transient vs permanent vs valid-empty, and where each is handled

Solid

Retry transient failures inside the subagent; escalate what it cannot resolve with full context; treat '0 results' as a finding; never silently succeed and never kill the whole workflow.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Errors sort into three buckets and the response differs completely for each. Transient failures — a network timeout, a briefly-unavailable endpoint — are retried with backoff at the subagent level. Permanent failures — a malformed query, a syntax or validation error, a password-protected PDF, a binary file that will never parse as text, a permission denial — will fail identically every time; log them and continue rather than retrying. And a legitimate empty result is not a failure at all: '0 results from industry reports' is an informative finding, and conflating it with a timeout tells the coordinator something false about the world. Two absolute rules bracket all of this: never catch an error and silently return success, and never terminate the entire workflow because one subagent failed.

Why it works that way

Retry policy is where cost and correctness meet. Retrying a permanent failure burns cycles for a guaranteed loss; not retrying a transient one throws away recoverable work; and a silent success is the worst outcome of all, because the gap is now invisible.

Decision rule

Transient → retry locally with backoff. Permanent → log and continue. Empty → that is a finding. Never silent success; never global abort.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Catch the error inside the subagent and return an empty-but-successful result so the pipeline keeps moving.Explicitly prohibited. It masks a real failure as a success — the coordinator never learns the item needs handling.Exam 2, Exam 5, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Terminate the whole batch or run so an engineer can investigate the one failing item.Disproportionate — never terminate the entire workflow for one subagent failure. One unreadable file should not cost the other 26 repositories.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Report a rejected or failed query as 'zero relevant results'.A query that never ran is not a valid empty result. Conflating them tells the coordinator the wrong thing about the underlying data.Exam 3, Exam 5; KD #9
  • Retry indefinitely until it succeeds, or forward every exception to the coordinator including ones the subagent could resolve.Unbounded retry treats every failure as transient and never terminates on a permanent one; forwarding everything drags the coordinator into routine error handling that belongs at the subagent level.Exam 3, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Route every tool error straight to a human so no automated retry can mask a real problem.Discards the transient/permanent distinction that drives recovery, and adds unnecessary human load for errors a retry would clear.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 10; KD #9

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10. Exam 5 and Exam 7 both have their single D1 miss identified elsewhere (§1.6, §1.3), so these were correct. Never named as a miss in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught
