Key Distinction #9

Domain 2 · 18% of the exam · 11 of 60 questions

Tool Design & MCP Integration

D2 is the seam between Claude and everything outside it: how you define a tool, how you describe it so the right one gets picked, how results and errors travel back into the conversation, and how you wire in external capability through MCP servers, hooks, and Claude Code's built-in tools. Eleven of your sixty questions come from here. Almost every D2 question is the same choice wearing a different costume — a structural guarantee (a confirmation token, a hook, a tool_choice setting, a rewritten description) versus a probabilistic one (a stronger prompt, a reminder, an extra classifier layer). The corpus nearly always wants the structural fix, applied at the root cause, at the smallest level that actually solves it — not a heavier layer bolted on top of a bad signal.

35 concepts54/70 lifetime (77%)

Recall check — D2

Answer out loud before you open each one. Retrieval is what moves a concept from recognised to owned.

  1. A tempting answer says A PostToolUse hook can perform the work the application never did.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Claude only ever requests a tool call — your application executes the tool and appends a tool_result before the conversation can continue.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Hooks are a Claude Code harness feature that fires around calls the harness itself executes; a script calling the Messages API directly has no such mechanism, and even inside Claude Code a hook does not substitute for the application's own responsibility to run the tool.

  2. A tempting answer says Force the calls into separate sequential turns so results cannot be reordered.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: The id field on a tool_use block is what binds a result back to the call that asked for it — match on id, never on append order.

    Why the tempting answer fails: It gives up the parallel-execution latency benefit and still never fixes the underlying attribution bug.

  3. A tempting answer says auto plus a system-prompt instruction to always use a tool is equivalent to any.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: auto lets Claude decide, any forces some tool, and {"type":"tool","name":"X"} forces that specific tool.

    Why the tempting answer fails: auto permits a plain-text answer, and the instruction on top of it is probabilistic — exactly the failure already observed in production.

D2 §2.3

A business-rule denial is not a tool failure

Still open

A policy rejection is a valid answer that the action is disallowed — return retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation, never a bare error.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When process_refund rejects a refund because the order is past the 30-day window, or a settlement exceeds a coverage cap, or an item is final-sale, the tool did not fail. It answered correctly: this action is not allowed. Structure that as a business-category error with retriable: false and a customer-friendly explanation in the payload — 'Refunds are available within 30 days of purchase; this order is outside that window' — so the agent stops retrying and can state the policy to the customer without paraphrasing internal jargon. A bare isError: true makes the agent apologise for technical difficulties, promise to retry later, and inflate your ops dashboard's error rate with outcomes that were never errors.

Why it works that way

This is the category most likely to be mislabelled as transient, and mislabelling it wastes retries on an outcome that can never change while giving the customer a false story about what happened.

Decision rule

If the tool worked correctly and the answer is 'not allowed', the right response is retriable: false plus a plain-language explanation — never a retry, never a bare failure, never a fake success.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Classify it as transient with isRetryable: true so normal retry-with-backoff clears it.A policy limit does not move; retrying spends attempts on an outcome that can never change.Exam 10 Q4 (missed), Exam 2/Exam 3 (unscored, recurring)
  • Return a generic {"error": "Operation failed"} and let the agent decide.The agent cannot distinguish a policy denial from an outage, so it retries or escalates incorrectly — the behaviour already observed in the logs.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Return a successful result with the denial explanation buried in a message field.Returning success with embedded error metadata masks the failure — the corpus rules this out explicitly.Exam 10 Q4 (missed)
  • Keep the generic error and escalate every failure to a human.It floods humans with self-explanatory policy outcomes the agent could have explained itself given a proper category.Exam 10 Q4 (missed)

Your record on it

Answered correctly in Exam 6 and Exam 8, then MISSED in Exam 10 Q4 — treated a valid policy denial as a tool failure. This is the most recent D2 miss and has not been re-tested since; EXAM-LOG's Professor's Note for Exam 11 explicitly biases toward §2.3.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.3 · Exam 10 Q4 · Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block) · EXAM-LOG Professor's Note — Intent for Exam 11

D2 §2.8

Prompt-bundling beats composite tools

Still open

When two tools are habitually called in sequence, instruct the agent to request both in one turn — do not build a composite tool that hides the composition.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The scenario is always a pair of tools called one turn apart when both are known to be needed: lookup_order then check_return_eligibility, get_module_metadata then get_test_coverage, compile_report_body then append_source_index. An engineer proposes a combined tool. The corpus's preferred answer is the simpler one: prompt the agent to bundle the related requests into a single turn, because Claude can naturally issue several tool calls in one response. A composite tool works but is explicitly marked not preferred — it hides the composition behind a new interface. Watch for two false premises the exam builds distractors on: that Claude cannot issue two tool calls in one response (it can), and that the sequencing is structurally required (usually it is not — both calls take the same identifier the user already supplied).

Why it works that way

This is the domain's clearest test of proportionality: the corpus wants the lightest intervention that removes the round-trip, and every heavier option — a new tool, a hook, a coordinator pre-fetch — is a real but disfavoured answer.

Decision rule

Two tools always needed together equals a prompt instruction to bundle — reach for a composite tool, a hook, or a coordinator pre-fetch only if the prompt fix is unavailable.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Approve the composite tool — collapsing a habitually sequential pair into one definition is the standard remedy.A composite hides the composition; bundling-by-prompt is the documented preferred approach.Exam 6 Q24 (missed), Exam 10 Q6 (missed)
  • Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks the first tool unless the second is called in the same turn, or a PostToolUse hook that fires the second automatically.Hooks run deterministic code around a call the model has already committed to; they are not the mechanism for getting two calls issued together, and reaching for hook infrastructure is disproportionate where a prompt instruction suffices.Exam 8 Q11 (missed), Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Keep the calls sequential because the second depends on the first completing.Both calls take the same identifier the user already supplied — nothing structural forces sequencing; the extra turn is habit, not dependency.Exam 10 Q6 (missed)
  • Have the coordinator pre-fetch both, or increase max_tokens or the context window.Pre-fetching removes the subagent's own judgment about what it needs; token and window limits address response length and memory, not why two calls were split across turns.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

The most repeated open D2 gap. Correct in Exam 5 and Exam 7, but MISSED in Exam 6 Q24, Exam 8 Q11 (chose a PreToolUse hook over the simpler bundling instruction) and again in Exam 10 Q6 (recommended the composite). EXAM-LOG's Insights Round 2 names §2.8 as a cross-exam repeat that neither individual Professor's Note caught, and Exam 8's note ties it to a broader over-engineering reflex.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.8 · Exam 6 Q24 · Exam 8 Q11 · Exam 10 Q6 · EXAM-LOG Insights Round 2 · EXAM-LOG Exam 8 Observations

D2 §2.1

The tool-use loop is application-driven

Recovered

Claude only ever requests a tool call — your application executes the tool and appends a tool_result before the conversation can continue.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tool use is a five-step cycle. You define tools in the API request with a name, description, and JSON Schema input_schema. Claude returns a response with stop_reason: "tool_use" and a tool_use content block. Your application executes the tool. Your application appends a tool_result content block. Claude continues from that result. The step people skip is the third and fourth: Claude never executes anything itself, and it cannot proceed until a matching tool_result comes back. If your harness sees tool_use, does the work in its own database, and stops — or does the work but reports it as a plain user-role text message — the loop is left open and Claude will re-request the same call or reply confused.

Why it works that way

The API is a request/response protocol, not an execution engine; the responsibility boundary between model and application is exactly where most first implementations break. Nothing downstream — retries, hooks, tool_choice — can compensate for a loop that was never closed.

Decision rule

If Claude asked for a tool and nothing happened, ask 'who was supposed to run it?' — the answer is always your application, never Claude and never a hook.

Traps that have caught you here

  • A PostToolUse hook can perform the work the application never did.Hooks are a Claude Code harness feature that fires around calls the harness itself executes; a script calling the Messages API directly has no such mechanism, and even inside Claude Code a hook does not substitute for the application's own responsibility to run the tool.Exam 5 Q35 (missed)
  • Marking the outcome internally and ending the request is enough.Without a tool_result appended to the conversation, the loop stays open — the session re-attempts the same escalation on the next turn.Exam 6 Q2 (missed)
  • Report the result as a new plain-text user message describing what happened.Free text carries no id and is not the structured continuation the protocol expects; Claude's next reply is confused and may repeat the call.Exam 8 (Customer Support block)
  • Seeing a tool_use block in the response means the work is done.It inverts the control flow — tool_use is the signal to execute and continue, end_turn is the signal to stop.Exam 9 (Developer Productivity block, unscored)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 5 Q35 (picked a PostToolUse hook over the missing execution step) and Exam 6 Q2 (harness marked the case escalated in its own database and never executed the tool or returned a result). Answered correctly on its next scored appearance, Exam 8 (harness executed the tool but reported the outcome as a plain user-role text message) — inside a 10/11 D2 score whose only miss was Q11 (§2.8). Not re-tested as a D2-tagged item in Exam 10; the closest Exam 10 question is D1 §1.1-cited (execute EVERY tool_use block in a multi-tool response, D2 §2.1 appearing only in a distractor) and was also answered correctly.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.1 · Exam 5 Q35 · Exam 6 Q2 · Exam 8 (Customer Support block) · EXAM-LOG Exam 5/6 Traps missed

D2 §2.1

Bind every tool_result to its tool_use id

Recovered

The id field on a tool_use block is what binds a result back to the call that asked for it — match on id, never on append order.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Each tool_use content block carries a unique id (for example "toolu_abc123") alongside its name and input. When you append the tool_result, it must reference that same id. This matters the moment more than one tool call happens in a single turn: if your harness builds results without preserving the ids, or assumes results come back in the order the calls were issued, Claude cross-attributes one call's result to another. A retry that reorders results, or two parallel lookups appended in the wrong sequence, will silently produce answers about the wrong customer or the wrong record.

Why it works that way

Parallel tool calls in one turn are a latency win you only get to keep if attribution is explicit; ordering is not a contract the protocol makes, ids are.

Decision rule

Two tool calls in one turn plus any doubt about which result is which equals an id-matching bug, not a timing bug.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Force the calls into separate sequential turns so results cannot be reordered.It gives up the parallel-execution latency benefit and still never fixes the underlying attribution bug.Exam 7 (Customer Support block)
  • Increase retry backoff so out-of-order arrival is less likely.Timing is a probabilistic workaround; a result appended out of order is still perfectly identifiable by its id if the harness checked it.Exam 7 (Customer Support block)
  • input_schema validation lets Claude tell the calls apart.input_schema validates the shape of Claude's arguments before execution; it plays no role in matching a result back to a call.Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 6 Q2 (id-matched tool_result skipped entirely); answered correctly in Exam 7 (id-vs-append-order framing) and Exam 8, both within perfect/near-perfect D2 scores.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.1 · Exam 6 Q2 · Exam 7 (Customer Support block) · Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block)

D2 §2.1

The three tool_choice settings

Recovered

auto lets Claude decide, any forces some tool, and {"type":"tool","name":"X"} forces that specific tool.

The full lesson

What is actually true

tool_choice has exactly three shapes and each makes a different promise. {"type": "auto"} is the default and promises nothing — Claude may answer in plain text. {"type": "any"} guarantees the model calls some tool, never conversational text, but does not say which one. {"type": "tool", "name": "X"} guarantees that specific tool is called. Reading the guarantee correctly is the whole game: a question that needs 'always structured output' wants any, and a question that needs 'this exact step first' wants the named form. When tool_choice names a specific tool, Claude has no discretion to decline it based on its description.

Why it works that way

tool_choice is the only deterministic lever over response shape; prompt instructions about tool use are probabilistic by construction.

Decision rule

Ask what the scenario needs guaranteed — a tool call at all (any) or a named tool (tool) — and never accept a prompt instruction as a substitute for either.

Traps that have caught you here

  • auto plus a system-prompt instruction to always use a tool is equivalent to any.auto permits a plain-text answer, and the instruction on top of it is probabilistic — exactly the failure already observed in production.Exam 4 Q19 (missed)
  • Rewriting a tool's description will stop Claude calling it when tool_choice names it.Once tool_choice names a specific tool, selection is controlled by tool_choice, not the description.Exam 5 (Structured Data Extraction block)
  • tool_choice can fix how an already-executed tool's output is returned.It governs whether and which tool Claude calls next; it has no bearing on the harness's continuation format.Exam 8 (Customer Support block)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q19 (chose a prompt instruction over tool_choice "any"); correct in Exam 5, Exam 7 and Exam 10 appearances. Caveat: the closely-related 'specific tool vs any' distinction has been missed three exams running under its D4 §4.6 framing (Exam 7 Q51, Exam 8 Q17, Exam 10 Q48), so this is not fully safe territory.

Where this was taught

D2 §2.2

Descriptions are the primary selection lever

Recovered

Tool descriptions are what Claude actually reads to choose a tool — when misrouting happens, check descriptions first.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tool selection runs on descriptions, not on names, not on the user's phrasing, and not on any external routing. So when logs show a tool being called for the wrong kind of request 30-45% of the time, the first thing to inspect is whether the two competing descriptions actually distinguish the tools. Two tools each described as 'extracts relevant text from a source' or 'flags an item for review' give the model nothing to discriminate on, and near-identical names make it worse. The fix is to rewrite both descriptions — and rename where the names themselves are near-identical — before you add anything new to the system.

Why it works that way

Every alternative fix (a classifier, a prompt rule, a merge) leaves the bad signal in place and pays for a new component to compensate for it; fixing the signal removes the cause.

Decision rule

Fix the signal before adding a layer that compensates for the bad signal.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rename the tool to something more distinctive but leave the description unchanged.The description is what the model reads to decide; a rename alone adds no boundary information, so the ambiguity in purpose remains.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 7 (Customer Support block)
  • Add a system-prompt rule such as 'always prefer lookup_symbol for code questions.'A blunt always-prefer rule never teaches when each tool applies and misroutes the genuine cases for the other tool entirely.Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Add one few-shot example of the misrouted case being handled correctly.A single example addresses a single case while the description still lacks the boundary statement for every other request of the same shape.Exam 4 Q8 (missed)

Your record on it

Missed twice in one sitting — Exam 4 Q8 and Q47, both description-boundary cases in different scenarios; correct on every appearance since, including Exam 5 (search_web vs the doc-analysis fetch tool), Exam 6 (extract_snippets vs extract_excerpts), Exam 7, Exam 8 (lookup_symbol vs lookup_reference) and Exam 10. Note that Exam 6 also carried a second §2.2 question, Q3, which WAS missed — but on the input-format facet tracked under D2-07, not the description-boundary facet here.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.2 · Exam 4 Q8 · Exam 4 Q47 · Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block) · KD #10

Key Distinction #10

D2 §2.2

What a good tool description must state

Recovered

A description must say what the tool does, what input it accepts (with an example), when to use it over similar tools, and when NOT to use it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Four things belong in every description: purpose (not just a restatement of the name), accepted input formats including ID shapes and a concrete example, when to prefer this tool over a similar one, and the boundary cases where it should not be used at all. Both failure modes on the exam trace to a missing element. A process_refund tool described only as 'processes a refund for a given order' never states the refund-versus-exchange boundary, so the agent issues refunds for exchange requests. The same tool with no stated ID format gets called with the raw digits a customer typed instead of ORD-12345, and 9% of calls fail validation.

Why it works that way

The description is the tool's entire contract with the model — anything you leave out, the model guesses at, and it guesses consistently wrong in the cases you did not anticipate.

Decision rule

For any description-quality question, check the four elements in order — purpose, input format with example, when-to-use, when-NOT-to-use — and pick the option that adds the missing one.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a preprocessing step that silently reformats whatever the agent passes.Silent reformatting masks the description gap and risks quietly converting a genuinely wrong ID into a different, still-wrong, valid-looking one.Exam 6 Q3 (missed)
  • Rename the tool to process_refund_by_order_id so its purpose reads unambiguously.A clearer name disambiguates between tools but says nothing about the expected input format — and format, not tool ambiguity, is what is failing.Exam 6 Q3 (missed)
  • Add a routing classifier that extracts a well-formed ID before the tool is ever called.That is infrastructure compensating for an under-specified description; fix the description first.Exam 6 Q3 (missed)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 6 Q3 (the input-format-and-example facet specifically); the later §2.2 questions in Exam 7, Exam 8 and Exam 10 — including Exam 10's 'input formats, examples and an explicit boundary statement' option — were all answered correctly.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.2 · Exam 6 Q3 · Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)

D2 §2.2

The two non-fixes for tool misrouting

Recovered

Never merge two near-identical tools into one parameterised tool, and never add a pre-routing classifier — both leave the bad description in place.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Two wrong answers show up in almost every misrouting question, and you should be able to reject both on sight. The first is consolidation: merge get_customer and lookup_order into lookup_entity, or flag_ledger_entry and flag_reconciliation_run into flag_item with a scope parameter. This destroys the semantic precision that let the model tell the two cases apart and simply relocates the same ambiguity into a parameter value. The second is a pre-routing classifier that inspects the request and picks the tool before Claude sees either one — new infrastructure layered on top of a signal you could have simply fixed.

Why it works that way

Both options feel like engineering progress while leaving the actual cause untouched, and both add permanent maintenance cost for a problem a description rewrite would have closed.

Decision rule

In a misrouting question, cross out 'merge the tools' and 'add a classifier' first — then choose among what is left.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Merging removes the choice, so there is nothing left to get wrong.It loses the semantic precision that lets a subagent scope its own action; the ambiguity moves into the parameter, it does not disappear.Exam 9 (Code Generation block, unscored), Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • A classifier in front of the agent is a clean separation of concerns.It compensates for an under-specified signal instead of fixing it, and it cements the bad descriptions in place so every tool added later inherits the same problem.Exam 3, Exam 4 Q47, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8 (recurring distractor)
  • A PostToolUse hook can rewrite the wrong tool's call into the right one after the fact.The wrong tool has already fired with the wrong semantics; it patches the symptom rather than why the model chose wrong.Exam 4 Q47 (missed)

Your record on it

Exam 4 Q47 was one of the two §2.2 misses. Every §2.2 question answered correctly since Exam 4 carried at least one of these two distractors, so both have been rejected repeatedly (Exam 5, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 10). One caveat: Exam 6 Q3 was a §2.2 miss and a pre-routing classifier was among its options — EXAM-LOG records the corpus fact the question tested (input format with an example) but not which option was selected, so that instance cannot be counted as a clean rejection either way.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.2 · Exam 4 Q47 · KD #10

Key Distinction #10

D2 §2.3

The four error categories

Recovered

Transient, validation, business, and permission errors each demand a different agent response — only transient ones are retryable.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The exam splits tool errors into four categories. Transient (timeout, service unavailable) is retryable, ideally handled inside the tool or subagent before it ever surfaces. Validation (malformed ID) is not retryable as-is — fix the input and re-call. Business (a policy limit exceeded) is not retryable at all; explain the outcome to the user. Permission (auth failure, access denied) is not retryable either, but the response is different again: escalate or switch credentials. The exam's favourite scenario gives you a tool failing two ways at once — say a monthly cap on one account and an expired carrier credential on another — and asks how to restructure. Returning one generic error for both, or one retryable flag for both, is wrong: two non-retryable categories still need two different agent responses.

Why it works that way

The category is not documentation for humans — it is the input the agent uses to decide between retrying, fixing, explaining, and escalating. Collapse the categories and you collapse the agent's decision-making.

Decision rule

For every tool error, ask 'can a retry ever change this outcome?' — if no, ask which of fix-input, explain-policy, or escalate-credentials applies.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add exponential backoff to every retry so all failures eventually succeed.Backoff helps only the transient case; no amount of retrying resolves a permission denial, so uniform backoff burns retries for nothing.Exam 4 Q52 (missed)
  • Return an error flag for both and let the coordinator decide from the error text.Forcing the agent to guess the failure type from prose is explicitly ranked worse than structured categorisation.Exam 4 Q52 (missed)
  • Return both a compliance lock and an out-of-scope repository as permission errors, since neither is allowed.It collapses two categories the corpus keeps apart — a compliance lock is a business outcome to be explained, and treating it as permission sends the agent chasing credentials no escalation can fix.Exam 9 (Developer Productivity block, unscored)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q52 (conflated a permanent permission failure with a transient timeout); answered correctly in Exam 7 (the reissue_shipping_label business-vs-permission split) and Exam 8.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.3 · Exam 4 Q52 · Exam 7 (Customer Support block) · KD #9

Key Distinction #9

D2 §2.4

Two-tool token-binding for mandatory previews

Recovered

Split the operation into preview_X (returns a single-use confirmation token) and execute_X (requires that token) so skipping the preview becomes architecturally impossible.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When an irreversible operation must always be preceded by a preview, a dry_run: boolean on a single tool is not enough — the agent can simply call it with dry_run=false on the first attempt, and production logs show it does. Replace the single tool with two: preview_remove_member returns the impact details plus a single-use confirmation token, and execute_remove_member requires that token as a parameter. Because the token only exists after a genuine preview of that specific operation, executing without a preview is not merely discouraged, it is impossible. This is a code-level guarantee where every other option is a prompt-level hope.

Why it works that way

For an action that cannot be undone, the difference between 'the agent usually previews first' and 'the agent cannot execute without previewing' is the entire safety property.

Decision rule

For a mandatory-precondition question, pick the option where the precondition's artefact cannot exist unless the precondition actually ran.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a confirm: boolean or a confirmation string like CONFIRM_DELETE that must be supplied.It is just another parameter the agent can supply on the same first call — the same bypassable shape as dry_run, only renamed.Exam 5 Q54 (missed), Exam 6 Q12 (missed)
  • Change the default so the preview runs automatically unless a caller explicitly skips it.A bypassable parameter is still in place; nothing stops a caller overriding it on the first call, exactly as already happens.Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Add a PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook that logs and flags calls made without a prior preview.Logging is detection, not prevention — the unauthorised operation has already executed.Exam 4 Q2 (missed), Exam 6 Q12 (missed)

Your record on it

This project's single most persistent trap: missed three exams running (Exam 4 Q2, Exam 5 Q54, Exam 6 Q12), each time picking a bypassable parameter-level fix. Then answered correctly on BOTH seeded facets in Exam 7 (Q7 fix-selection, Q38 defend-the-pattern), correctly in Exam 8 Q41, and correctly again among Exam 10's ten KD-seeded questions. EXAM-LOG calls it 'durably cleared'.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.4 · Exam 4 Q2 · Exam 5 Q54 · Exam 6 Q12 · Exam 7 Q7 · Exam 7 Q38 · Exam 8 Q41 · KD #12 · KD #11

Key Distinction #12

D2 §2.4

Why token-binding beats every alternative

Recovered

It enforces the precondition inside the tool interface itself — no timing heuristic, no orchestration-layer dialog, no prompt instruction can make the same guarantee.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The exam also asks the defend-the-pattern version of this question, where the two-tool split already exists and a teammate proposes something simpler. Know the ranked alternatives and why each falls short. A server-side timing heuristic that rejects calls arriving too soon after session start is fragile: a fast legitimate call gets blocked and a deliberately delayed bypass slips through. An orchestration-layer confirmation dialog can work but requires separate infrastructure outside the tool contract, and the tool remains callable from another integration path. A prompt instruction with worked examples stays probabilistic no matter how well written. Also know what the benefit is NOT: it is not fewer tool calls, not a smaller tool catalog (the split actually adds a tool), and not a nicer audit trail.

Why it works that way

Being able to say precisely why the guarantee lives in the interface — and not in a layer, a timer, or a prompt — is what separates recognising the pattern from understanding it.

Decision rule

Ask where the guarantee lives — in the tool's own interface (best), in a separate layer (needs infrastructure), in a timer (fragile), or in the prompt (probabilistic).

Traps that have caught you here

  • The dialog and the token pattern guarantee the same outcome, so it is a matter of team preference.They are not equivalent — the dialog needs separate orchestration-layer infrastructure to intercept every call, which the token pattern avoids entirely.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Well-written few-shot examples make single-step prompt compliance as reliable as a structural precondition.This is exactly the misconception the pattern defeats: instructions and examples remain probabilistic, and the agent can still call execute directly.Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • The real benefit is fewer tool calls, or cleaner audit-trail entries.Both designs still take two calls, and audit logging is a side effect — it misidentifies the enforcement mechanism entirely.Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)

Your record on it

The defend-the-pattern framing was answered correctly in Exam 7 Q38 and Exam 8 (cancel_subscription vs a confirmed: boolean), after the three-exam miss streak on the fix-selection framing.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.4 · Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 7 Q38 · Exam 8 (Customer Support block) · KD #11 · KD #12

Key Distinction #11

D2 §2.5

tool_choice "any" guarantees a call, not which tool

Recovered

Use "any" when an agent sometimes replies in prose instead of calling a tool — it forces a structured call while still letting the model pick the right one.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Two scenarios both resolve to "any". First, an extraction or formatting agent that occasionally answers with an explanatory paragraph instead of calling any tool: "any" removes the free-text path entirely. Second, and more subtly, a pipeline with three document-type extraction tools where someone hard-coded tool_choice to one specific tool to guarantee structure — receipts and PO confirmations now come back full of invoice-shaped nulls. "any" keeps the structured-output guarantee while restoring correct per-document selection. The contrast to hold onto: "any" guarantees a call without dictating the tool; a named tool_choice dictates the tool and, applied indiscriminately, dictates the wrong one.

Why it works that way

Choosing between 'guarantee some call' and 'guarantee this call' is the highest-frequency tool_choice decision on the exam, and picking the named form when the situation needs "any" silently produces wrong-but-structured output.

Decision rule

If several tools could each be correct depending on the input, the answer is "any" — never a named tool.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Set tool_choice to auto and add 'you must use a tool' to the prompt.auto permits a plain-text answer and the instruction is probabilistic — the exact failure already being observed.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 4 Q19 (missed), Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Force one specific tool because it is the safest default for most inputs.It blocks the other legitimate choices entirely and runs the wrong extraction schema on every off-type document.Exam 5 (Structured Data Extraction block), Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Wrap the response in a JSON-repair library that reconstructs valid JSON from prose.It patches the symptom after the fact; forcing a tool call removes the free-text response at the source.Exam 2 (unscored)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q19 (chose a prompt instruction over "any"); correct in Exam 5 and Exam 10. Flagged caution: the mirror-image distinction (specific tool vs "any") has been missed three consecutive exams under D4 §4.6 — Exam 7 Q51, Exam 8 Q17, Exam 10 Q48 — which EXAM-LOG names this project's only confirmed-stubborn trap.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.5 · Exam 4 Q19 · Exam 5 (Structured Data Extraction block) · Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block) · EXAM-LOG Insights Round 2

D2 §2.9

Grep searches contents, Glob matches paths

Recovered

Find all callers of a function equals Grep; enumerate all files of a type equals Glob — and the wrong one silently under-counts.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Grep looks inside files for patterns — function names, call sites, imports, error messages. Glob matches file names and paths — **/*.test.tsx, **/*.snap. The exam runs the trap in both directions. Asked to locate every file referencing a deprecated helper, Glob('**/resolveShippingRate*') returns two matches inside the helper's own module and misses eleven call sites elsewhere, because a file that calls the helper need not be named after it. Asked to enumerate every snapshot test file, grepping contents for the word 'snapshot' misses files that never contain the literal word and matches unrelated files that mention it in a comment — that is a Glob job. The failure is quiet in both directions: you get an answer, just an incomplete one.

Why it works that way

The under-count looks like a complete result, so an agent that picks the wrong tool reports confidently and the engineer proceeds on a false all-clear.

Decision rule

Ask whether the target is what a file is named or what a file contains — name equals Glob, contains equals Grep.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Broaden the Glob pattern to catch the missing call sites.A wider path pattern still never looks inside a file — widening does not convert a name match into a content search.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 7 (Code Generation block)
  • A better Grep target string will find the files.When files are identified by naming convention rather than a reliably present internal string, any content search inherits the same mismatch.Exam 5 Q57 (missed)
  • The search tool hit a recursion-depth limit on deeply nested directories.Invents a limit the corpus never documents; the real cause is that Glob never inspects contents at all.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 5 Q57 on its first citable appearance (chose Grep for a file-name enumeration that needed Glob); correct in Exam 4, Exam 7 and Exam 8 Q43, which EXAM-LOG logs as 'KD#26 correct again'. Caveat worth noting: the recovered cases were all the Grep direction — the Glob direction that actually tripped you has not been re-tested since Exam 5.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.9 · Exam 5 Q57 · Exam 7 (Code Generation block) · Exam 8 Q43 · Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block) · KD #26

Key Distinction #26

D2 §2.9

Edit needs a unique anchor; fall back to Read + Write

Recovered

When Edit's anchor text appears more than once it fails — load the file with Read, modify it, and Write it back; never shorten the anchor and never reach for sed.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Edit works by unique text matching. If the anchor appears eleven, fourteen or nineteen times in the file, Edit cannot decide which occurrence to modify and fails. The sanctioned fallback is three steps: Read the full file, modify the content programmatically, Write the updated version. Two tempting wrong moves appear in almost every version of this question. Shortening the anchor — from 'return config;' to 'config', or 'catch (err) {' to 'catch (' — makes it MORE likely to be non-unique, not less, which is the exact inverse of the intuition. And forcing the change with Bash sed bypasses the tool designed for the job and rewrites occurrences that should have been left alone.

Why it works that way

The shorter-anchor intuition is backwards in a way that feels right, which is why the corpus flags it explicitly rather than leaving it to inference.

Decision rule

Edit failed on a non-unique anchor equals Read + Write — never a shorter anchor, never sed.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Retry Edit with a shorter, more generic anchor so it matches more precisely.Shorter strings are more likely to be non-unique — the opposite of what is needed.Exam 4 Q32 (missed), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Use Bash sed to force the replacement, optionally scoped to a line range.It bypasses the purpose-built tool and, as one scenario shows, rewrites two occurrences that should have been left alone; scoping the same bypass does not make it sanctioned.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 9 (unscored)
  • Split the anchor across two Edit calls, using surrounding lines to disambiguate.Edit matches a single anchor string, not a chained sequence of surrounding-line calls — the capability does not exist.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Hand the edit back to the engineer to do manually.Burden-shifting — a reliable Read + Write fallback exists.Exam 2 (unscored)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q32 (the shorter-anchor trap); answered correctly in Exam 6 (transform-utils wrapError, 15 occurrences). Also seeded in the unscored Exams 2 and 9.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.9 · Exam 4 Q32 · Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block) · KD #27

Key Distinction #27

D2 §2.5

Least privilege via constrained alternatives

Not yet tested

When an agent misuses a generic tool, replace it with a constrained one that enforces the boundary at the interface — not a prompt rule or a blocklist.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Each agent should have only the tools its scope requires; broader tools produce scope creep. The corpus's worked example is a document-analysis agent given a generic fetch_url tool, which starts downloading search-engine results pages. The right fix is to replace fetch_url with load_document, which validates that the URL points to a document format — the constraint now lives in the tool's own interface rather than in the model's judgment. Adding a prompt instruction is probabilistic, and blocking known search-engine domains is fragile and not future-proof.

Why it works that way

It is the same lesson as token-binding in a different costume: a boundary enforced by the interface holds; a boundary enforced by instruction or blocklist leaks.

Decision rule

If an agent is using a tool for something outside its role, narrow the tool rather than instructing the agent.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a prompt instruction telling the agent not to fetch search-engine pages.Probabilistic — the agent can still call the generic tool however it likes.corpus (Domain-2_v2 §2.5)
  • Block known search-engine domains at the network level.Fragile and not future-proof; a new domain reopens the hole.corpus (Domain-2_v2 §2.5)

Your record on it

Never appeared as a scored question — no exam in the corpus of nine seeded the fetch_url-to-load_document constrained-alternative facet; the §2.5 questions that were scored covered tool count, scoped cross-role tools, and tool_choice instead.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.5

D2 §2.9

Choosing among the built-in tools

Not yet tested

Glob finds files by name pattern, Grep searches inside contents, Read loads a file, Write creates or fully replaces one, Edit makes a targeted change via a unique text match, and Bash runs shell commands.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Six built-ins, six jobs. Glob for file-path patterns like **/*.test.tsx. Grep for content: function names, error strings, import statements. Read to load a file for analysis. Write to create a file or fully replace its contents. Edit for a targeted modification located by a unique text match. Bash for git, npm, tests and builds. The exam's distractors are usually built from reaching past the purpose-built tool: Bash find where Glob belongs, Bash grep or sed where Grep or Edit belongs, or a shell script where Glob's name-pattern matching already does the job. Note one semantic detail the exam tests: Write replaces the whole file, so writing only a corrected block discards everything else — which is precisely why the Edit fallback is Read plus Write, not Write alone.

Why it works that way

Half of §2.9's questions are decided purely by knowing which tool's job the task actually is; the other half are decided by not shelling out to Bash for a job a built-in already covers.

Decision rule

Name the job first — path pattern, content search, load, create/replace, targeted change, shell command — then take the built-in that owns it and do not reach for Bash.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Shell out to Bash find, sed, or a custom script for file discovery or replacement.It bypasses the tool designed for the job — the corpus's sanctioned tools are Glob for names, Grep for contents, Edit or Read+Write for changes.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 7 (Claude Code CI block)
  • Call Write with just the corrected block, since Write replaces contents.Write fully replaces the file, so writing only a fragment discards the rest — Read must load the full content first.Exam 9 (Code Generation block, unscored)
  • Built-in Grep cannot handle a codebase this large, so Bash grep is needed.It invents a size ceiling the corpus never documents.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

The reference table as a whole has never been a scored question; its individual rows are tested through the Grep-vs-Glob, Edit-fallback and incremental-investigation concepts below, so treat this as orientation rather than a separately-graded item.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.9

D2 §2.9

Trace across wrapper and re-export aliases

Not yet tested

Before searching for a function's callers, collect every exported name it travels under — the original plus each wrapper alias — then search for each one.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When calculateTax is wrapped by utils/tax.ts as getTax and re-exported again from index.ts, grepping only for calculateTax finds some call sites and misses every consumer that imports the wrapper. A rename based on that search breaks production. The strategy has two ordered steps: first identify all exported names by reading the wrapper and re-export modules, then Grep for each name across the codebase. A case-insensitive grep does not help — it is still searching for one name and will never discover a distinct alias. Globbing for tax-named files does not help either, since consumers of getTax need not live in files named after tax.

Why it works that way

Alias-blind searching produces a confident, incomplete list of callers, and the failure only shows up after the rename lands.

Decision rule

Enumerate the names before you search for them — one Grep per exported alias, never one Grep for the original name alone.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Grep the original name case-insensitively to catch stylistic variants.It still searches for one name and never discovers the distinct alias.Exam 2 (unscored)
  • Glob for files whose names reference the topic and assume those are the consumers.Path matching does not reveal what names a file imports; consumers can live anywhere.Exam 2 (unscored)
  • Read the whole repository once to memorise all imports.The bulk-read anti-pattern, and worse, it relies on catching the alias by eye rather than systematically enumerating exported names.Exam 2 (unscored)

Your record on it

Seeded only once, in Exam 2's Developer Productivity block (the calculateTax / getTax stem), generated 2026-07-06 and never attempted — so this concept has never appeared on a scored paper. It shows up twice in the extracted corpus only because Exam 2 exists as both an original and a retrofit file carrying the same questions; do not read that as two independent seedings.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.9 · Exam 2 (unscored)

D2 §2.1

Branch on stop_reason, never on text

Solid

Handle both response shapes structurally: execute tools on stop_reason "tool_use", return the reply to the user on "end_turn".

The full lesson

What is actually true

A harness that assumes every response contains a tool call will break the first time a customer says hello. With tool_choice at its default auto, Claude decides whether a tool is needed — a greeting or a thank-you comes back as plain text with stop_reason: "end_turn". A correct harness branches on that structured field: process the tool_use blocks when stop_reason is "tool_use", and return the text reply when it is "end_turn". You never parse the prose for a marker word, and you never manufacture a stop_reason yourself — stop_reason is returned by Claude, not set by the application.

Why it works that way

stop_reason is the protocol's own control signal; substituting string matching or a forced tool call replaces a reliable structured field with a fragile heuristic.

Decision rule

Any option that reads Claude's natural language to decide control flow is wrong when a structured field carries the same information.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Set tool_choice to "any" so every response is guaranteed to contain a tool call the harness can process.It forces a tool call on greetings where none is appropriate, manufacturing spurious invocations to paper over a harness defect.Exam 10 (Customer Support block)
  • Have Claude begin tool-free replies with a fixed marker word and string-match for it.Response handling belongs on the structured stop_reason field, not on marker text in the reply.Exam 10 (Customer Support block)
  • Switch the response's stop_reason to end_turn once the application detects the case is handled.The application cannot manufacture stop_reason to paper over a step it skipped — Claude returns it.Exam 6 (Customer Support block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 10 (end_turn on greetings) and answered correctly — Exam 10's only two D2 misses were Q4 (§2.3) and Q6 (§2.8).

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.1 · Exam 10 (Customer Support block) · KD #5

Key Distinction #5

D2 §2.1

Every request carries the whole conversation

Solid

The API is stateless — each call must include the full history so far, with the new tool_result appended, not the result alone.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There is no server-side session. When you continue after a tool call, you send the entire conversation to date — including the original tool_use block — with the tool_result appended to it. Sending only the result, in a fresh message, drops all prior context, and Claude responds as though it never asked for the file. There is no expiry on tool_use blocks and no session_id to carry state; the application owns the conversation array.

Why it works that way

Statelessness is the single assumption that makes the whole tool-use loop coherent — every reconstruction bug in the loop traces back to forgetting it.

Decision rule

If an option implies Claude remembers anything between requests, it is wrong — the application resends everything.

Traps that have caught you here

  • tool_use blocks expire after one turn, so a fresh one must be requested before attaching a result.No such expiry exists — it is a fabricated mechanic.Exam 8 (Claude Code CI block)
  • The id match is irrelevant; raise max_tokens on the follow-up call instead.It dismisses id-matching and points at an unrelated parameter; the defect is missing conversation history, not output length.Exam 8 (Claude Code CI block)
  • Put the tool's result into a new system prompt so Claude always sees the current state.The system prompt is for durable instructions, not turn-specific data; it does not fix the missing tool_result block and does not scale to later calls.Exam 8 (Customer Support block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 8 (Claude Code CI block) and answered correctly — Exam 8's only D2 miss was Q11 (§2.8). Worth watching anyway: the same stateless principle was missed in Exam 6 Q5 under its D5 §5.1 / KD #25 framing.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.1 · Exam 8 (Claude Code CI block) · EXAM-LOG Exam 6 Q5 (D5 §5.1 cross-reference)

D2 §2.3

Empty results are success, not errors

Solid

A query that ran and matched nothing is a successful empty result set; only a query that could not run gets isError: true.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Conflating these two corrupts agent behaviour in both directions. Return isError: true for zero matches and the agent retries and escalates a query that worked perfectly. Return an empty list when the database was unreachable and the agent tells the customer 'you have no orders' — a false statement caused by masking an access failure. The correct signalling is precise: search_orders returns {"results": [], "isError": false} when the customer genuinely has none, and isError: true with a category when the query could not execute at all. Do not let the agent infer the difference from response latency or any other proxy — the tool already knows which case it is and must say so.

Why it works that way

'Zero results' and 'timeout' look nearly identical in a response payload and require completely opposite agent responses; this is one of the most explicitly flagged traps in the corpus.

Decision rule

Ask 'did the query execute?' — if yes, it is a success regardless of how many rows came back.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Return isError: true for both and add a prompt rule to retry a few times before believing a customer has no orders.It treats a legitimate answer as a failure and papers over it with a probabilistic retry instruction instead of fixing the signal.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Return an empty list in both cases and let the agent infer reachability from latency.Latency is a fragile proxy, and masking the access failure produces a confidently false answer to the customer.Exam 2 (unscored)
  • Return an empty result set with isError: false for a record that could not be retrieved, so the coordinator moves on.Signalling a failed retrieval as a successful empty result makes the agent report 'no data found' when the data may well exist.Exam 9 (Multi-Agent Research block, unscored)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 5 (query_source_archive empty-vs-unreachable) and answered correctly; Exam 5's three misses were Q35, Q54 and Q57, none of them this question. Also seeded once in Exam 2 (the search_orders stem), which was never attempted — it appears twice in the extracted corpus only because Exam 2 exists as both an original and a retrofit file carrying the same questions.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.3 · Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 2 (unscored) · KD #9

Key Distinction #9

D2 §2.3

Structured error context beats a flag beats prose

Solid

Give the agent failure type, what was attempted, partial results and alternatives — a retryable boolean is second best, and prose the agent must parse is worst.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There is a clear ranking here and the exam tests every rung of it. Best: a structured payload carrying errorCategory, isRetryable, a description, any partialResults, and suggested alternatives — enough for a retry-with-feedback step to construct a genuinely different retry instead of resending the identical failing request. Next: a bare retryable boolean, which tells the agent whether to retry but nothing about what to change. Worst: an isError with only a prose description, forcing the coordinator to keyword-match its way to a retry decision, which breaks the moment the wording changes. Note the one qualifier the corpus adds: a retryable flag is still worse than handling transient errors inside the tool and only surfacing the ones that genuinely need a coordinator decision.

Why it works that way

Structured context is what turns a coordinator from a blind retry loop into something that can decide to retry with a modified query, continue with partial findings, or escalate.

Decision rule

Prefer the option that gives the agent enough to make a different decision, not just a different mood.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Only a boolean isRetryable: true is needed, so the pipeline knows a retry is worth attempting.It says whether to retry, not what to change — so the retry repeats the identical failing request.Exam 10 (Structured Data Extraction block)
  • Keyword-match the returned description text to decide which errors to retry.That is still guessing from prose, merely relocated into the coordinator, and it breaks whenever the wording changes.Exam 9 (Multi-Agent Research block, unscored)
  • Log the failure server-side for a human to review in the morning.An automated in-session retry step needs something to act on right now; a log gives it nothing.Exam 10 (Structured Data Extraction block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 10 (run_document_ocr structured payload) and answered correctly — Exam 10's D2 misses were Q4 (§2.3 business errors) and Q6 (§2.8), not this question.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.3 · Exam 10 (Structured Data Extraction block) · KD #8

Key Distinction #8

D2 §2.3

Handle errors at the right level

Solid

Retry transient failures inside the tool, recover locally inside the subagent, and surface to the agent only what needs a decision it alone can make — never return success with error metadata.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Error handling is layered. Inside the tool, retry transient failures with backoff before surfacing anything. Inside a subagent, recover locally where you can and propagate to the coordinator only what you could not resolve — along with partial results and what was attempted. Return an error to the agent only when the decision genuinely belongs to it: skip, retry with different parameters, or escalate. And there is one absolute prohibition: never return success with error metadata embedded in the payload, because that masks the failure entirely — the agent believes the operation succeeded when it did not.

Why it works that way

Pushing every failure up to the coordinator floods it with noise it cannot use, while swallowing failures silently corrupts everything downstream — the level you handle at determines whether the system stays diagnosable.

Decision rule

Push a failure up only if the layer above can do something the current layer cannot — and never disguise a failure as a success to keep the pipeline moving.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Silently cap the value at the policy limit and resubmit on the agent's behalf.It hides a real business-rule outcome behind an apparent success, masking the decision from the agent and from whoever must explain it later.Exam 3 (Structured Data Extraction block, unscored)
  • Retry internally up to five times without surfacing any diagnostic detail.Retrying a problem the tool cannot fix just repeats it, and still leaves the pipeline with nothing specific when the attempts run out.Exam 10 (Structured Data Extraction block)
  • Escalate to a human on the first rejection without returning any details to the subagent.It skips the structured-response mechanism that would have let the subagent resolve the situation itself.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)

Your record on it

The 'silently return success' and 'escalate everything' distractors have been correctly rejected in every scored §2.3 question through Exam 8 (Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8); no scored miss traces to this facet. §2.3 did produce a miss afterwards — Exam 10 Q4 — but EXAM-LOG assigns it to the business-error-vs-tool-failure facet (D2-10), and the fake-success option was one of that question's rejected distractors rather than the fact being tested. Treat this as solid but not independently re-confirmed since Exam 8, given the Professor's Note for Exam 11 biases §2.3 upward.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.3 · Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 10 (Structured Data Extraction block) · KD #8

Key Distinction #8

D2 §2.5

Too many tools degrades selection reliability

Solid

Tool count itself is a root cause — restrict each agent to the 4-5 tools its role needs, rather than describing 18 tools better.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The official guide's own numbers are 18 tools instead of 4-5. Each additional tool is one more candidate the model must discriminate between on every turn, producing more overlap, more near-miss descriptions, and more misrouting. The exam scenario usually takes the retrospective shape: a subagent that once selected correctly among 5 role-scoped tools has accreted a dozen convenience tools over several sprints and now picks wrong 20-25% of the time, while a peer subagent still at 5 tools selects correctly. The fix is to restrict the subagent back to the tools core to its role and move the rest to the agents or workflow stages where they belong. Watch for the prospective variant too — a product manager proposing to fold 13 more tools into a 5-tool subagent 'so it can handle anything in one place'. Nothing has failed yet, so the answer is to recommend against the expansion on the same tool-count reasoning, not to wait for the misrouting to show up.

Why it works that way

This is the one case where better descriptions are explicitly NOT the answer — the corpus names tool count as the root cause and says to reduce the decision space first.

Decision rule

When an agent's tool count has grown well past ~5, shrink the set before touching the descriptions.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Keep all the tools but write substantially more detailed descriptions for each.Descriptions help at the margin, but tool count is the named root cause here — description tuning does not reduce the number of near-miss candidates.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)
  • Give every agent the full catalog for flexibility, or extend the expanded catalog to a second subagent for consistency.Agents with tools outside their specialisation tend to misuse them; spreading the catalog spreads the reliability problem.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)
  • Add a routing classifier that pre-selects the likely tool before the subagent's turn.Infrastructure layered on top of an inflated tool set — it never reduces the subagent's actual selection burden.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 6 (14-tool web-search subagent) and Exam 8 (a proposal to expand a 5-tool subagent to 18), correct both times; neither appears in those exams' miss lists.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.5 · Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 8 (Customer Support block) · Exam 3 (unscored)

D2 §2.5

Scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs

Solid

Strict role scoping has one sanctioned exception: a narrowly scoped cross-role tool for a simple, high-frequency need, with complex cases still routing through the coordinator.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A synthesis agent that constantly needs to confirm individual facts, or a documentation subagent that keeps checking the current lint rule, would otherwise force a full round-trip through the coordinator on nearly every turn. The sanctioned answer is to give it a narrow tool — verify_fact, check_lint_rule, check_loyalty_tier — scoped to simple lookups only, while complex questions still route back through the coordinator to the specialist subagent. Note what is being traded: not scoping for convenience, but a narrow slice of cross-role capability in exchange for removing round-trips on a genuinely high-frequency simple need.

Why it works that way

It is the one place the corpus permits crossing role boundaries, and knowing the exception exists is what stops you defaulting to either extreme — full cross-role access or unconditional coordinator round-trips.

Decision rule

High frequency plus simple lookup equals a narrowly scoped cross-role tool; low frequency or complex equals coordinator round-trip.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Give the agent the specialist subagent's full tool set so it can handle any question itself.Cross-specialisation misuse — it starts doing open-ended work well outside its role, exactly what scoped tools prevent.Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 6 (Customer Support block)
  • Route every check through the coordinator regardless of frequency, to keep scope strictly separated.Correctly scoped but ignores the problem: the round-trip overhead on a high-frequency simple need is precisely what the exception exists to eliminate.Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 6 (Customer Support block)
  • Merge the two subagents since they interact so frequently.It collapses the separation of responsibilities the split was designed to create, for a benefit a scoped tool already delivers.Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 5 (documentation subagent's check_lint_rule) and Exam 6 (returns subagent's check_loyalty_tier), answered correctly both times — neither appears in those exams' miss lists.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.5 · Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 6 (Customer Support block)

D2 §2.5

The forced-first-step pattern

Solid

Force the specific tool on the one turn that must be guaranteed, then relax tool_choice back to auto — leaving it forced blocks every later step.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a pipeline must always extract metadata (or classify a document) before any enrichment tool runs, and a prompt instruction is only followed 88-90% of the time, set tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request. That guarantees the required first step deterministically. Then relax tool_choice back to "auto" (or "any") for the follow-up turns so the rest of the workflow can proceed. The two symmetrical failure modes are both on the exam: leaving it at auto with a stronger prompt gives you no guarantee, and leaving it forced on every turn means the model calls the metadata tool over and over and never reaches the analysis tools at all. The same mechanism appears in a second costume that is easy to miss: a compliance rule requiring that the moment a customer asks for a manager, the very next turn must call escalate_to_human. That is not the first turn of anything — it is a triggered turn mid-conversation — but the answer is identical, force {"type": "tool", "name": "escalate_to_human"} for that turn only and relax immediately after. Read the pattern as force-the-guaranteed-turn, not literally force-turn-one.

Why it works that way

Execution order is a sequencing guarantee, and tool_choice is the only lever that provides it — but the guarantee is scoped to the turn you apply it on, which is exactly what the second failure mode forgets.

Decision rule

Force the named tool on exactly the turn that must be guaranteed, relax immediately after — a forced tool_choice that never relaxes is always a wrong answer.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Set tool_choice to "any" for the whole session so a tool is always called."any" guarantees some tool call but not which one — the model can satisfy it by calling an analysis tool first, losing the ordering guarantee.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 9 (unscored)
  • Strengthen the prompt with more emphasis and repetition.Repetition does not turn a probabilistic instruction into a guarantee; the compliance gap already observed is the whole reason to reach for configuration.Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Leave the tool forced for every turn of the workflow.The model can then never call the enrichment or analysis tools at all — production logs show it calling the metadata tool repeatedly forever.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 9 (unscored)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 7 (extract_source_metadata forced first, then relaxed) and answered correctly within Exam 7's perfect 11/11 D2 score, and in Exam 4 (escalate_to_human forced for one triggered turn, cited to §2.1) — Exam 4's D2 misses were Q2, Q8, Q19, Q32, Q47 and Q52, so that one was correct even in D2's worst sitting. Also seeded in Exam 3 and Exam 9, both of which remain unattempted.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.5 · Domain-2_v2 §2.1 · Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 4 (Customer Support block) · Exam 3 (unscored) · Exam 9 (unscored) · KD #11

Key Distinction #11

D2 §2.6

The three MCP primitives

Solid

Tools are actions Claude calls, resources are read-only data Claude can access, and prompts are reusable templates.

The full lesson

What is actually true

MCP exposes exactly three primitive categories, and the exam tests whether you can assign a real system's pieces to the right one. Actions that change state — issuing a refund, escalating a case — are tools; think API endpoints. Read-only reference material the agent only ever consults — a policy document set, a schema, an issue catalog — are resources; think files or databases. Reusable instruction templates, like a standard escalation summary, are prompts. Wrapping everything as tools for a uniform interface collapses the action/data distinction and pays a tool-call round-trip for data that could simply be read; exposing state-changing actions as resources is impossible, since resources are read-only by definition.

Why it works that way

The mapping is the vocabulary the rest of §2.6 is written in — the resources-as-catalogs lesson only makes sense once you know a resource is readable data rather than a callable action.

Decision rule

Does it change state or compute a per-input answer? Tool. Is it a static body of readable data? Resource. Is it instruction text you reuse? Prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Define all three as tools so the agent has one uniform interface.It adds a tool-call round-trip for what should simply be readable data and collapses the protocol's action/data distinction.Exam 10 (Customer Support block)
  • Documents are prompts and templates are resources.It swaps the categories: prompts are reusable instruction templates, resources are the read-only data primitive.Exam 10 (Customer Support block)
  • Expose a per-item validation lookup as a resource because it is reference data.Resources are read-only catalogs the agent browses; a lookup that takes an input and returns a result is an action, so it is a tool.Exam 6 (Structured Data Extraction block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 10 (assigning refund actions, a policy document set, and an escalation template to the three primitives) and answered correctly.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Exam 10 (Customer Support block) · Exam 6 (Structured Data Extraction block)

D2 §2.6

All configured servers load at connection time

Solid

Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and are available to the agent simultaneously — no merging, activation, or per-turn server selection.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Connect three MCP servers — a news archive, a patent database, a regulatory-filing index — and the agent sees all of their tools at once. There is no orchestration code needed to merge tool lists, no list_servers call to activate the others, no single-server-at-a-time restriction, and no rule that only the first server in .mcp.json is live. The exam builds distractors here entirely out of fabricated mechanics, so recognising that they are fabricated is the skill being tested.

Why it works that way

Believing a limitation that does not exist leads teams to build orchestration code for a problem the protocol already solved — and on the exam, fabricated mechanics are almost always the wrong answer.

Decision rule

If an option invents a per-server activation or ordering rule, it is fabricated — reject it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Tools are available one server at a time and the agent must say which server to query.No such restriction exists in MCP.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • The agent must call a list_servers tool each session to activate the other servers.A fabricated mechanism — no such activation call is part of MCP's documented behaviour.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Only the server listed first in .mcp.json is available unless the others are re-authorised.Listing order does not gate availability; all configured servers' tools load together.Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)

Your record on it

Tested once, in Exam 6 (three servers wired to the web-search subagent), and answered correctly — Exam 6's four D2 misses were Q2, Q3, Q12 and Q24.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Exam 6 (Multi-Agent Research block)

D2 §2.6

.mcp.json vs ~/.claude.json, and ${VAR} substitution

Solid

Shared team servers go in project-root .mcp.json with ${VAR} env-var substitution for per-developer credentials; personal and experimental servers go in user-scoped ~/.claude.json.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The classic pattern: a team shares an MCP server but each developer holds their own token. Put the server in .mcp.json at the project root — version-controlled, identical for everyone on clone — and express the credential as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} or ${SUPPORT_TOKEN}, documenting the variable in the README. At runtime the variable is substituted from the environment, so the config is shared while no credential ever enters the repository. The rule also runs the other way: a server one engineer is personally evaluating, that no teammate uses, belongs in their own ~/.claude.json, not in shared project config. When per-researcher ~/.claude.json entries produce onboarding delays and stale endpoints, that is the symptom of a shared server wrongly placed in user scope.

Why it works that way

Scope choice determines whether tooling stays consistent across a team or drifts per developer, and env-var substitution is what makes the version-controlled option safe.

Decision rule

Shared and version-controlled equals .mcp.json; personal, experimental or credential-bearing equals user scope or ${VAR} — never a committed secret.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Each developer adds the shared server in their own ~/.claude.json with their token hard-coded.It produces inconsistent, unshared tooling — the opposite of the version-controlled config the team wants; user scope is for personal overrides.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 9 (unscored)
  • Commit .mcp.json with a placeholder (or one person's) token for people to edit locally.Committing any token, placeholder or real, is a security risk and invites accidental credential commits — env-var substitution exists precisely to avoid it.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Keep a personal experimental server in .mcp.json behind an ${EXPERIMENTAL} gate, or with a comment saying it is not team-approved.The scope itself is the problem, not the absence of a toggle or a note — the server still loads for every teammate.Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Store the token in CLAUDE.md so it loads with the shared tool descriptions.CLAUDE.md is loaded instructional context, not a credential store; it leaks the token into version control and misuses the memory file.Exam 2 (unscored)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 5 (shared market-data server with per-researcher keys) and Exam 10 (a personal experimental server wrongly committed to project config), answered correctly both times. Also seeded in the unscored Exams 2 and 9.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Exam 5 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 9 (unscored) · KD #2

Key Distinction #2

D2 §2.6

MCP resources as content catalogs

Solid

Expose a catalog — issue summaries, category indexes, schemas — as a resource so the agent reads a map of what exists instead of burning tool calls guessing.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The symptom is always the same: telemetry shows the agent spending four to eight tool calls per session issuing guessed search queries just to discover what categories, components or filings even exist, before it can search productively. The fix is to expose that index as an MCP resource. A resource gives the agent an immediate readable map of available data with no exploratory tool call and no LLM round-trip, and because resources are requested on demand it stays current. Contrast the two near-miss answers: a list_everything tool still costs an LLM call and depends on the agent remembering to invoke it first, and pasting the catalog into the system prompt or CLAUDE.md bloats every request and goes stale as the data changes.

Why it works that way

This is the clearest case in D2 where the right answer is a different MCP primitive rather than a better tool — the exploratory-call overhead disappears because reading a resource is not a tool call at all.

Decision rule

If the agent is burning calls to find out what exists, the answer is a resource — not another tool and not a prompt dump.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a list_all_X tool the agent must remember to call before searching.It still costs an LLM call and relies on the agent thinking to use it — a resource provides the same map as readable context without either dependency.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 4 (Claude Code CI block), Exam 7 (Code Generation block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)
  • Paste the full catalog into the system prompt or CLAUDE.md so it is always in context.A static dump bloats context on every turn regardless of need and goes stale; resources are requested on demand.Exam 3 (unscored), Exam 7 (Code Generation block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)
  • Build a custom server or a predictive classifier to solve the discovery problem.Infrastructure overkill for something exposing an existing index as a resource already solves, with nothing new to train or maintain.Exam 4 (Claude Code CI block), Exam 8 (Customer Support block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 4 (finding-category index), Exam 7 (component catalog) and Exam 8 (policy-category index) and answered correctly every time — none appears in those exams' miss lists.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Exam 4 (Claude Code CI block) · Exam 7 (Code Generation block) · Exam 8 (Customer Support block)

D2 §2.6

Community servers vs custom servers

Solid

Adopt existing community MCP servers for standard integrations; build custom servers only for workflows unique to your team.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a well-maintained community MCP server already wraps the exact integration you need — Jira, GitHub, Slack, a national business registry, the Federal Register — use it. Building your own 'for full control' reinvents a maintained standard integration and spends engineering effort where it is not needed. Reserve custom server development for the workflows genuinely specific to your team that no existing server covers. Note the variants the exam also rejects: pre-committing to a rebuild next quarter regardless of whether gaps appear, running both servers in parallel for failover, and bypassing MCP altogether to hit the raw API.

Why it works that way

Custom-server effort is a scarce resource; spending it on a solved integration means the unique workflows that actually need it never get built.

Decision rule

Standard integration plus a maintained community server equals adopt; unique team workflow equals build.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Full control over a widely-used integration justifies the build.'Full control' is the documented anti-pattern rationale for exactly this situation — it reinvents a maintained standard integration.Exam 6 (Structured Data Extraction block), Exam 8 (Structured Data Extraction block)
  • Use the community server now but budget a custom rebuild next quarter regardless.It repeats the same reinvention on a delay, with no evidence the community server actually falls short.Exam 3 (unscored)
  • Run both servers in parallel for failover, or call the raw API directly instead.Parallel servers double the maintenance for overlapping integrations; bypassing MCP discards the standardised tool/resource interface the rest of the architecture depends on.Exam 8 (Structured Data Extraction block), Exam 3 (unscored)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 6 (national business registry) and Exam 8 (international jurisdiction registry) and answered correctly both times.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Exam 6 (Structured Data Extraction block) · Exam 8 (Structured Data Extraction block) · Exam 3 (unscored)

D2 §2.6

MCP tools must out-describe familiar built-ins

Solid

When the agent keeps reaching for Grep or Bash instead of a more capable MCP tool, enhance the MCP tool's description — do not remove the built-in.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tool selection runs on descriptions, and built-in tools are familiar, so an MCP tool described only as 'Searches the codebase' or 'Returns test information' loses to Grep or Bash even when it offers semantic, index-backed, or typed call-graph capability the built-in cannot match. The fix is to rewrite the MCP tool's description to spell out what it uniquely does, what inputs it takes, what outputs it returns, and specifically what built-in tools cannot provide. Do not disable or remove Grep — that breaks legitimate literal-search cases and leaves the under-specified description untouched.
