And do not add a blanket 'always prefer MCP tools' rule, which is blunt, keyword-sensitive, and misroutes the cases where the built-in genuinely is right.

Why it works that way

It is §2.2's fix-the-signal rule applied to a new pair of competitors, and it is the one place where 'remove the competing tool' looks tempting and is explicitly wrong.

Decision rule

Fix the signal before adding a layer — or removing a tool — to compensate for the bad signal.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Remove or disable Grep (or Bash) so the agent has no alternative.It breaks legitimate content-search or full-suite cases; the root cause is an under-specified description, not the built-in's existence.Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 9 (unscored), Exam 10 (Code Generation block)
  • Add a system-prompt rule to always prefer MCP tools.Blunt and keyword-sensitive; it misroutes cases where the built-in is genuinely correct and still tells the model nothing about what the MCP tool does.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 10 (Code Generation block)
  • Add a pre-routing classifier, or replace the server with a differently-named one offering the same capability.Both leave the defective description in place — the description is what drives selection either way.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 6 (call-graph MCP server losing to Grep) and Exam 10 (semantic code search losing to Grep, a KD#29-seeded question), correct both times; EXAM-LOG records all ten KD-seeded questions in Exam 10 as correct.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.6 · Domain-2_v2 §2.9 · Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 10 (Code Generation block) · KD #29

Key Distinction #29

D2 §2.7

Hooks are deterministic, prompts are probabilistic

Solid

For anything safety- or cost-critical, a hook fires regardless of what the model decides; a system-prompt instruction is a hope with a compliance rate.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the governing distinction of §2.7 and it decides most of its questions before you look at the specifics. Hooks are deterministic code that runs around tool calls, intercepting tool interactions without relying on the LLM. System-prompt instructions, few-shot examples, stronger wording, bolder thresholds and self-reported counts are all probabilistic — and the exam always tells you the exact failure rate the prompt-only version is already producing (3%, 4%, 6%, 8%). Once a rule is stated as a hard requirement — must never exceed, must always carry, must route to sign-off — the answer is a hook.

Why it works that way

The scenario has already run the experiment for you: the prompt version is in production and leaking. Any option that strengthens the prompt is proposing more of what is already failing.

Decision rule

If the scenario states a compliance percentage, the fix is never a better prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Reword the instruction with bolder, more explicit threshold language.Still prompt-only enforcement, already shown failing at the stated rate — stronger wording adds no enforcement.Exam 4 (Customer Support block), Exam 6 (Customer Support block), Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Add few-shot examples of the agent pausing correctly at the threshold.More prompt guidance, not a deterministic block — it cannot guarantee the threshold is never crossed.Exam 4 (Customer Support block), Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Have the model self-report and self-enforce its own running count.Probabilistic and unverifiable — the same unreliable self-governance the corpus rejects in favour of deterministic gates.Exam 3 (unscored)

Your record on it

Every scored §2.7 question — Exam 4 ($1,000 refund sign-off), Exam 5 (50-file threshold), Exam 6 (bulk-refund threshold), Exam 7 and Exam 8 (normalization), Exam 10 (citation-purge threshold) — was answered correctly; no §2.7 miss appears in any EXAM-LOG traps list.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.7 · Exam 4 (Customer Support block) · Exam 6 (Customer Support block) · Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block) · KD #11

Key Distinction #11

D2 §2.7

PostToolUse for central output normalization

Solid

When tools you cannot all modify return mismatched formats, normalize them centrally in a PostToolUse hook — not in wrappers, not in a normalize tool, not in the prompt.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The scenario always mixes formats across sources: Unix epoch timestamps from one tool, ISO 8601 from another, numeric status codes from a third-party build tool you cannot change; or reliability scores as a 0-1 float, a 1-100 integer, and an A-F letter grade. A PostToolUse hook fires after each tool returns and normalizes all of them centrally — one point of control, working even for third-party tools, with no LLM call and no reliance on interpretation. The three rejected alternatives each fail a specific way: modifying the tools you own plus wrappers for the ones you do not fragments maintenance across code paths; a normalize_data tool the agent must remember to call adds an LLM round-trip and probabilistic compliance; documenting the formats in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md relies on the model converting correctly every single time.

Why it works that way

Normalization is a mechanical transformation with no judgment in it — putting it anywhere the model has to participate reintroduces variance into something that should have none.

Decision rule

Mismatched output formats from sources you cannot all modify equals PostToolUse, every time.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Modify the tools you control and write wrappers for the third-party one.Fragments the normalization logic across several places — exactly the maintenance problem a central hook avoids.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Add a normalize_data tool and instruct the agent to call it after every retrieval.Adds an LLM call each time and depends on the model remembering; the hook needs no model cooperation.Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block), Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Document each format in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md and let Claude convert.Relies on correct interpretation on every call — probabilistic, and already failing.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 7 (mismatched reliability scales) and Exam 8 (owner field in three formats), answered correctly both times; also seeded once in the unscored Exam 2 (the git_blame / pr_metadata / build-status stem, which appears twice in the extracted corpus only because Exam 2 exists as both an original and a retrofit file).

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.7 · Exam 7 (Multi-Agent Research block) · Exam 8 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 2 (unscored)

D2 §2.7

PreToolUse for thresholds and parameter validation

Solid

PreToolUse fires before execution — it is the only hook that can validate, block or modify a call; PostToolUse can only clean up afterwards.

The full lesson

What is actually true

PreToolUse is the hook for anything that must not happen: blocking a bulk deletion above 50 records, a refund above $1,000 without prior escalation, a purge affecting more than 25 sources, an Edit or Write touching more than 50 files, or a retrieval call missing a required date-range parameter. It fires before the tool executes and routes the call to escalation instead. PostToolUse cannot substitute: by the time it sees the result, the refund has been issued, the account closed, or the out-of-window records already retrieved. Logging a violation for later audit is detection, not prevention — and the exam consistently offers it as the near-miss answer.

Why it works that way

Pre versus Post is a question about timing, and timing is the whole enforcement property — a hook that runs after an irreversible action can never make that action conditional.

Decision rule

If the requirement is 'this must not execute', it is PreToolUse; if it is 'clean up what came back', it is PostToolUse.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a PostToolUse hook that logs threshold breaches for later review.It fires after the tool already executed — logging documents a violation that has already happened.Exam 4 (Customer Support block), Exam 6 (Customer Support block), Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)
  • Use a PostToolUse hook to discard results from non-compliant calls.The non-compliant retrieval has already run; §2.7 scopes PostToolUse to transforming, logging and normalizing output, not to preventing a call.Exam 9 (Multi-Agent Research block, unscored)
  • Add a confirm_bulk_change: boolean the automation must set before large edits.A parameter the caller sets itself is bypassable the same way dry_run=false is — nothing forces it to be set correctly.Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 4 (refund sign-off), Exam 5 (50-file threshold), Exam 6 (bulk refund threshold) and Exam 10 (citation purge), correct on all four; the PostToolUse-logging near-miss was rejected each time.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.7 · Exam 4 (Customer Support block) · Exam 5 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 6 (Customer Support block) · Exam 10 (Multi-Agent Research block)

D2 §2.9

Investigate incrementally: Grep, then Read, then repeat

Solid

Build codebase understanding by grepping for entry points, reading what surfaces, grepping for usages, and reading consumers — never by reading everything upfront.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The loop is: Grep to find an entry point (a definition or export), Read that file, Grep for its usages (imports, call sites), Read the consumers and follow the imports, and repeat until the picture is complete. Discovery is driven by content search, followed by targeted reads. The exam treats reading everything upfront 'to get full context' as the anti-pattern, and it names the disguised versions too: globbing the whole tree and reading every match before searching is the same anti-pattern routed through a different tool, and concatenating every file into one buffer via Bash is bulk reading with extra steps. Note the specific harm the scenarios show — it is not only wasted context, it is conflation: reading all 60 files under order/ makes the agent blend the cancellation flow with an unrelated returns flow living in the same directory.

Why it works that way

A bigger context window does not fix this. The problem is that most of the files are irrelevant to the trace, not that they do not fit — and irrelevant files actively degrade the answer, not just the budget.

Decision rule

Start with a content search, read only what it surfaces, and expand outward — any option that reads first and searches later is wrong.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Request a larger context window so all the files fit.The agent still reads irrelevant files and still risks conflating unrelated flows; the fix is targeted discovery, not more room.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block)
  • Glob the subtree and Read every match before doing any content search.Explicitly the same anti-pattern as bulk reading — discovery should be driven by content search first.Exam 2 (unscored), Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 7 (Claude Code CI block)
  • Parallelize the bulk read across agent instances, or have a teammate pre-triage the files.Parallelizing does not address why the strategy was wrong, and manual pre-filtering is not the sanctioned strategy and does not scale.Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block), Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block)

Your record on it

Tested in Exam 4 (order-cancellation trace), Exam 6 (duplicate-suppression flag across 85 files) and Exam 7 (unguarded null pattern across a 40-file service), answered correctly all three times.

Where this was taught

Domain-2_v2 §2.9 · Exam 4 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 6 (Developer Productivity block) · Exam 7 (Claude Code CI block) · KD #28

Key Distinction #28

Domain 3 · 20% of the exam · 12 of 60 questions

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

D3 is about how you shape Claude Code's behaviour through files on disk and flags on the command line, rather than through what you type into the prompt each time. You learn where instructions live (CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/, .claude/skills/, .claude/commands/), which scope shares them with the team and which keeps them personal, when to plan before executing, how to converge on correct output through iteration instead of blind re-prompting, and how to run Claude Code unattended in a pipeline with structured, parseable output. The through-line is that a configuration-level or structural mechanism beats a prompt-level request every time: if the fix can be a file, a glob, or a flag, it should not be a sentence you retype each session. Twelve of the sixty exam questions come from here, and most of them are 'which mechanism is the right one for this situation' rather than 'what does this flag do'.

40 concepts59/72 lifetime (82%)

Recall check — D3

Answer out loud before you open each one. Retrieval is what moves a concept from recognised to owned.

  1. A tempting answer says A directory-level CLAUDE.md takes precedence and replaces the root file's criteria for work in that directory.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: All discovered CLAUDE.md files load together from root down to the working directory — a lower-level file never replaces a higher-level one.

    Why the tempting answer fails: The files are concatenated, not overridden; both sets of instructions load together.

  2. A tempting answer says Imports only resolve inside the same directory as the referencing file.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: `@` sits immediately before the path, relative paths resolve against the file containing the import, both relative and absolute paths work, and nesting is capped at 5 levels.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Fabricated — relative paths resolve against the importing file, which supports cross-directory references.

  3. A tempting answer says Re-state the instruction louder in the prompt each session.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: When Claude follows a rule in some sessions but not others, run `/memory` to see which memory files actually loaded before changing anything.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Treats the symptom; the corpus explicitly rejects it in favour of checking what is actually loaded.

D3 §3.1

CLAUDE.md files concatenate, they do not override

Still open

All discovered CLAUDE.md files load together from root down to the working directory — a lower-level file never replaces a higher-level one.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Claude Code discovers CLAUDE.md at several levels — user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project root, and any subdirectory you are working in — and concatenates them all into context in load order. Every discovered file contributes its instructions; none of them silently wins over another. That means if a subdirectory file says one thing and the root file says the opposite, Claude sees both, and the only real fix is to edit the files so they agree. There is no documented override-precedence mechanism between CLAUDE.md levels, so any answer that turns on 'the closer file takes precedence' is wrong.

Why it works that way

If you believe in override precedence you will diagnose configuration bugs by deleting the 'winning' file, which removes instructions you still need and never explains the actual behaviour. Concatenation means conflicts are an authoring problem, not a resolution-order problem.

Decision rule

If two CLAUDE.md levels conflict, fix it by editing the files — never by assuming one level wins.

Traps that have caught you here

  • A directory-level CLAUDE.md takes precedence and replaces the root file's criteria for work in that directory.The files are concatenated, not overridden; both sets of instructions load together.Exam 4 Q46 (missed); Exam 8 Q12 distractor; Exam 9 Q1 distractor
  • Only the root CLAUDE.md loads in CI; subdirectory files are a local-development-only feature.Fabricated restriction — `-p` mode discovers the same hierarchy as an interactive session.Exam 4 Q46
  • Whichever file was modified more recently in git history wins for that run.No such mechanism exists; the documented model is concatenation by directory level.Exam 4 Q46

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q46, the only scored question whose correct answer is this fact (EXAM-LOG Exam 4 traps-missed list: 'root and subdirectory CLAUDE.md concatenate; neither overrides the other'). It has appeared since only as a distractor (Exam 8 Q12, Exam 9 Q1 — and Exam 9 is unscored), so there is no clean re-test showing recovery.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.1 · Exam 4 Q46

D3 §3.1

@import path rules and the depth-5 limit

Still open

`@` sits immediately before the path, relative paths resolve against the file containing the import, both relative and absolute paths work, and nesting is capped at 5 levels.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Four mechanical facts decide most @import questions. The `@` goes immediately before the path with no space. Both relative and absolute paths are supported. A relative path resolves relative to the file that contains the import — so `@standards/x.md` written inside `services/booking/CLAUDE.md` points at `services/booking/standards/x.md`, not at the repository root. And the maximum import nesting depth is 5, so a chain that goes six levels deep silently drops the deepest file. When an import appears not to load, check these in order: does the relative path resolve from the importing file, and is the chain deeper than five?

Why it works that way

These are the failure modes where a configuration looks correct in review but never actually loads — the import line is present and well-formed, yet the content it points at was never pulled in. Nothing in the syntax tells you which of the two causes applied, so you have to check both deliberately.

Decision rule

An import that does not load: check relative-path resolution first (it resolves from the importing file), then chain depth against the limit of 5.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Imports only resolve inside the same directory as the referencing file.Fabricated — relative paths resolve against the importing file, which supports cross-directory references.Exam 4 Q22 (missed)
  • Only the root CLAUDE.md's direct imports load; nested imports are ignored entirely.Fabricated — the actual limit is a numeric depth of 5, which presupposes nested imports do load up to that depth.Exam 4 Q22 (missed)
  • @import requires absolute paths, so relative ones are silently skipped.Both relative and absolute paths are supported.Exam 4 Q22 (missed); Exam 9 Q1 distractor
  • A single one-level import that fails must have blown the depth-5 limit.Right fact, wrong application — one import from one file cannot exceed a five-level cap.Exam 9 Q1 (unscored)

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q22 (the depth-5 fact). Since then the fact has appeared only as a distractor in Exam 9 Q1, which was never attempted, so there is no scored re-test showing recovery.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.1 · Exam 4 Q22 · Exam 9 Q1

D3 §3.11

Universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md; procedures become Skills

Still open

CLAUDE.md loads every session, so keep universal standards there and move every occasional-use procedure into a Skill — including the second one you were tempted to leave inline.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a CLAUDE.md grows to 400+ lines mixing coding standards with a quarterly-close checklist, a deploy-hotfix runbook, and an incident-postmortem template, the split is by trigger, not by size. Universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md because they must apply to every session automatically. Workflow-specific guidance moves to Skills, which load on demand when someone actually runs that workflow. Two failure directions to reject: moving *everything* to Skills means universal standards now need explicit invocation each session, and moving only *some* of the occasional-use procedures is a half-measure that still clutters every session with content only a handful of sessions need. Watch for the half-move framing in particular — 'move the longer one first and capture most of the savings', or 'a partial move is safer to review'. Both rationalise leaving the exact defect the proposal was meant to fix.

Why it works that way

Every line in CLAUDE.md is paid for in every session. A partial cleanup keeps paying that cost while feeling like progress.

Decision rule

Must apply every session → CLAUDE.md. Applies only when a specific workflow runs → a Skill. Move all of them, not some of them.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Move just one of the two occasional procedures out and leave the other inline to limit scope.The remaining procedure still loads in every session for content only a few sessions need — the defect is unchanged.Exam 10 Q27 (missed)
  • Move everything, universal conventions included, into Skills so nothing loads unless invoked.Universal standards would need explicit invocation every session, so conventions that must always apply stop being unconditional.Exam 3 Q25 (unscored), Exam 5 Q58, Exam 6 Q56, Exam 7 Q22, Exam 10 Q27, Exam 9 Q6 (unscored)
  • Move the content to .claude/rules/ scoped by file glob instead.Rules are path-scoped, not workflow-scoped — a quarterly close or an incident runbook is tied to an occasion, not a file pattern.Exam 5 Q58, Exam 6 Q56, Exam 9 Q6 (unscored)
  • Leave it in one file but add bold headings so engineers can skip to the relevant part.Better formatting does not change what loads into context; the token cost persists.Exam 3 Q34 (unscored), Exam 5 Q58
  • Delete the rarely-used checklist and rely on institutional memory.Discards real guidance instead of relocating it — a genuine capability loss.Exam 6 Q56, Exam 7 Q22

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q58, Exam 6 Q56 and Exam 7 Q22, but missed on Exam 10 Q27 — the half-move variant, and the only miss of this specific facet. EXAM-LOG counts §3.11 as 2-for-2 missed at section level (Exam 8 Q51 + Exam 10 Q27) and names it D3's priority item for Exam 11 — but the Exam 8 half of that tally is the rules-modularization facet tracked under D3-36, not this one.

Key Distinction #3

D3 §3.11

Modularize a bloated CLAUDE.md into .claude/rules/ topic files

Still open

For a 500+ line CLAUDE.md that is hard to navigate and collides in merges, split it into single-topic Markdown files under .claude/rules/ — one per topic.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There are two distinct §3.11 problems and they take different answers. If the file mixes always-needed standards with occasional workflows, the answer is Skills (see D3-35). If the file is simply too large and too contended — every engineer editing the same file for unrelated changes, weekly merge conflicts — the supported modularization approach is separate Markdown files under .claude/rules/, one per topic: testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md, release-notes.md. Engineers editing different topics then touch different files. `@import` is the complementary approach when the content should stay part of the concatenated CLAUDE.md context but live in its own file. Reject the half-split here too: leaving two topics sharing one file means the engineers who edit those two topics still collide.

Why it works that way

Choosing between the Skills answer and the rules answer depends on whether the pain is context cost or file contention. Reading the stem for which pain is described is the whole skill.

Decision rule

Pain is 'every session loads content it does not need' → Skills. Pain is 'one giant file everyone edits' → one topic file per subject under .claude/rules/.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Bundle everything into one .claude/skills/conventions/SKILL.md that loads on invocation.Still a single file competing for edits, and universal standards would now need explicit invocation.Exam 8 Q51 (missed)
  • Split only some topics out and leave the less-frequently-changed ones inline.A partial split leaves two topics sharing one file, so those editors still collide.Exam 8 Q51 (missed)
  • Have engineers coordinate CLAUDE.md edits in a chat channel before pushing.A process workaround that leaves the single-file structure causing the collisions untouched.Exam 8 Q51 (missed)

Your record on it

Missed on Exam 8 Q51, its only scored appearance, and not re-tested since — Exam 10's §3.11 question was the Skills half-split variant, not this one.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.11 · Exam 8 Q51

Key Distinction #3

D3 §3.12

Resume versus starting a new session

Still open

Resume when most of the session's tool results are still valid and you can name what changed; start fresh with a short summary when the ground the session mapped no longer exists.

The full lesson

What is actually true

`--resume` continues a previous named session with its saved context, including its tool results. That is useful when the code has barely moved and you can tell the session exactly which files changed so it re-analyses just those. It becomes a liability when the tool results are broadly stale — the retry layer the session mapped has been swapped for a different library, or a review session is being reused across different PRs — because the session then reasons over old tool output as though it were current. In that case the corpus prefers starting a new session and injecting a short summary of the prior findings: you carry forward the conclusions without carrying forward the stale evidence. The judgment turns on how much of the mapped ground is still true, not on how expensive the prior investigation was.

Why it works that way

Stale tool results are worse than no tool results, because they look authoritative. The whole point of the fresh start is to keep the conclusions and drop the evidence.

Decision rule

Ask how much of what the session mapped is still true. Mostly true and you can name the diff → resume with the changed files listed. Fundamentally changed → new session plus a short summary.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Resume as-is and let the session discover the changes naturally.It reasons over stale tool results as though they were current — exactly the failure a fresh start avoids.Exam 4 Q23, Exam 7 Q48, Exam 10 Q29 (missed)
  • Resume and tell it which layer changed so it re-analyses just that part.Targeted re-analysis fits when most context is still valid; it does not fit when the entire mechanism the session mapped is gone.Exam 10 Q29 (missed)
  • Use `fork_session` so the stale results stay isolated from new findings.Forking branches from a shared, still-valid baseline to compare approaches — it does not refresh a baseline that is itself obsolete.Exam 7 Q48, Exam 10 Q29
  • Resume across every PR on a fast-moving branch to save startup cost.Optimises the wrong variable — the resumed session treats a previous PR's file contents as current when reviewing a different diff.Exam 4 Q50
  • Run `/compact` first, then resume.Compaction risks losing exact details and does nothing about the tool results being stale.Exam 4 Q23, Exam 7 Q48

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q23 and Q50 and on Exam 7 Q48, but missed on Exam 10 Q29 — the case where the mapped layer had been wholly replaced and a fresh start, not targeted re-analysis, was correct. Exam 10's own observations name only Q27 among its two D3 misses; Q29 is confirmed as the second from the scored-attempt detail in `WIP-EXAM10/score_detail.txt` ('g29 [D3 §3.12]' in the all-six-wrong-answers list). Not re-tested since.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.12 · Exam 4 Q23 · Exam 4 Q50 · Exam 7 Q48 · Exam 10 Q29

D3 §3.1

`/memory` is the first diagnostic for inconsistent behaviour

Recovered

When Claude follows a rule in some sessions but not others, run `/memory` to see which memory files actually loaded before changing anything.

The full lesson

What is actually true

`/memory` shows and manages the memory files loaded in the current session. It is the documented first step whenever a previously reliable convention stops firing, or fires on one machine but not another, or differs between two developers on the same branch. The reason is that CLAUDE.md files load as a discovered, concatenated set — so 'why is this rule not applying' is almost always 'the file holding it is not in the discovered set for this session', which `/memory` answers as a fact rather than a guess. The instinctive alternative — appending 'remember the rule' to every prompt — treats the symptom and guarantees the inconsistency continues.

Why it works that way

It converts a diagnosis into an observation. Every other candidate fix (re-typing the rule, reinstalling, deleting a file you suspect is overriding) is a guess made before you know which files are loaded.

Decision rule

'Claude follows rule X sometimes but not always' → run `/memory` before changing any file or prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Re-state the instruction louder in the prompt each session.Treats the symptom; the corpus explicitly rejects it in favour of checking what is actually loaded.Exam 7 Q16 (missed); Exam 8 Q12 (missed); Exam 10 Q16 (correct)
  • A newly added subdirectory CLAUDE.md is silently overriding the instruction — delete it.CLAUDE.md files concatenate rather than override, so this theory is false and the deletion may remove something needed.Exam 8 Q12
  • Run `/compact` to rebuild the session's context from the repository's current state.`/compact` compresses an existing conversation; it has nothing to do with which memory files load at session start.Exam 8 Q12
  • Reinstall Claude Code — a convention that worked and stopped means a corrupted install.Nothing in the documented memory mechanism involves installation corruption; a file the new machine never picked up is far likelier.Exam 10 Q16

Your record on it

Missed Exam 7 Q16 and again Exam 8 Q12, then answered correctly on Exam 10 Q16 — EXAM-LOG records this explicitly as a closed gap after a third re-test.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.1 · Exam 7 Q16 · Exam 8 Q12 · Exam 10 Q16

D3 §3.3

`allowed-tools` scopes what a skill may do

Recovered

To limit a skill to safe operations, set `allowed-tools` in its SKILL.md frontmatter — that is the mechanism the exam expects.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The Official Exam Guide framing, which is what the exam tests, describes `allowed-tools` as restricting tool access during skill execution — for example limiting a cleanup skill to `[Write]` so it cannot shell out or read outside its directory. Current product docs frame the same key slightly differently, as a list of tools the skill may use without prompting the user for permission, with unlisted tools falling back to the normal permission flow rather than being hard-blocked. Both framings agree on the exam-relevant judgment: when a question asks how to scope what a skill is permitted to do, the answer is `allowed-tools` in SKILL.md frontmatter. The real-world nuance is to scope it minimally, since anything unlisted still surfaces a prompt.

Why it works that way

It is the only skill-level mechanism that constrains capability. Every alternative on offer — a renamed skill, a warning in CLAUDE.md, an isolated context — leaves the skill just as able to do the destructive thing.

Decision rule

'Stop this skill from being able to do X' → allowed-tools in SKILL.md frontmatter, scoped as narrowly as the task allows.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in isolation and cannot cause damage.fork isolates output from the main session; a destructive tool call still fires inside the fork.Exam 6 Q50 (missed); Exam 7 Q17 (correct)
  • Add an argument-hint warning that deletion is possible.argument-hint changes what is displayed at invocation, not which tools may execute.Exam 6 Q50
  • Rename the skill to make its read-only purpose clear, or document the restriction in CLAUDE.md.Neither changes tool access; a CLAUDE.md bullet is a probabilistic instruction, not an enforced restriction.Exam 6 Q50; Exam 7 Q17
  • A glob-scoped rules file warning not to touch source files.Rules load advisory prose when matching files are touched; they are not tied to a skill's execution and enforce nothing.Exam 7 Q17

Your record on it

Missed Exam 6 Q50 on its first appearance, then answered correctly on Exam 7 Q17.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.3 · Exam 6 Q50 · Exam 7 Q17 · CURRENT-DOCS-DELTA_v1 §D1

D3 §3.3

`context: fork` isolates a skill's output

Recovered

When a skill produces large or exploratory output, `context: fork` runs it in an isolated subagent context so only a summary returns to the main session.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A deep dependency scan, a codebase analysis, an exploration of rejected alternatives — all of these flood the main conversation with output that then competes with the task you were actually doing. `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent context, so the bulk never enters the main window and only a summary comes back. Crucially, it preserves the skill's full analytical depth: the documented alternatives — switching to a faster model, compressing the skill's output to a short summary, splitting it into two skills — either fail to fix pollution at all or fix it by throwing away the capability. Fork is for discovery, analysis, exploration, and brainstorming. It is the wrong choice for implementation work the developer intends to keep refining in the same conversation, because isolation removes exactly that continuity.

Why it works that way

It is the only option that keeps both properties you want — full depth in the skill and a clean main context — instead of trading one for the other.

Decision rule

Skill output is discovery you only need summarised → fork. Skill output is work you will keep refining in conversation → main session.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Switch to a faster model so the verbose output is processed more quickly.Speed does not stop the output from landing in the main window and displacing the original task.Exam 4 Q6, Exam 4 Q35 (missed), Exam 8 Q14
  • Compress the scan to a short summary before returning it.That sacrifices the analysis capability the skill exists to provide; forking isolates the work rather than discarding it.Exam 4 Q6, Exam 4 Q35, Exam 8 Q14
  • Split the skill into two smaller skills run back to back.Each still dumps its output into the main session; isolation, not smaller chunks, is the fix.Exam 4 Q35, Exam 8 Q14
  • `context: fork` is a safe default for any skill because it merges reasoning back for extra continuity.Inverts the mechanism — fork isolates rather than merges, and it removes the continuity implementation work needs.Exam 5 Q34

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q35, then correct on Exam 5 Q34 and Exam 8 Q14 (and correct on Exam 4 Q6 in the same sitting as the miss).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.3 · Exam 4 Q6 · Exam 4 Q35 · Exam 5 Q34 · Exam 8 Q14 · KD #13

Key Distinction #13

D3 §3.4

Legacy `.claude/commands/` is still supported

Recovered

.claude/commands/ and .claude/skills/ are unified — both create `/name` commands, and legacy command files keep working with `$ARGUMENTS` unchanged.

The full lesson

What is actually true

In current Claude Code, the older `.claude/commands/` location and the newer `.claude/skills/` folder form are unified: both produce a `/name` slash command, and `$ARGUMENTS` continues to work inside a legacy command file. Nothing about a legacy file is deprecated, broken, or on a migration deadline, and there is no requirement to duplicate it into both locations. This is a deliberate fabricated-obsolescence trap: the wrong answers all assert that a real, still-supported mechanism has stopped working.

Why it works that way

Fabricated-obsolescence distractors are hard because they sound like responsible engineering hygiene. Recognising that a mechanism is documented as still supported is what stops you migrating for no reason.

Decision rule

Before agreeing that something must be migrated, check whether the corpus says the old mechanism is still supported — for .claude/commands/ it is.

Traps that have caught you here

  • .claude/commands/ is deprecated and no longer processes $ARGUMENTS, so the file must move.Legacy commands are explicitly documented as still supported; the claim is simply false.Exam 5 Q36 (missed); Exam 10 Q21 (correct)
  • Legacy commands work, but the typed text is only accessible via an argument-hint frontmatter key.Confuses argument-hint (a displayed prompt) with $ARGUMENTS (the variable holding the text).Exam 5 Q36
  • It keeps working only if duplicated into .claude/skills/ so both paths stay in sync.Not a documented requirement, and it just creates two copies to maintain.Exam 10 Q21

Your record on it

Missed Exam 5 Q36 (fell for the fabricated-obsolescence distractor), then answered correctly on Exam 10 Q21.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.4 · Exam 5 Q36 · Exam 10 Q21

D3 §3.5

Personal skills override project skills of the same name

Recovered

A skill at ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md automatically takes precedence over the project skill of the same name, for that user only.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the mechanism for customising a shared command without forking it or affecting teammates. Put your version at ~/.claude/skills/<same-name>/SKILL.md and it wins for your sessions, automatically, with no registration step and no edit to the version-controlled file. Two failure modes follow from it. Choosing a different folder name does not override anything — it just creates a second, differently-named command and loses the familiar invocation. And an old, forgotten personal skill that happens to share a name will silently shadow the team's updated version indefinitely, even on a perfectly current checkout, which is the diagnosis when one person's output diverges from everyone else's for no visible reason.

Why it works that way

Precedence is resolved by name and scope alone. That is what makes personal customisation frictionless — and what makes an accidental name collision invisible until someone notices the divergence.

Decision rule

Want your own version of `/x` without touching the team's → same name, user scope. A different name is never an override.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Create the personal version under a different name to keep it clearly separate.A different name creates a different command; the override you wanted never happens.Exam 6 Q51 (missed), Exam 7 Q45, Exam 10 Q22, Exam 9 Q28 (unscored)
  • Project skills always win over personal ones.Inverts the documented precedence; §3.5 exists so an individual can customise without affecting teammates.Exam 3 Q17 (unscored), Exam 9 Q28 (unscored)
  • A personal skill needs an `override: true` frontmatter field, or a shared settings file must register it.Fabricated opt-in — precedence is determined by name and scope alone.Exam 7 Q45, Exam 9 Q28 (unscored)
  • Just edit the shared project skill directly and revert before committing.Risks affecting teammates mid-change and depends on manual discipline instead of the documented mechanism.Exam 6 Q51, Exam 10 Q22

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q11, missed on Exam 6 Q51, then correct again on Exam 7 Q45 and Exam 10 Q22.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.5 · Exam 5 Q11 · Exam 6 Q51 · Exam 7 Q45 · Exam 10 Q22 · KD #4

Key Distinction #4

D3 §3.6

Direct execution when the scope is already settled

Recovered

When scope, approach, and target files are all defined, skip planning mode — exploration adds overhead with no ambiguity left to resolve.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Direct execution is the right mode for a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, an implementation against a well-defined input/output spec, or a change whose type, default value, and call sites are already agreed in a design doc. Planning mode exists to resolve ambiguity; when there is none, running it re-explores questions that are already answered. This is the harder half of the planning-versus-execution judgment, because opening plan mode always feels like the careful choice. The corpus is explicit that it is not: process for its own sake on an already-scoped one-liner is overhead, not diligence. Watch for stems that hand you a scan result, a stack trace, or a design doc — those are the signals that the decisions have already been made.

Why it works that way

This is where the 'proportionate response' principle bites. Reaching for the heavier mechanism on a settled task is the same error class as reaching for a hook, a re-typed reminder, or a half-split elsewhere in D3.

Decision rule

If the stem already tells you the scope, the root cause, and the fix, the answer is direct execution.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Stay in planning mode anyway — this scope still benefits from review.Approving a plan for an already fully-specified change is process for its own sake.Exam 7 Q19 (missed), Exam 8 Q13 (missed), Exam 10 Q23 (correct)
  • Open planning mode to re-derive a type and default already settled in the design doc, or to re-check whether the deprecated helper appears elsewhere.Redundant exploration of a question the scan or the doc has already closed.Exam 8 Q13, Exam 10 Q23
  • Use planning mode for part of the change and direct execution for the rest.Splitting one small, already-scoped change across both modes matches neither mode's intended use.Exam 10 Q23
  • Spawn a planning subagent to weigh alternative fixes, or use fork_session to draft two candidate implementations.There is no genuine alternative to weigh when a single documented replacement is already known.Exam 7 Q19, Exam 8 Q13

Your record on it

Missed Exam 7 Q19 and again Exam 8 Q13, then answered correctly on Exam 10 Q23 — EXAM-LOG records the gap as closed on its third re-test.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.6 · Exam 7 Q19 · Exam 8 Q13 · Exam 10 Q23

D3 §3.10

Plan against the 24-hour worst case, not the observed typical

Not yet tested

Batch has no SLA, so any deadline plan must budget the full documented 24-hour window even if runs usually finish in an hour.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Teams observe that batches typically come back quickly and start scheduling against that observation. The corpus is explicit that there is no latency SLA: the documented window is up to 24 hours, and 'usually about an hour' is not a bound. If results must be ready by 8 a.m. Monday, the batch has to be submitted no later than 8 a.m. Sunday so that even a full-window run finishes in time. The same reasoning kills the variants that try to make batch behave synchronously — polling faster does not make a batch complete sooner, and a fifteen-minute timeout on a merge gate converts a cost saving into a check that fails whenever the batch is slower than the typical case the 24-hour window explicitly permits.

Why it works that way

Historical typical-case timing does not bound the worst case. Any schedule built on it fails the one week the batch is slow.

Decision rule

Deadline minus 24 hours is the latest safe submission time for a batch.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Submit Sunday evening — batches usually complete in about an hour and we have observed that for a month.Typical-case timing does not bound the worst case; one full-window run blows the deadline.Exam 3 Q43 (unscored)
  • Submission timing does not matter because batch requests have no deadline dependency.The downstream deadline is real even though the API has no SLA.Exam 3 Q43 (unscored)
  • Submit on the morning of the deadline — nobody is blocked anyway.Zero buffer against a documented 24-hour worst case means results can arrive a full day late.Exam 3 Q43 (unscored)

Your record on it

Its only two appearances are Exam 3 Q43 and Exam 9 Q57, and neither exam was ever attempted — so there is no scored evidence on this facet.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.10 · Exam 3 Q43 · Exam 9 Q57 · Domain-4_v2 §4.11

Key Distinction #14

D3 §3.6

Planning mode is deliberately read-only

Not yet tested

In planning mode Claude uses Read, Grep, and Glob only — no side effects — and that constraint is the feature, not a limitation to route around.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Planning mode explores with read-only tools: it will not run the test suite or make a scratch edit to check an assumption. Engineers sometimes read that as a defect and propose abandoning planning mode entirely. The corpus treats the read-only constraint as the point — it is what guarantees that nothing has been executed by the time you review the plan, which is what prevents the expensive rework. The correct response to the complaint is the combined workflow: plan the change up front with read-only exploration, approve the plan, then implement in direct execution where side effects are intended.

Why it works that way

Understanding why the constraint exists is what stops you from treating planning mode as a slower version of execution and abandoning it at the first friction.

Decision rule

Read-only exploration → approve → direct execution. Do not treat the read-only phase as an obstacle.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Because planning mode cannot run tests, drop it and start every task in direct execution.Side-effect-free exploration is the mechanism that prevents rework; the answer is to plan then execute, not to skip planning.Exam 9 Q3 (unscored)
  • Route every task through planning mode instead, including single-file fixes with a clear stack trace.Over-applies the mode — §3.6 lists that exact case as direct execution.Exam 9 Q3 (unscored)

Your record on it

Its only appearance as the key fact is Exam 9 Q3, and Exam 9 was generated but never attempted, so there is no scored evidence either way.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.6 · Exam 9 Q3

D3 §3.1

Project scope is shared, user scope is not

Solid

Project-level CLAUDE.md is version-controlled and reaches every teammate; ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md reaches only you and is never shared.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Configuration at the project level — root CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md — is checked into the repository, so everyone who clones or pulls gets it automatically. Configuration in your home directory at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to every project you work on but travels with you, not with the code. This is the mechanism behind the classic exam scenario: three engineers all follow a convention, a newly onboarded fourth does not, and everyone has the same up-to-date checkout. The convention was never in the repository — it lives in the original engineers' user-level file. The fix is to move it into the project file, not to re-state it more forcefully in the prompt. Run the same rule in reverse when you want something personal: a habit your teammates should not inherit belongs in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

Why it works that way

Scope is the single decision that determines whether a rule is a team standard or a personal preference. Getting it wrong produces exactly the failure mode where behaviour differs between developers on identical code.

Decision rule

Everyone must get it → project scope. Only you should get it → ~/.claude/ user scope.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The new engineer's clone is stale — have them pull again.The stem states the checkout is current; the guidance was never in the project file to begin with.Exam 2 Q15 (unscored)
  • Claude Code caches CLAUDE.md per user and the new engineer's cache is empty.A per-user CLAUDE.md cache needing a rebuild is a fabricated mechanism.Exam 2 Q15 (unscored)
  • Put a personal habit in .claude/rules/ with a match-everything glob..claude/rules/ is project-level and version-controlled — it is still shared with the whole team regardless of the glob.Exam 5 Q31

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q31, the only scored appearance (Exam 2 Q15 covers the same fact but Exam 2 was never attempted).

Where this was taught
