Key Distinction #1

D3 §3.1

@import keeps CLAUDE.md modular

Solid

A CLAUDE.md can pull in an external file with `@path`, so each package includes only the standards its maintainers care about instead of one giant global file.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Instead of pasting every standards document inline into one root CLAUDE.md, each file can reference external content with `@./standards/coding-style.md`. The imported content still becomes part of the concatenated context Claude sees — it just lives in its own file. This is the mechanism when a monorepo splits into packages and each package's maintainers want their own standards loaded without dragging in the other packages' standards. Note the boundary: `@import` is for content that should always be part of the context for that configuration, while .claude/rules/ is for content that should load only when specific file paths are in play. They solve different problems.

Why it works that way

Without imports, modularity forces you to choose between one bloated always-loaded file and duplicating content by hand in several places. @import gives you separate files with the same always-loaded behaviour.

Decision rule

Content that must always apply for this configuration but should live in its own file → @import. Content that should apply only when certain files are touched → .claude/rules/.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use .claude/rules/ with a per-package glob instead.Rules trigger on which file paths Claude is editing, not on which package's CLAUDE.md is loaded — a different problem.Exam 3 Q26 (unscored); Exam 6 Q14
  • Because CLAUDE.md files concatenate, there is no way to include only part of the content.True premise, wrong conclusion — @import exists precisely to control what any one file pulls in.Exam 3 Q26 (unscored)
  • Rely on Claude to skip the irrelevant section once it is loaded.Loaded content burns context tokens whether or not the model attends to it; this is not a configuration fix.Exam 6 Q14

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q14, the only scored appearance of @import-as-modularization (Exam 3 Q26 and Exam 9 Q1 cover it but both exams are unscored).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.1 · Exam 6 Q14 · Exam 3 Q26 · Exam 9 Q1

D3 §3.10

Batch API for non-blocking work, synchronous for blocking

Solid

If something or someone is waiting on the result, use the synchronous API; if nothing is blocked, batch it for the 50% saving.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The Message Batches API costs 50% less but has no latency SLA — the documented window runs up to 24 hours. That single trade-off decides every assignment question. A pre-merge style check, a blocking pre-deploy compatibility gate, or a live fact-check a person is waiting on must stay synchronous, because a batch that takes many hours would block the merge for exactly that long. A nightly test-generation run, an overnight tech-debt report, a weekly security audit, or a one-time bulk backfill are all batch-appropriate: scheduled, non-blocking, latency-tolerant. Watch two rationalisations: 'nightly implies urgency' misclassifies the classic batch case, and 'batch always saves money' ignores that the saving is irrelevant when a person is blocked.

Why it works that way

The cost saving is real but it is never the deciding variable. Latency tolerance is.

Decision rule

Is anything blocked on the result? Yes → synchronous. No → batch.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Batch everything, since the 50% saving applies regardless of who is waiting.A blocking check on an API with no latency SLA is unacceptable no matter what it costs.Exam 2 Q39 (unscored), Exam 5 Q45, Exam 6 Q55, Exam 10 Q44
  • Keep everything synchronous to avoid the unpredictable window.Forfeits the discount on exactly the workloads that tolerate the delay; scheduling off-peak does not reduce per-call cost.Exam 2 Q39 (unscored), Exam 6 Q55, Exam 10 Q44
  • Batch the interactive job and keep the nightly job synchronous, since 'nightly' implies urgency.Inverts the assignment — nightly non-blocking jobs are the textbook batch case.Exam 5 Q45, Exam 6 Q55, Exam 10 Q44
  • Move a blocking check to batch but poll every thirty seconds, or fail the check after fifteen minutes.Polling frequency does not change when a batch completes, and there is no latency guarantee to build a timeout against.Exam 9 Q57 (unscored)
  • Batch savings apply only to bulk data-extraction workloads, not code generation.Fabricated scope restriction — batch applies to any latency-tolerant workload.Exam 5 Q45

Your record on it

Correct on all three scored appearances: Exam 5 Q45, Exam 6 Q55, Exam 10 Q44.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.10 · Exam 5 Q45 · Exam 6 Q55 · Exam 10 Q44 · KD #14

Key Distinction #14

D3 §3.10

`custom_id` matches batch outputs to inputs

Solid

Every batch request carries a `custom_id`; give each one a unique, meaningful value so results can be matched back regardless of return order.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Batch results do not come back in submission order, so the only reliable way to know which output belongs to which input is the per-request `custom_id`. Setting them all to the same placeholder makes the mapping unrecoverable. Give each request a unique identifier with meaning to your pipeline — the source document's own ID is the natural choice. The workarounds all miss the point: smaller chunks do not fix a shared placeholder at any batch size, timestamps do not reconstruct the specific input-to-output mapping, and moving to the synchronous API abandons the discount to solve a problem the batch API already solves.

Why it works that way

It is the batch API's built-in answer to out-of-order results. Reaching for anything else means you have missed a feature you are already paying for.

Decision rule

Batch results cannot be matched to inputs → give every request its own meaningful custom_id.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Switch to the synchronous API because batch results do not preserve order.Abandons the discount for a problem custom_id already solves; nothing here needs synchronous latency.Exam 8 Q30
  • Submit in smaller chunks so order is easier to track manually.A shared placeholder custom_id breaks matching at any batch size.Exam 8 Q30
  • Add a timestamp to each request and sort results back into order.A timestamp does not reconstruct the specific input-to-output mapping that custom_id provides directly.Exam 8 Q30

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q30, its only appearance across all nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.10 · Exam 8 Q30

D3 §3.10

Batch cannot do multi-turn tool calling

Solid

Batch requests are fire-and-forget — the API cannot execute a tool mid-request and feed the result back to Claude, so iterative tool-using workloads cannot use it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the hard limitation that disqualifies an otherwise batch-shaped workload. An iterative code review that fetches related files via tool calls in the middle of its analysis needs a request to pause, receive a tool result, and continue — and batch cannot do that. Be precise about the boundary: batch requests can include tool definitions; what they cannot do is execute a tool mid-request and return the result within that request. And there is no pause-and-resume mechanism for a single batch request, with or without a `custom_id`. So a workload's latency tolerance is necessary but not sufficient — if it needs multi-turn tool execution, batch is off the table regardless of how patient the deadline is.

Why it works that way

It is the one case where a non-blocking, latency-tolerant job still cannot be batched, which is exactly why the exam builds a question around it.

Decision rule

Does the request need a tool result mid-analysis? If yes, batch is impossible no matter how latency-tolerant the job is.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Batch supports full multi-turn tool calling, so mid-analysis fetches work as they do synchronously.This is precisely the documented limitation; batch cannot pause mid-request for a tool result.Exam 7 Q47
  • As long as a `custom_id` links the result to the file, a batch request can pause to run a tool and resume.No such pause-and-resume mechanism exists — a fabricated capability.Exam 7 Q47
  • Batch does not support tool definitions of any kind, so no tool-using workload can run under it.Overgeneralised — tool definitions are fine; mid-request multi-turn execution is not.Exam 7 Q47

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 7 Q47, its only appearance across all nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.10 · Exam 7 Q47 · KD #14

Key Distinction #14

D3 §3.12

`fork_session` to compare approaches from one baseline

Solid

Forking creates branches that inherit context up to the branch point and then diverge independently — the pattern for evaluating two designs against one expensive analysis.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When you have paid once for a deep analysis and now want to evaluate two competing designs against it, `fork_session` gives each evaluation the same baseline with none of the other's reasoning in view. Running both in the same session sequentially does not work: the second evaluation is anchored to the first, echoing its conclusions and even its ordering, and no instruction to 'disregard the previous analysis' fixes that — independence is a property of session structure, not of prompt wording. The two other tempting alternatives both cost you something real: two brand-new sessions each have to redo the expensive analysis (and may not reproduce it identically), and `/compact` compresses rather than partitions, so the first strategy's conclusions survive in summary form while precise details are lost.

Why it works that way

It is the only option that gives you both a shared, paid-for baseline and genuine independence between the branches.

Decision rule

One expensive shared baseline, two approaches to compare independently → fork_session.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Run both evaluations sequentially in the same session.The second is biased by the first's reasoning, which is still in context.Exam 6 Q57, Exam 9 Q58 (unscored)
  • Start two entirely new sessions and redo the analysis in each.Pays twice for the expensive analysis — the exact cost forking avoids — and risks two differing baselines.Exam 6 Q57, Exam 9 Q58 (unscored)
  • Instruct the session to disregard the first strategy's conclusions before evaluating the second.Independence is structural; the reasoning is still in context however the prompt is worded.Exam 9 Q58 (unscored)
  • `/compact` the analysis and paste the summary into two new sessions.Risks losing exact findings and values both evaluations need intact.Exam 6 Q57, Exam 9 Q58 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q57, its only scored appearance (Exam 9 Q58 covers it but Exam 9 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.12 · Exam 6 Q57 · Exam 9 Q58

D3 §3.12

`/compact` trades precision for space

Solid

`/compact` compresses context while preserving the gist, but exact numeric values, dates, and specific details can be lost in the summarisation.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Compaction is a real tool with a documented cost: it preserves essential information but summarises, and summaries lose precision. A session that had an exact test-coverage figure of 34.2% in a tool result may afterwards describe coverage as 'roughly a third'. It summarises the session's content broadly, including detail derived from tool output — it does not selectively spare tool results. So for work where exact figures matter, either extract those facts into a structured block that sits outside the summarised history, or start a new session instead of compacting. And do not reach for `/compact` mid-task when the next phase needs the precision you are about to compress away.

Why it works that way

The loss is silent. Nothing warns you that a figure became an approximation, so the mitigation has to be chosen before you compact, not after.

Decision rule

If exact numbers matter later, pull them into a structured facts block before compacting — or start a new session instead.

Traps that have caught you here

  • `/compact` only summarizes assistant messages and never touches tool outputs.It summarizes the session's content broadly, including tool-output-derived detail.Exam 8 Q52
  • Use `fork_session` instead, since forking preserves full history in both branches.Forking does not solve the token-budget problem that forced compaction; both branches still need managing.Exam 8 Q52
  • The precision loss is expected and downstream tooling should round anyway.Dismisses a real figure that genuinely existed in the tool output.Exam 8 Q52

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q52, its only appearance as the key fact across all nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.12 · Exam 8 Q52 · KD #21

Key Distinction #21

D3 §3.12

Explore subagent for verbose discovery

Solid

When a discovery phase would fill the context window before implementation starts, run it in an Explore subagent that returns a concise summary.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Enumerating every call site of a helper across 45 files, or surveying 90 functions before writing tests, produces exactly the kind of bulky output that leaves no room for the design conversation that has to follow. Running discovery in an Explore subagent isolates the verbose listing in its own context and returns only a summary to the main session. The instinctive alternative — `/compact` partway through discovery — is worse, because it trades away the precise file- and line-level details the implementation phase still needs. A larger context window only postpones the same collision, and skipping discovery risks missing exactly the call sites nobody remembers. This is the same isolation principle as `context: fork` for skills, applied to an ad-hoc discovery phase.

Why it works that way

Discovery output is high-volume and low-reuse; implementation needs the conclusions, not the transcript. Isolation gives you the conclusions without the transcript.

Decision rule

Verbose discovery that would crowd out the next phase → Explore subagent, never `/compact` mid-task.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Run `/compact` partway through discovery to free up space.Loses exact file and line-level detail the design conversation still needs — it trades precision for space instead of isolating the output.Exam 5 Q59
  • Switch to a model with a larger context window.The listing still crowds out the design conversation within the same session; it only delays the same problem at a bigger ceiling.Exam 5 Q59
  • Skip discovery and work from the call sites the engineer already remembers.Risks missing exactly the call sites discovery exists to find.Exam 5 Q59

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q59, its only appearance as the key fact across all nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.12 · Exam 5 Q59 · KD #22

Key Distinction #22

D3 §3.2

.claude/rules/ for path-scoped conventions

Solid

Conventions that depend on which file is being touched belong in .claude/rules/ with a `paths` glob in YAML frontmatter, so they load automatically and only when they apply.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A rules file is a Markdown file under .claude/rules/ whose frontmatter declares the globs it applies to — for example `paths: ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.test.tsx"]`. Claude loads it automatically, and only when it is working on matching files, which keeps irrelevant conventions out of context and saves tokens. This is the right mechanism whenever different file types or directories need different conventions and the affected files are scattered rather than neatly confined — co-located test files are the canonical case. The frontmatter glob is what makes it deterministic: matching happens on the file path, not on the model inferring which heading of a long CLAUDE.md applies right now.

Why it works that way

Path-scoped rules replace model inference with file-path matching. That is the difference between a convention that usually gets applied and one that reliably does.

Decision rule

'Apply this automatically based on which files are being touched' → .claude/rules/ with a glob. If the trigger is a task rather than a file path, it is not a rule.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Put every convention under headings in one root CLAUDE.md and let Claude pick the right section.Relies on model inference rather than deterministic file-path matching — and it also leaks the rule onto lookalike files that should not receive it.Exam 4 Q21, Exam 5 Q32, Exam 6 Q49, Exam 7 Q14, Exam 8 Q46, Exam 10 Q17, Exam 9 Q43
  • Put a separate CLAUDE.md in every subdirectory that needs a distinct convention.Breaks down as soon as the affected files (scattered tests, generated output) live across many directories; you end up duplicating the rule everywhere.Exam 4 Q21, Exam 6 Q49, Exam 10 Q17
  • Write one skill per convention and have engineers invoke the matching one before editing.Skills are invoked on demand; a convention that must apply automatically cannot depend on someone remembering.Exam 4 Q41, Exam 5 Q32, Exam 8 Q46
  • Create the rules file with no `paths` frontmatter and let Claude infer when the directory applies.Fabricates how rules work — the YAML `paths` glob array is the trigger; omitting it does not produce inference-based loading.Exam 5 Q32

Your record on it

Correct on every scored appearance: Exam 4 Q21 and Q41, Exam 5 Q32, Exam 6 Q49, Exam 7 Q14, Exam 8 Q46, Exam 10 Q17.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.2 · Exam 4 Q21 · Exam 4 Q41 · Exam 5 Q32 · Exam 6 Q49 · Exam 7 Q14 · Exam 8 Q46 · Exam 10 Q17 · KD #3

Key Distinction #3

D3 §3.2

Choosing between CLAUDE.md, rules, and Skills

Solid

Always-applies → CLAUDE.md; applies when specific file paths are touched → .claude/rules/; applies when a specific workflow is running → a Skill.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Three mechanisms, three different triggers. CLAUDE.md loads in every session, so it is for universal standards. A .claude/rules/ file loads when Claude touches files matching its glob, so it is for path-scoped conventions. A Skill loads when someone invokes `/name`, so it is for workflow-specific guidance like a PR-review checklist, a deploy procedure, or a migration runbook. Most D3 configuration questions are really this three-way choice in disguise, and the discriminator is always the trigger: is it every session, a file path, or a task the human is deliberately starting?

Why it works that way

Picking the mechanism whose trigger does not match the requirement is how you end up with rules that never fire or standards that need to be invoked by hand.

Decision rule

Ask what the trigger is — every session, a file path, or a task the user starts — and pick the mechanism whose trigger matches.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use .claude/rules/ for a quarterly-close or incident-response procedure.Rules are path-scoped, not workflow-scoped — a calendar-driven procedure is not tied to a file glob.Exam 3 Q25 (unscored); Exam 5 Q58; Exam 6 Q56
  • Use a Skill for a convention that should apply automatically whenever certain files are edited.Skills require deliberate invocation, which is exactly the reliability gap path-scoping closes.Exam 4 Q41; Exam 9 Q43

Your record on it

Every scored question that turns on this three-way choice was answered correctly (Exam 5 Q32 and Q58, Exam 6 Q49 and Q56, Exam 7 Q14 and Q22, Exam 8 Q46), with two exceptions — both §3.11 applications tracked separately under D3-35 (Exam 10 Q27, the Skills half-move) and D3-36 (Exam 8 Q51, the rules-modularization case).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.2 · Domain-3_v2 §3.11 · Exam 5 Q58 · Exam 6 Q56 · Exam 7 Q22 · KD #3

Key Distinction #3

D3 §3.3

Skill anatomy and its frontmatter keys

Solid

A skill is a folder under .claude/skills/ containing SKILL.md, whose frontmatter carries `description`, `argument-hint`, `context: fork`, and `allowed-tools`.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Skills live at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md and create a `/name` slash command. Four frontmatter keys carry almost all the exam weight, and each does exactly one job. `description` is the text shown in the slash-command menu. `argument-hint` is displayed when the command is invoked and prompts for required arguments. `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent context. `allowed-tools` scopes which tools the skill may use during execution. Exam questions frequently offer the wrong key as a plausible fix — the discipline is to name the symptom precisely, then pick the key whose documented job matches it.

Why it works that way

Because all four keys sit in the same block, the distractors are always other real keys. Knowing each key's exact job is what separates a confident answer from a coin flip.

Decision rule

Match the symptom to the key: menu text → description; missing argument → argument-hint; context pollution → context: fork; unsafe tool use → allowed-tools.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Tool scoping for a skill is configured in .mcp.json, CLAUDE.md, or a config.json commands array.It lives in SKILL.md frontmatter, nowhere else.corpus (Domain-3_v2 §3.3)
  • `context: fork` and `argument-hint` interact — fork only affects skills without an argument-hint.Fabricated interaction; they are independent keys with no documented gating relationship.Exam 5 Q34

Your record on it

Every scored question that hinges on picking the right frontmatter key was answered correctly (Exam 5 Q34, Exam 7 Q17, Exam 10 Q19), other than the first-appearance allowed-tools miss tracked under D3-10.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.3 · Exam 5 Q34 · Exam 7 Q17 · Exam 10 Q19 · Exam 9 Q2

D3 §3.3

`argument-hint` signals a required argument

Solid

`argument-hint` is displayed when the command is invoked, prompting the user for the argument the skill needs.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When users keep invoking a skill bare and it silently does something too broad — backfilling every region, scaffolding placeholder-named files — the missing piece is a signal at invocation time that an argument is expected. That is `argument-hint`'s documented job: it is shown when the command is invoked and prompts for required args. Note the near miss: `description` also appears in the slash-command menu, but as the summary line, not as an argument prompt at invocation. Rewriting the description to mention the argument in prose does not close the gap.

Why it works that way

It is the only frontmatter key that changes what the user sees at the moment they invoke the command, which is the moment the mistake happens.

Decision rule

The problem is that the user does not know an argument is expected → argument-hint.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Expand the `description` so the menu entry states that an argument is required.description is the menu summary line, not a prompt shown at invocation.Exam 10 Q19; Exam 9 Q2 (unscored)
  • Use `allowed-tools` so the skill cannot write more than intended.allowed-tools scopes which tools may run, not whether the skill knows what to scope its writes to — a legitimate Write still touches everything.Exam 10 Q19; Exam 9 Q2 (unscored)
  • Use `argument-hint` to narrow a scan's scope so it stops polluting context.argument-hint only displays a prompt; it does not isolate output — that is context: fork's job.Exam 4 Q6

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 10 Q19, its only scored appearance as the key (Exam 9 Q2 covers the same fact but Exam 9 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.3 · Exam 10 Q19 · Exam 9 Q2

D3 §3.4

Project commands are shared, personal commands are not

Solid

.claude/commands/ in the repo is version-controlled and reaches everyone on clone; ~/.claude/commands/ stays on your machine.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The scope rule for CLAUDE.md applies identically to commands and skills. A command file placed at .claude/commands/<name>.md inside the repository is checked in, so every teammate — and the CI runner, which checks out only the repository — gets `/name` automatically with no per-machine setup. A file in ~/.claude/commands/ is outside version control and never surfaces for anyone else. When the requirement is 'available to everyone the moment they pull, no manual steps', the answer is always the repository location; when the requirement is 'personal, teammates should not see it', it is always the home directory.

Why it works that way

Distribution is a filesystem-location decision, not something a wiki page, a manual copy step, or a note in CLAUDE.md can substitute for.

Decision rule

Shared and automatic on clone → .claude/commands/ (or .claude/skills/) in the repo. Personal only → ~/.claude/.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Leave it in ~/.claude/commands/ and add a wiki note telling everyone to copy it.Manual copying is exactly the per-machine setup being eliminated, and it drifts out of sync on the next change.Exam 3 Q16 (unscored), Exam 4 Q59, Exam 6 Q27
  • Convert it to a skill under ~/.claude/skills/ so it upgrades to the current form.Still a user-scoped location invisible to the team — the fix is the project-scoped directory, not the command-vs-skill format.Exam 3 Q16 (unscored)
  • Paste the check's logic into project CLAUDE.md as a documented convention.CLAUDE.md supplies instructions the model reads; it cannot reproduce an invocable `/name` command.Exam 6 Q27
  • Commit a personal skill to a feature branch — skills stay private by default.Anything committed in-repo surfaces to teammates; in-repo skills are not private.Exam 7 Q18

Your record on it

Correct on every scored appearance: Exam 4 Q59, Exam 6 Q27, Exam 7 Q18.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.4 · Exam 4 Q59 · Exam 6 Q27 · Exam 7 Q18 · Exam 3 Q16 · KD #1

Key Distinction #1

D3 §3.4

`$ARGUMENTS` holds the text typed after the command

Solid

Whatever the user types after the command name is available inside the command file as `$ARGUMENTS` — no other variable name receives the substitution.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A command file reads its argument by referencing `$ARGUMENTS`. If a command file uses any other name — `$INPUT`, `$1`, a made-up placeholder — the substitution simply never happens and the literal string appears in the output. And if the file references nothing at all, the typed text is passed but never read, so Claude ends up asking which value was meant on every invocation. Two adjacent mechanisms get confused with this one: `argument-hint` displays a hint at invocation but does not create or rename the substitution variable, and `context: fork` has nothing to do with arguments at all. One command file with `$ARGUMENTS` serves every possible value — creating one command file per value is the anti-pattern.

Why it works that way

It is the parameterization mechanism for commands. Without it, teams either duplicate command files or push the argument back onto the user as a follow-up message.

Decision rule

Typed text not reaching the command → reference `$ARGUMENTS` inside the file; nothing else substitutes.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add an `argument-hint` field so Claude knows to substitute the typed text.argument-hint only displays a hint at invocation; it does not create the substitution variable.Exam 8 Q47
  • Rename the command file so its name matches the argument variable.The filename and the argument-variable name are unrelated.Exam 8 Q47
  • Create one command file per value so each names its own.Encodes the belief that commands cannot be parameterized; $ARGUMENTS exists precisely so one file serves every value.Exam 9 Q44 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q47, its only scored appearance (Exam 9 Q44 covers it but Exam 9 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.4 · Exam 8 Q47 · Exam 9 Q44

D3 §3.5

A personal override never reaches CI

Solid

CI checks out only the repository, so a pipeline always runs the project-scoped skill regardless of what any developer has in ~/.claude/skills/.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Because personal skills live outside version control in the user's home directory, they are invisible to anything that only clones the repository — which is exactly what a CI runner does. A developer trialling a stricter local override changes nothing about what the pipeline runs. There is no sync mechanism that pushes personal skills into CI, a same-name collision does not cause a startup failure, and the two versions do not merge into a blended prompt: precedence means one applies, and in CI it is always the project one.

Why it works that way

This is the practical guarantee that a local experiment cannot leak into a shared pipeline — and the reason a personal trial cannot be used to validate CI behaviour.

Decision rule

If it is not in the repository, CI cannot see it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • CI picks up the personal override on the next push because Claude Code syncs personal skills into the pipeline.No such sync exists; a non-version-controlled file never propagates to CI.Exam 8 Q48
  • The CI job fails to start because two skills now share a name.A same-name pair does not collide into a startup failure; the personal copy simply overrides locally for that one user.Exam 8 Q48
  • CI merges both versions' instructions into one combined prompt.Overrides do not merge — precedence means one applies, not a blend.Exam 8 Q48

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q48, its only appearance across all nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.5 · Domain-3_v2 §3.4 · Exam 8 Q48

Key Distinction #4

D3 §3.6

Planning mode for large or undecided work

Solid

Use planning mode when scope is large, the design is unsettled, or several approaches are viable — Claude explores and proposes a plan before anything is executed.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Planning mode is for the cases where premature execution costs you rework: restructuring a monolith into services, a library migration touching 45+ files, adding an integration where several approaches are defensible, a cross-module change whose data representation has not been decided. Claude explores and designs first, presents a plan, and only executes after approval. The documented combined workflow is planning for investigation and design, then user approval, then direct execution to implement. Two ways to get this wrong: fragmenting the work into many independent sessions never resolves the cross-cutting design question, and generating several competing implementations multiplies unreviewed code without deciding anything.

Why it works that way

The expensive failure in agentic coding is confidently building the wrong thing across dozens of files. Planning mode buys the design decision before the edits exist.

Decision rule

Many files plus an unsettled decision → plan first. Never plan reactively after execution has started.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Start in direct execution and switch to planning mode only if it turns out harder than expected.The corpus's named trap — reactive switching is expensive because executed work has to be unwound; plan upfront when the task demands it.Exam 2 Q21 (unscored), Exam 4 Q20, Exam 4 Q37, Exam 5 Q38, Exam 6 Q52, Exam 7 Q19, Exam 9 Q3 (unscored)
  • Split the work into one direct-execution session per file or per module.Never resolves the open architectural question and loses cross-file consistency a single plan would establish.Exam 4 Q20, Exam 5 Q38, Exam 6 Q52
  • Ask the engineer to pre-decompose the change into single-file tickets first.Burden-shifting — the boundary decisions are precisely what planning mode is meant to explore and propose.Exam 2 Q21 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on every scored appearance where planning mode is the answer: Exam 4 Q20 and Q37, Exam 5 Q38, Exam 6 Q52.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.6 · Exam 4 Q20 · Exam 4 Q37 · Exam 5 Q38 · Exam 6 Q52

D3 §3.7

Matching the refinement technique to the failure mode

Solid

Missing requirements → interview; failing edge case → test; inconsistent output shape → examples; interacting fixes → one message.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The four §3.7 techniques are not interchangeable, and the exam tests that by offering the wrong one as a very plausible distractor. Diagnose from the symptom. If each generation misses a *different* requirement in a domain you do not know, requirements were never gathered — interview. If one specific input class keeps coming out wrong after repeated prose descriptions, you need an objective target — a failing test. If the same instruction produces a differently *shaped* output each run, the format is underspecified — concrete examples. If several review findings interact, the problem is how you are batching feedback — one message. Getting the technique right matters as much as knowing the technique exists.

Why it works that way

Applying the wrong refinement technique costs another full iteration cycle and can make the diagnosis harder, because the symptom does not change.

Decision rule

Name the symptom first (missing requirement / wrong on one input class / wrong shape / conflicting fixes), then pick the matching technique.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use concrete examples when the developer does not yet know the domain's rules.Examples anchor a known transformation; they cannot surface requirements nobody has stated.Exam 5 Q39
  • Use example pairs when the spec already names the edge cases unambiguously.Examples still leave no machine-checkable definition of done across the full edge-case surface — that is what a test suite provides.Exam 9 Q4 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q39, where the interview pattern had to be chosen over the concrete-examples near-miss; no scored miss on any §3.7 question across six scored exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.7 · Exam 5 Q39 · Exam 9 Q4

D3 §3.7.1

The interview pattern for unfamiliar domains

Solid

When you do not know what you do not know, have Claude interview you before it implements anything.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Instead of generating from an underspecified brief and then discovering requirements one failed iteration at a time, ask Claude to interview you first — to surface the questions you had not thought to answer. It pays off in unfamiliar domains (fintech, healthcare, tax, a vendor taxonomy you have never worked in), on tasks with non-obvious implications like cache invalidation or retroactive re-tagging, and where several approaches are viable and the choice depends on context only you hold. The diagnostic signature in an exam stem is that each successive generation misses a *different* requirement — ordering, then an exempt category, then a combination case. That pattern means the requirements were never gathered, not that the code needs another patch.

Why it works that way

One interview turn replaces several correction cycles, and correction cycles are worse than slow — each fix can disturb the last.

Decision rule

Each iteration misses a different requirement and the domain is unfamiliar → restart with the interview pattern.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Asking Claude to interview you wastes a turn — it is faster to generate first and correct after.For underspecified tasks, requirements surfaced up front prevent the rework that fix-by-fix iteration creates.corpus (Domain-3_v2 §3.7.1); Exam 5 Q39
  • Write the paragraph brief more precisely, with more adjectives about correctness and completeness.More descriptive language cannot surface domain unknowns the author does not know they are missing; only a dialogue does that.Exam 3 Q18 (unscored)
  • Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples instead.Examples fix an ambiguously-described transformation when requirements are known; they do not surface rules the developer never stated because they did not know them.Exam 5 Q39
  • Generate several alternative implementations in parallel and compare their edge-case handling.All the alternatives face the same unknown-domain gap; you would be comparing them against a spec that does not exist yet.Exam 3 Q18 (unscored), Exam 5 Q39

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q39, its only scored appearance, where the tempting near-miss distractor (use examples instead) was correctly rejected.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.7.1 · Exam 5 Q39 · Exam 3 Q18

D3 §3.7.2

Test-driven iteration beats prose re-description

Solid

Write the test first — a concrete failing case with exact expected output — then iterate on the failures until it passes.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tests are an objective, machine-checkable definition of done; prose acceptance criteria are not. The pattern is to write the suite first, covering expected behaviour, edge cases, and performance bounds, then feed Claude the concrete failures so each iteration is targeted rather than guesswork. This is the specific remedy for an edge-case bug you keep re-describing — null values in a migration, a rounding order on split-currency refunds, a daylight-saving transition, special characters in a JSON payload. Each prose re-description fixes only the case you named; a sample input plus its exact expected output fixes the class. Note the distinction the corpus draws: writing tests *after* generation is verification, not test-driven iteration. It gives you a pass/fail at the end instead of a failure signal to iterate against.

Why it works that way

Edge cases are exactly where natural language is interpreted inconsistently. A test converts an ambiguous requirement into a checkable target that cannot be partially satisfied.

Decision rule

Repeated partial fixes to an edge case → supply one concrete failing input with its exact expected output and iterate against it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Re-describe the bug more emphatically — 'really handle ALL nulls this time'.Prose descriptions of edge cases are interpreted inconsistently run to run; emphasis does not change that.Exam 3 Q23 (unscored), Exam 6 Q53, Exam 7 Q20, Exam 8 Q49
  • Ask Claude to write tests after the next fix to confirm it worked.That is verification, not test-driven iteration — it never anchors generation to a concrete failure signal.Exam 6 Q53, Exam 9 Q4 (unscored)
  • Ask Claude to write its own test suite with no concrete case supplied, or to self-confirm the fix is complete.It tests the same assumptions that already produced two incomplete fixes; there is no external check.Exam 3 Q23 (unscored), Exam 7 Q20
  • Switch to a larger context window to reason through more cases at once.A bigger window does not resolve an ambiguous prose requirement.Exam 6 Q53

Your record on it

Correct on all three scored appearances: Exam 6 Q53, Exam 7 Q20, Exam 8 Q49.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.7.2 · Exam 6 Q53 · Exam 7 Q20 · Exam 8 Q49 · Exam 3 Q23 · Exam 9 Q4

D3 §3.7.3

Two or three concrete input/output examples

Solid

When a transformation described in prose comes out differently on every run, add 2-3 concrete input→output example pairs.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Examples are the most effective way to communicate an expected transformation. They show format and decision logic unambiguously — the exact casing of a status value, whether prices are decimals or integer minor units, whether tracking fields nest or flatten — and the model generalises the pattern to new inputs rather than merely repeating the samples. Reach for this when the requirements are actually known but the prose describing them is being read differently each run. The tell in a stem is *shape* inconsistency across runs on the same instruction, as opposed to a missing requirement (which points to the interview pattern) or a specific failing edge case (which points to a test).

Why it works that way

Adding text to a failing instruction does not fix it. Examples change the kind of signal you are giving, not just its length.

Decision rule

Output shape varies run to run on a known requirement → 2-3 concrete example pairs, not more prose.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Well-chosen examples make the model copy the samples instead of generalising.Examples demonstrate the pattern; the model applies it to novel inputs.corpus (Domain-3_v2 §3.7.3)
  • Lengthen the prose with more adjectives, or expand it into a longer numbered checklist.A longer checklist is still prose — the description is already failing, and more of it does not disambiguate.Exam 2 Q22 (unscored), Exam 10 Q25
  • Lower the temperature so the output structure stops varying.Temperature controls randomness, not which structure the model chooses; this is an underspecified-format problem.Exam 2 Q22 (unscored)
  • Generate once and post-process the output into the right shape.Patches the symptom downstream instead of fixing the ambiguous spec that produces it.Exam 2 Q22 (unscored), Exam 10 Q25

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 10 Q25, its only scored appearance (Exam 2 Q22 covers it but Exam 2 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.7.3 · Exam 10 Q25 · Exam 2 Q22 · KD #16

Key Distinction #16

D3 §3.7.4

Batch interdependent feedback, sequence independent feedback

Solid

Issues that interact go in one detailed message; issues that do not interact can go one at a time.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When two fixes affect each other — a locking change and a backoff calculation that depends on the new locking behaviour — sending them separately lets the second patch be built against assumptions the first has just invalidated, which forces another round. Presenting interacting issues together lets Claude design one coherent change. Independent issues, like an unrelated typo in a log string, do not need that coordination and can ride along or go separately. The exam's favourite wrong answer is the plausible-sounding blanket rule 'always one issue per message so Claude can focus', which is precisely wrong for the interacting pair. The opposite blanket rule — always bundle everything — is not the documented rule either.

Why it works that way

The grouping decision is about dependency, not about count or report order. Get the dependency wrong and you pay for an extra correction round.

Decision rule

Ask whether fixing A changes what the fix for B should be. If yes, one message. If no, either way.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Always report one issue per message so Claude can focus.Separate fixes to interacting problems can contradict each other; interdependent fixes belong in a single message.Exam 3 Q28 (unscored), Exam 4 Q55
  • Bundle all findings regardless of relationship, since more context always helps.Not the documented rule — the independent issue does not need to be coupled to the interacting pair.Exam 4 Q55
  • Fix them in a specific numbered order, or oldest-issue-first.No such sequencing rule exists; what matters is whether the issues interact, and an arbitrary order does not substitute for presenting the pair jointly.Exam 3 Q28 (unscored), Exam 4 Q55
  • Ship the first fix, then raise the dependent one in a later sprint.Delays discovering the interaction and ships an interim state where the two are already out of sync.Exam 3 Q28 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q55, its only scored appearance (Exam 3 Q28 covers it but Exam 3 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.7.4 · Exam 4 Q55 · Exam 3 Q28

D3 §3.8

`-p` / `--print` for non-interactive CI

Solid

`claude -p "..."` processes the prompt, prints to stdout, and exits — without it, Claude Code waits for interactive input and the pipeline hangs.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the single most reliably-tested mechanical fact in D3. A CI step that invokes `claude "Review this PR"` with no flags never returns: Claude Code runs interactively, waits for input the runner will never provide, and the job sits until it is killed or the runner times out. `-p` (or `--print`) is the documented non-interactive mode. The three distractors are always the same and all three are worth memorising as non-answers: `--batch` is not a Claude Code flag at all (batching belongs to the Message Batches API), `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` is a fabricated environment variable, and redirecting `stdin < /dev/null` is an undocumented Unix workaround rather than the sanctioned approach.

Why it works that way

Every CI scenario in the exam starts from a working non-interactive invocation. If you cannot name the flag, you cannot reason about the structured-output and context questions that build on top of it.

Decision rule

Claude Code in any automated pipeline → `-p` / `--print`. Reject `--batch`, `CLAUDE_HEADLESS`, and stdin tricks on sight.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Set `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` so Claude Code detects the CI context.The variable does not exist; setting it changes nothing.Exam 2 Q31 (unscored), Exam 3 Q31 (unscored), Exam 5 Q41, Exam 9 Q56 (unscored)
  • Add a `--batch` flag so the job queues the work and exits.Not a Claude Code CLI flag — it borrows a Message Batches API concept and would be an unrecognised argument.Exam 5 Q41, Exam 9 Q56 (unscored)
  • Redirect `stdin < /dev/null` so there is no interactive channel to wait on.An undocumented Unix workaround, not the sanctioned mechanism, and it leaves the pipeline depending on shell plumbing.Exam 5 Q41, Exam 9 Q56 (unscored)
  • Run the job interactively so an engineer can correct it each time.Abandons the automation rather than informing it; `-p` is the documented way to run in a pipeline.Exam 10 Q14

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q41, its only scored appearance; also correct in Exam 10 Q14 where reverting to interactive mode was one of the distractors.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.8 · Exam 5 Q41 · Exam 2 Q31 · Exam 3 Q31 · Exam 9 Q56 · KD #15

Key Distinction #15

D3 §3.8

CLAUDE.md gives CI-invoked Claude its project context

Solid

CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for giving a headless run the project's testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A CI job that invokes Claude with only a diff and a two-line prompt has no idea what the team's conventions are, so it invents fixtures, improvises mocks, and flags deliberate documented patterns as bugs. The fix is project context, and CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for supplying it: testing standards, fixture conventions, mocking patterns, review criteria, and documented behaviours that should not be flagged. It improves generation quality and reduces low-value output on every run, without anyone maintaining a per-job prompt. The alternatives on offer are all weaker versions of the same idea — a longer prompt reminder cannot convey specifics the model has never seen, pasting a manual into every invocation duplicates content that belongs in version control, and post-processing filters the symptom.

Why it works that way

It is durable, version-controlled context that every run inherits, as opposed to a per-invocation instruction someone has to remember to maintain.

Decision rule

CI-invoked Claude keeps getting a convention wrong → put the convention in CLAUDE.md, not in the per-run prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add 'follow all our testing conventions' to the top of the CI prompt.A one-line reminder cannot convey what those conventions actually are, so the model keeps improvising.Exam 2 Q41 (unscored), Exam 7 Q46
  • Raise `max_tokens` so generated tests have room for proper setup.Token budget governs length, not adherence — you get a longer version of the wrong pattern.Exam 2 Q41 (unscored), Exam 6 Q54
  • Paste the full policy manual into each night's prompt.Duplicates version-controlled content per job and bloats every invocation.Exam 10 Q14
  • Post-process the output to delete findings mentioning the pattern, or add a second CI step that rewrites invented fixtures.Censors or patches the symptom every run and would also hide a genuine problem; the defect is missing context.Exam 6 Q54, Exam 10 Q14
  • Lower the review's strictness uniformly across all finding categories.Blunt — it damages accurate categories too and never addresses the specific misunderstanding.Exam 7 Q46

Your record on it

Correct on all three scored appearances: Exam 6 Q54, Exam 7 Q46, Exam 10 Q14.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.8 · Exam 6 Q54 · Exam 7 Q46 · Exam 10 Q14 · Exam 2 Q41

D3 §3.8

Existing test files in context prevent duplicate tests

Solid

Claude can only avoid re-testing scenarios it can see — put the existing test files in context when generating new tests.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a CI test-generation step proposes tests that duplicate scenarios the suite already covers, the missing input is the coverage map, not a better instruction. Include the module's existing test files in the context so Claude can see what is already tested and generate genuinely new scenarios. Instructing it to 'only generate tests not already covered' is useless when it has no visibility into what is covered — the instruction cannot compensate for missing context. Capping the number of generated tests assumes the duplicates fall off the end of a priority-ordered list, and keyword-matching the output against existing test names misses semantically identical tests worded differently while dropping distinct tests that happen to share a name.

Why it works that way

It is the clearest instance of a recurring D3/D4 principle: context beats instruction. You cannot instruct a model around information it does not have.

Decision rule

Duplicate output → give the model what already exists, do not instruct it to avoid what it cannot see.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Instruct Claude to generate only tests for scenarios not already covered.The instruction cannot compensate for missing context — the model has no visibility into the existing suite.Exam 2 Q37 (unscored)
  • Cap the number of generated tests so fewer duplicates appear.Assumes tests are priority-ordered and duplicates fall off the end; it may drop novel tests and keep duplicates.Exam 2 Q37 (unscored)
  • Post-process with keyword matching against existing test names.Fragile — misses semantic duplicates worded differently and drops distinct tests sharing a name.Exam 2 Q37 (unscored)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q54, whose correct answer pairs CLAUDE.md conventions with the existing test files; the standalone version (Exam 2 Q37) sits on an exam that was never attempted.

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.8 · Exam 6 Q54 · Exam 2 Q37 · Domain-4_v2 §4.18

D3 §3.8

Re-runs should carry the prior review's findings

Solid

When a review re-runs after new commits, feed it the previous run's findings and instruct it to report only new or still-unresolved issues.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A blank-slate re-run has no memory of what it already said, so it re-derives the same findings in slightly different words and floods the PR with near-duplicate comments on unchanged code — and, worse, it can silently drop findings the author has not addressed. Including the prior findings in the re-run prompt keeps the reviewer consistent across runs and lets it explicitly report which items remain open. Reject the 'objectivity' rationale on sight: starting fresh each time does not make the review more objective, it makes it inconsistent. Also reject the downstream patches — de-duplicating comment text after the fact cannot distinguish a reworded old finding from a genuinely new one, and a separate tracking database leaves the review bot's own prompt just as blank as before.

Why it works that way

Consistency across runs is an input problem. Nothing you do to the output can reconstruct information the model was never given.

Decision rule

Duplicate or dropped findings across re-runs → put the prior findings in the prompt and ask for new-or-unresolved only.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Each re-run should start from a blank slate so the review stays objective.A blank-slate re-run re-litigates settled findings and floods the PR; prior findings in context are what keep it consistent.Exam 2 Q38 (unscored)
  • De-duplicate afterwards by comparing new comment text against previously posted comments.Fragile text matching misses reworded duplicates and cannot tell a new issue from a reworded old one.Exam 2 Q38 (unscored)
  • Raise `max_tokens` so the response has room to list every historical finding.More output room does not give the model memory of a run it never saw.Exam 8 Q50
  • Track findings in a separate database, or run the bot twice and report only what both runs agree on.Adds infrastructure while the bot's prompt still starts blank; consensus voting suppresses genuinely unresolved findings.Exam 8 Q50

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q50, its only scored appearance (Exam 2 Q38 covers it but Exam 2 was never attempted).

Where this was taught

Domain-3_v2 §3.8 · Exam 8 Q50 · Exam 2 Q38

D3 §3.8

Use an independent instance to review generated code

Solid

The same session that generated the code is less effective at reviewing it, because it retains its own reasoning and is less likely to challenge its own decisions.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Session context isolation matters for review quality. A session that just produced a change carries the reasoning that produced it, which makes it disinclined to question the decisions it already made — its self-review reliably comes back clean while a human reading the diff cold finds the bug in minutes. For review, use a second, independent instance that receives only the diff and the review criteria. Two adjacent moves that look like fixes and are not: giving the same instance more reasoning (extended thinking, a second pass, a sterner 'review your own work carefully' instruction) leaves the same anchored context in place, and passing the generating session's reasoning transcript to the independent reviewer re-contaminates it — the isolation is the point, so the transcript is the one thing to withhold. This is the same isolation logic that motivates `context: fork` for skills and Explore subagents for discovery, applied to the review step of a pipeline.

Why it works that way

Review is only useful if the reviewer can disagree with the author. Reusing the authoring session — or feeding the author's reasoning to a fresh one — structurally reduces the chance of that happening.

Decision rule

Never review generated code in the session that generated it — spin up an independent instance, and give it the diff and criteria only, never the generator's reasoning.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Ask the same session for a second review pass, or tell it to look harder this time.A same-conversation pass still carries the full generation reasoning in context, so the model re-reads and reaffirms its own justification rather than evaluating the diff.Exam 7 Q20-family (D1 §1.17), Exam 10 Q20, Exam 6 (D4 §4.13)
  • Enable extended thinking on the generating instance so it catches the issue while writing the change.More reasoning by an already-anchored instance is not independent scrutiny; the corpus rejects extended thinking as a fix for the self-check limitation.Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10 (D1 §1.17 / D4 §4.13)
  • Use an independent reviewing instance but pass it the generating session's reasoning transcript alongside the diff.The reviewer then reasons from the generator's own justification and concurs every time — independence requires withholding the transcript, not just changing instance.Exam 9 (D1 §1.17)
  • Add a stronger self-review instruction to the generation prompt.A probabilistic instruction inside the same context inherits the same blind spots that produced the miss.Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10 (D1 §1.17 / D4 §4.13)

Your record on it

Corrected from 'untested': the idea is tested repeatedly across the mock exams, just never under a D3 §3.8 citation — every instance is tagged D1 §1.17 or D4 §4.13 (Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7 twice, Exam 9 twice, Exam 10 Q20). D3 §3.9

`--output-format json` plus `--json-schema` for structured CLI output

Solid

To guarantee parseable output from `claude -p`, pair `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` — a prompt instruction or a CLAUDE.md section will not do it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Whenever a downstream consumer needs named fields — one inline GitHub comment per finding with file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix; a ticketing API; a metrics dashboard; a compliance ledger — the mechanism is `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` pointing at a schema that defines the fields. This is enforcement at the CLI level, not a request the model may or may not honour. Note the sharper version of the fact: `--output-format json` on its own does not guarantee which fields are present, so a run can return valid JSON that is simply missing `severity`; marking the field required in the schema is what closes that gap. The rejected alternatives are always the same family — an 'Output Format' section in CLAUDE.md is not guaranteed consistent, a format instruction in the prompt has variable compliance, and a more forgiving regex or a JSON-repair library patches the symptom while the generator stays free to vary.

Why it works that way

The failure mode is intermittent — one run in twelve, or only on the zero-result case where a clean batch tips the model into a sentence instead of a record. Only a structural guarantee removes an intermittent failure.

Decision rule

Downstream tooling must parse it → enforce with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, never with an instruction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add an 'Output Format' section to CLAUDE.md describing the exact shape.CLAUDE.md is guidance loaded into context, not an enforcement mechanism — explicitly rejected by the corpus for this purpose.Exam 5 Q43, Exam 6 Q37, Exam 7 Q21, Exam 8 Q29, Exam 10 Q56
  • Add a strong prompt instruction to 'always respond with valid JSON only, no prose'.Variable compliance — the model can still return a preamble or a markdown fence, which is exactly the failure already occurring.Exam 5 Q43, Exam 6 Q37, Exam 8 Q29, Exam 10 Q56
  • Harden the parser — a wider regex, a JSON-repair library, or stripping text before the first brace.Treats the symptom; the source keeps varying, so the parser needs expanding indefinitely.Exam 5 Q43, Exam 6 Q37, Exam 8 Q29
  • Have the consumer substitute a default value when a field is missing.Silently fabricates data the pipeline never confirmed and hides the reliability problem.Exam 7 Q21, Exam 8 Q29, Exam 10 Q56

Your record on it

Correct on all five scored appearances: Exam 5 Q43, Exam 6 Q37, Exam 7 Q21, Exam 8 Q29, Exam 10 Q56.

Domain 4 · 20% of the exam · 12 of 60 questions

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

D4 is about getting Claude to produce output you can actually build a pipeline on — the right shape, the right content, reliably, every time. It splits into two halves that the exam keeps testing against each other: prompting technique (few-shot examples, reasoning cues, system-prompt placement, prefilling, chaining, escalation criteria) and structured output engineering (JSON schema design, tool_use as a structure guarantee, programmatic validation, retry loops, self-correction fields, batch processing). The single deepest idea running through the whole domain is that a schema can guarantee shape but never meaning — so almost every question is really asking whether you know which failure class you are looking at and which lever actually reaches it. The exam's favourite wrong answers are the ones that sound responsible but are probabilistic where the corpus wants a structural guarantee: another instruction, a lower temperature, a bigger context window, a post-processing patch, or one more retry.

36 concepts59/72 lifetime (82%)

Recall check — D4

Answer out loud before you open each one. Retrieval is what moves a concept from recognised to owned.

  1. A tempting answer says Reasoning cues never hurt, so apply them everywhere.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Add 'think step by step' when the task is multi-step math, multi-stage analysis, comparison across N items, or step-wise transformation — and not otherwise.

    Why the tempting answer fails: The corpus explicitly says do NOT add for single-step tasks; overgeneralizing the technique contradicts stated guidance.

  2. A tempting answer says Lower the temperature to reduce variation in how responses open.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: To kill 'Certainly!' or 'I apologize for the inconvenience', append a partial assistant message with the direct opening and let Claude continue from it.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Temperature controls randomness broadly, not a specific recurring phrase — a low-temperature model can still consistently pick the same apology opening.

  3. A tempting answer says Use tool_choice 'any' to make sure a specific mandatory step runs first.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: 'auto' guarantees nothing, 'any' guarantees SOME tool is called, and {type:'tool', name:'X'} guarantees THAT tool — pick by which guarantee you actually need.

    Why the tempting answer fails: 'any' guarantees SOME tool is called and lets the model pick — an extraction tool can still run before the mandatory redaction or metadata step.

D4 §4.17

Restore trust by disabling noisy categories

Still open

When high-false-positive categories make developers skim past everything, temporarily disable those categories and keep only the high-precision ones.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The scenario always gives you per-category dismissal or precision numbers with a clear split — correctness dismissed 6-9%, style and documentation dismissed 44-51% — plus the crucial detail that developers have started skimming past everything, including the accurate findings. The noisy categories are bleeding trust into the precise ones. The fix is surgical: temporarily stop posting the high-false-positive categories while their prompts are rebuilt, keeping the high-precision categories live and useful. Displaying confidence scores fails because it still surfaces every noisy finding to people who have stopped reading. A uniform strictness reduction fails because it damages the categories that were already accurate to compensate for problems isolated elsewhere. Adding few-shot examples across all categories is the right long-term repair on the wrong timeline — it takes weeks, and trust keeps eroding throughout.

Why it works that way

Trust is the shared resource. Once it is gone, even correct findings stop being read, so stopping the bleed comes before improving the noisy prompts.

Decision rule

Trust bleed already in progress? Stop the noise now, fix the prompts after.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Attach a confidence score to every finding so developers can judge which to trust.Still surfaces all the noise to people who have already stopped opening the comments; it does not stop the bleed.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 9
  • Apply a uniform strictness reduction across all categories.Damages the already-precise categories to compensate for category-specific problems; the response must be as targeted as the problem.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 9
  • Keep everything active and gradually add few-shot examples across every category.The right long-term fix on the wrong timeline — trust keeps eroding for the weeks it takes, and effort is wasted on accurate categories.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 5 Q42 (missed), Exam 9

Your record on it

Missed Exam 5 Q42 — EXAM-LOG records: 'chose the slow, eventual few-shot fix over surgically disabling the two noisy finding categories immediately — correct general direction, wrong urgency for a trust-bleed already in progress.' §4.17 has not appeared on a scored exam since (its only later corpus appearance is Exam 9, still unattempted), so the miss stands uncorrected.

D4 §4.6

tool_choice: auto vs any vs a specific tool

Still open

'auto' guarantees nothing, 'any' guarantees SOME tool is called, and {type:'tool', name:'X'} guarantees THAT tool — pick by which guarantee you actually need.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the single most-missed concept in Ram's exam history, so read it slowly. Three modes, three different guarantees. `{"type": "auto"}` lets the model decide whether to call a tool at all — it can still answer in free text, so it offers no structure guarantee whatsoever. `{"type": "any"}` forces a tool call but lets the model pick which one; use it when several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown, or when a 'no issues found' path also needs to be a tool. `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` forces one named tool; use it when a specific step must run first — a mandatory redaction pass, a metadata extraction other steps depend on, a resubmit-correction turn where an older tool is still sitting in the tool list. The trap is treating 'any' as if it were the strong guarantee. It is not: 'any' guarantees a tool call, not that tool.

Why it works that way

Sequencing and structure are two different requirements. 'any' solves structure; only the named form solves sequencing. Choosing 'any' where you needed the named form leaves exactly the gap you were trying to close, and it will look like it works most of the time.

Decision rule

Need SOME structure every time → 'any'. Need THIS tool this turn → {type:'tool', name:'X'}. Never rely on 'auto' plus an instruction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use tool_choice 'any' to make sure a specific mandatory step runs first.'any' guarantees SOME tool is called and lets the model pick — an extraction tool can still run before the mandatory redaction or metadata step.Exam 6, Exam 8 Q17 (missed), Exam 10 Q48 (missed)
  • Force one specific tool to guarantee structured output when several tools are defined.Forcing a specific tool blocks the other legitimate paths — e.g. it forces flag_finding on a clean PR where report_no_issues is the correct call.Exam 7 Q51 (missed)
  • Use 'auto' plus a strong prompt instruction that the model must always call a tool.'auto' permits a plain-text answer regardless of any instruction — that IS the observed failure mode.Exam 3, Exam 7, Exam 10
  • Remove the stale tool from the tool list entirely so only the right one can be called.Permanently removing the tool breaks the earlier stage for every future document; the fix must apply to this turn's decision.Exam 10 Q48 (missed)
  • Strengthen the prompt instruction 'always call X first' rather than changing tool_choice.A prompt instruction is probabilistic — the scenario's own 85% compliance rate is the evidence.Exam 6, Exam 8

Your record on it

Missed on three consecutive scored exams — Exam 7 Q51, Exam 8 Q17, Exam 10 Q48 — each a genuinely different concrete situation. EXAM-LOG's Insights Round 2 names this 'the only trap in this project's history to miss three consecutive scored exams' and recommends reading Domain-4_v2 §4.6 directly rather than relying on further exam exposure. Answered correctly only in Exam 6.

D4 §4.9

Retry cannot conjure absent information

Still open

If the data was never in the source, no retry count and no feedback wording will produce it — make the field nullable and stop retrying.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Retry-with-feedback only fixes errors the model can correct from the context it was given: format, structure, arithmetic. It cannot help when the information is genuinely absent from the source document, or when it lives in a document the pipeline never receives — a purchase-order number on an invoice that never had one, a CVE for a genuinely novel finding, a tracking number that only appears on a separate shipping label. In those cases retries burn tokens for nothing and, worse, the repeated pressure to fill a required field pushes the model toward fabrication. The correct design is schema-level: make the field nullable, accept null as a legitimate answer, and have the pipeline treat 'not found' as a real outcome rather than a failure to retry.

Why it works that way

This is where §4.9 and §4.5 meet. Loop tuning is the wrong layer; the fix is the contract. Keeping a field required 'for data quality' guarantees fabricated values on exactly the documents that lacked it.

Decision rule

Before tuning retries, ask whether the answer is in the document at all. If it is not, the fix is schema design, not loop tuning.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Raise max retries from 3 to 10 (or 5 to 15) so the model has more chances to find the value.Absent information stays absent regardless of retry count — it burns tokens and invites fabrication.Exam 2, Exam 7, Exam 8 Q22 (missed)
  • Strengthen the retry feedback message to demand the value more forcefully.No feedback can conjure data that is not in the document; a more forceful demand only raises fabrication pressure.Exam 2, Exam 7, Exam 8
  • Keep the field required for data quality / downstream reporting completeness.Guarantees fabricated values on documents that lack it, and treats a legitimate 'not present' as a defect.Exam 2, Exam 8 Q22 (missed)
  • Have the model generate a placeholder identifier so downstream tooling always has a value.Forcing a placeholder guarantees fabrication — exactly the outcome nullable fields exist to prevent.Exam 7

Your record on it

Correct in Exam 7 (cve_id nullable), then missed in Exam 8 Q22 — EXAM-LOG lists it as '§4.9 nullable-when-absent' among Exam 8's fresh-section misses. Not re-tested since: Exam 10's §4.9 question tested detected_pattern instead, so the miss stands uncorrected.

D4 §4.14

Prompt chaining for combined tasks

Recovered

When one prompt does two jobs at once and both come out shallow, split it into sequential focused prompts where step 1's output is step 2's input.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The signature is a single prompt asked to do two things — identify issues AND write fixes, enumerate call sites AND rewrite them, decide test scenarios AND write the test code, find citable claims AND draft the narrative. The result is uneven: the first two or three items get real depth, the rest get one-liners, some items are missed and some are handled twice. The fix is to break it into a chain: one prompt whose only job is enumeration or identification, and a second prompt that takes that list as input and does the work. Each stage gets the model's full attention on one well-defined job. Watch the near-miss options: asking for the list first within the same response is not a chain, because the second stage never actually consumes the first stage's output as input.

Why it works that way

Two objectives inside one pass compete for the same attention. Chaining removes the competition without discarding any finding, which is why it beats capping the number of items or asking the model to try harder.

Decision rule

One prompt, two jobs, uneven output? Chain them — step 1's output becomes step 2's input.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Keep one prompt but lengthen it with more detailed instructions for both jobs.Still asks one pass to do two competing jobs at once; more detail on a failing combined instruction does not fix it.Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 10
  • Ask for both in the same response but request the list first.Not a chain — the second stage still does not consume the first stage's actual output as its input.Exam 10
  • Cap the number of items flagged so more effort goes into each one.Trades completeness for depth instead of removing the attention competition; chaining does both.Exam 3
  • Raise max output length, enlarge the context window, or give one stage a bigger token budget.More room does not fix a rushed single-pass reasoning problem — the model is still doing both jobs at once.Exam 5, Exam 8, Exam 10

Your record on it

Missed Exam 5 Q13 (chose a clearer prompt instruction over splitting citation-identification and drafting into a sequential chain, per EXAM-LOG), then correct on scored Exams 8 and 10. Also correct in Exam 4.

D4 §4.19

State assumptions and proceed

Recovered

On a vague request, make a reasonable assumption, say what you assumed, do the work, and invite correction — do not block to ask, and never assume silently.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Asking four or more clarifying questions before doing anything drives 35-40% abandonment, so the corpus's answer for a vague request is to proceed with explicitly stated, reasonable assumptions and invite corrections. Two failure modes sit either side of the correct answer and both are tested every time. Bundling the questions into one compound message is still blocking — it changes packaging, not the demand for upfront effort, and the people who were not going to reply still will not. Silently picking a default is worse than asking, because the requester never learns what was assumed and a review that skipped the path they cared about reads like a clean bill of health. The pattern applies identically to user-facing assistants, automated CI jobs holding a merge queue, and multi-agent systems where a synthesis agent should not block awaiting coordinator clarification.

Why it works that way

A stated assumption is cheap to correct and produces work immediately. A question produces nothing until someone answers, and a hidden default produces work nobody can audit.

Decision rule

Proceed with a stated assumption. Blocking to ask and assuming silently are both wrong; the difference between them is not the point.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Ask all the clarifying questions in one compound message.Still demands upfront effort before anything happens — the compound form is explicitly not the fix.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Pick a sensible default silently and proceed without mentioning it.Hidden defaults leave the requester unable to tell what was assumed when the output does not match intent.Exam 3, Exam 4 Q54 (missed), Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Keep asking one question at a time until every detail is confirmed.Sequential clarification changes pacing, not the number of questions — the exact pattern tied to 35-40% abandonment.Exam 4, Exam 7
  • Keep the blocking question but add a shorter timeout so the queue is not held.Frees the queue by producing nothing — on the requests where nobody replies, the author now gets no work at all.Exam 9

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q54 ('for ambiguous automated requests, proceed with a stated assumption rather than blocking to ask or silently guessing', per EXAM-LOG), then correct on scored Exams 5, 7 and 10.

Key Distinction #19

D4 §4.2

Reasoning cues only for multi-step tasks

Recovered

Add 'think step by step' when the task is multi-step math, multi-stage analysis, comparison across N items, or step-wise transformation — and not otherwise.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A step-by-step reasoning cue measurably improves accuracy, but only on tasks that genuinely have steps. The four documented triggers are multi-step mathematical reasoning, multi-stage analysis, comparison across N items, and step-wise transformation. Comparing retry budgets across five services, computing an effective tax rate from line-item codes and exemptions, or checking every line item against every other for duplicates all qualify. Copying an explicitly labelled value out of a document does not — adding the cue there buys nothing. Watch for the exam pairing this against few-shot: the two techniques fix different failure modes, and swapping one for the other is a documented trap.

Why it works that way

Reasoning cues buy accuracy by forcing enumeration before conclusion. On a one-step task there is nothing to enumerate, so the cue is cost without benefit — and picking it signals you are pattern-matching a technique instead of diagnosing the failure.

Decision rule

Ask whether the task has enumerable steps. If yes, cue it; if it is a single lookup or copy, do not.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Reasoning cues never hurt, so apply them everywhere.The corpus explicitly says do NOT add for single-step tasks; overgeneralizing the technique contradicts stated guidance.Exam 5, Exam 10
  • Add few-shot examples instead — format consistency is the real issue.Few-shot fixes inconsistent format; a reasoning cue fixes reasoning depth. The two solve different failure modes and are not interchangeable.Exam 5 Q60 (missed), Exam 8 (N-item duplicate comparison)
  • Lower the temperature so the multi-step derivation comes out the same way every run.Temperature governs sampling randomness, not whether a multi-step derivation is calculated correctly.Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 8
  • Increase max_tokens so the model has more room to answer.The model is not running out of room — it is making a reasoning error. Wrong lever.Exam 6

Your record on it

Missed three scored exams running — Exam 5 Q60 (swapped a few-shot format fix for a reasoning cue), Exam 6 Q35 (tax-rate calculation), Exam 8 Q19 (chain-of-thought for N-item comparison) — then answered correctly in Exam 10, where the keyed answer was the inverse case: skip the cue for a single-step label copy.
