D4 §4.20

Behavioural drift: accumulated responses dilute the system prompt

Recovered

When a rule holds for a dozen turns then quietly stops at 2,500 tokens, the cause is accumulated assistant output diluting the system prompt — not context overflow.

The full lesson

What is actually true

As assistant responses accumulate in the conversation history, the system prompt's influence dilutes relative to the growing body of the model's own generated content, and the model increasingly pattern-matches its own prior outputs. The scenario always plants two disqualifying facts: the rule held fine for the first N items, and the session is far below any context limit — 2,500, 2,800, 4,000 tokens. Those rule out context-window overflow explicitly. They also rule out the other named misconception: the system prompt does NOT apply only to the first message; it is sent with every single API request, just with diluting relative influence. Watch for plausible-sounding fabricated mechanisms too — a hidden token cap on system prompts, a harness that silently stops re-sending the system prompt, a later document overwriting the rule. None of these exist.

Why it works that way

Correctly naming the mechanism is what points you at the right fix. Drift is a proportion problem, so the fixes change the proportion; overflow would be a capacity problem with completely different remedies.

Decision rule

Rule decays over turns at a low token count? Accumulated assistant output, every time.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The context window has been exceeded, so earlier instructions are being dropped.Impossible at 2,500-4,000 tokens — the scenario's own token count rules overflow out.Exam 5, Exam 6 Q42 (missed), Exam 7, Exam 8
  • The system prompt only applies to the first message in a session.False and explicitly named in the corpus — the system prompt is included in every request.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8
  • A hidden token cap, a silently-dropped system prompt, or a later document overwrote the rule.Fabricated mechanisms with no support in the scenario, competing against the real documented one.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 8

Your record on it

Missed Exam 6 Q42 (first-ever miss of KD #23, per EXAM-LOG), then answered correctly in Exam 8 Q53 — EXAM-LOG's Exam 8 Observations record it as 'recovered', and Exam 10's KD #23 re-confirmation (g13) was also correct. Also correct in Exams 5 and 7.

Key Distinction #23

D4 §4.4

Prefilling to suppress filler phrases

Recovered

To kill 'Certainly!' or 'I apologize for the inconvenience', append a partial assistant message with the direct opening and let Claude continue from it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Prefilling means putting the beginning of the assistant's message into the API call so Claude continues from it rather than generating a fresh response. It is the corpus's designated fix for one specific recurring opening phrase — greetings, apologies, or a prose preamble before JSON. Seeding an opening brace makes the model continue straight into JSON; seeding a direct first sentence makes it skip the pleasantry. The three rival options are all ranked below it: a system-prompt instruction not to greet is probabilistic compliance, lowering temperature targets randomness rather than a specific phrase, and stripping the phrase in post-processing is a fragile downstream patch.

Why it works that way

Prefilling works at generation time and is deterministic about the first tokens — you are not asking the model to avoid something, you are removing the position where it would appear.

Decision rule

One specific unwanted opening phrase, and you control the API call? Prefill it away.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Lower the temperature to reduce variation in how responses open.Temperature controls randomness broadly, not a specific recurring phrase — a low-temperature model can still consistently pick the same apology opening.Exam 5, Exam 7 Q50 (missed), Exam 8
  • Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model never to open with a greeting.Explicitly ranked less reliable than prefilling for suppressing one narrow opening pattern.Exam 7 Q50 (missed), Exam 8
  • Post-process the output to strip greeting phrases before it ships.A fragile workaround that treats the symptom and drifts the moment the preamble is worded differently.Exam 5, Exam 7, Exam 8

Your record on it

Missed Exam 7 Q50 (chose a system-prompt instruction over prefilling), then correct in Exam 8 Q16 — the only one of Exam 7's four flagged sections that cleared on its Exam 8 re-test, per EXAM-LOG's Exam 8 Observations. Also correct in Exam 5.

D4 §4.7

Syntax errors vs semantic errors

Recovered

Strict schemas via tool_use eliminate the entire syntax-error class and do nothing at all for the semantic class.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the domain's organising distinction. Syntax errors are schema violations — malformed JSON, wrong field type, missing required field — and a programmatic validator catches 100% of them deterministically; tool_use with a schema eliminates them at the source. Semantic errors are valid JSON with wrong content: line items that do not sum to the stated total, a value placed in the wrong field, a hallucinated value, a wrong category, a line number that does not belong to the file. These sail through schema validation by definition, because the JSON is valid and only the meaning is wrong. So when a team migrates to tool_use and parse failures drop to zero while reconciliation still finds mismatches, that is the expected outcome, not evidence that something broke. The remaining failures need business-rule validation, cross-field checks, retry-with-feedback and self-correction fields.

Why it works that way

Knowing which class you are in tells you which lever can possibly reach it. Tightening a schema against a semantic error is unfalsifiable work — no JSON Schema constraint can express that numbers sum correctly or that a date belongs in this field rather than that one.

Decision rule

Is the JSON valid? If yes, no schema change can help — you are in the semantic class and need code-side validation.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The schema must be too loose — keep tightening it until the mismatches stop.No schema constraint can verify arithmetic, cross-field placement, or that a value came from the right source line. Tightening cannot reach this defect class.Exam 2, Exam 4 Q51 (missed), Exam 5, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • tool_use is unreliable — revert to prompt-based JSON.Reverting reintroduces the syntax class on top of the unchanged semantic class — strictly worse, two failure classes instead of one.Exam 2, Exam 5, Exam 7, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • A passing validator means the extraction is correct, so nothing further is needed.A validator proves only structural validity; semantic errors clear it by definition. This is the section's named misconception.Exam 2, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Ask the model to double-check its confidence before responding.A vague self-check gives no structural mechanism; the documented answer to this class is cross-field validation or self-correction fields.Exam 8

Your record on it

Missed Exam 4 Q51 ('schema validation guarantees syntax only, never semantic correctness', per EXAM-LOG's Exam 4 traps list), then answered correctly on scored Exams 5, 7, 8 and 10 — four consecutive correct data points on the most heavily repeated concept in the domain.

D4 §4.11

SLA planning: budget the 24-hour worst case

Not yet tested

Submission deadline = downstream deadline minus 24 hours. Plan against the worst case, never the typical one.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Because there is no latency SLA, every batch deadline calculation has to absorb the full 24-hour window. If results are needed in 30 hours, your submission window is 30 minus 24 equals 6 hours. For a recurring pipeline against a 30-hour SLA, split submissions into 4-hour windows so every batch still has its full 24-hour buffer before its own deadline. Planning around 'batches usually finish in an hour' is the documented misconception — the one run that takes 23 hours blows the deadline. Note also that slicing a large job into many small sub-batches does not create margin: each sub-batch needs its own full buffer, so arbitrary hourly slicing just guarantees the late slices have none.

Why it works that way

Latency you cannot bound must be planned as if it will always take the maximum. Anything else is a bet you will lose exactly once, on the run that matters.

Decision rule

Submission deadline = downstream deadline − 24h. Always.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Submit at any point in the window, since batches this size have historically finished within hours.Planning around typical completion ignores the absence of an SLA — the run that takes close to 24 hours blows the deadline.Exam 3
  • Split into hourly sub-batches so results are always trickling in before the deadline.Each sub-batch still needs its own 24-hour buffer; arbitrary slicing does not guarantee that for the late slices.Exam 3
  • Submit the evening before — 'the day before' comfortably covers the timeline.Leaves almost no margin against the documented worst case, and real submission/processing overhead eats the thin remainder.Exam 3

Your record on it

Keyed only in Exam 3, which was generated 2026-07-07 but never attempted (attempted_date null in DASHBOARD-DATA.jsonl). No scored exam has tested batch SLA planning.

D4 §4.11

Tool use IS supported in batches

Not yet tested

A batch request's params mirror a normal Messages API call, tools and multi-turn history included — what it cannot do is execute a tool mid-request.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The v2 corpus corrects an older claim here, so know the current framing. The Batch API does support tool use and multi-turn conversations: a batch request's params are the same as a regular Messages API call, including a tools array and a full message history. Materials claiming 'batches cannot use tools' are wrong. The real constraint is narrower and about the loop, not the fields: each batch request is self-contained, so if the model responds with tool_use, that request completes with that response. Your client cannot execute the tool and return a tool_result mid-request. Continuing the loop requires submitting a follow-up request — in a new batch or synchronously — with the tool result appended.

Why it works that way

The distinction changes what you can architect. You may batch tool-enabled requests; you may not expect a batch request to pause while your client answers a tool call.

Decision rule

Tools in a batch request: fine. Expecting the batch to run the tool for you mid-request: not fine.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The Batch API strips out the tools field, so tool definitions are silently ignored.False — batch accepts tools in a request's params exactly as the synchronous Messages API does. The limitation is mid-request execution, not the field.Exam 3
  • Batch requests can only carry a single fresh message, not a multi-turn history.Batch requests can include full multi-turn histories; this misstates the narrow limitation as a much broader one.Exam 3
  • A batch request can execute a tool call and continue end-to-end like a synchronous loop.Each request is one shot: submit, then a single model response. It cannot pause mid-processing to receive a tool result.Exam 3

Your record on it

Keyed only in Exam 3, which has never been attempted. NOTE A CORPUS CONFLICT: Key Distinctions #14 (v1.1) says batch multi-turn tool calls are 'Not supported — fire-and-forget', while Domain-4_v2 §4.11 v2.0 explicitly marks that claim outdated and false, verified against platform docs 2026-07-06. The Domain-4 v2 framing is the one the mock exams teach.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.11 · Exam 3 · KD #14

Key Distinction #14

D4 §4.13

Confidence scores: a narrow routing aid, not a fix for anything

Not yet tested

Confidence has exactly two documented legitimate uses — a field_confidence float in a schema, and routing findings out of a verification pass — and is a rejected distractor almost everywhere else.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The corpus gives confidence scores two legitimate homes. At schema level (§4.5), where you need a per-field trust signal, add `field_confidence: float [0,1]` alongside the field. At architecture level (§4.13), within an independent verification pass, have the reviewing model self-report confidence alongside each finding so downstream routing can be calibrated — high-confidence findings auto-comment, low-confidence findings go to a human. Now learn the boundary, because this is where the exam actually tests it: confidence is a routing aid applied to output from an already-well-specified process, never a replacement for specifying it. It is explicitly rejected as a substitute for written escalation criteria (§4.15), as a fix for a vague flagging instruction (§4.16), as a fix for a vocabulary gap in an enum (§4.5, D4-08), and as a way to restore developer trust in a noisy review bot (§4.17, D4-32). The reason is the same in every one of those cases: the model is confident and wrong, so the bad output scores high and the threshold never fires.

Why it works that way

Across scored exams, 'add a confidence score' has been a distractor far more often than an answer. Knowing its two narrow legitimate uses is what lets you reject it everywhere else without hesitating.

Decision rule

Confidence routes output from a process that is already well specified. If the criteria, the vocabulary, or the nullability is what's broken, fix that instead.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Use self-rated confidence with a numeric threshold to decide what escalates or auto-applies.Rejected in §4.15 — self-rated confidence is uncalibrated, and the model can be confidently wrong; it adds infrastructure without fixing unclear decision boundaries.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Display confidence scores on every finding to restore developer trust.Rejected in §4.17 — this still surfaces all the noisy findings to people who have stopped opening them, so trust keeps eroding.Exam 2, Exam 3, Exam 5, Exam 9
  • Keep a required field but add a confidence score so low-confidence values can be filtered downstream.Rejected in §4.5 — the schema still demands a value, so the model fabricates one and scores it confidently; the fix is nullability, not measurement.Exam 3, Exam 8

Your record on it

Confidence has never been the keyed answer on any mock exam, scored or unscored — all §4.13 questions test the independent-instance concept (D4-27), and the §4.5 field_confidence row has never been keyed either. It appears only as a rejected distractor, under §4.5 (Exams 3, 8), §4.15 (Exams 3, 6, 7, 9, 10) and §4.17 (Exams 2, 3, 5, 9) — Ram rejected it correctly every time on a scored exam, which is evidence he knows where it is wrong, not that he knows where it is right.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.13 · Domain-4_v2 §4.5 · Domain-4_v2 §4.15 · Domain-4_v2 §4.17

D4 §4.20

The three fixes for behavioural drift

Not yet tested

Inject user-role reminders at conversation breakpoints, replace verbose abstract rules with few-shot examples, or prefill a partial response — matched to which drift you have.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Once you have named drift correctly, the corpus gives three fixes and pairs each with a situation. Persistent behavioural-constraint drift takes user-role reminder messages injected at conversation breakpoints. A long system prompt full of abstract rules that stops being followed after ten to fifteen turns takes something different: replace the verbose rules with few-shot examples demonstrating the behaviour — the exam explicitly prefers this over periodic reminder injection in that case, because reminders address the symptom while the abstract-rules format is the root cause. And where you need to suppress one specific response pattern, prefill a partial assistant response.

Why it works that way

Two of these fixes look interchangeable and are not. Reminder injection maintains a constraint; replacing verbose rules with examples fixes why the constraint was fragile in the first place.

Decision rule

Verbose abstract rules failing after many turns → few-shot examples. Constraint drift generally → reminders at breakpoints. One specific pattern → prefill.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Inject a periodic reminder every 4-5 turns when a 2,800-token system prompt of abstract rules stops being followed.Addresses the symptom, not the root cause — the corpus prefers replacing the verbose rules with few-shot examples in this case.corpus (Domain-4_v2 §4.20 exam scenario)

Your record on it

Never keyed on any mock exam, scored or unscored — all four §4.20 corpus questions test root-cause diagnosis (D4-35), not fix selection. This content exists only in Domain-4_v2 §4.20's Fixes table.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.20

D4 §4.5

Build escape hatches into the enum: 'other' and 'unclear'

Not yet tested

An enum with no escape hatch forces a lie — add 'other' plus a companion detail field for values outside the vocabulary, and 'unclear' for cases the model genuinely cannot decide.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A closed enum is a contract that one of these members is correct, and when none is, the model picks the nearest wrong bucket confidently. The corpus gives two distinct escape hatches for two distinct situations, and the exam tests the difference. When the vocabulary is basically right but new values will keep appearing, add an explicit 'other' member plus a companion free-text detail field, so a novel case is recorded as what it actually is rather than mis-filed — an expired licence header filed as 'style' gets buried in triage. When the value itself is knowable but the model cannot confidently choose among the existing members, the hatch is a different one: add 'unclear' to the enum, because an honest 'unclear' beats a confident wrong category. Keep them apart — 'other' says the vocabulary is incomplete, 'unclear' says the evidence is. Neither is the same as nullable, which is for a value that is genuinely absent or ambiguous in the source (§4.5, D4-07); an unset category on a finding that plainly exists carries no routing signal at all.

Why it works that way

A short vocabulary silently converts novel findings into mislabeled ones, and mislabeled findings get buried in triage. Designing the escape hatch into the schema beats maintaining the enum by hand every time something new appears — and it beats every downstream mechanism, because by the time the wrong label is written the information about why it was wrong is gone.

Decision rule

Vocabulary will grow → 'other' + detail field. Model genuinely cannot decide between existing members → 'unclear'. Value absent or ambiguous in the source → nullable (D4-07).

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a new enum member each time triage discovers a type the vocabulary does not cover.A process patch for a schema problem — every genuinely novel type still gets mis-filed once before anyone can add its member.Exam 9
  • Make the category field nullable so the model can leave it unset when nothing fits.Nullable is for genuinely absent information. Here the finding exists and is describable; an unset category carries no routing signal at all.Exam 9
  • Add a category_confidence score and route low-confidence items to manual triage.Per-field confidence is a routing aid for uncertain values, not a fix for a vocabulary gap — the model is confident and wrong, so it scores high and never routes. See D4-28 for where confidence scores are legitimately useful.Exam 9

Your record on it

Keyed only in Exam 9, which was generated 2026-07-19 but has never been attempted (attempted_date null in DASHBOARD-DATA.jsonl). No scored exam has tested the enum/'other'/'unclear' facet.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.5 · Exam 9

D4 §4.6

tool_use is the structured-output guarantee

Not yet tested

Define a tool whose input schema IS your desired output structure, then read the tool_use block — this is the most reliable way to get schema-compliant JSON.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The tool does not need to do anything. Its purpose is to force schema-conformant JSON, and defining one whose input schema is your target output structure is the corpus's designated mechanism for guaranteed structure. This eliminates the entire class of JSON syntax errors — missing braces, trailing commas, wrong field types. Contrast it with asking nicely in the prompt: 'respond only with valid JSON matching this schema' is a request the model may or may not honour, and prompt-based JSON still returns prose preambles, markdown fences and malformed output. Post-processing free text with a JSON repair library is explicitly rejected as treating the symptom — tool_use removes the problem at the source.

Why it works that way

A pipeline that must always receive parseable structure cannot be built on probabilistic compliance. Tool use moves the guarantee from the model's cooperation into the API's contract.

Decision rule

If a downstream consumer must never see unparseable output, the answer is tool_use with a schema — not a better-worded prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a prompt instruction: 'always respond with JSON matching this schema.'No guarantee — syntax errors and prose wrappers still occur regardless of how the instruction is worded.Exam 3, Exam 7
  • Post-process free-text responses with a JSON repair library.Repairing after the fact treats the symptom; tool_use prevents the prose response from being generated at all.Exam 3
  • tool_use with a strict schema guarantees the output is correct.It guarantees syntactically valid, schema-shaped output. Values can still be semantically wrong — see §4.7.corpus (Domain-4_v2 §4.6 misconception block)

Your record on it

The pure 'tool_use vs prompt-based JSON vs JSON repair' framing was keyed only in Exam 3, which has never been attempted. On scored exams it appears only as a rejected distractor inside §4.6 tool_choice questions and §4.7 questions — so there is no clean scored data point for this proposition on its own.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.6 · Exam 3

D4 §4.8

tool_use does not make code validation redundant

Not yet tested

Tool use enforces structure at generation time; your code still has to check the meaning and defend everything downstream.

The full lesson

What is actually true

It is tempting to argue that if the tool's schema already guarantees shape, a second check in code is dead weight. The corpus is explicit that it is not. Tool use enforces structure at generation time only. Your code still needs to validate the semantic and business rules no JSON schema can express, and to provide defence-in-depth for whatever consumes the output downstream. What tool use genuinely does make redundant is the raw JSON parse check — which is precisely the part you would be keeping if you trimmed the layer down to 'just a parse check', discarding the layer's actual value. And wrapping ingestion in a silent try/except compounds the mistake by discarding failures without any signal anyone can act on.

Why it works that way

The schema constrains shape; validators check meaning. Deleting the meaning check because the shape check exists is the exact confusion §4.7 warns about, applied to your own architecture.

Decision rule

Keep the code layer. Delete only the parse check if you want to trim something.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Drop the separate validation module — tool_use already enforces the schema.Tool use enforces structure at generation time; code should still check business rules like sum(line_items) == total and guard downstream consumers.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Keep only a JSON parse check, since tool_use already guarantees every field's type.The parse check is the one part tool use genuinely does make redundant — keeping only that discards exactly the semantic checks that mattered.Exam 9
  • Wrap ingestion in a try/except so anything that slips through is skipped quietly.Business-rule violations reach production unchallenged, and the ones that do not vanish without a signal anyone can act on.Exam 9

Your record on it

Keyed only in Exam 9, which has never been attempted. On scored exams it appears only as a rejected distractor (Exams 6 and 7, both answered correctly), so there is no direct scored data point for it as the keyed answer.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.8 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 9

D4 §4.1

Few-shot examples beat instruction refinement

Solid

When prose instructions already produce inconsistent output, add examples — not more instructions.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When your output format is inconsistent and you have already written the instruction, writing the instruction again more explicitly is the losing move. The instruction is the thing that is failing; adding adjectives and emphasis to it gives the model more text to interpret, not a pattern to reproduce. Three to four few-shot examples showing the exact required shape — identified issue, precise location, concrete change — give the model something concrete to copy. This is one of the exam's cleanest either/or pairs: 'refine the instruction further' is a distractor almost every time it appears against a few-shot option. The corpus also names the four situations where few-shot is the designated technique in the first place: prose instructions that produce inconsistent output, ambiguous tool selection, multi-issue requests where the examples must demonstrate correct decomposition and sequencing, and escalation calibration ('escalate this / don't escalate this' — see §4.15). All four are pattern-transmission problems, which is why examples rather than more prose are the lever in each.

Why it works that way

Format consistency is a pattern-matching problem, and examples are the highest-bandwidth way to transmit a pattern. Instruction text competes with everything else in the prompt for interpretation; an example is unambiguous.

Decision rule

If an instruction has already been written once and output is still inconsistent, the next move is examples, never a longer instruction.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Expand the instruction with more explicit adjectives and a longer definition of what 'concrete' and 'actionable' mean.The instruction is already failing — more text does not resolve format inconsistency. Few-shot beats instruction-refinement here.Exam 2 (Claude Code CI block); recurs as a distractor in Exams 4 and 8
  • Lower the temperature so the field is generated more deterministically.Temperature controls randomness, not adherence to a specific output structure. Wrong mechanism entirely.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 8
  • Add a post-processing pass that rewrites vague output into a more detailed version.Patches the symptom downstream; it cannot invent a concrete fix the model never reasoned about.Exam 2

Your record on it

§4.1 appeared on three scored exams (4, 5, 8) with zero misses. An instruction-refinement distractor was present and rejected on two of them — Exam 4 ('rewrite the instruction to state even more explicitly') and Exam 8 ('rewrite the prose instruction with a longer, more explicit list of phrasing rules'); Exam 5's §4.1 question offered no instruction-refinement option at all, so it is not evidence for this proposition. The pure format-consistency framing itself was only keyed in Exam 2, which was never attempted — so the signal here rests on distractor rejection, not on a keyed answer.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.1 · Exam 2 · Exam 4 · Exam 8 · KD #16

Key Distinction #16

D4 §4.1

Target 4-6 examples at the ambiguous cases

Solid

Aim a small set of examples exactly where the model gets it wrong, each with a rationale — never pad the prompt with clear cases.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The exam is emphatic about example selection: 4 to 6 examples aimed precisely at the borderline cases the model currently misroutes, each carrying a short rationale for why that choice was made over the alternative. Do not add 10 to 15 examples of clear, unambiguous cases — those cover exactly the requests the model already handles correctly and teach it nothing about the edge it is failing on. This applies identically to ambiguous tool selection, ambiguous document classification, severity-boundary judgements, and normalizing messy phrasings into an enum: find the failure region, then build the examples there.

Why it works that way

Examples are expensive prompt real estate. Spending them on cases the model already gets right is pure waste; spending them on the decision boundary is where they change behaviour.

Decision rule

Count the examples and check where they point: 4-6, all aimed at the failure region, each with a rationale.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add 10-15 examples of clear, unambiguous requests so the model sees many correct mappings.Clear-cut examples do not address the ambiguous edge cases where misrouting actually occurs — the documented anti-pattern.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 8
  • Add a single example of the most common ambiguous request and let the model generalize.One example is too thin to cover the range of ambiguous phrasings; the corpus calls for 4-6.Exam 2 ('one worked example per tool' and 'a single example of the most common ambiguous request'), Exam 5 ('a single detailed example per tool')
  • Draw examples at random from the historical archive, regardless of whether routing succeeded on them.Random sampling is not targeted at the known failure mode and mostly reinforces cases already handled correctly.Exam 5 (Structured Data Extraction block)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4 (twice — test-file placement and severity-boundary), 5 (receipt/donation borderline) and 8 (payment-terms normalization); correct every time. No §4.1 miss appears anywhere in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.1 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · Exam 8 · KD #18

Key Distinction #18

D4 §4.10

Self-correction is structural, not conversational

Solid

Build the re-derivation into the output schema — stated value, independently calculated value, and a conflict boolean — so contradictions surface as data on every extraction.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Have the model emit both the value as written in the source and a value it independently re-derives, plus a boolean flag when they disagree: stated_total, calculated_total, conflict_detected. This catches arithmetic drift — the extraction grabbed a subtotal, or the source document itself is internally inconsistent — and lets your pipeline route conflicts to review at extraction time instead of silently trusting either number. The pattern generalizes well beyond financial totals: stated vs computed severity, a stated exhibit count vs the headings actually found, a self-reported package count vs the actual diffs, an enumerated list of API changes vs the compatibility verdict derived from them. The section's named misconception is that self-correction means asking 'are you sure?' after the answer. It does not — that produces no machine-readable signal and nothing the pipeline can act on.

Why it works that way

Detection at extraction time beats detection in a later reconciliation, and a boolean beats a paragraph. The whole design is about producing a signal a pipeline can route on, automatically, on every single record.

Decision rule

Extract both the claimed value and an independently derived one, and flag disagreement with a boolean.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a prompt instruction to 'be especially careful with totals' or 'double-check before finalizing'.A vague instruction with no detection mechanism — it cannot surface a mismatch as a signal the pipeline can act on.Exam 2, Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Run a monthly (or weekly) reconciliation report to catch mismatches.Detects after posting, on a sample; the pattern's entire point is moving detection to the moment of extraction, on every record.Exam 2, Exam 6, Exam 8, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Ask the model, right after it answers, whether it is sure the value is correct.The section's named misconception — self-correction is built into the schema, not requested as a conversational follow-up.Exam 2, Exam 6
  • Add a free-text notes field where the model explains its reasoning for reviewers.Not machine-readable and does not structurally flag disagreement — a reviewer must still read every note.Exam 4
  • Run a full second independent extraction pass and compare the totals.Duplicates the cost of the entire extraction instead of adding a lightweight structural re-derivation of one value.Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 6, 8 and 10 — four different framings (severity, package count, exhibit count, parts cost) and correct every time. No §4.10 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.10 · Exam 2 · Exam 4 · Exam 6 · Exam 8 · Exam 10

D4 §4.11

Batch vs synchronous: match API to latency tolerance

Solid

Batch gives 50% off with no latency SLA and up to a 24-hour window — so anything a human or pipeline is blocking on stays synchronous.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The Message Batches API costs 50% of synchronous calls, processes within a window of up to 24 hours, and carries no latency SLA — most batches finish much faster, but you cannot rely on that. The routing rule is latency tolerance, not frequency, volume or cost. A pre-merge PR check blocks a developer, so it stays synchronous no matter how often it runs. A live single-document lookup a support rep waits on during a call stays synchronous. An overnight tech-debt report, a nightly test-generation job, a weekly security audit, a 10,000-document backlog, a nightly re-run of yesterday's failures — all non-blocking, all batch. Refusing batch everywhere because of the SLA risk discards real savings on genuinely non-blocking work; batching everywhere for the discount leaves someone waiting up to a day.

Why it works that way

The discount is real and worth capturing, but it is bought with latency you cannot bound. Sorting workloads by who is waiting is the only assignment rule that survives contact with production.

Decision rule

Is a human or a blocking pipeline waiting on this result? Synchronous. Otherwise batch.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Batch the most frequently-run job to maximize savings.Frequency is not the deciding factor — a blocking pre-merge check is exactly what batch is wrong for, however often it runs.Exam 4
  • Move everything to batch — every job eventually completes and the savings apply across the board.'Eventually completes' ignores that some tasks need an immediate response; developers would block for up to 24 hours with no SLA.Exam 4, Exam 5
  • Keep everything synchronous — the lack of a latency SLA is too risky to use anywhere.Discards real savings on workloads that are genuinely non-blocking; the mismatch applies only to the blocking task.Exam 4
  • Batch is just a 50%-cheaper synchronous API with a delay, so poll faster.The section's named misconception — there is no latency SLA, and every deadline calculation must absorb the full 24-hour worst case.corpus (Domain-4_v2 §4.11 misconception block)

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4 (three CI analyses) and 5 (three extraction workloads, tagged KD #14) — correct both times. No §4.11 miss appears in EXAM-LOG across Exams 4-10.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.11 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · KD #14

Key Distinction #14

D4 §4.11

custom_id is the join key

Solid

Batch results can arrive in any order — custom_id is the only correct way to match a result back to its request.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There is no guaranteed correspondence between submission order and result order in a batch. Assign a meaningful, unique custom_id to every request in every batch — something like 'doc-invoice-2024-001' — and use it to link each result to its originating document, to identify exactly which items failed, and to avoid re-processing the ones that succeeded. Matching results back by position is the documented anti-pattern, and its failure mode is the dangerous kind: it does not error, it silently mis-joins your data. Note also what custom_id cannot do — it tells you which requests failed, but it cannot repair a systematic prompt defect that caused all of them to fail the same way.

Why it works that way

A silent mis-join corrupts data without raising anything you can alert on. The join key is cheap insurance against the failure you would never notice.

Decision rule

Never rely on batch result ordering. Every request gets a meaningful unique custom_id.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Match results back to inputs by submission order and re-run any position that returned no output.Ordering is not guaranteed — this silently mis-joins data rather than failing loudly.Exam 2
  • Skip prompt validation and rely on custom_id to sort out failures afterwards.custom_id identifies which requests failed; it cannot fix a systematic prompt defect, and the answer may simply be 'all of them'.Exam 2

Your record on it

Carried inside Exam 10's selective-re-submission question ('identify the 12 failures by custom_id'), answered correctly. The 'match by submission order' misconception appears only as a distractor in Exam 2, which is unscored — so this concept has never been keyed on its own in a scored exam.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.11 · Exam 2 · Exam 10

D4 §4.11

Selective re-submission after partial failure

Solid

Re-submit only the failures, identified by custom_id, and fix the cause first — never the whole batch, never unchanged.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The canonical scenario: you submit 100 (or 200, or 400) documents, most succeed, a handful fail because they exceeded a per-request limit. Two things must both be true in the correct answer. First, re-submit only the failures — identified by custom_id — because re-submitting the whole batch pays again for every success and may produce duplicate downstream results. Second, modify the strategy before re-submitting: those items failed for a structural reason, so chunk the oversized documents. Context-limit errors are not transient; re-submitting them unchanged fails again, and the batch discount does not make cost-tolerant repetition correct. Waiting for the next scheduled run is equally wrong — it neither fixes the cause nor stops the delay.

Why it works that way

Partial failure is the normal case at batch scale. Handling it well is the difference between a pipeline that self-heals and one that quietly doubles its bill or its data.

Decision rule

Only the failures, by custom_id, and only after changing what made them fail.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Re-submit the entire batch so everything is processed uniformly.Pays again for every success and can produce duplicate downstream results.Exam 2, Exam 10
  • Re-submit the failures unchanged — the batch discount makes retries cheap.They failed for a structural reason; unchanged re-submission repeats the same failure.Exam 2, Exam 10
  • Let the next scheduled nightly run pick up the failures alongside new documents.Does not fix the underlying cause and needlessly delays items already identified by custom_id.Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 10 (12 of 200 inspection reports exceeded a per-request limit) — answered correctly. Exam 2's version is unscored. No §4.11 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.11 · Exam 2 · Exam 10

D4 §4.11

Sample-first iteration before a large batch

Solid

Validate the prompt synchronously on a small representative sample, refine until it passes, and only then submit the full volume.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Before committing 8,000 or 240,000 documents to a batch, run the extraction prompt synchronously on a small representative sample for fast feedback, refine prompt and schema until the sample validates cleanly, and only then submit the whole thing. This maximizes first-pass success and avoids paying — and waiting up to 24 hours — to discover a prompt defect replicated across every request. Submitting the full batch and iterating on it costs a full batch plus up to a day per iteration, and the discount does not make that cheap. Splitting into two untested halves still commits the unvalidated prompt at scale, twice. Spreading submissions across the day addresses scheduling, not correctness.

Why it works that way

A prompt defect at batch scale is replicated instantly across every request. The cost of finding it on ten documents versus ten thousand is the entire argument.

Decision rule

Never send an unvalidated prompt to a large batch. Sample synchronously, refine, then commit.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Submit the full batch now and iterate on the whole batch if validation rates look low.Each iteration costs a full batch and up to 24 hours; the defect is replicated across every request before it is caught.Exam 2, Exam 8
  • Split into two halves so a prompt defect only affects half.Still commits the unvalidated prompt at scale, twice, without ever checking correctness on a small sample first.Exam 8
  • Split into hourly sub-batches submitted through the day.Addresses scheduling, not the risk that a prompt defect ruins the whole run.Exam 2
  • Skip the batch entirely and run everything synchronously overnight.This is a non-blocking latency-tolerant workload — exactly what batch fits; abandoning it does not address prompt correctness.Exam 8

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 8 (8,000-file nightly vulnerability scan) — answered correctly. Exam 2's 240,000-document version is unscored. No §4.11 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.11 · Exam 2 · Exam 8

D4 §4.12

Multi-pass review beats one big pass

Solid

Inconsistent depth across many items is attention dilution — fix it with a focused pass per item plus a separate integration pass, not a bigger context window.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The symptom is unmistakable: thorough, specific analysis on the first two or three items, then shallow one-liners for the rest, plus contradictory verdicts where the same pattern is flagged in item 3 and missed in item 9. The root cause is attention dilution from processing many items at once, and the fix is structural — one focused pass per file or document for local issues, plus a separate integration pass that examines cross-item data flows. The exam's flagged trap is switching to a larger model with a bigger context window: a larger window does not fix attention quality, and the items already fit. Once the per-item split is in place, a defect that spans files (a helper's return type changes and three callers elsewhere go unflagged) needs the integration pass specifically — giving every per-file pass the whole diff as background just reinstates the dilution.

Why it works that way

More tokens available is not the same as consistent attention per token. The quality problem is about how much the model is holding at once, which is a decomposition question, not a capacity one.

Decision rule

Front-loaded thoroughness that fades across items = attention dilution. Split into focused passes, then add an integration pass.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Switch to a larger model with a bigger context window so everything fits with headroom.The exam's explicitly flagged trap — larger context does not fix attention quality, and the items already fit.Exam 5, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Cap the batch or PR size so every review gets the depth the first items received.Papers over the problem instead of fixing it for realistic sizes, and leaves the remainder unplanned.Exam 5, Exam 7
  • Repeat the instruction to 'check every item equally' within the same combined pass.An instruction does not address attention dilution; the root cause remains structurally unaddressed.Exam 6, Exam 7
  • Give every per-file pass the full diff as background.Reintroduces the many-items-at-once condition that caused the dilution in the first place.Exam 9

Key Distinction #17

D4 §4.13

Independent review needs a separate instance

Solid

A model that generated the output is anchored to its own reasoning — real review means a fresh request containing only the artifact, never a second pass in the same conversation.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Self-review inside the generating session does not work, and the reason is specific: the model still has its own generation reasoning in context, so it re-reads its own justifications and confirms them. The blind spots that produced the bug survive the re-check. True independence means routing the artifact to a second Claude instance with no access to the first instance's reasoning — a fresh request containing only the code or draft plus the review criteria, not the generation conversation. Without the generator's rationalizations in context, the reviewer evaluates the work on its own merits. Three rival options all fail identically: adding 'review your own work thoroughly' to the generator's prompt, enabling extended thinking so the same anchored instance reasons longer, or asking for a second (or third) pass in the same conversation.

Why it works that way

This is an architecture decision, not a prompting one. Anchoring is a property of what is in context, so the only lever that removes it is a context boundary.

Decision rule

If the reviewer can see why the generator did it, it is not an independent review.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Ask for a second review pass within the same conversation.The section's named misconception — the same-conversation pass still carries the full generation reasoning and tends to reaffirm it.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Enable extended thinking on the generating instance before it reviews.More reasoning by the same anchored instance is not independent scrutiny.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Add 'review your own work thoroughly before finishing' to the generation prompt.Self-review inside the same context inherits the same blind spots that produced the original output.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 6 and 7 — correct every time. No §4.13 miss appears in EXAM-LOG. Exam 9's synthesis-subagent framing is unscored.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.13 · Exam 4 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D4 §4.15

Explicit escalation criteria, not confidence thresholds

Solid

When an agent escalates the easy cases and attempts the hard ones, the decision boundary is undefined — write explicit escalate-when / resolve-when criteria with few-shot examples.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The diagnostic signature is inverted routing: the human queue is full of routine cases the agent was authorized to handle, while genuinely complex edge cases were settled autonomously and later reversed. That pattern means no written guidance defines which cases go where. The fix is explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt — 'escalate when [scenario]' and 'resolve autonomously when [scenario]' — paired with few-shot examples distinguishing simple from complex. Every alternative is rejected for a named reason: a self-rated confidence score with a routing threshold is uncalibrated infrastructure that leaves the boundary undefined (raising the threshold from 8 to 9 just applies a stricter cutoff to a broken measure); a separately trained classifier is overkill for what is a prompt-design problem, and it inherits the same ambiguity; and blunt proxies like customer sentiment, currency count, or 'escalate everything by default' flood the queue without stating a boundary at all.

Why it works that way

Routing quality is a function of how clearly the boundary is written down. Adding a layer that guesses the boundary cannot outperform simply stating it.

Decision rule

Escalating simple cases while attempting complex ones = undefined boundary. Write the boundary, with examples of both sides.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Have the model self-rate confidence 1-10 and auto-route below a threshold.Self-reported confidence is uncalibrated — confidently wrong cases sail through, which the reversed decisions already demonstrate.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Train a separate classifier model to pre-route every case.Overkill infrastructure for a prompt-design problem; the classifier inherits the same unclear boundary.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9, Exam 10
  • Use a blunt proxy — negative sentiment, more than one currency, always escalate by default.Proxies do not track real complexity and flood the human queue with resolvable cases, worsening the metric they were meant to fix.Exam 6, Exam 9, Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 6, 7 and 10 — correct every time. No §4.15 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.15 · Exam 6 · Exam 7 · Exam 10

D4 §4.16

Replace abstract instructions with testable criteria

Solid

'Flag anything unusual' produces arbitrary output — replace vague intent with a criterion you could check by hand.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When identical situations get different verdicts across runs and reviewers say the behaviour feels arbitrary, the root cause is an abstract instruction, not randomness. 'Rate severity appropriately', 'check that comments are accurate', 'flag risky changes', 'report code that is no longer used', 'make sure new endpoints have good test coverage' — each leaves the model to invent a definition per run. Replace them with explicit, testable criteria: 'flag a comment only when the behaviour it claims contradicts the code's actual behaviour'; 'flag a symbol only when the diff removes its last remaining caller'; 'flag a change only when a function used outside its own service directory has its signature, return type, or behaviour altered'; define critical/high/medium/low each with a concrete example. The test is whether two people applying the criterion would reach the same verdict.

Why it works that way

Inconsistency from an underspecified concept is not stochastic noise, so no sampling parameter reaches it. The model needs a rule, and only a rule fixes it.

Decision rule

If you cannot write the criterion as something you could check by hand, the model cannot apply it consistently either.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Reword the instruction more emphatically — 'use better judgment', 'ALWAYS be REALLY comprehensive', 'apply the criteria consistently'.Still the same abstract instruction; intensity is not specificity, and restating a vague word without defining it adds no signal.Exam 3, Exam 4, Exam 5, Exam 10
  • Lower the temperature so behaviour is more deterministic run to run.The inconsistency comes from an underspecified concept, not sampling variance.Exam 3, Exam 8
  • Move to a larger model or a bigger context window so it infers the intended scope.A larger model does not fix an under-specified instruction — the definitional gap survives any model size.Exam 2, Exam 4, Exam 9
  • Shift the threshold — flag more, flag less, or always err toward flagging when uncertain.A volume adjustment changes how much is flagged without fixing which things get flagged.Exam 8, Exam 10
  • Add a self-confidence score, a consensus filter across two runs, or a second independent reviewer.Scoring or filtering sits on top of the ambiguity instead of removing it — a confidently-applied wrong definition scores high and reproduces across runs.Exam 2, Exam 5, Exam 9, Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 5, 8 and 10 — four different framings (test coverage, tax_id flagging, cross-service impact, unusual inspection values) and correct every time. No §4.16 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Domain-4_v2 §4.16 · Exam 4 · Exam 5 · Exam 8 · Exam 10

D4 §4.18

Give Claude what already exists

Solid

Claude can only avoid duplicating what it can see — put the existing tests, config, or prior findings in the prompt.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a tool suggests ten test cases and six duplicate existing ones, or re-proposes a fix already merged in a sibling service, or re-raises a suggestion a developer already replied to, the cause is simply that the relevant context was never in the prompt. Include the existing test file, the existing vendor-mapping config, the already-merged diff, or the prior round's findings and replies. The rejected alternatives are all indirect: reducing the requested count assumes a priority ordering that has nothing to do with duplication; keyword-matching post-processors are fragile and miss semantically identical items phrased differently; and an instruction like 'check whether a similar fix exists' or 'never repeat a prior suggestion' asks the model to recall information it was never given.

Why it works that way

Deduplication is a knowledge problem, not a filtering problem. Nothing downstream can reliably reconstruct what the model should have known upstream.

Decision rule

Duplicate suggestions mean missing context. Put the existing artefact in the prompt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Reduce the number of suggestions requested so only the best ones appear.Assumes a priority ordering unrelated to whether something already exists; may suppress genuinely new items.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7
  • Post-process with keyword matching against prior names, comments or commit messages.Fragile surface-level matching that misses semantically identical items phrased differently.Exam 3, Exam 6, Exam 7
  • Add an instruction to check for existing work, or never repeat a prior suggestion.Without the prior context in the prompt, the instruction has nothing concrete to check against.Exam 3, Exam 7
  • Have a second instance regenerate the list independently and merge the two.Neither instance can see the existing set, so both carry the same duplication risk.Exam 6

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 6 (vendor-mapping config) and 7 (prior review round's findings and replies) — correct both times. No §4.18 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Domain-4_v2 §4.18 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D4 §4.3

Persistent behavioural rules live in the system prompt

Solid

Tone, persona, standing behavioural rules and response-format requirements belong in the system prompt — nowhere else holds authority for a whole conversation.

The full lesson

What is actually true

If a constraint has to hold for the entire conversation — stay terse, always cite the policy section, never guess at an unstated rule, always render dates as ISO-8601, never wrap JSON in prose — it belongs in the system prompt, which is sent with every single request. The three distractors are always the same three and each fails for its own reason: the first user message loses authority as the conversation grows around it; an environment variable never reaches the model at all, so it has zero effect on behaviour; and a first assistant message is just prior output the model is free to drift away from. Prefilling is a fourth near-miss — it is a mechanism for steering one specific response, not for setting a standing rule.

Why it works that way

The system prompt is the only position in the request that carries the same standing weight on turn 1 and turn 50. Everything else is content the model weighs against everything else in context.

Decision rule

If the rule must survive to the last turn, it goes in the system prompt. Placement, not reinforcement.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Put the rules in the first user message of each request so they are the first thing the model sees.A user message loses authority as the conversation accumulates; it is not re-asserted with standing weight on every request.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • Set the rules as environment variables the deployment or CI step exports.Environment variables configure the process, not the model — nothing in an exported variable reaches Claude's context.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 7, Exam 9
  • State the rules in the first assistant message as an opening commitment.A first assistant message is prior output the model can deviate from; it carries strictly less authority than a system prompt.Exam 4, Exam 6, Exam 9
  • Re-send the rules as a user-role reminder after every few turns.Each reminder is just another user message that later content dilutes again — repetition patches the symptom and leaves the constraint outside the only position that holds.Exam 9

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 4, 6 and 7 — all correct; no §4.3 miss appears in EXAM-LOG. Exam 9's version remains unscored.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.3 · Exam 4 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D4 §4.4

Injecting real-time context mid-session

Solid

New information that arrived mid-conversation goes as a prefix on the next user message, not as a system-prompt rebuild or a synthetic turn.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When something changes during a live session — a webhook fires saying the package shipped, a specialist corrects a misread vendor name on document 14 — you need that fact in the model's context for the very next response. The documented mechanism is to prefix it to the next user message: 'Your package has shipped. Now: [user message].' Rebuilding the system prompt would mean reconstructing the session; sending a standalone synthetic user message breaks the natural dialogue flow; batching corrections to the end of the session delays the fact past the point where it was needed.

Why it works that way

The API is stateless — the only way a new fact reaches the model is by riding in on the next request. Prefixing the user message is the lightest-weight way to do that without restructuring anything.

Decision rule

Mid-session fact that must land on the next response? Prefix the next user message.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rebuild the system prompt to include the new information.Requires reconstructing session context — heavy and unnecessary compared with a message prefix.Exam 6
  • Send the update as a separate synthetic user message.A synthetic message unrelated to the actual submission breaks the natural flow of the conversation.Exam 6
  • Batch all corrections and apply them at the end of the session.Delays the correction past the point it was needed — the very next document.Exam 6

Your record on it

Tested once on a scored exam — Exam 6 (mid-session vendor-name correction) — answered correctly; no §4.4 context-injection miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.4 · Exam 6

D4 §4.5

Nullable fields prevent fabrication

Solid

Mark a field required and non-nullable only if the data is ALWAYS in the source — otherwise the schema itself pressures the model to invent a value.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the highest-frequency schema question in the domain and it always has the same shape: an audit finds that some percentage of extractions carry a plausible-looking identifier that traces to nothing real, and investigation shows those source documents simply never contained one. The cause is the schema. A required, non-nullable field is a contract demanding a value, and when the data is genuinely absent the model satisfies the contract by fabricating. The fix is a schema change — make the field nullable and drop it from required so the model can honestly return null — and 'not found' becomes a legitimate pipeline outcome, not a failure. The same lever covers the adjacent case in the §4.5 table: where a value is present in the source but genuinely ambiguous, nullable lets the output preserve the ambiguity instead of resolving it by guess. Every rival option leaves the pressure in place: an anti-fabrication instruction is probabilistic compliance competing against the schema's own constraint; a confidence score only measures the fabrication after it happens; a downstream reconciliation job detects it later; and replacing the field with free text throws away structure for cases that extract fine.

Why it works that way

Completeness by fabrication is worse than honest absence, because a fabricated value looks exactly like a real one to every downstream consumer. Nullability is the one lever that removes the pressure rather than measuring its output.

Decision rule

Required and non-nullable only when the value is always present in the source. Anything sometimes absent is nullable.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Keep the field required but add a system-prompt instruction never to invent a value.The prompt cannot reliably override a structural demand the schema is still making — the fix is the schema, not another instruction.Exam 2, Exam 8
  • Keep the field required and add a confidence score so low-confidence values can be filtered later.A confidence score does not relieve the pressure — the model still must supply some value, confidently wrong or not.Exam 3, Exam 8
  • Keep the field required and add a format/plausibility validator.A plausible fabricated value matches the format by construction; this is a semantic error and no format constraint can catch it.Exam 3, Exam 6
  • Remove the field entirely, or replace it with free text, since it cannot always be found.That discards the genuinely available values along with the fabricated ones — nullable preserves the real data while allowing absence.Exam 6, Exam 8
  • Lower the temperature so the model stops generating fabricated identifiers.Temperature controls randomness, not schema-driven pressure to fill a required field.Exam 2

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 6 (publication_year) and 8 (vat_registration_number) — both correct. No §4.5 miss appears in EXAM-LOG. Note the sharp split inside Exam 8 itself: this §4.5 framing (audit finds fabricated values) was answered correctly, while the near-identical §4.9 framing (retry loop keeps failing on an absent value, Q22) was missed — see D4-17. Mastery here is of the fabrication-audit entry point, not of the retry-loop entry point.

Domain-4_v2 §4.5 · Exam 2 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 8

D4 §4.5

Format normalization belongs in the prompt

Solid

The schema constrains the output's shape; the prompt governs how messy source formats map into it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When source documents write dates as '3/14', '14 March' and '2024-03-14', or durations as '3.5 hrs', '3h30m' and '210 min', the strict output schema alone will not resolve them. Put explicit normalization rules for each source format directly in the extraction prompt, alongside the schema. The two work together and are not substitutes. Loosening the schema to accept any string and normalizing downstream reintroduces exactly the inconsistency the schema exists to prevent; adding a 'format' enum records which style was seen instead of converting it; and retrying does nothing, because nothing about the request has changed.

Why it works that way

A schema is a shape contract, not a transformation spec. Mapping rules are semantic instructions, so they have to live where the model reads instructions.

Decision rule

Messy inputs, strict outputs? Schema for shape, prompt for the mapping rules — both, not one.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Loosen the schema to accept any string and normalize in a downstream script.Reintroduces the inconsistency the schema exists to prevent and pushes the work downstream instead of solving it at extraction.Exam 10
  • Add a format enum so the model flags which style it encountered.Records the style instead of converting it — downstream consumers still handle three value shapes.Exam 10
  • Retry the extraction until the output finally complies.Treats a format-mapping gap as a random model error; nothing about the request changed, so nothing about the output will.Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested once on a scored exam — Exam 10 (inspection-report dates and labor hours) — answered correctly; Exam 10's only D4 miss was Q48 on §4.6.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.5 · Exam 10

D4 §4.8

Programmatic validation lives in your code

Solid

The validation layer sits in your code AFTER the model responds — typed models check structure deterministically and custom validators encode the business rules no schema can express.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Never trust model output unvalidated. Pydantic (or any equivalent typed-schema library) gives you four things: deterministic structural validation of types, requiredness and enum membership; semantic validation through custom validators that encode business logic like sum(line_items) == total or start_date < end_date or 'this line must fall inside a changed hunk'; a validation error message that becomes the feedback for the retry prompt; and a single definition that can generate the tool's JSON Schema. When a schema cannot express an ordering relationship between two fields — both are perfectly valid ISO-8601 strings — a code validator is the only thing that can check it.

Why it works that way

Schemas describe shape. Business rules describe relationships between values, and those relationships are where real-world extraction quality lives.

Decision rule

If the rule relates two values to each other or to the outside world, it is a code validator, not a schema constraint.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a boolean field and have the model self-report whether the rule holds.Not independent verification — the same model that got it wrong can just as easily misjudge its own flag.Exam 10
  • Add tighter string-format constraints to both fields.Both values are already valid and correctly typed; no format tightening can express an ordering relationship between two separate fields.Exam 10
  • Add a system-prompt reminder that the rule must hold.Probabilistic guidance — and a batch that already passed schema validation while violating the rule is the evidence it is not reliably followed.Exam 10
  • Replace the validation layer with a weekly audit of sampled outputs.Sampling detects a fraction of violations after they have shipped, and gives the retry loop no per-item error to feed back.Exam 9

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 10 (inspection_date vs next_due_date ordering) — correct. No §4.8 miss appears anywhere in EXAM-LOG across Exams 4-10.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.8 · Exam 9 · Exam 10

D4 §4.8

One source of truth for the schema

Solid

Generate the tool's JSON Schema from your typed model so the tool contract and the code validator can never drift apart.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The classic failure is two hand-maintained definitions of the same structure — the tool's JSON schema in one file, a validation class in another — that quietly diverge when someone adds a field or a severity level to one and not the other. Findings then fail validation silently in production until someone traces it. The architectural fix is to define the structure once as a Pydantic (or equivalent) model and generate the tool's input schema from it, so both consumers derive from one definition. Every rival option is a process patch on an architecture problem: a PR checklist item, a two-reviewer sign-off rule, a nightly job that diffs the two files, or merging them under whoever edited last. All of them leave two artefacts someone must remember to keep in sync — which is exactly the failure that already happened.

Why it works that way

Drift between a generation-time contract and a validation-time contract fails silently, which is the worst failure mode there is. Making drift structurally impossible beats making it detectable.

Decision rule

Two definitions of one structure is the bug. Generate one from the other; never keep both by hand.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a code-review checklist item requiring both files to be updated together.A process patch for an architecture problem — it depends on every future editor remembering, which is the failure that already occurred twice.Exam 3, Exam 6
  • Add a nightly job that diffs the schema file against the validation class and alerts on mismatch.Still two independently maintained files that can drift; it detects the problem after the fact instead of eliminating it.Exam 7
  • Require two reviewers to sign off on any change to either file.A process control that does not touch the underlying duplication causing the drift.Exam 7
  • Increase the retry limit so transient mismatches resolve themselves.A definitional mismatch is not transient — retrying the same request produces the same failure every time.Exam 3

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exams 6 and 7 (both drift scenarios) — correct both times. No §4.8 miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.8 · Exam 3 · Exam 6 · Exam 7

D4 §4.9

Retry with the SPECIFIC validation error

Solid

A retry request carries three things — the original document, the previous failed extraction, and the exact validation error. 'Try again' carries none of them.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The validate-then-retry loop is: send document plus prompt, receive JSON, validate against schema and business rules, and on failure resend with the original document, the previous incorrect extraction, and the specific error — 'Field total = 150, but sum(line_items) = 145. Re-check values.' The specificity is the whole mechanism. When the feedback is a generic 'extraction failed, please retry', the model has no idea which field was wrong, so it edits the wrong one and the loop burns attempts without converging. This class of error — wrong date format, misplaced currency symbol, a value in the wrong field, an arithmetic inconsistency — is exactly what retry CAN fix, provided the model is told precisely what is wrong. Dropping the previous failed output to 'start clean' removes one of the three required ingredients.

Why it works that way

Retry is an information channel, not a lottery. Its success is bounded by what you put in the message, not by how many attempts you allow.

Decision rule

Before tuning the retry count, check whether the retry message actually names the field, the constraint, and what was found.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Raise the retry ceiling so the loop has more chances to converge.The loop is information-limited, not retry-count-limited — every extra attempt receives the same uninformative feedback.Exam 5, Exam 9
  • Drop the failed output and resend the original prompt unchanged so the model starts clean.Removes one of the three ingredients a retry needs; without seeing its previous output the model can reproduce the same error.Exam 9
  • Route every document that fails once straight to human review.Burns human capacity on errors the model could fix itself if simply given the specific validation error.Exam 5

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 5 (generic 'extraction failed' feedback) — answered correctly. Exam 9's version (rejected line vs hunk ranges) is unscored. No miss on this facet appears in EXAM-LOG.

Where this was taught

Domain-4_v2 §4.9 · Exam 5 · Exam 9

D4 §4.9

detected_pattern for systematic analysis

Solid

Tag each finding or extraction with the construct that triggered it, so failures and dismissals aggregate by cause instead of being read one at a time.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Add a detected_pattern field to structured findings identifying which construct produced them. That single field converts a pile of isolated events into a signal you can group. When developers dismiss findings, grouping dismissals by detected_pattern tells you which patterns drive false positives instead of leaving you guessing. Across retries, tracking which patterns repeatedly fail validation reveals a systematic prompt or schema weakness rather than a series of unrelated one-offs. The rejected alternatives all fail on the same axis: free-text dismissal reasons and free-text notes do not aggregate, verbose reasoning logs still leave you reading prose per item, and a raw retry-count dashboard shows volume with no attribution to cause.

Why it works that way

You cannot fix what you cannot group. Structure at the point of generation is what makes downstream analysis cheap.

Decision rule

If the question is 'which kinds of X are noise', the answer is a structured category field, not free text.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Ask developers to type a free-text reason on every dismissal, then read them periodically.Unstructured text does not aggregate — the team cannot cleanly group by pattern, which is the analysis they need.Exam 2
  • Add a free-text notes field where the model explains why the attempt likely failed.Same problem — prose cannot be counted or grouped by cause the way a structured pattern field can.Exam 10
  • Increase logging verbosity to capture the full model reasoning behind every finding.Bloats storage and still leaves per-finding prose to read; no aggregate per-pattern signal.Exam 2
  • Build a dashboard counting total retries per day.Shows volume but nothing about cause — the attribution is the entire point.Exam 10

Your record on it

Tested on scored Exam 10 (which source-document construct drives first-pass failures) — answered correctly. Exam 2's version is unscored. No §4.9 detected_pattern miss appears in EXAM-LOG.

Domain-4_v2 §4.9 · Exam 2 · Exam 10

Domain 5 · 15% of the exam · 9 of 60 questions

Context Management & Reliability

This domain is about one hard fact and everything that follows from it: Claude's API has no memory. Every request you send must carry the entire conversation with it, which means context is a budget you spend, a resource that degrades, and a thing that vanishes the moment a process crashes. D5 teaches you how to spend that budget well — what to keep verbatim, what to compress, what to trim before it ever enters the window, and what to push out to a subagent or a file. It also covers the reliability half: when an agent should stop and escalate to a human, how to design confidence and sampling so errors do not slip through automation, and how to make source attribution survive every summarization step between raw evidence and final report.

30 concepts50/52 lifetime (96%)

Recall check — D5

Answer out loud before you open each one. Retrieval is what moves a concept from recognised to owned.

  1. A tempting answer says Adding a `session_id` parameter would let the API retrieve prior turns server-side.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Claude remembers nothing between calls; the only memory that exists is the prior turns your application re-sends in the messages array on every single request.

    Why the tempting answer fails: No such capability exists. The API holds no session state for an ID to attach to, so the parameter cannot do the work being claimed for it.

  2. A tempting answer says Widen the retained window (25 pairs to 60, 15 exchanges to 40) so earlier commitments stay in context longer.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Recent exchanges verbatim, a running summary of older ones, and a structured facts block that is never dropped — a pure sliding window always eventually discards something critical.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Any fixed window still discards early turns eventually; a sufficiently long case reproduces the exact same contradiction.

  3. A tempting answer says The context window overflowed and the system prompt was truncated out.

    State the correct model, then check

    Right model: Rule-following that decays after a dozen turns at only a few thousand tokens is accumulated assistant responses diluting the system prompt — not overflow, and not a first-turn-only system prompt.

    Why the tempting answer fails: Impossible at roughly 2,500–3,400 tokens — the window is orders of magnitude larger. This is the corpus's explicitly ruled-out explanation.

D5 §5.1

The API is stateless — memory is the messages array

Recovered

Claude remembers nothing between calls; the only memory that exists is the prior turns your application re-sends in the messages array on every single request.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Every call to the Messages API is fully independent. There is no server-side session, no conversation store Claude can look up, and no parameter that turns one on. When an agent 'forgets' something a customer said two turns ago, the diagnosis is almost always the same: your application's request builder is not including the prior turns. This applies to every path that constructs a request, not just the happy path — a retry queue, a background worker, or a page-refresh handler that resends only the newest message will produce an agent that treats a continuing case as brand new, even when your own database still holds the conversation ID. Fabricated fields like `session_id` or `persist_context: true` show up in exam options precisely because they sound plausible; neither exists.

Why it works that way

Statelessness is the root constraint the entire domain is built on — it is why cost grows with turns, why summarization strategies exist at all, and why nothing survives a crash unless you persisted it yourself.

Decision rule

If an agent 'forgot' something, check what your code put in `messages[]` before you reach for any API parameter — the parameter you are imagining does not exist.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Adding a `session_id` parameter would let the API retrieve prior turns server-side.No such capability exists. The API holds no session state for an ID to attach to, so the parameter cannot do the work being claimed for it.Exam 4 Q5; Exam 6 Q5; Exam 7 Q11; KD #25
  • Setting `persist_context: true` makes the API retain conversation state once a conversation ID is supplied.`persist_context` is not a real parameter. The corpus consistently plants fabricated flags that imply server-side memory; recognising them as invented is the test.Exam 6 Q5 (missed)
  • The context window overflowed and silently dropped the earliest turns.In a two-turn or single-retried-message scenario there is nothing near a window limit. This misdiagnoses a request-construction bug as a capacity problem.Exam 4 Q5; Exam 7 Q11
  • Claude needs a vector database to hold conversational memory.Vector retrieval addresses long, multi-session histories. It does nothing for a request builder that simply omits prior turns, and it is not how standard multi-turn memory works.Exam 4 Q5; Exam 7 Q11; KD #25
  • Claude Code's `--resume` flag can restore the session for a customer-facing web widget.`--resume` is a Claude Code CLI concept for developer sessions, not a mechanism available to an application calling the Messages API directly.Exam 6 Q5 (missed)

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q5 (session_id framing); MISSED on Exam 6 Q5 (fabricated `persist_context` field) — flagged in the Exam 6 Professor's Note as one of only two D5 misses in the project's history; answered correctly again on Exam 7 Q11 (retry-queue framing), which the log records as confirming the Exam 6 dip was attempt-specific.
