Key Distinction #25

D5 §5.13

The hybrid window beats the sliding window

Recovered

Recent exchanges verbatim, a running summary of older ones, and a structured facts block that is never dropped — a pure sliding window always eventually discards something critical.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Keeping only the last N message pairs is the most natural cost-control instinct and it fails predictably: an accessibility requirement, an agreed store credit, a corrected loyalty tier, a rounding rule for multi-currency line items — stated early, still binding — falls out of the window, and the agent contradicts it. Widening the window from 25 pairs to 60, or from 15 exchanges to 40, only delays the same failure, because any fixed window eventually discards early turns and a long enough case will reproduce the contradiction. The hybrid design fixes it structurally: recent turns verbatim for coherence, a running summary of earlier discussion for continuity, and a structured facts block holding the agreed values that is never dropped at all. This section is closely related to §5.3 and §5.4 — think of §5.13 as those two ideas applied to conversation-level state design.

Why it works that way

Any policy that decides what to keep by position rather than by importance will eventually throw away the one thing that mattered.

Decision rule

Never let position alone decide what survives — agreed facts get a block that is exempt from both the window and the summarizer.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Widen the retained window (25 pairs to 60, 15 exchanges to 40) so earlier commitments stay in context longer.Any fixed window still discards early turns eventually; a sufficiently long case reproduces the exact same contradiction.Exam 2 Q7; Exam 6 Q44 (missed); Exam 7 Q12
  • Summarize the entire history uniformly instead.Uniform summarization compresses a precise rule or corrected value into something vaguer, losing exactly the precision that mattered.Exam 6 Q44 (missed); Exam 7 Q12
  • Switch to a larger-context model so the whole conversation fits.It raises cost, postpones dropping, and larger inputs invite lost-in-the-middle attention gaps rather than reliably preserving the early commitment.Exam 2 Q7
  • Replay the full untrimmed history on every request so nothing is ever lost.That is precisely what makes cost and latency scale with conversation length — unbounded history is the problem the window was introduced to solve.Exam 2 Q7
  • Ask the model to remind itself of earlier corrections at the start of each new item.It relies on the model reliably recalling something it has no structural guarantee of retaining.Exam 6 Q44 (missed)

Your record on it

MISSED on Exam 6 Q44 (interactive correction session keeping only the last 15 exchanges) — one of only two D5 misses in the project's history, named in the Exam 6 Professor's Note and Insights Round 1's focus recommendation; deliberately re-tested and answered CORRECTLY on Exam 7 Q12 (loyalty-tier dispute), which the log records as confirming the Exam 6 dip was attempt-specific.

Where this was taught

D5 §5.13

System-prompt instruction drift over long conversations

Recovered

Rule-following that decays after a dozen turns at only a few thousand tokens is accumulated assistant responses diluting the system prompt — not overflow, and not a first-turn-only system prompt.

The full lesson

What is actually true

You will recognise this by its numbers. A stated rule holds for the first eight to twenty turns and then quietly stops being followed, and the session is at two or three thousand tokens with no summarization or trimming configured. Context overflow is impossible at that size, and the idea that a system prompt applies only to the first turn is simply false — it is included in every request. What is actually happening is dilution: as the model's own prior output accumulates, the system prompt's authority weakens relative to the growing body of assistant turns. The preventive patterns are to inject reminder messages at conversation breakpoints, keep the rules concrete and minimal, and replace verbose abstract rule lists with few-shot examples, because examples hold a behavioural pattern longer than abstractions do. Repeating the rule in capitals at the top of the same static system prompt does not address drift across turns.

Why it works that way

It is a behavioural failure with no capacity component, so every capacity-shaped fix — bigger window, summarization, louder emphasis — misses the mechanism entirely.

Decision rule

Behaviour degrades but the token count is small → dilution. Reinforce at breakpoints and swap abstract rules for concrete examples.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The context window overflowed and the system prompt was truncated out.Impossible at roughly 2,500–3,400 tokens — the window is orders of magnitude larger. This is the corpus's explicitly ruled-out explanation.Exam 4 Q28; Exam 5 Q44; Exam 10 Q13; KD #23
  • The system prompt only applies to the first turn unless restated.False — the system prompt is included with every request and never expires after turn one.Exam 4 Q28; Exam 5 Q44; Exam 10 Q13; KD #23
  • A summarization pass compressed the rule out of retained history.In these scenarios no summarization or trimming is configured, so nothing was evicted — the rule is still present, just increasingly outweighed.Exam 10 Q13
  • The instruction was never loaded; a `/memory` check would show the file missing.The scenario shows the convention was followed correctly for the first fifteen turns, which rules out a never-loaded file.Exam 4 Q28
  • Repeat the rule in all-caps at the top of the system prompt for stronger emphasis.The rule is already stated once at the top; the problem is drift across accumulated turns, not weak initial emphasis.Exam 8 Q45
  • Move to a much larger context window so the system prompt stays available longer.The conversation stays well within token limits throughout; this is instruction drift, not a context-budget problem.Exam 8 Q45

Your record on it

Correct on all four D5-tagged appearances — Exam 4 Q28 (CLAUDE.md convention drift), Exam 5 Q44 (backward-compatible parameter rule), Exam 8 Q45 (refund-timeline rule, testing the preventive half: reminders at breakpoints plus a few-shot example) and Exam 10 Q13 (order-ID restatement rule). However Key Distinction #23 itself was MISSED on its first-ever scored appearance at Exam 6 Q42 (tagged D4 §4.20, format drift), then answered correctly on its re-tests at Exam 8 Q53 and Exam 10 Q13; the Exam 10 log records all ten KD-seeded questions correct that sitting.

Key Distinction #23

D5 §5.1

Cost and latency scale with conversation length

Not yet tested

A long conversation gets slower and more expensive because every request re-sends the whole history, not because the model writes more or the database slows down.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Because the API is stateless, turn 60 sends everything from turns 1 through 59 along with the new message. Input tokens grow monotonically, and cost and latency grow with them. The tell-tale signature is a session that started fast and cheap and is now several times more expensive per turn while the assistant's replies are the same length as before and the conversation is still comfortably inside the context window. The cost curve starts rising from turn one — long before any window boundary is in play — so a rising-cost symptom is never evidence of overflow.

Why it works that way

This is the economic reason every context-management strategy in this domain exists; if history were free to carry, you would never compress anything.

Decision rule

Rising cost-per-turn in a healthy-length conversation means growing input tokens — look at history size, not at model behaviour or infrastructure.

Traps that have caught you here

  • The model generates progressively longer responses as detail accumulates.The corpus explicitly rules this out, and the scenario states reply length is unchanged. The growth is on the input side.Exam 9 Q45; corpus §5.1
  • The conversation exceeded the context window and the overflow drives the added cost.The session is stated to be well within the window, and cost has been rising since long before any limit was approached.Exam 9 Q45
  • The application's growing stored history makes database reads slow each turn.The corpus rules out slowing database operations. The growth is in tokens sent to the API, not in the storage layer.Exam 9 Q45

Your record on it

Taught only in Exam 9 Q45 (Developer Productivity block). Exam 9 was generated 2026-07-19 and has never been attempted, so this facet has never appeared on a scored exam.

Where this was taught

D5 §5.11

Separate well-established findings from contested ones

Not yet tested

Structure the final report with explicit sections distinguishing what is well-established from what is contested, preserving each source's original characterization and methodological context.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The last piece of provenance is presentational. A report that mixes settled findings and disputed ones in a single undifferentiated narrative forces every reader to re-derive which is which. Give contested material its own explicit section, and preserve how the original source characterized its own finding along with the methodological context — a figure a source hedged should not arrive at the reader as flat assertion. This complements the conflict-annotation rule in §5.10: annotation preserves the disagreement inside the pipeline, and this structuring makes it legible in the output.

Why it works that way

Provenance that survives the pipeline still fails the reader if the final document presents contested and settled claims with identical confidence.

Decision rule

If two claims have different evidentiary standing, the report structure should say so before the reader has to work it out.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Present all findings in one uniform narrative regardless of how contested they are.It strips the reader of the ability to weight claims, and loses the source's own hedging and methodological framing.corpus §5.11

Your record on it

Stated in the syllabus §5.11 closing paragraph but never appeared as the key or as a named distractor in any D5 question across the nine mock exams.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.11

D5 §5.14

Terminate the agent loop on stop_reason

Not yet tested

Exit the agent loop when `stop_reason` is `end_turn` — never by parsing Claude's prose for something that sounds like a conclusion.

The full lesson

What is actually true

The §5.14 reliability table opens with the non-terminating agent loop, and its root cause is not checking `stop_reason`. The harness should branch on the structured field: `tool_use` means execute the requested tools, append the results, and continue the loop; `end_turn` means Claude has finished and the loop stops. Reading the model's natural-language output for a phrase like 'I'm done' substitutes an unreliable textual signal for a reliable structural one. This concept is primarily examined under D1 agent-loop mechanics, but it is listed in D5's reliability summary because a loop that never terminates is a reliability failure.

Why it works that way

Structured protocol fields are deterministic; prose is not, and control flow should never depend on interpreting text.

Decision rule

Branch on `stop_reason`, never on what the response says.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Parse Claude's text for a phrase indicating it is finished.Natural-language parsing is unreliable control flow; the API already exposes a structured `stop_reason` for exactly this decision.KD #5; corpus §5.14

Your record on it

Listed in the §5.14 reliability summary table but never appeared as the key or a distractor of any D5-tagged question across the nine mock exams; it is examined under D1 instead.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.14 · Key-Distinctions_v1 #5

Key Distinction #5

D5 §5.2

Fix input volume at its source, not downstream

Not yet tested

When upstream agents flood a synthesis step with raw pages and reasoning traces, change what they emit — structured facts, quotes, relevance scores — rather than bolting on a summarizer.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There is a second, harder variant of the lost-in-the-middle problem: the input is not just badly ordered, it is far larger than the synthesis step can reliably handle, because upstream subagents are returning full page content and complete reasoning traces. The correct move is to change the upstream contract so each subagent returns structured key facts, direct quotes, and relevance scores instead of everything it saw. That shrinks the input at its origin and improves its signal density at the same time. Inserting an intermediate summarization agent between the subagents and the synthesizer looks reasonable but adds latency and another component that can fail, while leaving the verbose upstream behaviour untouched.

Why it works that way

Root-cause fixes at the producing end are the corpus's consistent preference over compensating layers added at the consuming end.

Decision rule

When input is too big AND too noisy, change the producer's output contract before adding any consumer-side machinery.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add an intermediate summarization agent to compress the combined output before synthesis.It adds latency and another point of failure, and treats the volume symptom downstream instead of stopping the verbose output being produced.Exam 3 Q15
  • Reorder the subagents so a different one's output leads.A finding sitting in the middle of one subagent's own large block stays in the middle regardless of which subagent comes first.Exam 3 Q15
  • Truncate each subagent's output to its first 20K tokens.Truncation discards exactly the load-bearing findings that happen to fall later in a subagent's own content, without addressing why the content is verbose.Exam 3 Q15

Your record on it

Taught only in Exam 3 Q15 (Multi-Agent Research block). Exam 3 was generated 2026-07-07 and has never been attempted, so this facet has never appeared on a scored exam.

Key Distinction #20

D5 §5.6

Subagents receive only what the coordinator passes

Not yet tested

A subagent inherits none of the coordinator's history — anything it needs must be written explicitly into its prompt, never referenced by pointing at an earlier step.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Context isolation cuts both ways. The same property that makes an Explore subagent useful means a subagent cannot see prior findings, earlier tool results, or the coordinator's reasoning unless the coordinator puts them in the prompt. Telling a synthesis subagent to 'use the findings from the review step' passes a reference, not the findings. When a downstream subagent behaves as though it is missing upstream results, the fix is at the coordinator: include the actual content it needs. Related to this, letting each subagent independently rediscover shared structure instead of giving them one shared map wastes effort and leaves the coordinator's own decomposition just as uninformed as before.

Why it works that way

Most 'the subagent failed' diagnoses are actually coordinator prompt-construction failures, and the fix is at a different layer than the symptom.

Decision rule

Before dispatching a subagent, read its prompt as if you knew nothing else — if a needed fact is not literally in it, the subagent will not have it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Skip the shared survey and let each delegated subagent discover the relevant files during its own subtask.Without a shared map every subagent re-discovers the same structure, duplicating work and leaving the coordinator's decomposition uninformed.Exam 5 Q6
  • A subagent can pick up results from a prior step just by being told which step to use.Subagents have isolated context and cannot see prior findings by reference alone; the coordinator must include the findings themselves.Domain-5_v2 §5.14 reliability table; corpus

Your record on it

Taught in the syllabus (§5.6 opening statement and the §5.14 reliability table row 'Subagent lacks upstream results') and appears as a distractor rationale in Exam 5 Q6, but has never been the scored key of a D5 question on any attempted exam. Note: the closely related D1 §1.5 version of this idea was missed on Exam 10 Q35, which is logged under D1, not D5.

Where this was taught

D5 §5.8

Frustration is not a request for a human

Not yet tested

Acknowledge the emotion, offer a concrete resolution, and escalate only if the customer reiterates that they want a person.

The full lesson

What is actually true

There is a deliberate asymmetry in the escalation rules that is easy to collapse. 'This is outrageous, I'm very unhappy!' is an expression of dissatisfaction — the right response is to acknowledge it and propose a concrete fix. 'No, I want to talk to someone!' is an explicit request — the right response is to escalate immediately. A first expression of frustration is not a request for a manager, and treating it as one is the same mistake as escalating on sentiment. But once the customer restates the desire for a human, the acknowledge-then-offer pattern is finished and you escalate without another attempt.

Why it works that way

Getting this boundary right is what separates an agent that resolves most cases from one that either stonewalls upset customers or hands every unhappy message to a person.

Decision rule

Emotion → acknowledge and offer. Explicit or repeated request for a person → escalate now.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Treat any expression of anger or dissatisfaction as a request to be transferred.Mood does not equal a human request; escalating on first frustration floods the human queue with cases the agent could have resolved.corpus §5.8; Exam 2 Q10 rationale
  • Keep applying acknowledge-then-offer after the customer has explicitly asked for a person.Once the request is explicit, the pattern no longer applies and continuing to offer alternatives violates the immediate-escalation rule.Exam 10 Q9

Your record on it

Taught in the syllabus §5.8 nuanced-escalation pattern and appears as a distractor rationale in Exam 10 Q9 (correctly rejected), but has never been the scored key of a question on any attempted exam.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.8 · Exam 10 Q9

D5 §5.9

Field-level confidence, calibrated on labeled data

Not yet tested

Emit a confidence score per extracted field, not one per document, and tune review thresholds against a labeled validation set rather than trusting raw self-reports.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A single 1–10 confidence score per document is too coarse and too uncalibrated to route review well: reviewers find high-confidence documents that are wrong on specific fields, and flagged documents that are perfectly fine. Two changes fix it together. First, granularity — score each extracted field, so oversight lands on the specific values that are actually uncertain instead of on whole documents. Second, calibration — tune the review thresholds against a labeled validation set with known ground truth, because raw self-reported confidence means nothing until it has been mapped to real accuracy. Raising a cutoff on an uncalibrated score, or averaging two self-ratings from the same model, does neither of these things. Once calibrated, the signal drives a two-way route: high confidence in a segment whose accuracy has been independently validated goes to automated processing, while low-confidence extractions — and, separately, anything extracted from ambiguous or contradictory source documents — go to human review. Source ambiguity is a routing trigger in its own right, not something the confidence number is expected to catch.

Why it works that way

Calibrated field-level confidence is what makes targeted human oversight possible at all — without it you are choosing between reviewing everything and reviewing blind.

Decision rule

Confidence is only a routing signal after it has been calibrated against labeled ground truth — and it should be per field, not per document.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Keep the single document-level score but raise the review cutoff.Raising a cutoff on an uncalibrated score floods review with correct documents while still missing per-field errors hidden under a high document score.Exam 2 Q55
  • Ask the model to re-rate its confidence and average the two scores.Averaging two self-ratings from the same model does not calibrate anything against ground truth — it can be confidently wrong twice.Exam 2 Q55
  • Route a fixed random 10% of documents to review regardless of confidence.An unstratified flat slice wastes reviewer capacity on easy segments and undersamples the fields where errors actually cluster.Exam 2 Q55; Exam 7 Q42
  • Trust the model's self-reported confidence directly as the routing signal.Uncalibrated confidence is unreliable until tuned on a labeled validation set; the threshold itself may be miscalibrated per segment.Exam 2 Q54; Exam 3 Q56; Exam 7 Q42

Your record on it

The field-level-plus-calibration redesign is the scored key only in Exam 2 Q55, and Exam 2 has never been attempted. The related trap 'trust self-reported confidence directly' was correctly rejected as a distractor on Exam 7 Q42.

Where this was taught

D5 §5.1

Vector databases are for long histories, not multi-turn memory

Solid

A vector database solves retrieval across months of accumulated history — it is never the answer to 'Claude forgot what I said three turns ago'.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Two different problems get conflated in exam options. Ordinary multi-turn memory is solved by the `messages[]` array and nothing else. Retrieval across a very large, multi-session history — months of discussion, dozens of archived projects — is where embeddings and semantic search legitimately belong (see §5.7). If the scenario is a short conversation, a single retried message, or a page refresh, proposing a vector database is over-engineering a bug that lives in your request builder. Learn to spot which of the two problems a stem is actually describing.

Why it works that way

It stops you reaching for retrieval infrastructure to fix an application bug, and stops you reaching for a bigger window when the real need is genuine retrieval.

Decision rule

Ask how far back the needed fact lives: same session → messages array; months and many sessions → semantic retrieval.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Claude needs a vector database keyed on case ID to recall the conversation across queue retries.Vector retrieval is for long histories spanning months, not for restoring a message that was simply never resent by the retry path.Exam 7 Q11
  • A vector database is the standard mechanism for conversational memory.Simple conversation memory is the `messages[]` array. Vector databases address retrieval over long histories, a different problem entirely.Exam 4 Q5; KD #25

Your record on it

Appeared as a distractor Ram correctly rejected on Exam 4 Q5 and Exam 7 Q11, both scored exams where D5 finished 9/9.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.1 · Domain-5_v2 §5.7 · Key-Distinctions_v1 #25 · Exam 4 Q5 · Exam 7 Q11

Key Distinction #25

D5 §5.10

Annotate conflicts — do not resolve them, do not block on them

Solid

When two credible sources disagree, finish the analysis carrying both values, mark the conflict with source attribution, and let the coordinator or a human reconcile it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This concept tests two boundaries at once, and most wrong answers violate one of them. The first boundary: a subagent must not resolve a genuine conflict between credible sources on its own. Picking the government figure, applying a precedence rule, computing a credibility score, or averaging the two all abandon a decision that sits above the subagent's scope — and averaging is worse still, because it fabricates a number neither source reported. The second boundary: it must not stop the pipeline either. Halting to ask the coordinator before completing the analysis blocks progress unnecessarily. The correct behaviour is to do both things at once — complete the work with both values preserved, and annotate the disagreement explicitly with which source said what, so the reconciliation decision can happen downstream with full visibility.

Why it works that way

It keeps evidence and judgement at the right layers — the subagent owns gathering and flagging, the coordinator owns deciding — without either losing information or stalling the pipeline.

Decision rule

Complete the work, carry both values, name the sources, keep moving — never pick, never average, never halt.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Apply a heuristic (prefer government sources, prefer the delivery confirmation, prefer the more plausible figure) and report one value.Heuristic selection abandons a reconciliation decision above the subagent's scope and silently discards a credible data point.Exam 3 Q6; Exam 6 Q28; Exam 7 Q43; Exam 8 Q26; Exam 9 Q26; Exam 10 Q36
  • Stop and ask the coordinator which figure to use before completing the analysis.Blocking the pipeline is unnecessary — the subagent can finish its work and flag the conflict for a decision that can happen later.Exam 3 Q6; Exam 6 Q28; Exam 7 Q43; Exam 8 Q26; Exam 9 Q26; Exam 10 Q36
  • Average the two figures and report a blended value.Averaging manufactures a number neither source actually reported, destroying attribution and creating false precision.Exam 3 Q6; Exam 6 Q28; Exam 7 Q43
  • Keep resolving autonomously but log the discarded value to an internal audit trail.The subagent is still deciding; only the evidence trail changes. The conflict must be visible in the analysis output where reconciliation actually happens.Exam 9 Q26
  • Discard both figures and mark the record unextractable.It throws away real, credible findings instead of preserving them with attribution for downstream reconciliation.Exam 10 Q36

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q28 (rollout-timeline disagreement, in the one exam where D5 dipped), Exam 7 Q43 (near-miss rates), Exam 8 Q26 (invoice vs delivery-confirmation quantities) and Exam 10 Q36 (compliance-cost estimates) — four scored appearances, no misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.10 · Exam 3 Q6 · Exam 6 Q28 · Exam 7 Q43 · Exam 8 Q26 · Exam 9 Q26 · Exam 10 Q36

D5 §5.11

Claim-to-source mappings must survive synthesis

Solid

Every claim carries its own structured source mapping through the whole pipeline, and each downstream agent preserves and merges those mappings — a bibliography at the end is not attribution.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Attribution gets lost the moment findings are compressed without their provenance attached. The requirement is that subagents emit structured claim-to-source mappings — the claim text, the source URL or document name, the page or excerpt location, the publication date, sometimes a confidence — and that every downstream synthesis step preserves and merges them rather than flattening them away. A consolidated bibliography listing every source used somewhere in the document is the classic near-miss: it looks like attribution but restores nothing at the claim level, because no individual figure can be traced to any particular entry. Sorting the bibliography, or dropping in-body citations in favour of it, both make things worse. So does re-deriving attributions at the end by searching the sources again — expensive, error-prone, and unnecessary if the mapping was carried through the pipeline in the first place.

Why it works that way

Auditors and reviewers do not need to know which sources were consulted; they need to know which source supports this specific number, and only per-claim mappings can answer that.

Decision rule

If you cannot point at one sentence and name its source and page, your provenance design has already failed — no end-matter can repair it.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a general bibliography of all sources at the end of the report.A document-level list leaves individual claims untraceable — the auditor still cannot tie a particular total to a particular page.Exam 2 Q57; Exam 7 Q44; Exam 8 Q27; Exam 9 Q27; Exam 10 Q42
  • Sort the bibliography alphabetically so reviewers can scan it faster.A better-organised document-level list is still a document-level list; it does nothing for claim-level traceability.Exam 10 Q42
  • Re-derive attributions at the end by searching the original sources again.Reconstruction after the fact is expensive and error-prone; the mapping should be preserved as the pipeline runs, not rebuilt at compile time.Exam 2 Q57; Exam 7 Q44; Exam 8 Q27; Exam 9 Q27; Exam 10 Q42
  • Drop in-body citations entirely and rely on the bibliography alone.It removes the last connection between claims and sources, making the traceability problem strictly worse.Exam 10 Q42

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 10 Q42 (report-generation subagent dropping per-claim mappings for a consolidated bibliography); the same bibliography and re-derivation traps were correctly rejected on Exam 7 Q44 and Exam 8 Q27.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.11 · Exam 2 Q57 · Exam 7 Q44 · Exam 8 Q27 · Exam 9 Q27 · Exam 10 Q42

D5 §5.11

Publication dates prevent false contradictions

Solid

Require a publication or collection date on every structured output, so two sources describing different time periods are read as change over time rather than as a conflict.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Without dates, normal temporal change looks exactly like disagreement. 'Source A says 10%, source B says 15%' reads as a contradiction; 'Source A (2023) says 10%, source B (2024) says 15%' reads as roughly five points of growth in a year. The same problem shows up in extraction pipelines when an original contract and a later amendment cover the same price clause and reconciliation flags a data conflict. The fix is metadata, not adjudication: capture publication, effective, or data-collection dates in every structured output and let downstream logic treat a later-dated document covering the same term as an update. Flagging every numeric disagreement as a conflict is the failure mode itself; blending figures from different years, or discarding the older one, both destroy the temporal signal that resolves the apparent conflict.

Why it works that way

It is the difference between a pipeline that surfaces genuine contradictions worth a human's time and one that generates false conflicts on every ordinary year-over-year change.

Decision rule

Before calling two figures contradictory, check their dates — different periods are data, not disagreement.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Flag every numeric disagreement between sources as a conflict.Without dates this misreports normal temporal change as contradiction — the exact failure the corpus names.Exam 3 Q12; Exam 5 Q23; Exam 7 Q44; Exam 8 Q27
  • Average figures from different years into a single blended statistic.A blend describes neither year accurately and destroys the very temporal signal that explains the difference.Exam 3 Q12
  • Keep only the most recent figure and drop the earlier one.It discards legitimate historical context and sidesteps the fix — the two figures were never in conflict once dated.Exam 3 Q12
  • Silently take whichever value was processed most recently.It discards the audit trail, and a later amendment does not necessarily supersede the original for every downstream purpose.Exam 5 Q23
  • Merge the original and every amendment into one document before extraction.Pre-merging destroys provenance and does not scale as more amendments arrive; the fix is metadata, not document flattening.Exam 5 Q23

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q23 (contract amendment falsely flagged as a data conflict) and Exam 7 Q44 (filings gathered fourteen months apart); also taught in unattempted Exam 3 Q12.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.11 · Exam 3 Q12 · Exam 5 Q23 · Exam 7 Q44

D5 §5.11

Render each content type in its own form

Solid

Financial and tabular data belongs in tables, time series in chronological order, technical findings in structured lists — do not flatten everything to uniform prose.

The full lesson

What is actually true

A synthesis step that converts every finding to narrative prose 'for a consistent house voice' makes precise data imprecise and hard to verify. Due dates, amounts and payment references across dozens of vendor statements need to be scannable and cross-checkable line by line, which a paragraph per vendor destroys. Per-ward rates across twelve hospitals belong in a table; a five-year trend belongs in chronological order; technical findings belong in structured lists. Tightening the prose does not help, because the problem is the form, not the length. Note this is a distinct §5.11 failure from losing attribution — you can preserve every claim-to-source mapping perfectly and still produce an unusable report by rendering a rate table as sentences.

Why it works that way

Verification is a real workflow, and formats that resist scanning and cross-checking impose a real cost on every reviewer downstream.

Decision rule

Ask what the reader will do with each block of data — scan, compare, or read — and render it in the form that supports that.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Convert all findings to uniform narrative prose for consistency.Tabular financial data becomes imprecise and harder to verify once flattened into sentences — the documented failure this rule exists to prevent.Exam 2 Q57; Exam 8 Q27; Exam 9 Q27
  • Shorten the narrative so the figures stand out more within the prose.A symptom-level edit — tabular and time-series data expressed as prose stays imprecise no matter how tightly the prose is written.Exam 9 Q27
  • Append a bibliography so readers can locate the underlying figures themselves.It neither restores claim-level traceability nor does anything about a rate table dissolved into sentences.Exam 9 Q27

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q27 (reconciliation report flattened to one paragraph per vendor), its only scored appearance as the key; also taught in unattempted Exam 9 Q27.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.11 · Exam 2 Q57 · Exam 8 Q27 · Exam 9 Q27

D5 §5.12

Scratchpad files and context degradation

Solid

Write intermediate findings to a scratchpad file as you go and read it back at each continuation — it is what stops a long task drifting into generic 'typical patterns'.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tasks that run across many tool calls — a 200-endpoint migration, a 300-page clause extraction, a multi-day conversion picked up by a different engineer each morning — cannot hold every discovered specific in conversation history. Past a certain point you see context degradation: the model starts giving inconsistent answers about earlier work and reaching for 'typical' patterns instead of the specific quirks it actually found. Writing key findings and progress to a scratchpad file as they emerge, and reading it at the start of each continuation, lets the task survive both context limits and session boundaries. Note the difference from summarization: summarizing exact quirks is what blurs them into generic patterns; the scratchpad preserves them verbatim outside the conversation.

Why it works that way

It moves the durable record out of a medium that compresses and expires and into one that does not, which is the only way long multi-session work stays specific.

Decision rule

If a finding will still matter after the next context boundary, write it to a file — not into the conversation.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Summarize older findings more aggressively to free room for new ones.Aggressive summarization of exact quirks is what turns them into generic patterns in the first place — it is the cause, not the cure.Exam 10 Q30
  • Use `/compact` periodically to shrink the conversation.`/compact` risks losing the exact text and specific detail the later work needs, and it does nothing once a session has ended or crashed.Exam 3 Q30; Exam 6 Q43
  • Rely on conversation history to carry the prior session's findings forward.The API is stateless and an ended session's context is gone; nothing carries into the next morning's session regardless of intent.Exam 3 Q30; Exam 9 Q10
  • Restart the session periodically, or re-run discovery each day, so history never grows large.Restarting discards findings a scratchpad would have preserved, re-losing exactly the specifics that were expensive to establish.Exam 9 Q10; Exam 10 Q30
  • Raise `max_tokens` so the model can restate more context each turn.A larger response budget does not address why the model has lost track of prior specific findings.Exam 6 Q43

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q43 (300-page clause extraction drifting to 'typical contract language') and Exam 10 Q30 (200-endpoint migration losing per-endpoint quirks); also taught in unattempted Exams 3 and 9.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.12 · Exam 3 Q30 · Exam 6 Q43 · Exam 9 Q10 · Exam 10 Q30

D5 §5.12

Structured state export and manifest for crash recovery

Solid

Each agent exports its status and findings to a known location and the coordinator loads a manifest on restart, so a crash resumes from the checkpoint instead of the beginning.

The full lesson

What is actually true

In a multi-agent or long-batch system, design for the restart before it happens. Each unit of work writes structured state — status, completed IDs, key findings, coverage, gaps — to a known location, and a manifest records which stages are completed, in progress, and not started. When the host process dies, the coordinator reads the manifest, injects the persisted findings into the relevant prompts, and picks up where the work actually stood. The three wrong answers are all versions of not persisting: relying on conversation history to survive is impossible because the API is stateless and a crashed process's context is gone; re-running the whole investigation wastes hours of completed work; and keeping findings inside each agent's own context window means both that the window fills and that nothing outlives the process.

Why it works that way

Crash recovery is an architectural property you either designed in or did not — there is no way to recover state that was never written down.

Decision rule

Ask what a cold restart would know. If the answer is 'nothing', you need state exports plus a manifest — not a smaller batch.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Rely on the conversation history to reconstruct progress after the restart.The API is stateless and the process itself crashed — there is no server-side session and no surviving context to reconstruct from.Exam 3 Q50; Exam 8 Q15
  • Re-run the whole batch or migration from the beginning to be safe.It discards substantial completed work — 40 of 120 modules, thousands of claims — that a checkpoint would have preserved, and risks re-applying changes.Exam 3 Q50; Exam 8 Q15
  • Keep completed-work state only inside each agent's own context window.In-memory context disappears the moment the process holding it dies; nothing survives for the coordinator to resume from.Exam 3 Q50; Exam 8 Q15
  • Reduce the batch size so a crash loses less, while still reprocessing from the start of each chunk.Shrinking the blast radius does not tell the restart script what was already completed; it still reprocesses from the start of whatever chunk it was in.Exam 3 Q50

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 8 Q15 (coordinator host crash mid-migration, 40 of 120 modules done), its only scored appearance; also taught in unattempted Exam 3 Q50.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.12 · Exam 3 Q50 · Exam 8 Q15

D5 §5.14

PostToolUse hook for centralized format normalization

Solid

When several tools return the same kind of data in different formats, normalize them all deterministically in one PostToolUse hook before anything reaches the model.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the second, distinct use of the same hook. §5.5 trims tool output for volume; §5.14 normalizes it for consistency. Three lookup tools returning dates as Unix epoch, DD/MM/YYYY and MM-DD-YYYY, or three analyzers reporting severity as 1/2/3, low/medium/high and info/warn/error, will produce contradictory summaries and country-ambiguous misreads. A single `PostToolUse` normalization point converts every tool's output to one shared representation deterministically, at the moment it enters context. The alternatives all reintroduce probability or fragmentation: a system-prompt note asking the model to reconcile the scales relies on interpretation every time and leaves all three raw formats in context anyway; a separate `normalize_dates` tool adds an LLM call and depends on the model remembering to invoke it; patching some tools and wrapping others splits one problem across several maintenance points.

Why it works that way

Format reconciliation is deterministic work, and deterministic work belongs in code at a single choke point rather than in the model's judgement on every turn.

Decision rule

Same data, different shapes, multiple sources → one hook at the boundary, not an instruction, an extra tool, or per-tool patches.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Add a system-prompt note listing each tool's format for the model to interpret.It relies on the model reconciling the mismatch every time, and the raw divergent formats still accumulate in context regardless.Exam 6 Q45; Exam 7 Q25
  • Add a `normalize_dates` tool the pipeline calls after every lookup.It adds an extra LLM call and a tool-selection dependency — the model must remember to invoke it every single time.Exam 6 Q45
  • Modify the tools you control and write a wrapper for the third-party one.Fragmented maintenance — separate fixes for controlled and external tools instead of one centralized normalization point.Exam 6 Q45
  • Replace the several tools with a single tool to avoid the mismatch.Discarding tools that each catch different issue classes throws away real coverage — disproportionate to what is a normalization problem.Exam 7 Q25

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 6 Q45 (three date formats, in the exam where D5 otherwise dipped) and Exam 7 Q25 (three severity scales) — two scored appearances, no misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.14 · Domain-5_v2 §5.5 · Exam 6 Q45 · Exam 7 Q25

D5 §5.2

Lost in the middle — primacy summary plus headings

Solid

Claude attends reliably to the beginning and end of a long input and least reliably to the middle; fix it with a key-findings summary at the start and explicit section headings throughout.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Feed a model a very long input and its attention is not uniform across it. Content at the start and at the end is processed reliably; content buried in the middle is systematically at greater risk of being missed. You will recognise this in exam stems by a specific shape: the output accurately covers the opening material and the closing material but silently omits something load-bearing from the middle third. The two documented mitigations are positional, not volumetric — put the critical information where attention is strongest by leading with a key-findings summary, and give the model navigational structure with explicit section headings so it can find mid-input content deliberately rather than by chance.

Why it works that way

It is a property of how attention distributes across position, so the only fixes that work are ones that change where information sits or how navigable it is — not how much of it there is.

Decision rule

If the beginning and end came through but the middle did not, restructure position and navigation — never shrink, reorder, or enlarge.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Summarize the whole input to under ~20K tokens first so there is less to process.Aggressive pre-summarization risks discarding exactly the buried detail you are trying to surface, before extraction or review even runs.Exam 4 Q29; Exam 5 Q19; Exam 8 Q58; Exam 10 Q58; KD #20
  • Rotate which section or which agent's output appears first across runs to average out position bias.Rotation does not change the attention pattern — whatever ends up in the middle is still at risk, regardless of which content that is.Exam 4 Q29; Exam 5 Q19; Exam 8 Q58; Exam 10 Q58; KD #20
  • Switch to a model with a larger context window so the whole thing fits comfortably.The content already fits and is still missed. A bigger window changes capacity, not attention quality at a given position.Exam 4 Q29; Exam 5 Q19
  • Raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to describe everything in detail.`max_tokens` governs output length. The limiting factor is what gets noticed while reading the input, not how much can be written back.Exam 8 Q58; Exam 10 Q58

Your record on it

Tested on four scored exams and correct every time: Exam 4 Q29 (consolidated diff), Exam 5 Q19 (45-page merger agreement), Exam 8 Q58 (60K-token PR bundle), Exam 10 Q58 (compiled inspection binder). Never missed.

Where this was taught

Key Distinction #20

D5 §5.2

A bigger context window is never the fix

Solid

Switching to a larger-context model raises cost and postpones the problem — it does not improve attention, remove noise, or preserve precision.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This distractor appears across almost every section of this domain, dressed differently each time, and it is wrong for a different reason each time. Against lost-in-the-middle, a bigger window does not change where attention is strongest. Against verbose tool output, it leaves the same irrelevant fields distracting the model, just with more room to hold them. Against precision loss in long conversations, it does not decide which content matters. Against context degradation and crash recovery, it does not persist anything. In every case it costs more and delays the same failure. Learn to hear 'bigger window' as a capacity answer, then ask whether the problem you are looking at is actually a capacity problem — it usually is not.

Why it works that way

Recognising this one anti-pattern lets you eliminate a plausible-looking option in a large share of D5 questions before you evaluate the rest.

Decision rule

Before accepting 'use a larger context window', name the failure — attention, noise, precision, isolation, or persistence. A bigger window addresses none of them.

Traps that have caught you here

  • A larger context window fixes attention on content buried in a long input.Lost-in-the-middle is a positional attention pattern, not a capacity limit; the content already fits and is still missed.Exam 4 Q29; Exam 5 Q19
  • A larger context window fixes context flooded by verbose tool results.Cost goes up and the noise problem remains — the irrelevant fields still enter context and still compete for attention.Exam 2 Q8; Exam 3 Q36; Exam 8 Q25; Exam 9 Q8; Exam 10 Q59
  • A larger window means nothing needs to be summarized or dropped in a long conversation.It raises cost and only delays the same problem; the precise facts are still sitting unstructured in a pile of turns, at risk of being paraphrased away.Exam 4 Q15; Exam 6 Q15; Exam 10 Q24; Exam 2 Q7
  • A larger window prevents context degradation over a very long task.Degradation is not stopped by raw capacity; the documented fix is persisted state in a scratchpad or state export.Exam 10 Q30
  • A larger window lets a verbose discovery pass run in the main session after all.The inventory still lands in the main session and still crowds out the design and implementation phases; the fix is isolation in a subagent, not capacity.Exam 8 Q60; Exam 9 Q8

Your record on it

Appeared as a distractor on scored exams 4, 6, 7, 8 and 10 across §5.2, §5.3, §5.5, §5.6 and §5.12 questions and was rejected correctly every time. Exam 6 is the one exam where D5 did not finish 9/9 — it carried only 7 D5 questions and scored 5/7 — but both of its misses were D5 questions with no larger-window option in play (Q5, §5.1, fabricated `persist_context`; Q44, §5.13, sliding window widened from 15 exchanges to 40), while the bigger-window distractor that did appear that exam, on Q15, was rejected correctly. Exams 4, 5, 7, 8 and 10 all finished D5 9/9.

D5 §5.3

The hybrid context-management approach

Solid

Extract critical structured data verbatim, summarize the low-density discussion, and keep the most recent exchanges untouched — all three, not one of them.

The full lesson

What is actually true

This is the single most-tested pattern in the domain. When a long conversation must shrink, split it into three treatments. First, pull the precision-critical items — amounts, dates, IDs, allergies, error codes, commit SHAs, agreed config values — into a compact structured block that is preserved word for word. Second, summarize the routine, low-information-density back-and-forth, which is where most of the tokens are and where compression costs you nothing. Third, keep the last few exchanges verbatim so the current turn stays coherent. Pure summarization fails because precision dissolves — 'the 15% discount I mentioned' becomes 'promotional pricing was discussed'. A pure recency window fails because anything agreed early falls outside it and disappears entirely.

Why it works that way

Different content has different information density; treating it uniformly either wastes tokens on chatter or destroys the exact values the work depends on.

Decision rule

Sort the content by information density first: exact values get a verbatim block, chatter gets summarized, the last few turns stay as they are.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Summarize the entire history uniformly once it passes a token threshold.Uniform summarization turns exact values — an order ID, a gate code, a commit SHA, a TTL — into vague paraphrase, losing precisely what needed preserving.Exam 4 Q15; Exam 4 Q30; Exam 6 Q15; Exam 7 Q23; Exam 8 Q59; Exam 9 Q7; Exam 10 Q24
  • Keep only the most recent N tokens or N messages and drop everything earlier.A fixed recency window drops early-established facts entirely, even when those facts are still operative for the current turn.Exam 4 Q15; Exam 6 Q15; Exam 8 Q59; Exam 9 Q7; Exam 10 Q24
  • Raise the threshold at which summarization triggers so it happens less often.Delaying compression only postpones the same precision loss; the same values get blurred whenever it finally runs.Exam 7 Q23; Exam 9 Q7
  • Start a new session and re-run the investigation.Restarting discards genuine progress. This is a cost-management problem, not a stale-results problem.Exam 8 Q59

Your record on it

The most heavily tested D5 concept — correct on Exam 4 Q15, Exam 4 Q30, Exam 6 Q15, Exam 7 Q23, Exam 8 Q59 and Exam 10 Q24, six scored appearances with no misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.3 · Exam 4 Q15 · Exam 4 Q30 · Exam 6 Q15 · Exam 7 Q23 · Exam 8 Q59 · Exam 9 Q7 · Exam 10 Q24

D5 §5.4

The persistent case-facts block

Solid

Keep transactional facts in a block that sits outside the summarized history and is included in every prompt, so compression can never reach them.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Long support and correction sessions have a signature failure: an exact commitment stated early — a 15% discount, a $12,450 credit, a pinned library version, a routing rule naming one specific tool — gets compressed into a vague reference, and twenty turns later the agent acts on the vagueness. The structural fix is to maintain a 'case facts' block that is updated whenever a new fact appears and injected into every prompt, held entirely outside whatever gets summarized. It survives compression because it is never subject to compression. The three tempting alternatives all share one weakness: they keep the fact inside the summarizer's reach and then hope the summarizer behaves.

Why it works that way

It converts precision from something you hope a summarization step preserves into something the architecture guarantees.

Decision rule

If losing a value would produce a wrong action, that value belongs outside the summarizer, not inside it with better instructions.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Raise the summarization threshold so compression triggers later.It only buys turns. The fact still eventually gets compressed and blurred.Exam 2 Q9; Exam 4 Q27; Exam 5 Q29; Exam 5 Q37; Exam 8 Q24; KD #21
  • Revise the summarization prompt to instruct it to always preserve exact numbers.This still depends on the summarizer executing perfectly every single time. The facts block removes that dependency instead of strengthening it.Exam 2 Q9; Exam 4 Q27; Exam 5 Q29; Exam 5 Q37; Exam 8 Q24; KD #21
  • Move the facts into an external database and retrieve them each turn.External storage plus retrieval is overkill for facts that only need to live for one session; the documented fix is a compact in-prompt block.Exam 2 Q9; Exam 5 Q37; Exam 8 Q24
  • Restart the session periodically so summarization never accumulates enough turns to compress the early exchanges.It loses conversational continuity and just resets the clock without addressing why precise facts get compressed.Exam 5 Q29

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q27 (error code and line number), Exam 5 Q29 (agreed credit amount), Exam 5 Q37 (pinned SDK version and timeout) and Exam 8 Q24 (vendor routing rule) — four scored appearances, no misses.

Where this was taught

Key Distinction #21

D5 §5.5

Trim verbose tool output with a PostToolUse hook

Solid

A tool returning 40+ fields when five matter should be filtered by a PostToolUse hook before the result enters context — not mentally ignored afterwards.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Tool results consume tokens completely out of proportion to their relevance, and unlike a single long input they keep arriving: every call adds another payload, and every payload stays in the conversation for every subsequent turn. A `lookup_order` returning warehouse routing and carrier metadata, an OCR pass returning per-character confidence and font metrics, a coverage tool returning ninety days of trend history — each floods the window and degrades quality on later work. Trim at the boundary with a `PostToolUse` hook that keeps only the fields the task actually needs, so the irrelevant ones never enter context at all. The classic wrong answer is telling the model in the system prompt to ignore the extra fields: the tokens are still paid for and the attention cost remains.

Why it works that way

This is where the corpus draws the line between removing tokens and asking the model to disregard them — only the former actually conserves the window.

Decision rule

Filter tool output at the boundary it crosses into context; never ask the model to ignore tokens you could have deleted.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore the irrelevant fields.The tokens are already in context and still consumed. The attention cost and clutter remain; the fields must be removed before they enter, not skipped over.Exam 2 Q8; Exam 2 Q29; Exam 2 Q56; Exam 3 Q36; Exam 4 Q40; Exam 8 Q25; Exam 9 Q60; Exam 10 Q59
  • Summarize the whole conversation more aggressively once it grows.This treats the symptom while the verbose results keep flooding in on every subsequent call; summarization then runs harder and loses precision later work needs.Exam 2 Q8; Exam 3 Q36; Exam 8 Q25; Exam 9 Q60; Exam 10 Q59
  • Switch to a larger-context model so the extra fields fit.Cost rises, the noise persists, and the model still reads every irrelevant field alongside the work. This is a noise problem, not a capacity problem.Exam 2 Q8; Exam 4 Q40; Exam 8 Q25; Exam 10 Q59

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q40 (semantic-search tool), Exam 8 Q25 (`run_ocr_pass`) and Exam 10 Q59 (`run_document_ocr`); also taught in unattempted Exams 2, 3 and 9. No misses on any scored exam.

Where this was taught
