D5 §5.6

Explore subagent for verbose discovery

Solid

Run the noisy discovery phase in a subagent whose context is separate, and let it return only a concise summary — so the main session keeps its window for design and implementation.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Context isolation is usually described as a constraint on subagents, but here it is the feature you want. Mapping 120 files, enumerating 90 route handlers, surveying fourteen adapter modules, cataloguing 90 functions — this kind of work produces a long, detailed inventory that will fill the main session before the real conversation begins. Delegate it to an Explore subagent: the verbose output stays in the subagent's own context, and only a concise summary of the findings comes back. Your main session then still has room for the design discussion and the implementation the discovery was for. The rejected alternatives are worth memorising: `/compact` mid-task loses the precision the implementation phase still needs, and splitting across sessions joined with `--continue` or `--resume` adds coordination overhead and consistency risk without isolating anything.

Why it works that way

Discovery and implementation have different context needs; isolating the first protects the second instead of forcing a lossy trade between them.

Decision rule

If a phase will produce far more output than the decisions that follow it need, run that phase somewhere else and bring back the summary.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Run `/compact` partway through the discovery pass and continue in the same session.Mid-task compaction loses exact details — specific file paths, which adapters overlap on which logic — that the design and implementation phases still need.Exam 3 Q19; Exam 4 Q43; Exam 5 Q6; Exam 7 Q24; Exam 8 Q60; Exam 9 Q8; Exam 10 Q28; KD #22
  • Split the discovery across several sessions joined with `--continue` or `--resume`.Multiple sessions add coordination overhead and consistency risk between phases, and never actually isolate the verbose output.Exam 3 Q19; Exam 4 Q43; Exam 7 Q24; Exam 8 Q60; Exam 9 Q8; Exam 10 Q28
  • Run the discovery in the main session anyway, since the full inventory is context the design discussion will need.That is exactly the described failure mode — it consumes the room the design discussion requires.Exam 10 Q28; Exam 5 Q6
  • Ask the same session to periodically self-summarize its own notes as it goes.The tokens are already spent by the time a summary is requested; isolation must happen in a separate context, not through in-session compression.Exam 3 Q19
  • Hand the remaining exploration to the human engineer to keep the session light.It shifts the burden off the mechanism designed for it. Verbose discovery belongs in a subagent, not offloaded to a person.Exam 4 Q43

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q43, Exam 5 Q6, Exam 7 Q24, Exam 8 Q60 and Exam 10 Q28 — five scored appearances across four different scenarios, no misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.6 · Key-Distinctions_v1 #22 · Exam 3 Q19 · Exam 4 Q43 · Exam 5 Q6 · Exam 7 Q24 · Exam 8 Q60 · Exam 9 Q8 · Exam 10 Q28

Key Distinction #22

D5 §5.7

Semantic retrieval for long-term recall

Solid

To recall one specific exchange out of months of history, index the full history for semantic retrieval — do not window it, summarize it, or tag it.

The full lesson

What is actually true

When a conversation or archive spans many sessions — an eleven-week design discussion, fourteen months of research projects, a quarter of session transcripts — and someone asks for a specific past decision, caveat, or tradeoff, you need retrieval, not compression. Embeddings over the full history let you pull back precisely the relevant past exchange on demand, without having decided in advance what would matter. Each alternative destroys something you will need: a rolling window discards the early sessions where the answer usually lives, progressive summarization compresses specific quoted conclusions into abstractions that can no longer be recalled precisely, and manually tagging conclusions with XML both fails to scale and does nothing for the history already written.

Why it works that way

Compression is a bet about what will matter later; retrieval removes the need to bet at all, which is the right trade once history is large.

Decision rule

If the question is 'what did we conclude about X, months ago', the answer is retrieval over full history — never a window and never a summary.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Keep a rolling window of only the most recent sessions or projects.It discards exactly the early history the question is about — the week-three decision is the first thing a rolling window drops.Exam 3 Q24; Exam 5 Q15; Exam 6 Q30; Exam 9 Q9
  • Maintain a progressively compressed running summary of the whole history.Progressive summarization turns specific quoted conclusions into vague abstractions, so a niche detail or a particular accepted tradeoff simply vanishes.Exam 3 Q24; Exam 5 Q15; Exam 6 Q30; Exam 9 Q9; KD #24
  • Add XML tags around each concluded decision so future questions can be answered by scanning tags.Tagging does not solve retrieval at this scale, depends on remembering to tag consistently, and does nothing for the history already accumulated.Exam 3 Q24; Exam 6 Q30; Exam 9 Q9
  • Add section headings to each report so the coordinator can navigate faster.Headings address lost-in-the-middle attention within one long input — a different problem from retrieving a specific exchange out of months of separate archives.Exam 5 Q15

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q15 (research archive caveat) and Exam 6 Q30 (14-month niche subtopic) — notably Exam 6 Q30 was answered correctly even in the one exam where D5 dipped to 5/7.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.7 · Key-Distinctions_v1 #24 · Exam 3 Q24 · Exam 5 Q15 · Exam 6 Q30 · Exam 9 Q9

Key Distinction #24

D5 §5.8

Escalate on structural signals, not inferred emotion

Solid

Trigger escalation on explicit human requests, policy gaps, missing data and repeated failures — never on sentiment analysis or the model's own confidence score.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Reliable escalation keys off things that are structurally true about the case: the customer asked for a person, the policy is silent or ambiguous on what they want, required data is missing, a lookup has failed repeatedly, or a financial operation crosses a threshold (best enforced by a hook rather than a prompt). What does not work is inferring difficulty. Sentiment does not track complexity — a calm message can describe a tangled multi-account billing error, and an irate one can be about a trivially fixable typo — so an anger threshold floods the human queue with resolvable cases while missing the calm-but-hard ones. Model self-rated confidence fails for a different reason: it is uncalibrated, and the model can be confidently wrong. Note that none of the usual patches help — lowering the threshold, having a second instance re-score, or switching from 1–10 to high/medium/low all keep the same unreliable signal. The syllabus is also specific about how you implement this, and it is the ✅ option in its escalation-design exam pattern: write explicit escalation criteria into the system prompt with few-shot examples showing when to escalate versus when to resolve autonomously. That is a rule set the agent applies, not a score it has to invent — so if an option offers 'explicit escalation criteria plus few-shot examples' against sentiment thresholds, self-rated confidence, or a minimum-attempts rule, it is the answer.

Why it works that way

Escalation design decides where scarce human attention goes; keying it to a signal that does not correlate with difficulty wastes that attention and misses the cases that needed it.

Decision rule

Ask whether the escalation trigger is a fact about the case or a guess about the case — escalate on facts, written down as explicit criteria with few-shot examples.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Escalate whenever sentiment analysis detects anger.Customer mood does not correlate with case complexity, so this floods the human queue with easy cases and leaves calm, complex ones unescalated.Exam 2 Q10; Exam 7 Q13
  • Have the model rate its own confidence 1–10 and escalate below a cutoff.Self-reported confidence is uncalibrated and poorly correlated with actual difficulty — testing showed confidently-scored cases resolved wrongly and low-scored ones that were straightforward.Exam 2 Q10; Exam 7 Q13; Exam 10 Q9
  • Lower the confidence cutoff, or re-score with a second agent, or use a coarser high/medium/low label.Every variant still rests on the same unreliable self-rating; changing the cutoff, duplicating it, or simplifying its scale does not calibrate it.Exam 7 Q13
  • Train an automatic complexity classifier to score each message.Over-engineering that requires training data the team likely does not have; the sanctioned approach is structural signals, not a bespoke model.Exam 2 Q10

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 7 Q13 (self-rated confidence routing for merge disputes); the same principle appeared as the rejected option on Exam 10 Q9 and was also correctly rejected. Also taught in unattempted Exam 2 Q10. Caveat on the implementation facet: the 'explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples' option is stated in the syllabus §5.8 escalation-design exam pattern but has never been the key of a D5-tagged question — the few-shot-escalation-criteria framing that does appear in the mock corpus is tagged D4, so that specific facet is untested within D5.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.8 · Domain-5_v2 §5.8 escalation-design exam pattern · Exam 2 Q10 · Exam 7 Q13 · Exam 10 Q9

D5 §5.8

Explicit human request means escalate immediately

Solid

When a customer asks for a person, escalate on the spot — no attempt counter, no 'let me try one more thing', no confidence check.

The full lesson

What is actually true

An explicit request for a human is a structural signal that overrides everything else in your escalation design. The agent must not attempt to solve the issue first. This is the specific reason a rule like 'never escalate until three resolution attempts have been made' is wrong: it is a sensible-sounding policy that directly violates the immediate-escalation requirement, and in practice it produces exactly the transcript you never want — the customer asks for a person, the agent offers another remedy, and the customer repeats the demand, angrier. Any minimum-attempts budget must yield to an explicit request.

Why it works that way

It is the one escalation case with no judgement in it, which is why exam stems dress it up with a competing policy and see whether you let the policy win.

Decision rule

Explicit request for a human beats every other escalation rule you have written, including your own attempt counter.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Continue offering alternative resolutions until the three-attempt budget is exhausted, then escalate with a summary.A minimum-attempts rule violates the immediate-escalation requirement for explicit human requests — the documented trap of gating escalation behind N attempts.Exam 10 Q9
  • Acknowledge the frustration and propose one more concrete resolution first.Acknowledge-then-offer is the pattern for expressions of dissatisfaction without a human request; 'I want to talk to a person' is explicit, so applying it here misreads the signal.Exam 10 Q9
  • Have the agent rate its confidence in resolving the case and escalate only below a threshold.Self-rated confidence is uncalibrated and irrelevant once a structural signal has already fired.Exam 10 Q9

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 10 Q9, its only scored appearance (Exam 10 D5 finished 9/9).

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.8 · Exam 10 Q9

D5 §5.8

Multiple-match disambiguation — ask, never guess

Solid

When a lookup returns several plausible matches, request an additional identifier — never pick one by recency, position, or risk reasoning.

The full lesson

What is actually true

If a customer lookup returns several accounts under the same name, or a config change matches three environment files with different values, the agent has genuine ambiguity that it is not entitled to resolve on its own. Ask for one more identifier — an email address, an order number, which environment is intended. Every heuristic shortcut is the same failure class dressed differently: 'take the most recently active' is arbitrary, 'take the first result' is arbitrary, 'update all of them for consistency' silently over-scopes, and 'assume production because it is highest-stakes' is still a guess wearing risk-analysis clothing. Note also that escalating to a human here is unnecessary — the ambiguity is resolvable by simply asking.

Why it works that way

Heuristic selection among genuine matches produces misidentified accounts, wrong refunds, and unintended production changes — errors that look like confident correct behaviour until someone audits them.

Decision rule

Several genuine matches and no disambiguator in the request → ask for one more identifier before touching anything.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Select the most recently active or most recently modified match.Recency is an arbitrary tiebreaker with no bearing on intent; the corpus explicitly rejects heuristic selection among lookup matches.Exam 5 Q40; corpus §5.8
  • Apply the change to all matches, since consistency is safer than picking one.It silently over-scopes the change to avoid asking — risking an unintended production edit, the opposite of the caution required.Exam 5 Q40
  • Choose the highest-stakes target (e.g. production) as the most likely intent.Still a guess, just dressed as risk reasoning, instead of confirming the actual intended scope.Exam 5 Q40
  • Escalate to a human immediately.Unnecessary — the ambiguity is fully resolvable by asking the customer or requester one clarifying question.corpus §5.8

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q40 (feature-flag timeout defined in dev/staging/prod configs), its only scored appearance.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.8 · Exam 5 Q40

D5 §5.9

The aggregate-accuracy masking trap

Solid

A reassuring overall accuracy number can hide a catastrophic failure rate on one rare segment — validate by document type and by field before reducing human review.

The full lesson

What is actually true

97% overall accuracy sounds like a mandate to automate. It is not, because an aggregate averages away segment-level failures: the same 97% is consistent with a rare document type failing 40% of the time. The corpus repeats this with different numbers — 96% aggregate hiding 33% failure on windshield-only glass claims, 91% resolution hiding a much worse rate on billing disputes — because the shape is what matters. Before you reduce human review anywhere, break accuracy out by document type and by field and require every segment to clear the bar independently. The giveaway in a stem is always the same: someone points out that a particular category is a small fraction of total volume.

Why it works that way

Rare segments are exactly where automation errors concentrate and exactly where aggregate metrics are least able to see them.

Decision rule

Never act on an aggregate accuracy figure when someone can name a segment that is a small share of volume — break it out first.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Auto-process everything above the aggregate confidence threshold, since the overall number clears the bar.This is the masking trap itself — the average conceals that a rare segment may fail dramatically underneath it, and those failures post as real downstream errors.Exam 2 Q54; Exam 3 Q56; Exam 4 Q10; Exam 7 Q42
  • Nudge the global confidence threshold slightly stricter and keep automating the rest.A blunt aggregate-level tweak does not address a systematically underperforming segment, which needs its own investigation and likely its own handling.Exam 3 Q56
  • Check whether the figure was measured over a week or a month, since a longer window is more trustworthy.Window length does not reveal per-segment masking — a longer window averages the same problem away just as effectively.Exam 4 Q10
  • Benchmark the aggregate against competitors' reported rates.External comparison says nothing about whether your own aggregate is hiding a segment-level failure; the fix is internal segment analysis.Exam 4 Q10

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 4 Q10 (91% resolution rate, billing disputes) and Exam 7 Q42 (91% aggregate, regulatory facts); also taught in unattempted Exams 2 and 3. No misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.9 · Exam 2 Q54 · Exam 3 Q56 · Exam 4 Q10 · Exam 7 Q42

D5 §5.9

Stratified random sampling of the automated stream

Solid

Regularly audit a random sample of what you auto-accepted, stratified across document types and field categories — otherwise novel error patterns in the automated path never surface.

The full lesson

What is actually true

Calibrated confidence tells you where to send today's uncertain cases. It tells you nothing about whether the automated path is still correct six months from now, when a major vendor has introduced a new invoice layout that nobody validated. The safeguard is ongoing stratified random sampling of the high-confidence, auto-processed stream — stratified across document types, layouts and field categories rather than drawn from the top of the review queue. That is what measures the true error rate of automation and catches novel error patterns before they compound. Reviewing only what was flagged low-confidence leaves the automated path permanently unexamined, and an unstratified flat 10% spends reviewer capacity on the easy, common segments while undersampling the rare ones where errors live.

Why it works that way

The automated path is the one nobody looks at by construction, so it is the one that needs a deliberate, structured audit designed into it.

Decision rule

Sample the stream nobody reviews, and stratify the sample — random alone is not enough.

Traps that have caught you here

  • Route a fixed 10% of all documents to review at random, without stratifying.Unstratified sampling over-samples easy, common segments and under-samples the rare, problem-prone ones where errors actually cluster.Exam 2 Q55; Exam 7 Q42; Exam 9 Q25
  • Lower the confidence threshold so more documents fall into the review queue.Enlarging the low-confidence queue still never inspects the auto-accepted stream, which is where the undetected error lives.Exam 5 Q26; Exam 9 Q25
  • Have humans re-review every document until the problem is understood.Universal re-review defeats the automation calibration exists to enable and does not scale; the point is targeted oversight, not blanket inspection.Exam 5 Q26; Exam 9 Q25
  • Wait for downstream reconciliation complaints to surface the problem.Reactive detection lets the error compound; stratified sampling exists precisely to catch it before it reaches reconciliation.Exam 5 Q26

Your record on it

Correct on Exam 5 Q26 (unvalidated new vendor layout after six months) and Exam 7 Q42 (paired with the aggregate-masking check); also taught in unattempted Exam 9 Q25. No misses.

Where this was taught

Domain-5_v2 §5.9 · Exam 5 Q26 · Exam 7 Q42 · Exam 9 Q25

Cross-domain · 29 high-yield traps

The Key Distinctions

These are the pairs the exam most likes to blur. Every one of them has been seeded into your mock exams at least once, and as of Exam 10 the tracker holds zero weak rows — your remaining gaps have moved off this list and onto whole corpus sections.

KD #1 · D3

Project scope vs user scope for CLAUDE.md

Not yet tested
True

Project scope is version-controlled and reaches every team member, so it is where shared conventions and team standards belong; user scope reaches only that one developer and is for personal preferences and personal workflow.

Commonly believed

That a convention some teammates follow and a new joiner does not must be a defect in the project file — when the real cause is that the convention only ever lived in the existing members' personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is not shared via version control.

The full lesson

When behaviour differs between people on the same repository at the same commit, the difference is per-person, so look at per-person configuration first. Project files are version-controlled and reach everyone; `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` reaches exactly one machine and is never shared. Put shared conventions in the project file and keep only your own preferences at user scope. The tell on the page is a stem that carefully establishes that everyone is on the same commit.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 1 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 2; seeded Exam 2 Q15 and Exam 5 Q31). Exam 2 is unscored; Exam 5 Q31 is not among Exam 5's eight recorded misses, so it was answered correctly, but the tracker was never promoted off 'unknown'. No EXAM-LOG.md miss cites KD #1. The coaching doc's Theme 9 associates KD #1 with D3 §3.1, whose two Exam 4 misses (Q22 `@import` depth, Q46 concatenation) were logged without a KD tag.

KD #2 · D2

`.mcp.json` vs `~/.claude.json`

Not yet tested
True

A team that shares one MCP server but each holds a different token puts the server definition in `.mcp.json` and injects the secret with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` environment-variable substitution — one shared config, per-developer credentials.

Commonly believed

That per-developer credentials force per-developer config, so each engineer must define the server in their own `~/.claude.json`, or that a real secret can be committed into the shared file.

The full lesson

Separate the shape of the configuration from the secret inside it. The server definition is shared and belongs in version-controlled `.mcp.json`; the token is personal and gets referenced as `${VAR}` so each developer's environment supplies their own. Reach for `~/.claude.json` only for genuinely personal auth and personal overrides across all your projects.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 2 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 2; seeded Exam 2 Q4 and Exam 5 Q9, the latter with its citation trimmed for the KD cap per PB-14). Exam 2 is unscored; Exam 5 Q9 is not among that exam's recorded misses. No EXAM-LOG.md miss cites KD #2.

KD #3 · D3

`.claude/rules/` vs CLAUDE.md vs Skills

Not yet tested
True

Choose the destination by trigger condition — universal standards go in CLAUDE.md, path-scoped conventions go in a `.claude/rules/` file with a glob, and workflow-specific guidance that should load only when asked for becomes a Skill.

Commonly believed

Treating the three as interchangeable places to 'put the instructions', so path-specific or workflow-specific content gets loaded into every session via CLAUDE.md, or universal standards get buried behind a glob or a slash command that rarely fires.

The full lesson

Ask one question before you choose: when does this content need to be in context? Always, on matching paths, or only when someone asks for it. That answer picks the destination on its own — CLAUDE.md, `.claude/rules/` with a glob, or a Skill. Getting this wrong does not usually produce an error; it produces content that is either always in the way or never present when needed.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 3 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 3; seeded Exam 3 Block B, Exam 4 Q41, Exam 5 Q32). Exam 3 is unscored; Exam 4 Q41 and Exam 5 Q32 are not among their exams' recorded misses, so both were answered correctly without the tracker being promoted. Related but untagged: Exam 8 Q51 and Exam 10 Q27 both missed D3 §3.11 (CLAUDE.md-vs-Skills modularization) — the Exam 10 Professor's Note calls §3.11 'now 2-for-2 missed' and D3's priority item for Exam 11.

KD #4 · D3

Project skills vs personal skills with the same name

Not yet tested
True

The personal skill overrides the project skill for that individual only — which is precisely the point: one person can customise the behaviour without forking the team command, editing the shared version-controlled file, or inventing an unfamiliar command name.

Commonly believed

That a name collision is an error to be avoided, that the project (shared) version must win, or that customising requires renaming the command or editing the team's file.

The full lesson

This is the one genuine override in the Claude Code configuration story, and it runs personal-over-project. Use it when you want your own behaviour behind the same familiar command without touching what your teammates share. Keep it filed separately from CLAUDE.md, where levels concatenate and nothing overrides anything — mixing the two mechanisms up is the trap.

Flagged discrepancy: EXAM-LOG.md Exam 6 Q51 is a recorded miss on exactly this lesson — 'a personal skill of the same name overrides a project skill only for that individual, without editing the shared version-controlled file. Domain-3_v2 §3.5' — but it is logged with a section citation and no KD number, so the tracker never registered it. Treat the 'untested' label as a tracker artefact; there is one documented miss on the underlying content.

KD #5 · D1

`stop_reason: "tool_use"` vs `stop_reason: "end_turn"`

Not yet tested
True

The orchestrator branches on the structured `stop_reason` field — on `tool_use` it executes the tool, appends the result, and calls again; on `end_turn` it stops the loop and returns the response.

Commonly believed

Parsing Claude's natural-language text for a completion signal such as 'I'm done' — substituting prose inspection for the structured field the API already gives you.

The full lesson

Loop control is a protocol question, not a reading-comprehension question. The API hands you an explicit `stop_reason`; branch on it and nothing else. Any option that has your harness inspecting Claude's wording to decide whether to continue is wrong by construction, because the same sentence can appear in a turn that still wants a tool.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 5 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 3; seeded Exam 2 Q1, Exam 4 Q1, Exam 5 Q47). Exam 2 is unscored; Exam 4 Q1 and Exam 5 Q47 are not among their exams' recorded misses. No EXAM-LOG.md miss cites KD #5. The coaching doc files KD #5 under Theme 7 ('Who runs the loop'), whose three misses (Exam 5 Q35, Exam 6 Q2 on D2 §2.1; Exam 6 Q5 on D5 §5.1) are adjacent protocol facts rather than the stop_reason branch itself.

KD #6 · D1

Coordinator hub pattern vs direct subagent-to-subagent communication

Not yet tested
True

The coordinator is the hub: it sees all exchanges, handles errors centrally and uniformly, and decides what each agent is allowed to see.

Commonly believed

Letting agents talk directly — which leaves the coordinator blind to exchanges it never saw, pushes error handling down into each agent independently, and breaks the hub-and-spoke pattern.

The full lesson

Multi-agent designs in this corpus are hub-and-spoke, and the coordinator's visibility is the reason. Once two subagents talk directly, the coordinator can no longer reason about what was tried, cannot recover uniformly from a failure, and loses control over information flow. Direct inter-agent chat looks like an efficiency; treat it as a loss of the coordinator's only source of truth.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 6 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 1; seeded only Exam 5 Q1). Exam 5 is scored and Q1 is not among its eight recorded misses, so the single scored appearance was correct, but the tracker was never promoted off 'unknown'.

KD #7 · D1

Root cause of incomplete coverage: narrow decomposition, not subagent performance

Not yet tested
True

When every subagent reports success but the aggregate output covers the wrong ground, the fault is upstream in how the coordinator partitioned the work — fix the coordinator prompt.

Commonly believed

Diagnosing it as subagent capability, search-query quality, a tool-description problem, or a synthesis-stage gap-detection failure.

The full lesson

Read the success reports as evidence, not noise. If all subagents succeeded and the coverage is still wrong, no subagent can be at fault — they each did exactly what they were asked, and what they were asked is the defect. The coordinator's job is to partition the space explicitly before delegating, not to deduplicate or patch afterwards. 'Every subagent reported success' is the tell that sends you upstream.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 7 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 1; seeded only Exam 3 Block A, which is unscored). Flagged discrepancy: EXAM-LOG.md records two untagged misses on exactly this lesson — Exam 4 Q39 ('when subagents all succeed but coverage is wrong, the root cause is the coordinator's task decomposition, not subagent execution. Domain-1_v2 §1.6') and Exam 5 Q21 ('misattributed a coverage gap to a tool-description problem instead of the coordinator's own narrow task decomposition'). Both logged with a section citation and no KD number. The coaching doc ranks this Theme 3 (5 misses, ~80 marks index), while noting D1 has since held 93.8% for three consecutive exams.

KD #8 · D1

Structured error context vs a generic failure status

Solid
True

Always return the structured context, because it is what lets the coordinator recover intelligently — retry with a modified query, continue on partial results, or route around the failure.

Commonly believed

Returning a generic failure status, which collapses the coordinator's whole decision space down to retry-or-abort.

The full lesson

An error message is an input to the coordinator's next decision, so design it for that consumer. Say what failed, what was attempted, what you got anyway, and what else could be tried. A bare 'failed' throws away everything the coordinator needs and leaves it guessing between two blunt options.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 8 records 'strong — correct in Exam 10' (cycle 3; seeded Exam 3 Blocks A and D, Exam 5 Q5, and Exam 10 Q49 on the OCR-failure structured-retry-feedback facet). Exam 10 Q49 is not among that exam's six recorded misses, and EXAM-LOG.md Exam 10 Observations state 'All 10 Key-Distinction-seeded questions were answered correctly (KD#8, #9, #10, #11, #12, #14, #19, #20, #23, #29)'. No recorded miss on this KD in any scored exam.

KD #9 · D1

Transient vs permanent errors in MCP tool design

Solid
True

Retry transient failures with backoff inside the tool before surfacing them; return permanent failures immediately with details. '0 results' is a valid result, not an error; a timeout is an access failure that needs a coordinator decision.

Commonly believed

Applying one uniform retry policy to every failure, or collapsing 'the query succeeded and matched nothing' into the same bucket as 'we could not reach the source' — which makes the agent report absent data that may actually exist.

The full lesson

Sort every failure into retryable and not before you decide anything else, and hand the agent that classification rather than making it infer retryability from prose. Retrying a permission error or a not-found is pure waste no matter how many attempts you allow. And guard the '0 results' boundary hard: a successful query with no matches is an answer, while a timeout masquerading as 'no data' is a silent correctness bug.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 9 records 'strong — correct in Exam 10' (cycle 3; seeded Exam 3 Block A, Exam 5 Q50, Exam 10 Q5 on the coordinator error-handling-ownership facet), and EXAM-LOG.md Exam 10 Observations confirm all ten KD-seeded questions were correct. Flagged nuance: adjacent, untagged D2 §2.3 error-taxonomy items have been missed twice — Exam 4 Q52 ('permission errors are non-retryable regardless of attempt count; timeouts are transient/retryable — conflating the two wastes retries') and Exam 10 Q4 (business-error vs protocol-error semantics; treating a valid policy denial as a tool failure). The KD itself is clean; the surrounding section is not.

KD #10 · D2

Fix the tool descriptions before adding a routing layer

Recovered
True

Fix the descriptions first — misrouting means the descriptions do not distinguish the similar tools, and the description is the primary input to selection.

Commonly believed

Adding a pre-routing classifier (or any other layer), which adds infrastructure while leaving the ambiguous signal exactly where it was; likewise merging two semantically distinct tools to dodge the ambiguity.

The full lesson

Fix the signal before adding a layer that compensates for a bad signal. When two tools get confused, the repair lives in the text the model reads to choose between them: what it does, what input it accepts with an example, when to use it, and explicitly when not to. A classifier in front leaves both descriptions just as ambiguous as they were, and merging the tools trades the ambiguity for lost semantic precision.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 10 now reads 'strong — correct in Exam 10' (cycle 3; Exam 2 Q16 area, Exam 3 Block A, Exam 4 Q47, Exam 10 Q34 on extract_key_findings-vs-extract_citations description ambiguity), but the history is a recovery: EXAM-LOG.md Exam 4 logs 'Q8, Q47 — tool description must state scope/boundary to disambiguate near-duplicate tools (two independent misses, same corpus section, different scenarios). Domain-2_v2 §2.2; Key-Distinctions #10.' Two tagged misses in Exam 4, then correct in Exam 10.

KD #11 · D1

Prompt instructions vs programmatic preconditions for critical sequencing

Recovered
True

When the sequencing is safety- or security-critical, enforce it programmatically — code makes it deterministic. Prompt instructions remain the right default for general, non-critical guidance.

Commonly believed

Trusting a prompt instruction to guarantee an ordering, when prompt compliance is probabilistic and the corpus records real failure rates for exactly this pattern.

The full lesson

Ask of every proposed fix: after this change, can the model still do the wrong thing? If yes, you have bought guidance, not enforcement. Reserve the deterministic mechanisms for the cases that genuinely need a guarantee — irreversible actions, mandatory ordering, capability grants — and note that a compliance percentage in the stem is the exam telling you the probabilistic layer has already been tried and failed.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 11 records 'strong — correct in Exam 10' (cycle 4; Exam 3 Block A, Exam 4 Q11, Exam 5 Q46, Exam 10 Q7 identity-verification enforcement plateau). The recovery history is in EXAM-LOG.md Exam 4, whose Q2 miss is tagged 'Key-Distinctions #11/#12', and whose Professor's Note groups Q34, Q19 and Q52 as sharing 'the same shape: a probabilistic prompt-level fix chosen over the structural/configuration-level guarantee'. Correct on its most recent scored appearance (Exam 10).

KD #12 · D2

Two-tool token binding vs a single tool with a `dry_run` boolean

Recovered
True

The two-tool token binding makes skipping the preview architecturally impossible — the token cannot exist without a prior preview call. That is a code-level guarantee.

Commonly believed

A `dry_run` boolean, a `confirmed: true` parameter, or a confirmation string — all of which the agent can simply set or pass directly, making them prompt-level hope rather than enforcement. Near-miss wrong answers also include a server-side timing heuristic (fragile to timing) and an orchestration-layer confirmation prompt (extra infrastructure).

The full lesson

When a preview is mandatory, make the skip impossible rather than merely discouraged. Token binding does that because the second call cannot be constructed without the artefact the first call produces. Any single-tool variant — a boolean, a flag, a confirmation string — leaves the agent free to call straight through, which is exactly what audit logs in these stems keep showing.

Your record on it

This was the project's most persistent trap and is now durably cleared. Missed three consecutive exams (EXAM-LOG.md Exam 4 Q2, Exam 5 Q54, Exam 6 Q12 — Insights Round 1 names it as the only KD missed in all three exams of that window), then correct on both seeded facets in Exam 7 (Q7, Q38), correct again in Exam 8 Q41 and Exam 10 Q37. GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 12: 'strong — CORRECT four consecutive exams now (Exam 7 both facets, Exam 8, Exam 10), durably cleared... this project's former single most persistent trap remains resolved.'

KD #13 · D3

`context: fork` in skills vs running in the main session

Recovered
True

Use `context: fork` for discovery, analysis, exploration and brainstorming — work that generates large or exploratory output you do not want polluting the main window. The main session is for implementation, design and conversation.

Commonly believed

Treating `context: fork` as a general 'make this skill better behaved' switch and confusing it with `allowed-tools`; or fixing context pollution by switching to a faster model, compressing results to a short summary (which loses analysis capability), or splitting into two skills (which does not prevent leakage).

The full lesson

Ask what the skill is doing wrong — filling the window, or reaching too far. Output volume, lost main-session focus, exploratory material bleeding into later turns is a `context: fork` problem; destructive or out-of-scope tool use is an `allowed-tools` problem. Both keys live in SKILL.md frontmatter and nowhere else, and forking isolates context, not side effects.

Your record on it

Tracker override: GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md row 13 still reads 'unknown', but EXAM-LOG.md explicitly tags a miss — Exam 4 'Q35 — `context: fork` isolates a skill's large/exploratory output from the main session. Domain-3_v2 §3.3; Key-Distinctions #13.' The KD was then seeded again at Exam 5 Q34, which is not among Exam 5's recorded misses, so it was answered correctly. Related untagged miss: Exam 6 Q50, confusing `allowed-tools` with `context: fork` (D3 §3.3) — the coaching doc ranks that pair Theme 8.

KD #14 · D4

Message Batches API vs the synchronous API

Solid
True

Batch is for scheduled, non-blocking work. Synchronous is for blocking checks, interactive use, and anything that needs multi-turn tool calls.

Commonly believed

Reaching for batch purely on cost, in a workflow that needs tool calls mid-request — batch is fire-and-forget and cannot execute a tool during a request and return the result to Claude.

The full lesson

Two questions decide it: does anything block on the answer, and does the work need tool calls mid-flight? An iterative code review that fetches related files while reviewing fails the second test outright, so no amount of cost saving makes batch eligible. Save batch for work you can start and collect later.

KD #15 · D3

`-p` / `--print` vs invented headless mechanisms for CI/CD

Not yet tested
True

`-p` / `--print` is the documented way to run Claude non-interactively and print output to stdout — the correct answer for CI/CD invocation.

Commonly believed

`CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` and `--batch` do not exist; the stdin redirect is a workaround, not a documented approach.

The full lesson

This is a fabricated-flag trap, and the defence is knowing the real flag cold rather than reasoning about which invented one sounds most plausible. Distractors here are built from real-looking environment variables and switch names precisely because they read like something you would find in a CLI. If an option names a mechanism you cannot place in the documentation, that is the signal, not the wording.

Your record on it

KD #16 · D4

Few-shot examples vs instruction refinement for format consistency

Not yet tested
True

Few-shot examples showing the exact required format — they give the model a concrete pattern to match.

Commonly believed

More detailed or more explicit instructions, when instructions are already the thing that is failing; adding more text does not help.

The full lesson

Read the stem for what has already been tried. When the instruction has been rewritten three times and the output still comes back in four shapes, the instruction channel has been tested and found wanting — a fourth rewrite is the same experiment again. Format problems get examples; that is the mapping.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 16 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 1; seeded only in an Exam 2 question area, and Exam 2 is unscored). No EXAM-LOG.md miss cites KD #16. Adjacent evidence that the technique-to-failure-mode mapping is genuinely shaky in both directions: Exam 5 Q60 'swapped a few-shot format-consistency fix for a step-by-step reasoning-depth cue' and Exam 6 Q35 needed the reasoning cue and reached for few-shot or temperature instead — the coaching doc's Theme 5.

KD #17 · D1

Per-file review passes vs a single-pass full-PR review

Solid
True

Per-file passes hold attention quality high and give every file consistent depth; cross-file concerns get their own integration pass. This is the correct pattern for large PRs.

Commonly believed

A single pass over everything, which dilutes attention across files and produces variable depth — and, specifically, 'use a larger model with a bigger context window', which does not fix attention quality at all.

The full lesson

More tokens available is not the same as consistent attention per token, so a bigger window does not repair a dilution problem. When the symptom is that some files got a deep review and others got a shallow one, split the passes. Keep a separate integration pass so the cross-file issues a per-file split would miss still get caught.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 17 records 'strong (first-ever scored instance, Exam 6 Q38, correct)' (cycle 3; Exam 2 Q area, Exam 5 Q48, Exam 6 Q38 under a D4 framing). Exam 6 Q38 is not among Exam 6's eleven recorded misses. Single scored data point, so the label rests on one confirmed-correct appearance rather than a streak.

KD #18 · D4

Examples targeted at ambiguous cases vs generic clear examples for misrouting

Not yet tested
True

The small, targeted set covering the ambiguous boundary, with rationale — that is where the model is actually failing.

Commonly believed

The larger set of clear-cut examples, which demonstrates cases the model already gets right and never touches the edge where the routing breaks.

The full lesson

Example count is not the lever; example placement is. Misrouting happens at a boundary, so the examples have to sit on that boundary and say why each case falls where it does. Ten clean examples of obvious calls teach the model nothing it did not already know.

Your record on it

Neither question appears in its exam's recorded misses (Exam 4's fifteen misses and Exam 5's eight are both fully enumerated in EXAM-LOG.md), so both scored appearances were correct without the tracker being promoted.

KD #19 · D4

State explicit assumptions vs asking multiple clarifying questions

Recovered
True

Proceed with the assumptions stated out loud and an invitation to correct them; this eliminates abandonment while keeping the user in control.

Commonly believed

Asking four or more clarifying questions up front, which drives a 35-40% abandonment rate; or applying hidden defaults without stating them, which leaves the user confused when the output does not match intent.

The full lesson

Vagueness is not a reason to stop, it is a reason to be explicit. Name the assumption, act on it, and make correcting it cheap. The two failure modes sit either side of that: stalling the user with a questionnaire, or quietly guessing and never telling them what you guessed.

Your record on it

The recovery: EXAM-LOG.md Exam 4 logs 'Q54 — for ambiguous automated requests, proceed with a stated assumption rather than blocking to ask or silently guessing. Domain-4_v2 §4.19; Key-Distinctions #19' as a tagged miss, and Exam 10 Observations confirm all ten KD-seeded questions correct.

KD #20 · D5

Mitigating "lost in the middle"

Solid
True

Put a key-findings summary at the start and add explicit section headings, so the material buried in the middle is surfaced and navigable.

Commonly believed

Rotating which agent's output appears first, which does not change the underlying attention pattern; or summarising everything down under 20K tokens, which risks losing critical information outright.

The full lesson

The failure is positional: content in the middle of a long input gets less attention than content at either end. Fix it by changing where the important material appears and by signposting the structure, not by shuffling the order or by shrinking the whole document. Rotation just moves which item gets buried.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 20 records 'strong — correct in Exam 10' (cycle 3; Exam 2 Q area, Exam 5 Q19, Exam 10 Q58 on the buried-mid-binder site-report defect facet). EXAM-LOG.md Exam 10 Observations confirm all ten KD-seeded questions were correct. No recorded miss on this KD in any scored exam.

KD #21 · D5

A persistent case-facts block vs better summarization

Not yet tested
True

The case-facts block, because it survives compression — the exact numbers and amounts are held somewhere summarisation never touches.

Commonly believed

Revising the summarisation prompt to preserve numbers, which still depends on perfect execution every time; or raising the summarisation threshold, which buys time without addressing the precision loss at all.

The full lesson

If a value must survive compression, do not ask the compressor to be careful with it — take it out of the compressor's path. A structured facts block that is never dropped gives you a guarantee; a better summarisation prompt gives you a probability. Raising the threshold only postpones the same loss.

Your record on it

GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 21 records Learner Signal = 'unknown' (cycle 1; seeded only Exam 4 Q27, which is not among Exam 4's fifteen recorded misses, so that single scored appearance was correct). No EXAM-LOG.md miss cites KD #21. Closely related untagged miss: Exam 6 Q44 (D5 §5.13) on the hybrid context window — 'recent verbatim + running summary + a never-dropped structured facts block' — the same never-dropped-facts idea in a different section.

KD #22 · D5

Subagent isolation for discovery vs main-session discovery

Not yet tested
True

The Explore subagent isolates the verbose output and hands back only the summary, leaving the main session's context intact for the work that follows.

Commonly believed

Running `/compact` mid-task after the main session has already filled up, which loses precision the implementation phase still needs.

The full lesson

Decide where the noisy work happens before you start it, not after it has already consumed your window. A subagent contains the exploration and returns only what matters; compaction after the fact is a lossy repair that costs you exactly the detail you were about to use. This is the same instinct as `context: fork` for skills, applied to discovery.

KD #23 · D5

Behavioral drift: accumulated responses, not context-window overflow

Recovered
True

The accumulated assistant responses dilute the system prompt's influence as the session grows; the model drifts toward whatever pattern its own recent output established.

Commonly believed

Blaming context-window overflow, which is impossible at 2,500 tokens; or believing the system prompt 'only applies to the first turn', which is false — it is included in every request.

The full lesson

Check the token count in the stem before you reach for an overflow explanation. A few thousand tokens over a handful of turns is nowhere near any limit, so the drift has to come from somewhere else — and it comes from the model's own accumulated responses outweighing a fixed system prompt. The system prompt is resent every time; it is not being forgotten, it is being outvoted.

Your record on it

Missed on its first-ever appearance (EXAM-LOG.md Exam 6 Q42, tagged 'Domain-4_v2 §4.20; Key Distinction #23 (first-ever miss of this KD)'), then correct in Exam 8 Q53 (PR-description-generator drift) and again in Exam 10 Q13 (order-ID restatement drift, ~2,700 tokens, no summarization). No further re-test urgency; drop to occasional periodic confirmation only.'

KD #24 · D5

Semantic retrieval vs progressive summarization for long-term recall

Not yet tested
True

Semantic embeddings with retrieval, when the requirement is recalling something specific out of a very long history (the corpus case is 85K tokens across months).

Commonly believed

Progressive summarization, which compresses specific conclusions into abstractions that can no longer be recalled precisely.

The full lesson

Match the mechanism to the shape of the recall you need. Summarisation is lossy by design — it trades specifics for gist, which is fatal when the question is 'what exactly did we decide on that one occasion'. Keep this scoped correctly, though: retrieval is for long-horizon history, not for ordinary multi-turn conversation state, which is just the messages array.

KD #25 · D5

The stateless API memory pattern

Recovered
True

The API is fully stateless. Claude appears to remember only because the application includes the prior messages in every request; the application owns conversation state.

Commonly believed

That Claude needs a `session_id` parameter (it does not exist), or that a vector database is required for conversation memory — vector databases serve retrieval over months of history, not standard multi-turn conversation.

The full lesson

When an agent loses the thread, walk the request your own application sent and look for the step it skipped. If an option adds state or memory on the API side, it is wrong by construction. And check the token count before accepting a context-window explanation — a three-turn conversation under 3,000 tokens cannot have overflowed anything.

KD #26 · D2

Grep (content search) vs Glob (path pattern match)

Recovered
True

Grep for anything about file contents — function names, error strings, imports, call sites. Glob for enumerating files by name or extension, such as `**/*.test.tsx`.

Commonly believed

Globbing `**/formatDate*` to find files that *use* `formatDate` (that only matches files *named* that), or grepping for the word 'test' to find test files (which matches unrelated files and misses test files that never contain the literal word).

The full lesson

Decide first whether your target is inside the files or is the file names themselves. 'Every caller of this function' is content, so it is Grep. 'Every TypeScript test file' is a naming convention, so it is Glob. Both wrong answers fail in the same visible way — partial results that look complete.

Your record on it

Missed on its first-ever citable appearance (EXAM-LOG.md Exam 5: 'Q57 — chose Grep (content search) over Glob (path-pattern match) for file-name enumeration... Domain-2_v2 §2.9; Key-Distinctions #26'), then correct in Exam 7 Q29 and Exam 8 Q43 (legacyDiscountRate variable trace). GENERATION-INTELLIGENCE.md tracker row 26: 'strong — CORRECT two consecutive exams (Exam 7, Exam 8) after the original Exam 5 miss; durably cleared, no re-test urgency.'

KD #27 · D2

Edit's unique-text anchor vs the Read + Write fallback

Solid
True

When Edit fails because the anchor is not unique, fall back to Read + Write for a reliable full-file modification.

Commonly believed

Retrying Edit with a *shorter* anchor — shorter strings are more likely to be non-unique, not less — or forcing it through Bash `sed`, which bypasses the tool designed for the job when a sanctioned fallback exists.

The full lesson

Non-uniqueness is a property of the anchor's specificity, so shortening it moves you in exactly the wrong direction. If you cannot make the anchor unique, stop trying to make Edit work and switch to the sanctioned Read + Write path. Reaching for shell `sed` is the same instinct as the shorter anchor: forcing a tool past the condition it told you about.

KD #28 · D2

Incremental investigation (Grep then Read) vs reading everything upfront

Solid
True

Incremental: Grep to find the entry points, then Read to trace outward — context is spent only on files that turned out to matter.

Commonly believed

Bulk reading upfront, which burns the context window on irrelevant files. Globbing the whole tree and reading each match before searching is the same anti-pattern in a different costume.

The full lesson

Discovery should be driven by content search and then targeted reads, never by exhaustive upfront reading. The bulk-read option is attractive because 'full context' sounds like diligence, but it spends your window before you know what is relevant. Watch for the Glob-then-read-everything variant, which is the same mistake with an extra step.

KD #29 · D2

MCP tool vs built-in tool preference — fix the description, do not remove the built-in

Solid
True

Enhance the MCP tool's description — spell out its unique capability, its outputs, and what the built-in tools cannot provide. Tool selection runs on descriptions, so an under-specified description is why the agent keeps defaulting to familiar built-ins like Grep or Read.

Commonly believed

Removing or disabling Grep so the agent has no alternative (which breaks legitimate content-search cases and leaves the real cause untouched), or adding an always-prefer-MCP system-prompt rule (blunt and keyword-sensitive, misrouting the cases where the built-in genuinely is right).

The full lesson

This mirrors the tool-description rule exactly: fix the signal before adding a layer — or removing a tool — to compensate for a bad signal. If the agent keeps choosing the familiar built-in, the description of the better tool has not told it what it would gain. Removing the built-in destroys a capability you still need, and a blanket preference rule misroutes every case where the built-in was the right call.

Outside the mock-exam loop

The rest of what you were taught

Before the mock exams existed there were two courses, an academy track, and eight practice sets. This material never appears in your score data, so it is invisible to every weakness report — but it is where a lot of the groundwork was laid.

claude-101 33 lessons

Anthropic's official 'Claude 101' Skilljar course (14 lessons, 5 sections) captured lesson-by-lesson into a source-of-truth markdown file and rebuilt as a single self-contained interactive HTML course. It teaches the product-level vocabulary the exam assumes: what Claude is, prompt anatomy, Projects, Artifacts, Skills, Connectors/MCP, Enterprise Search, Research mode, and the desktop Chat/Cowork/Code split. Six architect-level extension lessons were then researched from live Anthropic docs and bolted on to take the same surface areas down to builder/API depth.

cross

Claude is a steerable thinking partner, not a chatbot

The lesson

Claude is trained under Constitutional AI to be helpful, harmless and honest, which is why it is steerable — you can direct its personality, tone and behaviour rather than working around a fixed voice. Treat it as a thought partner for complex problems, not a Q&A box. Its large context window (200K+ tokens, up to 1M on Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) is what lets you hand it whole documents instead of pasting fragments.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D4

The three-part prompt: set the stage, define the task, specify the rules

The lesson

Every good prompt does three things — sets the stage (your role, objective, context), defines the task (the specific action you want taken), and specifies the rules (style, tone, format, examples). This framework is adapted from the 4D Framework for AI Fluency (Dakan and Feller): Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence. Speak to Claude like a coworker; the real power comes from continued iteration, not a single perfect prompt.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D4

Fix generic output with context, not volume — and run evals to know if it worked

The lesson

Each common failure has a specific cause: generic output means missing context, wrong length means Claude is guessing, format misses mean you told it what but not how, and confident-but-wrong output means you need citations or web grounding. Evals are how you find out whether Claude is actually good at your task: gather 5-10 real examples, write prompts that should reproduce them, compare, then refine. This is the Discernment competency of the 4D framework, and it is the discipline the exam expects before you reach for prompt engineering.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D3

Chat vs Cowork vs Code — and why Cowork and Code share one engine

The lesson

The desktop app gives you three modes: Chat for quick exchanges, Cowork for sustained multi-source work producing finished deliverables, and Code for building software. Cowork and Code both run on Claude Code underneath — local to your machine, able to spin up subagents and sustain long tasks. Code adds three interaction modes that control autonomy: Ask (propose every change), Code (apply file edits, check before terminal commands), and Plan (outline the whole approach first). Cowork adds folder access, scheduled tasks, subagents, plugins, and a contained sandbox it cannot escape.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D5

Projects and the automatic RAG switch

The lesson

A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own knowledge base, instructions, chat history and memory. Instructions apply to every conversation in the project — treat them as programming Claude's behaviour for that work stream. Crucially, when the knowledge base approaches the context limit, Claude silently enables Retrieval Augmented Generation mode, expanding capacity by up to 10x by retrieving only relevant slices instead of loading everything. Name your files descriptively, because Claude uses file names to decide what to retrieve.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D3

Skills perform tasks; Projects store knowledge

The lesson

The one-line distinction to hold is 'projects store knowledge, skills perform tasks.' A Project is the what — reference material available across every conversation in it. A Skill is the how — a folder of instructions, scripts and resources that encodes the steps, order of operations and methodology so Claude executes the same way every time. They compose: a skill can pull from the knowledge stored in a project. Skills can contain executable code, so only install custom skills from trusted sources.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D2

Connectors, and MCP as the USB-C port for AI

The lesson

Connectors turn Claude from an assistant into an informed collaborator by giving it your actual tools and data, and they are powered by the Model Context Protocol — the universal standard often described as 'USB-C for AI.' Two types exist: web connectors to cloud services and desktop extensions that reach local files and native apps. Security rests on three properties: access is scoped per permission, Claude sees only what you can see, and any connection is revocable.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D1

Research mode is agentic, not a bigger search

The lesson

Research does not run one search — it operates agentically, planning an approach with extended thinking automatically enabled, then running many searches that build on each other while deciding what to investigate next from what it found. Reports typically take 5-15 minutes, up to 45 for complex investigations, and every claim carries a citation. Choose it over plain web search when you need synthesis across many sources; choose extended thinking instead when the answer comes from reasoning rather than gathering, and Enterprise Search when the answer lives inside your organisation.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D2

Enterprise Search is a pre-built Project for your whole organisation

The lesson

Enterprise Search adds an 'Ask {Your Org}' entry that searches and synthesises across SharePoint, Slack, Gmail and Drive, always citing sources. Think of it as a Project whose knowledge base is your company, configured by an admin with custom instructions. It only surfaces what you already have permission to see in the source tool, and your connected data is not indexed or stored separately.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/source/claude-101_source.md

D2

EXTENSION — The tool-use loop is a contract keyed on stop_reason

The lesson

Tool use is a contract: you declare what operations exist and what shape their inputs and outputs take; Claude decides when to call them but never executes anything itself. The canonical loop is a while loop on stop_reason — send tools plus the user message, get back stop_reason 'tool_use' with tool_use blocks, execute them, return tool_result blocks in a user message, repeat. The loop exits on any other stop reason ('end_turn', 'max_tokens', 'stop_sequence', 'refusal'). The Claude API has no dedicated 'tool' or 'function' role: assistant messages carry tool_use blocks, user messages carry the matching tool_result blocks.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/tool-use-agent-loop_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/tool-use-agent-loop.html

D2

EXTENSION — Three tool buckets, and who is responsible for each

The lesson

Tools differ by where the code executes, and the bucket decides what you must handle. User-defined client tools: you write the schema, execute the code, drive the loop. Anthropic-schema client tools (bash, text_editor, computer, memory): Anthropic publishes the schema — trained-in, so Claude calls them more reliably — but you still execute and loop. Server tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search): Anthropic runs them in its own loop; you never construct a tool_result and never handle is_error. If the server loop hits its iteration cap you get stop_reason 'pause_turn' — resend the conversation to continue.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/tool-use-agent-loop_citations.md

D2

EXTENSION — tool_choice, parallel calls, and the ordering rules that 400 you

The lesson

tool_choice has four values: auto (default when tools are present), any (must call some tool), tool (must call this named tool), and none. Only 'any' or a named tool guarantees a call; with either, the API prefills the assistant turn so you get no natural-language preface. Two ordering rules cause 400 errors: tool_result blocks must immediately follow their tool_use message with nothing in between, and tool_result blocks must come first in the content array with any text after them. When Claude emits several tool_use blocks in one turn, all matching results must return in a single user message — splitting them teaches Claude to stop calling tools in parallel.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/tool-use-agent-loop_citations.md

D2

EXTENSION — The tool description is the highest-leverage thing you write

The lesson

Anthropic states plainly that the description is by far the most important factor in tool performance — aim for at least three to four sentences covering what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, what each parameter means, and any caveats. Consolidate related operations under an action parameter rather than shipping create_pr, review_pr and merge_pr as three tools; namespace names meaningfully; return only high-signal data. Add strict: true to guarantee tool inputs match your schema exactly. The heuristic to remember: if you find yourself writing a regex to extract a decision from model output, that decision should have been a tool call.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/tool-use-agent-loop_citations.md

D2

EXTENSION — MCP architecture: one client per server, two layers

The lesson

MCP follows host/client/server: the host is the AI application, and it creates one MCP client per MCP server, each maintaining a dedicated connection. That one-client-per-server rule is the single most testable architecture fact — two connections to the same remote server means two clients. Underneath sit two layers: the data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0, lifecycle management, the core primitives) and the transport layer (stdio or Streamable HTTP, framing, authorisation). 'Server' describes a role, not a location — servers can run local or remote.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/mcp-at-a-builder-level_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/mcp-at-a-builder-level.html

D2

EXTENSION — The three server primitives and who controls each

The lesson

Servers expose three building blocks, and the exam-critical fact is who controls them. Tools are model-controlled: functions Claude decides to call, discovered via tools/list and invoked via tools/call. Resources are application-controlled: passive, read-only data addressed by URI (file:///path, or templated like travel://activities/{city}/{category}) that the application decides whether to include. Prompts are user-controlled: instruction templates that require explicit invocation, usually surfacing as slash commands. Mnemonic: Model / Application / User.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/mcp-at-a-builder-level_citations.md

D2

EXTENSION — Client primitives: sampling, roots, elicitation

The lesson

Clients offer three features back to servers. Sampling (sampling/createMessage) lets a server request an LLM completion through the client, so a server author can stay model-independent and never ship an SDK or pay for inference — with human review both before and after the call. Roots (roots/list) communicate filesystem boundaries using file:// URIs, but they are advisory coordination, not enforcement: the spec says servers SHOULD respect them, and real security must come from OS permissions or sandboxing. Elicitation (elicitation/create) lets a server pause and request specific structured input from the user mid-task, and never asks for passwords or API keys.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/mcp-at-a-builder-level_citations.md

D2

EXTENSION — Transports: stdio, Streamable HTTP, and what was actually deprecated

The lesson

MCP defines two standard transports. stdio launches the server as a subprocess exchanging newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout — the server must never write non-MCP output to stdout, though stderr is fine for logging. Streamable HTTP serves many clients over a single endpoint supporting POST and GET, optionally using SSE to stream, with session identity in Mcp-Session-Id and version in the MCP-Protocol-Version header. The nuance people get wrong: SSE is not gone — it survives inside Streamable HTTP. What was deprecated is the standalone two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport from protocol version 2024-11-05.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/mcp-at-a-builder-level_citations.md

D5

EXTENSION — Context windows, context rot, and the shared budget

The lesson

The context window is working memory — everything the model can reference, including its own response. More is not automatically better: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon Anthropic names context rot, so curating what is in context matters as much as how much fits. The budget is shared: prior history, the current message, tool definitions, tool results, thinking tokens and generated output all draw on it. Thinking blocks from previous turns are auto-stripped by the API — the one exception is a tool-use turn, where the thinking block must be returned alongside the tool results.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/context-management-reliability_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/context-management-reliability.html

D5

EXTENSION — Compaction and context editing are different instruments

The lesson

Server-side compaction is the primary strategy for long-running agents: at a trigger (default 150,000 input tokens, minimum 50,000) Claude summarises the conversation into a compaction block, and on subsequent requests the API drops everything before it. Context editing is the finer instrument — clear_tool_uses_20250919 clears oldest tool results with placeholders, clear_thinking_20251015 manages thinking blocks — and it applies server-side, so your client keeps the full unmodified history. Know the costs: compaction adds a sampling step you pay for, cannot use a cheaper model, and may fail when tools are defined because the model calls a tool instead of summarising.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/context-management-reliability_citations.md

D5

EXTENSION — Context engineering: the smallest set of high-signal tokens

The lesson

Context engineering is broader than prompt engineering — it curates the whole context state (system instructions, tools, MCP, external data, message history) across many turns, and the maxim is to find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that produce the outcome you want. Prefer just-in-time retrieval — keep lightweight identifiers like file paths and load data at runtime — over pre-loading everything. Practical tactics: keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, prefer CLI tools over MCP servers for context efficiency, use hooks to pre-filter verbose output, delegate noisy operations to subagents so only the summary returns, and /clear between unrelated tasks.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/context-management-reliability_citations.md

D5

EXTENSION — Prompt caching: the mechanism and the break-even arithmetic

The lesson

cache_control marks the last block of the prefix you want cached, and the cached region is always a contiguous prefix built in the fixed order tools, then system, then messages — so changing anything earlier invalidates everything after it (editing a tool definition busts the entire cache). Hits require 100% identical segments. The economics are exact: a 5-minute write costs 1.25x base input, a 1-hour write 2x, and a read 0.1x. That means the 5-minute cache pays for itself after one read and the 1-hour cache after two, with steady-state savings approaching 90% on the cached prefix.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-caching-economics_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/prompt-caching-economics.html

D5

EXTENSION — When caching silently fails to pay off

The lesson

Caching backfires in four situations. A prefix under the model's minimum (1,024 or 4,096 tokens depending on model) is silently not cached with no error returned. Single-shot prompts pay the write premium and never collect a read. A prefix with anything dynamic at the front — a timestamp or user name injected into the system prompt — fails exact-match and re-writes every call. And bursty traffic with gaps longer than the TTL turns every request into a fresh write, which is worse than not caching; switch to the 1-hour TTL for that shape. Verify it is working by watching cache_read_input_tokens rise while cache_creation_input_tokens falls.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-caching-economics_citations.md

D4

EXTENSION — The prompt-engineering ladder, cheapest lever first

The lesson

Climb the techniques in rough order of cost and leverage and stop when your evals pass: be clear and direct, add examples, let Claude think, structure with XML tags, assign a role in the system parameter, chain prompts, then handle long context. Clarity is free and fixes the most failures — the golden rule is that if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by your prompt, Claude will be too. Adding the motivation behind an instruction helps Claude generalise. And remember Anthropic's own caveat: not every failing eval is a prompting problem — latency and cost are often better fixed by changing model.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-engineering-depth_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/prompt-engineering-depth.html

D4

EXTENSION — Examples are the highest-leverage rung

The lesson

Few-shot examples are the most reliable way to steer format, tone and structure; three to five is the documented sweet spot. Good sets are relevant (mirroring your real case), diverse (covering edge cases so Claude does not latch onto an unintended pattern), and structured (wrapped in <example> tags inside <examples> so they are distinguishable from instructions). Positive examples beat negative instructions — show the target rather than enumerating what to avoid. Examples also compound with thinking: put <thinking> tags inside your examples and Claude generalises that reasoning style.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-engineering-depth_citations.md

D4

EXTENSION — Structured Outputs replaced prefill

The lesson

Output control comes in three tiers: prompt-level format instructions, XML output contracts, and Structured Outputs — the hard guarantee via constrained decoding, either JSON output through output_config.format or strict tool use with strict: true. The version break that invalidates older study material: prefilling the last assistant turn is no longer supported on Claude 4.6+ models and returns a 400. Its classic uses migrate cleanly — forcing JSON becomes Structured Outputs, killing preambles becomes a direct system-prompt instruction. Know the limits too: no recursive schemas, no external $ref, no numeric or string-length constraints, and additionalProperties must be false.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-engineering-depth_citations.md

D4

EXTENSION — Model selection is a peer lever to prompting, and effort is the second dial

The lesson

Opus, Sonnet and Haiku trade capability against speed and cost, and the effort parameter is an orthogonal dial inside any model — so you tune quality and spend on two axes, not one. The practical strategy is to start with a capable model to establish a quality ceiling, then optimise down to the cheapest model that still passes your evals, escalating to Opus only for the hardest long-horizon work. A prompt is portable across models as a starting point, but you must re-run your evals after any model change — verbosity, literalness, effort calibration and tone all shift between generations.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-engineering-depth_citations.md

D4

EXTENSION — Prompt-engineering anti-patterns on current models

The lesson

Two anti-patterns are specific to modern models. Over-prompting: where you once wrote 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...', normal phrasing like 'Use this tool when...' now works better — aggressive language causes overtriggering, and tools that undertriggered on older models will trigger appropriately now. And manual budget_tokens extended thinking is removed on Opus 4.7+ in favour of adaptive thinking plus an effort setting; prefer general instructions ('think thoroughly') over hand-written step-by-step plans, because Claude's own reasoning frequently exceeds what a human would prescribe.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/prompt-engineering-depth_citations.md

D3

EXTENSION — Claude Code configuration: four scopes, and the settings-vs-permissions trap

The lesson

Configuration is organised by scope — Managed (enterprise policy) beats command-line arguments, which beat Local, then Project, then User. The trap to memorise: settings override by that precedence, but permission rules merge across scopes. CLAUDE.md behaves differently again — all discovered files are concatenated broadest-to-most-specific rather than overriding each other, imports use @path with a maximum depth of four hops, and managed-policy CLAUDE.md cannot be excluded. Remember that CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement: to block an action regardless of what Claude decides, you need a PreToolUse hook.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md · courses/claude-101/extensions/claude-code-configuration.html

D3

EXTENSION — Permissions evaluate deny then ask then allow

The lesson

Rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow, first match wins, so a deny at any level cannot be re-allowed anywhere. A bare tool name like Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely; a scoped rule like Bash(rm *) leaves the tool visible and blocks matching calls. Path patterns have a nasty anchor: /Users/alice/file is relative to the project root, not absolute — you need //Users/alice/file for a true absolute path. Argument-constraining Bash patterns are fragile, so for reliable URL filtering deny curl and wget and use WebFetch(domain:...) instead. Permissions are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md

D3

EXTENSION — Hooks: only exit code 2 blocks

The lesson

Hooks are shell commands fired at lifecycle events and are the deterministic control surface. The counter-intuitive fact that costs marks: only exit code 2 blocks the action — exit 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and Claude proceeds, even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code. If your hook enforces policy, it must exit 2. The roster is far larger than the classic eight (roughly thirty events now), and blocking capability is per-event: PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop and PreCompact can block; PostToolUse cannot, because the tool already ran.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md

D3

EXTENSION — Extension surfaces: skills, subagents, plugins, marketplaces

The lesson

Custom slash commands have been merged into skills — a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both produce /deploy, but skills are now the primary mechanism, and a skill wins over a command of the same name. Pick the surface by need: CLAUDE.md for always-on soft guidance, rules for topic-scoped guidance, skills for on-demand procedures, subagents for isolated context plus tool restriction, hooks for hard deterministic enforcement, MCP for external integration. Plugins bundle all of these for distribution; note that plugin subagents cannot use hooks, mcpServers or permissionMode frontmatter for security reasons.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md

D3

EXTENSION — Headless mode, the Agent SDK, and CI

The lesson

claude -p runs non-interactively and is the same surface as the Agent SDK via CLI — the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code. The flag that trips people up is --bare: plain -p still auto-discovers hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, while --bare skips all of it for reproducible CI (and is slated to become the -p default). For structured CI output use --output-format json (which includes total_cost_usd) with --json-schema. Authenticate CI via claude setup-token into CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN.

Where this was taught
