courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md

D3

EXTENSION — The canonical Claude Code workflow: explore, plan, code, commit

The lesson

Enter plan mode first so Claude reads and answers without changing anything, then have it produce a detailed implementation plan you approve, then switch out of plan mode to implement against that plan, then commit. Letting Claude jump straight to coding produces code that solves the wrong problem. Give it a check it can run — tests, a build, a screenshot — and gate on it, optionally with a Stop hook that blocks the turn from ending until the check passes. Between tasks, /clear frequently; after two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt rather than continuing to patch.

Where this was taught

courses/claude-101/extensions/source/claude-code-configuration_citations.md

introduction-to-subagents 17 lessons

Anthropic's 200-level 'Introduction to Subagents' course (4 lessons, captured with zero source gaps) rebuilt as self-contained interactive HTML, plus three researched extension lessons and one deep-mastery '202' rebuild. The base course teaches what a subagent is, how to create one with /agents, the four design patterns that make subagents reliable, and when not to use them. The extensions generalise this into the five orchestration patterns, subagents as a programmable SDK primitive, and orchestrator-worker at production scale with its failure modes.

D1

What a subagent buys you, and what it costs

The lesson

A subagent runs in its own conversation context window, does its work, and returns only a summary to the main thread — all the file reads, searches and tool calls stay isolated and never clutter your main conversation. It receives exactly two things: a custom system prompt from its config, and a task description written by the parent. When it finishes, the entire subagent conversation is discarded. The tradeoff is real and worth stating out loud: you lose visibility into how it reached its conclusion.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D3

Creating a subagent: scope, tools, model, and the config file

The lesson

Use the /agents command rather than hand-writing files. You first choose scope — project-level (this project only) or user-level (all projects on your machine) — then let Claude generate the name, description and system prompt from your description of the job. Restrict tools deliberately: a code reviewer does not need edit tools, though keeping execution tools lets it run git diff. Pick a model to match the work (Haiku for fast lightweight tasks, Sonnet as a middle ground, Opus for complex analysis, or inherit). The result is a markdown file at .claude/agents/<name>.md whose YAML frontmatter is the config and whose body is the system prompt.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D1

The description does double duty — it decides when AND what

The lesson

The name and description of every available subagent are injected into the main agent's system prompt; that is how the parent decides which one to launch. But the description has a second job: when the parent writes the input prompt to kick off the task, it uses the description as guidance for writing that prompt. So the description shapes not only when a subagent runs but what it is told to do. Adding a line like 'You must tell the agent precisely which files you want it to review' changes the parent's delegation from a vague 'use git diff to find changes' into a specific file list.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D1

Four design patterns that make a subagent finish reliably

The lesson

Effective subagents share four traits. Specific descriptions steer both trigger and instructions. A defined output format in the system prompt is the single most important improvement — it creates natural stopping points, so the agent knows it is done when every section is filled, and without it subagents struggle to decide when enough research has happened and run far too long. An 'Obstacles Encountered' section surfaces workarounds, environment quirks and required flags so the main thread does not rediscover them. And limited tool access prevents side effects and clarifies each agent's role: read-only gets Glob/Grep/Read, a reviewer adds Bash for git diff, only a modification agent gets Edit and Write.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D1

The decision rule: does the intermediate work matter?

The lesson

Ask one question before delegating — does the intermediate work matter to your main thread? If you just need the final result, delegate. If you need to see and react to what happens along the way, keep it in the main thread. Subagents shine for research and exploration, for code reviews (Claude reviews code more effectively when it reads as someone else's work, and a reviewer subagent has no memory of writing it), and for tasks needing a genuinely different system prompt such as copywriting or styling against a design system.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D1

Three subagent anti-patterns

The lesson

Expert-persona subagents ('you are a Python expert') add nothing — Claude already has that knowledge, so there is nothing the so-called expert can do that your main thread cannot. Sequential pipelines fail when each step depends on the previous step's discoveries — a reproduce/debug/fix chain loses information at every handoff, and bug fixing almost always has that dependency. Test runners hide what you need: when tests fail you want full output to diagnose, and an agent that returns 'tests failed' forces you to build debug scripts to recover detail that would have been visible directly. Anthropic's testing found the test-runner pattern performed worst of all configurations.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/source/introduction-to-subagents_source.md

D1

EXTENSION — Workflows versus agents, and the augmented LLM under both

The lesson

Anthropic draws a hard line inside 'agentic systems': workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage. The dividing question is who controls the path — your code, or the model at runtime. Every pattern is composed from one repeated unit, the augmented LLM: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. Before reaching for any multi-step pattern, make sure that single augmented call is well built, because the patterns compose augmented LLMs, they do not substitute for getting one right.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestration-patterns_citations.md · courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/orchestration-patterns.html

D1

EXTENSION — The five orchestration patterns and when each fits

The lesson

Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a fixed sequence where each call processes the previous output, with programmatic gate checks between steps — use it when decomposition is clean and you can trade latency for accuracy. Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a specialised followup, giving separation of concerns and letting you send easy queries to a cheaper model. Parallelisation splits into sectioning (independent subtasks in parallel) and voting (the same task run several times for confidence). Orchestrator-workers has a central LLM break down tasks dynamically — the key difference from parallelisation is that subtasks are not pre-defined but determined at runtime. Evaluator-optimizer loops a generator against a critic, and needs clear evaluation criteria to be worth it.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestration-patterns_citations.md

D1

EXTENSION — The simplicity-first decision ladder

The lesson

Anthropic's core rule is to find the simplest solution possible and only increase complexity when needed — which may mean not building an agentic system at all. Start with a single augmented call plus retrieval and in-context examples; escalate to prompt chaining for fixed decomposable steps, routing for distinct categories, parallelisation for independent subtasks or multi-attempt confidence, orchestrator-workers when subtasks are unpredictable, evaluator-optimizer when criteria are clear and iteration measurably helps, and only then an autonomous agent loop for open-ended problems with no hardcodable path. Workflows give predictability; agents give flexibility at the cost of higher spend and compounding errors.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestration-patterns_citations.md

D1

EXTENSION — AgentDefinition: the subagent as a code object

The lesson

In the Agent SDK a subagent is an AgentDefinition with two required fields — description (which drives routing) and prompt (the system prompt) — plus optional tools, disallowedTools, model, skills, memory, mcpServers, maxTurns, background, effort and permissionMode. Omitting tools inherits all of them; specifying tools is an allow-list, and disallowedTools is applied first as a denylist. Programmatically defined agents take precedence over filesystem agents of the same name, and the filesystem ladder runs managed settings, then --agents, then project, then user, then plugin. The Python gotcha: AgentDefinition fields are camelCase even in Python, so passing snake_case raises a TypeError.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/subagents-as-sdk-primitive_citations.md · courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/subagents-as-sdk-primitive.html

D1

EXTENSION — One channel in, one channel out, and no nesting

The lesson

The only channel from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string, so every file path, error message and prior decision the subagent needs must be written into that prompt. It receives its own system prompt, the delegation prompt, CLAUDE.md and its tool definitions — never the parent's conversation history, tool results or system prompt. On the way out, only the final message returns, verbatim, as the tool result. And subagents cannot spawn their own subagents: never put Agent in a subagent's tools list. For nested delegation use skills, chain workers from the main conversation, or graduate to the Workflow tool.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/subagents-as-sdk-primitive_citations.md

D1

EXTENSION — When to graduate from subagents to a Workflow

The lesson

Subagents work well for a few delegated tasks per turn. When you need dozens to hundreds of coordinated agents, or you want the orchestration codified as a rerunnable script, use the Workflow tool — it moves orchestration into a script the runtime executes outside the conversation, so intermediate results live in script variables and Claude's context holds only the final answer. The decisive distinction is who decides what runs next: with subagents it is Claude turn by turn; with a workflow it is the script. Workflow runtime caps are 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run; ordinary subagent parallelism has no documented per-turn cap.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/subagents-as-sdk-primitive_citations.md

D1

EXTENSION — Orchestrator-worker at scale: why it wins and what it costs

The lesson

Anthropic productionised this in Research: a lead agent analyses the query, develops a strategy, spawns parallel subagents each with its own context window, then a dedicated CitationAgent attributes the claims. Three rationales justify it — context compression through parallel windows, separation of concerns that reduces path dependency, and parallelism that cut research time by up to 90%. The numbers to hold: multi-agent beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval, token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance, and multi-agent systems burn about 15x the tokens of a chat. It wins largely because it is a mechanism for spending more tokens productively in parallel.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestrator-worker-at-scale_citations.md · courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/orchestrator-worker-at-scale.html · courses/introduction-to-subagents/deep-mastery/orchestrator-worker-at-scale-202.html

D1

EXTENSION — The orchestrator's four jobs, including effort scaling

The lesson

At scale the lead agent does four things: decompose and delegate with detailed task descriptions, scale effort to complexity, synthesise results, and run a separate verification pass. Delegation must give each subagent an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries — without that, agents duplicate work or leave gaps. Anthropic embedded explicit scaling rules in the prompt because agents judge effort badly: simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, complex research more than 10 subagents with divided responsibilities. Verification is architecturally separated as its own worker.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestrator-worker-at-scale_citations.md

D5

EXTENSION — Eight failure modes at scale

The lesson

Learn these by mechanism, not name. Errors compound because agents are stateful across long runs. Context exhaustion truncates the plan itself. Token cost blows up at ~15x. Coordination overhead grows pairwise (10 agents means 45 potential interactions) and synchronous fan-out blocks on the slowest worker. Vague delegation produces duplicated work and coverage gaps — Anthropic's own example had two subagents redundantly researching 2025 supply chains while 2021 history went uncovered. Partial failure can stall a whole batch. Non-determinism makes failures unreproducible. And deploying mid-run can destroy hours of stateful work.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestrator-worker-at-scale_citations.md

D5

EXTENSION — Reliability patterns that design those failures out

The lesson

Match each failure to its counter-measure. Durable resumable execution instead of restart-from-scratch, because restarts are expensive and frustrating. Checkpoints plus deterministic retry logic wrapped around the adaptive agent. Model-driven graceful degradation — telling the agent a tool is failing and letting it adapt works surprisingly well. External memory: save the plan and phase summaries so truncation cannot destroy strategy, and spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts and careful handoffs as limits approach. Full production tracing for diagnosability. End-state rather than turn-by-turn evaluation, with discrete checkpoints. And rainbow deployments that shift traffic gradually so in-flight agents finish on the version they started.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestrator-worker-at-scale_citations.md

D1

EXTENSION — When to refuse orchestrator-worker at scale

The lesson

Four gates say no. It fails the economics gate when the task is not valuable and parallelisable enough to justify roughly 15x the tokens. It fails when agents need shared state or have tight interdependencies — Anthropic notes most coding tasks have far fewer truly parallelisable subtasks than research. It fails for latency-sensitive work, because synchronous fan-out blocks on one slow subagent and spawn-plus-synthesis adds overhead a single agent avoids. And it fails the default-to-simplest principle: fall back to a single agent or a fixed workflow whenever the dynamic multi-agent machinery is not earning its cost.

Where this was taught

courses/introduction-to-subagents/extensions/source/orchestrator-worker-at-scale_citations.md

academy 23 lessons

A 37-session, ~29-hour interactive exam-prep program run by an AI 'Professor' persona (concept teaching) and an 'Exam Coach' persona (drills, scenarios, mocks), covering all five CCA-F domains exhaustively across seven phases. It was built by extracting every sub-domain from the official exam guide, auditing the 12 existing HTML course files for coverage, and writing dedicated Professor sessions for every gap the HTML did not reach. The HTML courses are explicitly NOT assigned reading — everything is taught through dialogue, with a persistent learner model carrying mastery state between sessions.

D1

GAP — Hooks are deterministic; prompts are probabilistic

The lesson

A PostToolUse hook intercepts a tool result before the model ever sees it — use it to normalise date formats across three MCP tools, or to trim a 40-field order response down to the 5 fields that matter. A PreToolUse hook inspects and can block an outgoing call — block a refund over $500 and redirect to escalation rather than failing silently. The distinction that decides your architecture: a hook is a 100% deterministic guarantee because code runs regardless of model reasoning, while a prompt instruction is probabilistic compliance the model can reason around. If failure has financial, legal or safety consequences, use a hook, not a prompt.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D1

GAP — Escalate by category and impact, never by a fail counter

The lesson

Three escalation patterns exist: immediate (the customer asks for a human — escalate now, do not try to solve first), attempt-then-escalate (in-scope issues you try first), and nuanced (acknowledge the emotion, propose a concrete solution, escalate only if they reiterate wanting a human). Escalate when policy is silent rather than guessing, and ask for identifiers when multiple customer records match rather than heuristically picking one. The traps: sentiment analysis is unreliable because mood does not predict case complexity, model self-rated confidence is unreliable because the model can be confidently wrong, and 'escalate after N failed tool calls' both ignores an explicit human request and waves through a high-value transaction that succeeded first try.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D1

GAP — The structured handoff payload

The lesson

The human operator receiving an escalation sees only your summary, never the conversation transcript, and cannot ask follow-up questions. So the payload must be complete and self-contained: customer_id, issue_summary, order_id, root_cause, actions_taken, refund_amount, recommended_action, escalation_reason. Dumping the raw transcript is an explicit anti-pattern, and so is handing over a bare customer ID that forces the human to reconstruct everything. Think of it as a doctor's referral letter — 'patient has a problem' is not a referral.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D1

GAP — Session management: resume, fork, or start fresh

The lesson

--resume brings back a named session with its saved context, which is right for long investigations spanning days — but carries a real risk: if files changed since, the saved tool results are stale. fork_session branches independently from a shared point, so you can compare two approaches (Redux vs Context API) that both inherit context up to the branch and then diverge. The judgement call: resume when files are unchanged and results still valid; start fresh when results are stale or significant time has passed, because a short written summary of what you found is more reliable than resuming with old tool data.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D1

GAP — Fixed pipelines vs dynamic decomposition vs multi-pass

The lesson

Use a fixed pipeline (prompt chaining) when the task structure is predictable and all steps are known upfront — metadata extraction, then data extraction, then validation, then enrichment. Use dynamic adaptive decomposition when the scope is unknown and each step depends on what the last one found, as in root-cause investigation. And for reviewing many files, do not run one pass across all of them: attention dilutes, comments get inconsistent, bugs get missed. The correct shape is per-file analysis in parallel subagents followed by a separate cross-file integration pass in the coordinator.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D3

GAP — Skills frontmatter, and the allowed-tools trap

The lesson

context: fork runs a skill inside an isolated subagent so its verbose output never pollutes the main session — reach for it when a skill produces a large catalog or exploratory dump. The exam trap is allowed-tools: the name sounds restrictive but the behaviour is permissive — it pre-approves the listed tools while the skill is active and does not remove the others, which stay callable subject to existing permissions. To actually remove tools you need disallowed-tools. argument-hint prompts the user when the skill is invoked with no argument.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D3

GAP — CI/CD: -p is necessary, --bare is what people forget

The lesson

The -p (--print) flag is the only correct way to run Claude in a CI pipeline: it processes the prompt, prints to stdout and exits without waiting for input. But -p alone still auto-loads every local config source — hooks, CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto-memory — so claude -p is not equivalent to claude -p --bare. If a pipeline mysteriously picks up an unexpected CLAUDE.md rule or hook, the missing --bare is your answer. Pair with --output-format json and --json-schema so results can be parsed into inline PR comments, and use a separate Claude instance for review, because the instance that wrote the code retains its reasoning context and will not challenge its own decisions.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D4

GAP — Validation, retry-with-feedback, and the Type 1 / Type 2 gate

The lesson

A retry only works if you send three things: the original document, the previous incorrect extraction, and the specific error — 'Field total = 150, but sum(line_items) = 145. Re-check values.' Retry helps with format errors, structural errors and arithmetic inconsistencies. It will never help when the information is simply absent from the source document or lives in a different document — that is a Type 2 failure and needs enriched input, not another attempt. Classify the failure before retrying. Pydantic gives you structural validation, custom semantic validators for business rules, and JSON Schema generation for tool_use from one source of truth.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D4

GAP — Self-correction by design

The lesson

Rather than hoping the model gets arithmetic right, design the schema so contradictions become visible: extract both stated_total and calculated_total, and emit conflict_detected: true when they diverge. This turns a semantic error that validation cannot catch into a structured signal downstream code can route on. It is the same principle as confidence fields — make the model's uncertainty a first-class output field instead of something you infer from prose.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D4

GAP — Message Batches API: the 24-hour gate

The lesson

Batch costs 50% less than synchronous calls but runs in a processing window of up to 24 hours with no latency SLA, and it does not support multi-turn tool calling — one request, one response. The custom_id field links request to response and lets you re-submit only the failures. The decision is entirely about who is waiting: a pre-merge PR check or interactive review must be synchronous; an overnight tech-debt report, a weekly security audit, or 10,000 documents belongs in batch. Do the SLA arithmetic — if you need results in 30 hours and the window is 24, you must submit at least 6 hours before the deadline.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D4

GAP — Multi-instance review and the interview pattern

The lesson

A model reviewing its own output is structurally, not capability-, limited: it retains its reasoning context and is unlikely to challenge its own decisions, so an independent instance with no generation context finds subtle issues the author misses. Combine with multi-pass structure — parallel per-unit analysis then a sequential integration pass — to avoid attention dilution. The interview pattern is the complement on the input side: have Claude ask clarifying questions before implementing when the domain is unfamiliar, the implications are non-obvious, or several approaches are genuinely viable. The trigger is genuine ambiguity, not every task.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

GAP — Tool description is the selection mechanism, always present

The lesson

The description — not the name, not the schema — is the primary mechanism Claude uses to pick a tool, and descriptions are always present in context influencing every selection, not lazily loaded when needed. A good one states what the tool does and returns, input formats with example values, edge cases and constraints, and explicitly when to use this tool rather than a similar one. Near-identical descriptions on analyze_content and analyze_document cause misrouting; the fix is renaming to eliminate functional overlap. Watch for system-prompt side effects too: 'always verify the customer' makes the model overuse get_customer even when it is unnecessary.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

GAP — Two error channels, four error categories

The lesson

Keep the channels straight: a JSON-RPC protocol error means the request itself failed — unknown tool, malformed arguments — and the JSON-RPC response is an error. isError: true is a tool-execution error carried inside a successful response. A timed-out orders API gives you isError: true; a call to a tool that does not exist gives you a protocol error. Then categorise: transient (timeout, 503) retries with backoff, validation fixes the input and retries, business (policy violation) explains and offers an alternative, and permission escalates. A generic 'Operation failed' leaves the coordinator with nothing to decide on — return category, retryability, message, attempted query and any partial results.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

GAP — Error-handling anti-patterns in multi-agent systems

The lesson

Four ways teams get this wrong. Generic status strings leave the coordinator unable to choose a recovery path. Silent suppression — treating an empty result as success — makes the coordinator believe there were no matches when there was actually a failure. Aborting the whole workflow on one subagent failure throws away every partial result the others produced. And infinite retries inside a subagent burn latency and tokens invisibly. The correct shape is local recovery of one or two retries for transient failures, then propagate a structured error upward with whatever partial results exist.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

GAP — Too many tools degrades selection

The lesson

Giving one agent 18 tools instead of 4-5 measurably reduces tool-selection reliability, and agents equipped with tools outside their specialisation tend to misuse them. The fix is domain-scoped subagents each holding only role-relevant tools plus a few cross-role utilities — not merging tools into a god-tool, and not patching around it with a content index that adds tokens without adding clarity. Pair with tool_choice: auto to let the model decide, any when you need a guaranteed structured call, and a named tool when you must guarantee the first action.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

GAP — Built-in tool selection and incremental investigation

The lesson

Grep searches inside file contents; Glob finds files by name or extension — that is the distinction most people invert. Read loads a whole file, Write creates one, Edit makes a precise change via a unique text match, Bash is for shell work. When Edit fails because the anchor is not unique, the fallback is Read the file, modify programmatically, then Write it back — shortening the anchor makes it more generic and therefore more likely to be non-unique, not less. Investigate incrementally rather than reading everything: Grep for entry points, Read those files, Grep for usages, Read the consumers, repeat.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D5

GAP — Persistent fact blocks and position-aware input

The lesson

Two failure modes compound in long sessions: lost-in-the-middle, where models reliably process the start and end of a long input but skip the middle, and progressive summarization risk, where exact numbers, dates and percentages degrade into 'about' and 'roughly'. The counter to both: extract key facts into a persistent CASE FACTS block that is included in every prompt regardless of how history is summarised, and structure input position-aware — KEY FINDINGS at the top, detail in the middle, ACTION ITEMS at the end. Never place your key findings in the middle.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D5

GAP — Scratchpad files and structured state persistence

The lesson

During a long investigation, have the agent write key findings to a scratchpad file as it goes; when context degrades or a new session starts, it consults the scratchpad instead of re-running discovery. For crash recovery in multi-agent runs, go further: each agent exports state to agent-state/{agent-id}.json with status, queries executed, results count, key findings and gaps, and the coordinator reads agent-state/manifest.json on resume to know which agents completed. Note the boundary carefully — a subagent should return a structured summary to the coordinator, not nothing at all.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D5

GAP — Confidence calibration and stratified sampling

The lesson

Have the model emit a confidence score per extracted field, then calibrate the thresholds against a labelled validation set — high confidence with proven accuracy routes to automated processing, low confidence or ambiguous sources routes to human review. The reason aggregate accuracy is dangerous: 97% overall can conceal 40% error on one document type. So audit by stratified random sampling across document types and fields, not just a global sample, and analyse accuracy per type and per field rather than only in total.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D5

GAP — Provenance survives only if it is structured

The lesson

Attribution is lost during summarization because a claim and its source drift apart in free text; keep them together as structured data — claim, source_url, publication_date, confidence — and the pairing survives every aggregation layer. When two sources conflict, preserve both with full attribution rather than arbitrarily choosing one. And always carry publication dates, because a temporal difference reads as a contradiction without them: 'Source A says 10%, Source B says 15% — contradiction' becomes 'Source A (2023) 10%, Source B (2024) 15% — likely growth' once dates are present.

Where this was taught

academy/SESSION-PLAN.md · academy/CURRICULUM.md

D2

Mock-surfaced — Two-tool token binding for destructive operations

The lesson

A single tool with a dry_run boolean the model sets itself is never an architectural guarantee, because the model controls the flag. Split it: preview_X returns a single-use token bound to the previewed payload, and execute_X requires that token. That makes skipping the precondition structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged, and it is the same defence-in-depth principle as enforcing compliance thresholds inside the tool against a server-controlled source instead of in the prompt.

Where this was taught

academy/LEARNER-MODEL.md

D1

Mock-surfaced — Partial failure means coverage-annotated synthesis

The lesson

When 2 of 8 files are unparseable and the other subagents complete fine, neither failing the whole report nor quietly omitting the gap is correct. Synthesise with what you have and explicitly annotate which conclusions are well supported and where a real gap exists. And when every subagent reports success but the combined output misses subtopics, the root cause is the coordinator's own decomposition — its task list never assigned them — not subagent execution or tooling.

Where this was taught

academy/LEARNER-MODEL.md

D4

Mock-surfaced — The stated-assumptions technique

The lesson

The interview pattern says to ask when there is genuine ambiguity — but in an automated pipeline, blocking to ask stalls the run. The right move is neither blocking nor silently guessing: proceed with a reasonable assumption and state it explicitly in the output so a human can correct it. Recognise which situation you are in — an interactive session can afford the clarifying question; an unattended pipeline needs the stated assumption.

Where this was taught

academy/LEARNER-MODEL.md

practice sets 17 lessons

51 original scenario- and anti-pattern-style MCQs across five domain-weighted banks (D1 14, D2 9, D3 10, D4 10, D5 8), each with an answer-free question section for genuine active recall and an answer key explaining why the tempting distractor fails, plus the sub-topic and a difficulty tag. Three cross-domain integration checkpoints then force learners to design an architecture cold before comparing against a model answer and named cross-domain traps. A separate held-out mock folder and an HTML mock-test also exist.

D1

Parallel elapsed time is max, not sum

The lesson

When you fan out N subagents, wall-clock time equals the longest worker, not the total of all of them — four chunks at 30s, 35s, 90s and 25s finish in about 90 seconds, not 180. The deeper lesson the question is really testing: balance chunks by expected effort, not by raw row count, or one dense chunk dominates the whole run. Common phasing to remember is serial decomposition, parallel execution, serial synthesis.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d1-agentic-architecture.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D1

Eight tool calls in one turn is not a smell by count

The lesson

Judging a design broken because the orchestrator issued eight tool calls in one turn is itself the misconception. Parallel calls to genuinely independent tools are good design and cut latency. It is only a smell when the calls are interdependent and need sequencing, when the orchestrator is doing worker grunt-work instead of delegating, or when it is runaway tool-calling. Judge the dependency structure, not the count.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d1-agentic-architecture.md · GAPS.md

D1

Do not delegate when you already hold the context

The lesson

Spawning a subagent to compute a loyalty tier from a record the orchestrator is already holding is pure overhead — delegation costs a tool call, a fresh empty context, and a separate invocation. Context isolation is not always worth it. The mirror-image failure is delegating with too little: a parent that spent 80,000 tokens on case history then delegates 'Draft the apology email' gets a generic email, because the subagent sees only the constructed prompt, never the parent's turns, tool results or memory.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d1-agentic-architecture.md

D1

Graceful degradation beats fake success

The lesson

When an SMS gateway times out and you cannot tell whether the message sent, do not retry (uncertain writes produce duplicates), do not report the whole flow as successful, and do not throw away a real partial success with a generic error. State what was verified, state what could not be confirmed, and offer a next step — never claim a side effect happened if you do not know that it did. Partial completion beats both fake success and a generic error.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d1-agentic-architecture.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D1

Compliance belongs in code, not in capital letters

The lesson

Enforcing 'no transaction over $10,000 without secondary approval' with a strongly worded CRITICAL system-prompt instruction is unsafe, and so is making the threshold a parameter the model passes — anything model-controlled is not an enforcement boundary. The check must live inside the tool, reading a server-controlled source. Think in defence-in-depth layers: the prompt biases behaviour, the tool enforces it, audit logs detect violations.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d1-agentic-architecture.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D2

MCP does not auto-solve the hard parts, and annotations are not security

The lesson

MCP standardises the exchange, not the operations concerns — auth, rate limiting, retries, caching, authorisation and performance are all still yours to build. Likewise the tool annotations readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint are untrusted UI hints, not security boundaries; security belongs in code. And use a resource, not a tool, when the thing is stable passive context such as a catalog or schema — resources answer 'what is true and stable', tools answer 'what actions can be taken'.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d2-tools-mcp.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D2

Tool design details that get tested

The lesson

Split a tool when its parameters have interdependent constraints rather than shipping one call with mutually exclusive arguments. Return structured, compact results carrying downstream IDs, not prose — and remember an empty array is not an error. For very large tool sets use progressive availability: a discovery tool returns a shortlist, then the relevant tools are registered. Descriptions must state what, when to use, when not to use, inputs, outputs and limits; format hints belong in descriptions, not in parameter names.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d2-tools-mcp.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D3

Settings override, permission rules merge

The lesson

This pairing is the classic Claude Code trap. Settings resolve by precedence — Managed beats CLI, which beats Local, then Project, then User — with the higher scope overriding. Permission rules do not work that way: they merge across scopes and then evaluate deny, ask, allow, with deny absolute and unrecoverable. Layer on the hook rule (only exit code 2 blocks; exit 1 proceeds) and the CLAUDE.md rule (concatenated context, not enforcement) and you have the three most-tested Domain 3 mechanics.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d3-claude-code.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D3

Plan mode is workflow control, not reasoning quality

The lesson

Plan mode gates thinking from doing — read-only exploration and a proposed plan before any edit — and is right for multi-file changes, architectural decisions and breaking changes. Extended thinking is about reasoning quality. They are different axes and they combine; treating them as alternatives is the trap. Separately, sessions are stored transcripts, not filesystem state: --continue resumes the most recent, --resume a specific one, --fork-session branches. For file isolation you need git branches or worktrees, not sessions.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d3-claude-code.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D4

Structured Outputs is the source fix; retry is the fallback

The lesson

When a pipeline emits malformed JSON at scale, the first lever is Structured Outputs via constrained decoding — output_config.format or strict tool use — which makes invalid output impossible at the source. Retry and dead-letter queues are the fallback, not the primary fix. Prevent at the source, then catch after. And remember the ceiling: valid JSON is not correct data. Schema catches syntax; semantic validation catches line-item sums, date ranges and ID formats, and a correction loop resending the document plus the prior extraction plus the exact errors beats blind retries.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d4-prompt-engineering.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D4

Schema design that reduces fabrication

The lesson

Making an absent field required creates hallucination pressure — the model will invent a value to satisfy the schema. Instead allow null, mark genuinely optional fields optional, give few-shot examples covering edge cases like missing data and informal units, preserve informal values verbatim, and add source grounding fields such as source_location and source_quote. Know the semantic difference between required, optional, nullable, an empty array and an 'other_detail' escape hatch — they are four different statements about the world, and strict enums with no escape hatch break in evolving domains.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d4-prompt-engineering.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D4

System-prompt salience decays; principles vs conditionals

The lesson

Attention to the system prompt weakens as a conversation grows — the instructions are not dropped, they are competed for — so reinforce key rules at phase breakpoints and use XML-tagged sections for salience. Write principles for judgement ('adapt depth to the user's expertise') and conditionals for safety bright-lines ('if this is an emergency, call 911'). For teaching a distinction, few-shot beats prose. And 'IMPORTANT/NEVER' is a salience device, not a reliability mechanism.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d4-prompt-engineering.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D5

Capacity is not attention — pick the strategy by what must survive

The lesson

A 200K window does not make every detail equally salient, so choose the technique by what has to survive. Sliding window drops old turns and is aggressive on RAG results. Progressive summarization replaces old blocks with a structured summary of decisions, preferences, open questions and facts while keeping recent turns verbatim. A persistent reference section holds things that must never blur (allergies, counts, definitions). A structured state object updated on change is more reliable than inferring state from a long transcript. And exact p-values or quotes belong in a retrieval or fact store, because summaries lose precision.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d5-context-reliability.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

D5

Returning users and mid-conversation updates

The lesson

When a user returns, open with a structured summary and fetch fresh state — never resume by replaying stale embedded tool results, which describe a world that may have moved. When external state changes mid-conversation, inject it into the system prompt or a dedicated context block, not as an unsolicited assistant message. And place cache_control after the stable prefix and before the per-turn variable content; putting it before something that changes every turn guarantees a cache miss on every call.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_practice_d5-context-reliability.md · EXAM-DIGEST.md

cross

Checkpoint A — Customer support: escalation meets compaction

The lesson

The collision this checkpoint drills is that D5 context techniques can destroy the D1 handoff. Do not compact away the original complaint that the escalation payload needs; do not cache per-conversation content (only the stable knowledge base belongs behind cache_control); and escalate by category and impact, not by a failed-call counter. Design the token budget explicitly: cached product knowledge, a persistent case-facts block, recent turns verbatim, and a reserved output allowance.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_checkpoint_A_support-agent_D1xD5.md

cross

Checkpoint B — CI/CD: headless flags meet output guarantees

The lesson

Two domains collide in an unattended pipeline. On the D3 side, a permission prompt will hang CI, and --bare is coupled to how you authenticate, so reproducibility depends on getting both right. On the D4 side, prompt-only JSON is not acceptable in an unattended pipeline — you need the Structured Outputs guarantee, because there is no human to notice a malformed response. Design the pipeline so neither a hanging prompt nor an unparseable result can occur.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_checkpoint_B_ci-cd_D3xD4.md

cross

Checkpoint C — Multi-agent research: orchestration meets tool design

The lesson

Seven design decisions have to compose: orchestrator-workers as the pattern, the constructed prompt as the only delegation channel, parallel elapsed time as max not sum, the tool-vs-resource-vs-prompt split for the MCP layer, an error surface architected by category rather than hoped for, provenance handled as an architecturally separate pass, and partial failure handled by graceful degradation. The named traps are dumping raw mega-outputs across the agent seam, forgetting subagent context isolation, and retrying uncertain writes.

Where this was taught

practice/CCA-F_checkpoint_C_multi-agent-research_D1xD2.md

Live teaching sessions 17 lessons

Mined from 19 Claude Code sessions on this project — explanations given in conversation that were never written into any project file. Each one is anchored to a verbatim quote from the transcript.

D2 · live session

A confirmation parameter is not a safeguard — token-binding across two tools is

The lesson

For an irreversible action, adding a dry_run or confirmation-string parameter to a single tool looks like the fix but isn't: the model can still call the tool and skip the safety step, because nothing structurally forces the check. The architecturally-guaranteed answer is to split it into two tools, where the first returns a token that the second requires as input — the safety step becomes unskippable by construction rather than by instruction. This is the project's single most persistent trap: the learner missed it on Exams 4, 5 and 6 in exactly the same shape before finally clearing it on Exam 7.

What prompted it

Exam 6 score-entry and Insights Round 1, explaining why Key Distinction #12 had now been missed three exams running

From the transcript

picking a parameter that still allows skipping the safety step over the architecturally-guaranteed two-tool split
cross · live session

Being able to defend a pattern is not the same as knowing when to reach for it

The lesson

The learner answered the 'why is this pattern better than the alternative' question correctly while still failing the 'which fix should you choose' version of the same concept. Justification and recognition are separate skills, and the exam tests both facets. Getting the rationale question right can mask a real selection gap, so a concept is only genuinely held when the scenario-selection facet also comes back correct.

What prompted it

Diagnosing why the learner got the paired defend-the-pattern question (Q22) right on Exam 6 while missing the fix-selection question on the same Key Distinction

From the transcript

you can defend the pattern, but aren't yet reliably recognizing when to reach for it
D2 · live session

The application executes tool_use, not Claude

The lesson

When Claude emits a tool_use block, Claude has not done anything — the calling application is what actually executes the tool and performs the side effect, such as writing the file. The learner reached for a PostToolUse hook instead, which is a Claude Code configuration mechanism, not the API-level execution boundary. Mixing up who runs the tool is a recurring source of wrong answers in the Tool Design domain.

What prompted it

Exam 5 score entry, cross-referencing the eight missed questions back to corpus sections (Q35, D2 §2.1)

From the transcript

must execute `tool_use` and write the file; picked a `PostToolUse` hook instead
D2 · live session

Grep searches content; Glob matches paths

The lesson

Grep is for finding content inside files; Glob is for enumerating files by name or path pattern. The learner picked Grep for a file-name-pattern enumeration task, which is the classic inversion. Related to this, the correct investigation strategy is incremental — let a content search drive a small number of targeted reads — rather than reading everything upfront, which is the anti-pattern.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q57, D2 §2.9), later hardened into Key Distinctions #26 and #28 in a separate session

From the transcript

chose Grep over Glob for file-name-pattern enumeration (content search vs. path pattern)
D4 · live session

Few-shot examples fix format; they do not fix reasoning depth

The lesson

Few-shot examples and reasoning-depth interventions solve different problems, and swapping one for the other is a distinct failure mode. If the output shape is wrong, add examples; if the model isn't reasoning far enough, that needs a reasoning intervention, not more examples. The learner substituted one for the other and lost the question on exactly that confusion.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q60, D4 §4.2)

From the transcript

swapped a few-shot format fix for a reasoning-depth fix; two techniques for two different problems
D3 · live session

Watch for the fabricated-obsolescence distractor

The lesson

One recurring distractor class asserts that a real, still-working feature has been deprecated or 'stopped working'. The learner fell for a version of this claiming that legacy `.claude/commands/` no longer functions. Treat any option whose entire argument rests on an unstated deprecation as suspect unless you can independently confirm the feature was actually removed.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q36, D3 §3.4)

From the transcript

fell for a fabricated-obsolescence distractor
cross · live session

Prefer the proportionate direct move over the heavier symptom-level fix

The lesson

About half of the learner's Exam 8 misses shared one meta-pattern: reaching for a heavier or symptom-level intervention — adding a hook, re-typing a reminder, switching to plan mode, splitting the work — when the correct answer was the smaller, direct fix aimed at the actual cause. This is the single highest-yield habit to correct, because it spans Prompt Engineering and Claude Code Config questions alike: when two options both plausibly help, the exam usually wants the one proportionate to the diagnosed problem, not the one that adds a layer.

What prompted it

Exam 8 scoring summary, naming a pattern visible across roughly half the missed questions

From the transcript

reaching for the heavier or symptom-level fix
D4 · live session

Prefilling and tool_choice are one mechanism family, not two topics

The lesson

Assistant prefilling (D4 §4.4) and tool_choice (D4 §4.6) are both ways of guaranteeing structured output, so they should be studied as one family rather than as unrelated techniques. The learner missed both in a back-to-back pair, which is diagnostic of a clustered conceptual gap in output-guarantee mechanisms rather than two isolated slips.

What prompted it

Exam 7 trap review, noting Q50/Q51 fell adjacent to each other

From the transcript

both in the same structured-output-guarantee mechanism family
D4 · live session

tool_choice: forcing a specific tool vs. forcing 'any' tool

The lesson

Setting tool_choice to a named tool compels that exact tool; setting it to "any" only compels that some tool be called, leaving the selection to the model. The learner has confused these repeatedly — missed on Exams 7, 8 and again on 10, at which point it was reclassified from noise into a confirmed-stubborn trap, with the advice to read Domain-4 §4.6 directly rather than hope more exam reps would fix it.

What prompted it

Exam 8 and Exam 10 scoring; the third consecutive miss changed the diagnosis from noise to a genuine gap

From the transcript

forced-specific-tool vs. `"any"`
D1 · live session

Coverage gaps in multi-agent work usually trace to the coordinator's decomposition

The lesson

When a multi-agent run misses part of the problem, the instinctive diagnosis is that a tool description was inadequate. More often the real cause is that the coordinator decomposed the task too narrowly in the first place — the subagents faithfully did the wrong-sized work they were given. The learner attributed a coverage gap to the tool description and lost the question on that misattribution.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q21, D1 §1.6)

From the transcript

misattributed a coverage gap to a tool-description problem instead of the coordinator's own narrow decomposition
D4 · live session

When one prompt carries too many steps, chain it — don't just word it better

The lesson

If a single prompt is being asked to carry several dependent steps, sharpening the wording does not fix the structural problem; the right move is to split it into a sequential chain where each stage handles one step. The learner chose 'clearer instruction' over chaining, which is the archetypal 'improve the prompt' reflex applied to a decomposition problem.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q13, D4 §4.14)

From the transcript

chose "clearer instruction" over splitting into a sequential chain
D4 · live session

Fix the noisy signal now rather than teaching around it slowly

The lesson

When a system is emitting noisy or low-value output categories, surgically disabling those categories is the immediate, proportionate fix; adding few-shot examples to gradually teach better behaviour is the slow, indirect one. The learner chose the slow route. This is the same underlying instinct as the broader 'fix the signal before adding a layer' principle that runs through several of the project's Key Distinctions.

What prompted it

Exam 5 trap review (Q42, D4 §4.17)

From the transcript

chose the slow eventual few-shot fix over surgically disabling the noisy finding categories now
D3 · live session

Plan mode versus direct execution is a real decision, not a default

The lesson

Plan mode is not a universally safer setting — choosing it when direct execution is warranted is itself a wrong answer, and it belongs to the same 'reach for the heavier control' habit flagged elsewhere. The learner missed this on Exam 7 and missed it again on the deliberate Exam 8 re-test, which converted it from a suspected slip into a confirmed gap in Claude Code Config (D3 §3.6), alongside the `/memory` diagnostic question (§3.1).

What prompted it

Exam 7 trap list and the Exam 8 targeted re-test of those same sections

From the transcript

plan mode vs. direct execution
cross · live session

How to tell a careless slip from a real conceptual gap

The lesson

A miss re-tested in a fresh scenario, and answered slowly rather than rushed, is a genuine wrong answer — not carelessness. Exam 8 deliberately re-tested four sections the learner had missed on Exam 7; three missed again, and one of those was the second-slowest question on the paper at 77 seconds. That combination — different scenario, plenty of time, still wrong — is the evidence standard used to promote a suspected gap to a confirmed one and to justify going back to the source material instead of doing more exam reps.

What prompted it

Exam 8 scoring, explaining why the targeted re-test design worked

From the transcript

these survived a fresh re-test in a different scenario, and they weren't rushed
D2 · live session

When an MCP tool loses to a built-in, improve its description

The lesson

If Claude keeps picking a built-in tool such as Grep over a purpose-built MCP tool, the fix is to make the MCP tool's description clearly signal when it should win — not to remove the built-in, and not to bolt a 'prefer MCP' rule onto the system prompt. It is the same root pattern as 'fix the signal before adding a layer', applied here to built-in-tool routing: repair the discriminating information rather than adding an enforcement layer on top of it.

What prompted it

Adding Key Distinctions #26-29 on built-in tool selection, grounded in Domain-2 §2.9 and official Exam Guide task 2.5

From the transcript

Enhance the MCP description — don't remove Grep or bolt on a "prefer MCP" rule
D2 · live session

Edit needs a unique anchor — a shorter anchor makes it worse

The lesson

The Edit tool requires a uniquely-matching anchor string. When an edit fails because the anchor is not unique, the instinct to shorten the anchor is backwards — a shorter string matches in more places and makes the ambiguity worse. The correct fallback is a full-file Read followed by Write.

What prompted it

Adding Key Distinction #27 on Edit failure fallback, grounded in Domain-2 §2.9

From the transcript

The official CCA-F domain numbers and weights

The lesson

The externally-grounded exam numbering is D1 Agentic Architecture (27%), D2 Tool Design & MCP (18%), D3 Claude Code Config (20%), D4 Prompt Engineering (20%), D5 Context Management (15%). This is distinct from any teaching-sequence module numbering used by a curriculum, and conflating the two is a real source of drift — when they disagree, the official exam weighting wins because it is grounded against the actual exam.

What prompted it

Resolving a domain-numbering inconsistency between the curriculum's module sequence and the official exam domain codes in the sibling mcq-practice-app

From the transcript

1=Agentic (27%), 2=Tool Design & MCP (18%), 3=Claude Code Config (20%), 4=Prompt Engineering (20%), 5=Context Management (15%)

The point of all of it

What to carry into the exam

Five durable models

  1. An architectural guarantee beats a parameter. When an option makes the bad outcome impossible and another makes it unlikely, the exam wants the impossible one. A flag can be ignored; a two-tool split cannot be.
  2. Match the size of the fix to the size of the problem. The proportionate direct move beats the heavier mechanism. A hook is not better than an instruction just because it is more machinery.
  3. Context is designed, not ambient. Nothing reaches a subagent unless something puts it there. Isolation is the default, and passing a reference is not passing the finding.
  4. Fix the cause the evidence names. The dramatic-sounding explanation is usually the distractor; read what the symptom actually implicates before choosing.
  5. Your remaining gaps are sections, not traps. Every Key Distinction is clean. What is left are whole corpus sections — and they respond to direct review, not to more exam exposure.

Ranked by domain. These are the only ones the record shows as unresolved — every other concept on this page is either solid or recovered.

  • D1 §1.5 Pass complete findings, not references to findings
  • D1 §1.8 The coordinator's iterative refinement loop
  • D1 §1.8 Knowing when to stop the refinement loop
  • D2 §2.3 A business-rule denial is not a tool failure
  • D2 §2.8 Prompt-bundling beats composite tools
  • D3 §3.1 CLAUDE.md files concatenate, they do not override
  • D3 §3.1 @import path rules and the depth-5 limit
  • D3 §3.11 Universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md; procedures become Skills
  • D3 §3.11 Modularize a bloated CLAUDE.md into .claude/rules/ topic files
  • D3 §3.12 Resume versus starting a new session
  • D4 §4.6 tool_choice: auto vs any vs a specific tool
  • D4 §4.9 Retry cannot conjure absent information
  • D4 §4.17 Restore trust by disabling noisy categories

Built from the CCA-F prep corpus: five domain files, the Key Distinctions set, 2,400 per-option rationales extracted from 10 mock exams, the exam log with its Professor's Notes and two Insights Rounds, two courses, the academy track, eight practice sets, and 19 Claude Code session transcripts. Concept text is drawn from those sources; nothing here is invented. Track records reflect the six scored exams (4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10) as of 29 July 2026. Exam 9 was generated but never attempted, so it contributes questions but no score data.
